title: Развитие инструментального мониторинга климатических параметров атмосферы
summary: Дистанционные измерения с помощью средств как наземного, так и космического базирования играют все более возрастающую роль в мониторинге климатических характеристик атмосферы. В работе приведены сведения о созданной в системе Росгидромета в
content: Дистанционные измерения с помощью средств как наземного, так и космического базирования играют все более возрастающую роль в мониторинге климатических характеристик атмосферы. В работе приведены сведения о созданной в системе Росгидромета в начале 2000-х годов сети станций инструментального мониторинга парниковых газов и стратосферного аэрозоля на основе дистанционных измерений с помощью новой отечественной аппаратуры, размещенной в различных географических зонах России. Организация такой сети создала предпосылки детального изучения пространственно-временных вариаций климатообразующих факторов и климатических параметров атмосферы над территорией России и выявления их связи с различными природными процессами. В работе кратко изложены основные результаты мониторинга параметров атмосферы, полученные с помощь этой аппаратуры, а также обработки спутниковой информации. На основе единого метода ИК Фурье-спектроскопии исследована многолетняя изменчивость содержания парниковых газов в толще атмосферы, их концентрации в приземном воздухе. Выполнено сравнение с данными европейских станций и спутниковыми измерениями. Оценены фазовые соотношения между вариациями приземных и средних в толще атмосферы концентраций углекислого газа и метана. Изложены результаты многолетнего лидарного зондирования сернокислотного стратосферного аэрозоля, аэрозоля природных пожаров, среднеширотных перистых облаков, позволяющие оценивать влияние аэрозоля на климат. По спутниковым данным выявлены существенные изменения характеристик струйных течений Северного полушария и площадей зон, занятых турбулентностью разной интенсивности как индикаторов климатической изменчивости. Сформулированы соображения о путях дальнейшего развития инструментального мониторинга климатических параметров атмосферы в ближайшей и среднесрочной перспективе.

title: Зависимость температурной чувствительности частоты молний и природных пожаров от типа внешнего воздействия на земную систему по расчётам с моделью ИФА РАН
summary: С помощью модели Земной системы ИФА РАН проведены численные эксперименты для 1850-2014 гг. с различными типами внешнего воздействия. Все воздействия были заданы в соответствии с условиями численного эксперимента "historical" проекта Coupled
content: С помощью модели Земной системы ИФА РАН проведены численные эксперименты для 1850-2014 гг. с различными типами внешнего воздействия. Все воздействия были заданы в соответствии с условиями численного эксперимента "historical" проекта Coupled Models Intercomparison project, phase 6 (CMIP6). В период 1997-2013 гг. Модель в сравнении со спутниковыми данными Lightning Imaging Sensor/Optical Transient Detector ‒ LIS/OTD реалистично воспроизводит частоту молний (ЧМ) ‒ как глобальные значения, так и пространственное распределение. При этом модель воспроизводит глобальный коэффициент чувствительности частоты молний к изменению приземной температуры только в ряде регионов при учете воздействия на климат за счёт изменения содержания антропогенных (сульфатных) аэрозолей в тропосфере. МЗС ИФА РАН воспроизводит годовую площадь выгорания из-за природных пожаров (ПП) с ошибками в отдельных регионах. Лучше всего модель воспроизводит чувствительность площади выгорания из-за ПП к изменению частоты молний в экспериментах с учетом антропогенного воздействия.

title: Policy brief on Soil carbon removals: The impact of non-permanence on climate mitigation
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The permanence of carbon removals in soils by carbon farming cannot be guaranteed, putting at risk the climate integrity of using such removals for CO2 emissions compensation. In the EU project MARVIC we quantified the impact of non-permane
content: The permanence of carbon removals in soils by carbon farming cannot be guaranteed, putting at risk the climate integrity of using such removals for CO2 emissions compensation. In the EU project MARVIC we quantified the impact of non-permanence of carbon removals in soils by carbon farming on climate change mitigation and on the effectiveness of such removals to compensate GHG emissions. This policy brief provides recommendations on the use of temporary soil carbon removals to compensate for greenhouse gas emissions and highlights the importance of longer project durations and monitoring periods for effective climate mitigation and credible carbon farming certification.

title: A Model-Based Digital Thread Approach for Managing the Complexity of Next-Generation Offshore Support Vessels Design, Build, Delivery and Beyond
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Objectives and Scope Growth in offshore wind, subsea construction, and carbon capture and storage is reshaping the missions OSVs are built to support. Traditionally designed to provide logistics, transportation, and operational support to o
content: Objectives and Scope Growth in offshore wind, subsea construction, and carbon capture and storage is reshaping the missions OSVs are built to support. Traditionally designed to provide logistics, transportation, and operational support to offshore oil and gas installations, modern OSVs are now expected to support a much wider range of missions. These include offshore wind farm installation and maintenance, subsea construction and inspection activities, carbon capture and storage (CCS), low-carbon energy infrastructure remote and autonomous operations, environmental monitoring and operations involving increasingly sophisticated power and propulsion systems. At the same time, vessel owners and operators face growing pressure to improve sustainability, reduce emissions, enhance operational efficiency, and maintain compliance with increasingly demanding regulatory and classification requirements. As a result, the design, construction, operation, and maintenance of OSVs have become substantially more complex than in previous generations of vessels. Modern vessels contain a greater number of integrated systems, including hybrid and electric propulsion architectures, advanced automation and control systems, dynamic positioning technologies, sensor networks, communication platforms, and mission-specific equipment. These interconnected systems generate large volumes of engineering, operational, maintenance, and regulatory information throughout the vessel lifecycle all the way from preliminary and initial designs to construction and further to operations and eventual refit. Managing this information effectively has emerged as one of the primary challenges facing both shipbuilders and vessel operators. In many organizations, critical lifecycle information remains fragmented across multiple disconnected systems, databases, spreadsheets, documents, and departmental processes. This fragmentation often results in inconsistent information, duplicated effort, reduced traceability, delayed decision-making, and increased lifecycle costs. It also creates challenges when managing vessel modifications, upgrades, certification activities, and maintenance programs throughout decades of operation.

title: Net-Zero Drilling Through Electrified Surface Support Systems: Scalable Compressor Technology Delivering Proven Carbon, Cost, and HSE Gains
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Temporary offshore surface-support packages continue to generate operational emissions during drilling, well-testing, intervention, and maintenance campaigns. This paper examines whether electrified compressor systems can reduce gr
content: Abstract Temporary offshore surface-support packages continue to generate operational emissions during drilling, well-testing, intervention, and maintenance campaigns. This paper examines whether electrified compressor systems can reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, operating cost, maintenance demand, and selected HSE exposure mechanisms in drilling-support operations. The field evidence is drawn from Deepsea Yantai and subsequent multi-rig deployments to assess whether electrified surface-support equipment provides repeatable operational and environmental benefits. Field deployment data are combined with a comparative cradle-to-grave lifecycle assessment of a diesel-driven compressor and an electrically driven equivalent delivering the same compressed-air duty. The evaluation covers carbon intensity, maintenance requirements, operating costs, reliability, and offshore integration factors across four power-supply scenarios: direct diesel drive, diesel-generated electricity, gas-turbine-generated electricity, and low-carbon grid electricity. The electrically driven compressor had lower lifecycle carbon intensity in all assessed scenarios. Relative reductions were approximately 24–25% with diesel-generated electricity, 32% with gas-turbine-generated electricity, and 83–94% with low-carbon grid electricity. Across more than 19,000 operating hours, field deployments demonstrated reduced maintenance requirements and reported operating-cost reductions typically in the range of 20–25%. The results indicate repeatable reductions in emissions, operating cost, and maintenance demand, while supporting reliability and selected HSE exposure benefits where suitable electrical infrastructure is available. Electrification is therefore positioned as a practical component of a broader drilling-decarbonisation strategy, not as a standalone route to net-zero drilling.

title: Immersive Virtual Reality for Zero-Emission Education: Exploring Environmental Literacy and Analytical Skills among Elementary Students
source: International Journal of Technology in Education and Science
summary: This study explores immersive virtual reality media to support environmental literacy and analytical skills among elementary school students within the context of zero-emission education. Employing an exploratory design integrating qualitat
content: This study explores immersive virtual reality media to support environmental literacy and analytical skills among elementary school students within the context of zero-emission education. Employing an exploratory design integrating qualitative analysis, descriptive statistics, and the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), data were collected through interviews, observations, expert evaluations, written feedback, and questionnaires involving three experts and 100 fifth-grade students across eight elementary schools. The results indicate a media feasibility score of 90.34% and a student response score of 81.99%. Specific ratings were 94.05% for content, 91.07% for pedagogy, and 85.71% for media quality. Performance metrics included 85.38% for analytical skills, 83.11% for environmental literacy, 86.89% for media presentation, and 70.81% for practical application. Student experiences were shaped through contextual exploration, environmental change simulations, decision-making, and visual feedback. The media assisted students in identifying problems, tracing cause-and-effect relationships, determining solutions, and drawing conclusions. The assessment prioritized responsible behavior, causal analysis, and solution determination. Successful implementation requires device orientation, simple navigation, clear instructions, and teacher guidance. The study establishes a concept for decision-based immersive environmental learning that emphasizes student agency, environmental consequence evaluation, and the integration of environmental literacy with analytical skills, providing both a theoretical foundation and practical implementation guidelines for schools.

title: Low-Emission LNG Production Through Electrified Liquefaction at Ruwais LNG
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Liquefied natural gas (LNG) production requires substantial refrigeration duty, making liquefaction one of the principal energy-consuming and greenhouse gas-emitting stages of the LNG supply chain. LNG facilities have historically
content: Abstract Liquefied natural gas (LNG) production requires substantial refrigeration duty, making liquefaction one of the principal energy-consuming and greenhouse gas-emitting stages of the LNG supply chain. LNG facilities have historically employed several energy architectures, including direct gas-turbine-driven compressors, steam-turbine-driven compressors supplied through fuel-fired steam systems, captive power generation and hybrid utility configurations. Although these arrangements have supported reliable commercial-scale production, they remain dependent on onsite fuel combustion and associated energy-conversion losses. This paper examines the transition from combustion-based LNG energy systems to clean-power electrified liquefaction through the case study of Ruwais LNG, a two-train development with a combined production capacity of 9.6 million tonnes per annum, located in Al Ruwais Industrial City, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Based on publicly available information, the project employs electric-driven refrigeration systems and is designed to operate using clean electricity. Publicly available references identify Ruwais LNG as a clean-power LNG development comprising two electric-drive liquefaction trains [29-32]. The assessment compares the energy-conversion, emissions and operational characteristics of combustion-based and clean-power electrified LNG architectures. Electrification restructures the facility energy system by reducing the largest continuous combustion requirement associated with liquefaction, separating refrigeration performance from onsite fuel conversion and supplying compressor shaft power through electricity with verified clean-energy attributes. Published studies indicate that refrigeration compression and associated power systems account for a substantial proportion of operational emissions in conventional LNG facilities, and that electrified liquefaction supplied by low-emissions electricity can deliver greenhouse gas reductions of more than 50% relative to conventional configurations under comparable operating conditions and assumptions [5,17-20]. Residual emissions from flaring, fugitive releases, emergency equipment and non-routine events remain within the facility inventory. The paper introduces a three-level classification comprising driver electrification, facility electrification and clean-power electrification. It also establishes a clearly bounded framework separating liquefaction-driver Scope 1 abatement, total facility Scope 1 emissions, location-based and market-based Scope 2 emissions, and lifecycle LNG emissions. For ADNOC Gas, the project illustrates the potential to combine reduced liquefaction-related emissions with commercial-scale LNG capacity, clean-power integration and robust carbon-accounting practices. For the global LNG industry, the case provides a transferable framework integrating process engineering, electrical performance, environmental-attribute management and greenhouse gas monitor

title: From Qatar to Europe - LNG Carrier Decarbonization Via Pre-Combustion Onboard Methane Splitting
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Methane splitting emerged as a promising methane decarbonization technology capable of producing low-carbon hydrogen while avoiding direct carbon dioxide emissions. Through the thermal decomposition of methane into hydrogen and sol
content: Abstract Methane splitting emerged as a promising methane decarbonization technology capable of producing low-carbon hydrogen while avoiding direct carbon dioxide emissions. Through the thermal decomposition of methane into hydrogen and solid carbon (CH4 → C + 2H2), the process enables decarbonization of methane across a range of hard-to-abate sectors while creating opportunities for carbon valorization. One particularly attractive application is the maritime industry where liquefied natural gas (LNG) has become an important transitional fuel but continues to generate greenhouse gas emissions during combustion. Integrated onboard LNG-fueled vessels, methane splitting functions as a pre-combustion carbon capture technology, producing hydrogen on demand for propulsion and auxiliary power without the need for hydrogen storage onboard, while capturing carbon in solid form that can be safely stored in ambient conditions and discharged at port. This study evaluates onboard methane splitting as a decarbonization strategy for large LNG carriers and benchmarks its performance against conventional post-combustion for onboard carbon capture systems (OCCS). A baseline assessment was first established through the evaluation of four post-combustion CO2 capture technologies: chemical absorption, membrane separation, adsorption, and cryogenic separation, using energy integration models representative of LNG-fueled ships. The analysis identified that thermal capture technologies, particularly absorption and adsorption, provide the most favorable performance when sufficient waste heat is available onboard. Building upon this benchmark, a model-based assessment of methane splitting was conducted for a representative steam-driven LNG carrier, considering process integration, energy requirements, onboard storage, and regulatory compliance economic performance. Heat integration between the methane splitting unit and the ship's existing energy system were evaluated to maximize overall process efficiency. For a carbon capture rate of 55%, the vessel's Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) improved from rating D to A and estimated compliance savings from FuelEU Maritime and EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) exceeded USD 134 million over the assessed period of 10 years (2030-2040), with projected CO2 price. Methane splitting substantially outperformed post-combustion capture in several key metrics, such as reduction of onboard storage requirements, from approximately 12,360 mVreturn trip for liquefied carbon dioxide to only 6,430 m3/return trip for solid carbon, less complex port logistics, and lower energy demand required per ton of CO2 avoided. The results demonstrate that methane splitting represents a technically viable and economically attractive decarbonization pathway for LNG powered vessels. By leveraging existing LNG infrastructure while producing low-carbon hydrogen and a marketable solid carbon co-product, the technology offers a practical pathway for extending t

title: From Flares to Fuels: Modular Conversion of Flare Gas into Lower-Carbon Liquids for Asset-Scale Decarbonization
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Routine flaring and venting of associated gas remain persistent operational, environmental, and value-loss challenges across upstream and midstream assets, particularly where gathering infrastructure, gas treatment capacity, or off
content: Abstract Routine flaring and venting of associated gas remain persistent operational, environmental, and value-loss challenges across upstream and midstream assets, particularly where gathering infrastructure, gas treatment capacity, or offtake markets are constrained. Methane-rich flare streams are especially important because real flare performance can be affected by intermittent flow, sub-stoichiometric combustion, flame instability, and operational upsets. These factors can increase methane slip and near-term climate impact. The World Bank's Global Gas Flaring Tracker and Zero Routine Flaring initiative reinforce this urgency by showing that routine flaring remains a global resource-efficiency and emissions challenge despite long-standing reduction commitments. This paper presents an engineered modular Flare-to-Fuels platform, with emphasis on Flare-to-Liquids, for upgrading variable off-gas into fungible, transportable products. The portfolio includes NGL recovery, CNG, LNG, methanol, synthetic fuels, and liquid fuel blendstocks that can use existing storage, transport, blending, or end-use infrastructure where specifications allow. The objective is to reduce routine flaring and methane slip while converting a waste stream into saleable products that improve asset economics, local energy security, and portfolio-level emissions performance. The solution focus is deployable process design rather than a theoretical single-route concept. The manuscript describes feed conditioning, brownfield tie- ins, operability under variable feeds, skid-based modularization, syngas generation, methanol synthesis, optional downstream upgrading, and quantified emissions outcomes through transparent lifecycle carbon-intensity accounting. The proposed screening framework links field conditions to monetization pathways and defines how technology configuration, operating envelope, lifecycle assessment, monitoring, reporting and verification, and policy-relevant design choices can be considered together. When modular process equipment, auditable carbon boundaries, and certification-ready data systems are integrated early, flare gas can be repositioned from an environmental liability into a transition-molecule value chain.

title: From Gas Processing to Climate Action; How Habshan-5 CRI Sets a Global Benchmark in CCUS
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Industrial decarbonization increasingly depends on integrating large-scale carbon-management infrastructure into existing assets rather than relying exclusively on greenfield developments. This paper presents the Habshan-5 CO2 Reco
content: Abstract Industrial decarbonization increasingly depends on integrating large-scale carbon-management infrastructure into existing assets rather than relying exclusively on greenfield developments. This paper presents the Habshan-5 CO2 Recovery and Injection (CRI) Project as an execution-stage case study of an integrated carbon capture, conditioning and utilization development within a major gas-processing facility. Habshan-5 CRI is designed to recover carbon dioxide from gas-processing-related streams, condition the recovered CO₂ through compression and dehydration, and deliver it for Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR). The project integrates these stages into a single, connected carbon-management value chain linked with the existing gas-processing ecosystem, and supports ADNOC Gas's stated objective of reducing operational (Scope 1 and Scope 2) greenhouse gas emissions intensity by up to 25% by 2030 against a Business-as-Usual baseline, as well as, to ADNOC's stated ambition to develop 10 million tonnes per annum of carbon-capture capacity by 2030. The study examines the project's strategic alignment, process architecture, brownfield integration, solvent-management provisions, thermal reclaiming, energy integration and environmental-assessment methodology. A central feature is the utilization of available low-pressure steam from the existing gas-processing complex for solvent regeneration, reducing reliance on wholly incremental thermal-energy generation and strengthening integration between the carbon-recovery facilities and the wider site-energy system. Environmental performance is evaluated using a design-stage assessment framework that compares a Reference or BAU Case, a CCUS Case and an Integrated CCUC Case. The methodology distinguishes gross CO₂ recovery from net greenhouse gas abatement by accounting for residual direct emissions and energy-related indirect emissions within the defined project boundary. Assessment results are reported using normalized indicators that enable evaluation without disclosure of confidential utility balances or project GHG inventories. The study also introduces complementary benchmarking frameworks covering net-abatement assessment practices and global industrial CCUS deployment experience, positioning Habshan-5 CRI within the broader carbon-management landscape. The findings demonstrate that the project's significance extends beyond capture technology. Its wider contribution lies in integrating a complete carbon-management chain into an existing gas-processing ecosystem through resource integration, lifecycle GHG assessment, operational flexibility and alignment with national and corporate decarbonization pathways. The resulting insights provide a transferable framework for future CCUS developments in gas processing and other hard-to-abate industrial sectors.

title: A New Approach for CO2 Flooding and Storage Dynamic Scheme Optimization Based on Deep Reinforcement Learning
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract As a win-win technology, CO2 flooding and storage can enhance oil recovery (EOR) while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, collaboratively optimizing injection-production schemes remain challenging. This study proposes a dy
content: Abstract As a win-win technology, CO2 flooding and storage can enhance oil recovery (EOR) while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, collaboratively optimizing injection-production schemes remain challenging. This study proposes a dynamic optimization method using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to maximize net present value (NPV) while considering carbon tax. The problem is formulated as a Markov decision process. An agent observes reservoir states and annually adjusts injection-production parameters. To support the numerous evaluations required by DRL, a two-level deep-learning surrogate model is trained using reservoir numerical simulation samples, reducing the evaluation time of a 30-year scheme from 9.17 min to 1.53s. The TD3 algorithm is employed and benchmarked against a genetic algorithm (GA). With an oil price of $460/ton, CO2 cost of $90/ton, and carbon tax of $60/ton, the reward converges after 1500 episodes, and NPV stabilizes at $267 million. During the first 15 years, the injection rate increases while bottom-hole pressure decreases, indicating an emphasis on EOR. During the final 15 years, the injection rate remains stable while bottom-hole pressure rises, improving storage efficiency. Compared with GA, DRL increases NPV by 7.71%, cumulative oil production by 11.55%, and CO2 storage efficiency by 9.50 percentage points. Trapped storage increases from 17100 to 216900 tons, and dissolved storage rises from 59100 to 66500 tons, reducing free CO2 and improving storage safety. The proposed method therefore simultaneously improves economic performance, EOR, storage efficiency, and security, providing an effective approach for designing collaborative CO2 flooding and storage schemes.

title: Integrated Power Generation Optimization
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper presents an electrical power generation optimization initiative implemented at the PTTEP Platong Complex in the Gulf of Thailand. The project was undertaken to address several operational challenges, including excessive
content: Abstract This paper presents an electrical power generation optimization initiative implemented at the PTTEP Platong Complex in the Gulf of Thailand. The project was undertaken to address several operational challenges, including excessive spinning reserve capacity, inefficient gas turbine generator utilization, elevated fuel gas consumption, and associated greenhouse gas emissions. The Platong Complex consists of two interconnected operational areas, namely Platong Complex 1 and Platong Complex 2, which contain gas turbine generators of different capacities and efficiencies. Prior to the project implementation, multiple gas turbine generators were operated simultaneously at relatively low loading conditions in order to maintain a high level of spinning reserve. Although this operating philosophy provided a high degree of electrical system reliability, it resulted in suboptimal fuel efficiency and increased maintenance requirements. Through comprehensive heat rate analysis and power system studies, the project identified an opportunity to redistribute electrical loads from smaller and less efficient gas turbine generators to larger, higher-efficiency units. This optimization strategy enabled the reduction of operating generators while maintaining acceptable system reliability and operational flexibility. The project involved integrating the electrical distribution systems of Platong Complex 1 and Platong Complex 2, allowing spinning reserve capacity from the larger gas turbine generators to support loads across both complexes. As a result, one Saturn 10 gas turbine generator could be removed from normal operation without compromising power system security. The optimization led to a significant reduction in fuel gas consumption, lower maintenance demand, and a measurable decrease in carbon dioxide (CO2) and greenhouse gas emissions. The project demonstrates how strategic power system integration and load redistribution can enhance operational efficiency while supporting sustainability objectives in offshore oil and gas production facilities.

title: First-Of-A-Kind Electrified Process Gas Heater Pilot for Direct Reduction Iron Decarbonization at EMSTEEL
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Natural-gas-based direct reduction produces iron with a lower carbon intensity than conventional coal-based ironmaking, but it still requires natural-gas combustion to provide the thermal energy required for heating the circulating
content: Abstract Natural-gas-based direct reduction produces iron with a lower carbon intensity than conventional coal-based ironmaking, but it still requires natural-gas combustion to provide the thermal energy required for heating the circulating reducing gas. This paper presents the design basis, integration method and pre-commissioning assessment of a 1.3-MW electric process-gas heater (ePGH) pilot plant at an operating direct reduction plant in Abu Dhabi. The unit is is being integrated in parallel with the existing fired process-gas heater and heats a controlled process-gas slipstream before the streams are recombined. This arrangement permits direct comparison with the conventional heating route while preserving the fired heater as the operating safeguard. The pilot programme is structured to evaluate heat-transfer performance, outlet-temperature control, pressure drop, electrical demand, dynamic load response, process stability, availability and maintainability under industrial conditions. Baseline testing, stepped-load trials, transient tests and an endurance campaign are combined with process and electrical modelling to determine the implications of larger electrified-heating installations. Engineering estimates indicate annual displacement of approximately 1,136,000 Nm3 of natural gas and direct avoidance of about 2,200 t CO2 when the pilot is operated for 8,000 h/year. At rated power, annual electricity demand is approximately 10.4 GWh. The estimated direct Scope 1 benefit is therefore clear, while the combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 benefit depends on the carbon intensity of the electricity supply; the calculated break-even electricity emission factor is approximately 0.212 kg CO2e/kWh. The project is consequently designed not only to validate the ePGH equipment, but also as a practical study of hybrid fired-electric operation, clean-power integration and scale-up constraints. No commercial-scale performance claim is made from the engineering estimates alone. The endurance test and reconciled plant data will provide the evidence required to assess whether direct electric process-gas heating can be expanded as an incremental decarbonization pathway for existing DRI assets.

title: Pilot Plant Demonstration of Saf Production Via Integrated Rwgs + Fischer-Tropsch Processes from Co2 and Green Hydrogen
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions requires the development of scalable technologies capable of converting captured carbon dioxide (CO2) into sustainable fuels using renewable hydrogen. Among the various Carbon Capture and
content: Abstract Achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions requires the development of scalable technologies capable of converting captured carbon dioxide (CO2) into sustainable fuels using renewable hydrogen. Among the various Carbon Capture and Utilization (CCU) pathways, Power-to-Liquid (PtL) processes have attracted increasing attention because they enable the production of drop-in synthetic fuels compatible with existing transportation infrastructures. However, the integration of the highly endothermic Reverse Water-Gas Shift (rWGS) reaction with the strongly exothermic Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis remains challenging owing to the contrasting thermal requirements of the two catalytic processes. This work presents an integrated Power-to-Liquid (PtL) pilot plant based on proprietary milli-structured Heat Exchanger Reactor (HER) technology developed by KHIMOD. The process integrates two catalytic reactors operating sequentially: a Reverse Water-Gas Shift (rWGS) reactor employing a proprietary PtFe-based catalyst for synthesis gas production, followed by a Fischer-Tropsch (FT) reactor using a proprietary cobalt-based catalyst for hydrocarbon synthesis. Both catalysts were specifically formulated for operation within the HER architecture, enabling efficient heat transfer, precise temperature control, and enhanced reactor performance. The pilot further incorporates dedicated recycle loops, an integrated process control system, and a modular design suitable for future industrial deployment. The paper describes the process design, reactor technology and commissioning of the pilot plant together with the first operational results obtained during the initial experimental campaign. Stable operation of the Fischer-Tropsch reactor was successfully demonstrated under representative operating conditions, resulting in the first production of liquid synthetic hydrocarbons. Product characterization showed that the synthetic crude was predominantly composed of middle-distillate hydrocarbons, with approximately 41 wt.% of the product distributed within the C9-C16 carbon-number range associated with Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) production after upgrading. The observed boiling-point distribution and carbon-number profile demonstrate the suitability of the reactor-catalyst combination to produce synthetic aviation fuel precursors. Beyond validating the operation of the pilot plant, the results confirm the effectiveness of milli-structured Heat Exchanger Reactor technology for integrating highly endothermic and highly exothermic catalytic processes within a compact modular architecture. The demonstrated process provides a promising pathway for decentralized CO2 utilization and contributes to the industrial deployment of Power-to-Liquid technologies to produce low-carbon synthetic fuels.

title: Operational and Economic Benefits of Drag Reducing Agents in Long-Distance Crude Oil Pipelines
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Objectives/Scope Long-distance crude export pipelines can become hydraulically constrained when higher throughput is required against elevated downstream network backpressure. This paper presents field evidence from an ADNOC Onshor
content: Abstract Objectives/Scope Long-distance crude export pipelines can become hydraulically constrained when higher throughput is required against elevated downstream network backpressure. This paper presents field evidence from an ADNOC Onshore pipeline-segment project where Drag Reducing Agent (DRA) injection enabled higher crude export flow within existing pressure and pump limitations while creating measurable energy and carbon-reduction potential. Methods, Procedures, Process The study integrated historical no-DRA baseline data, controlled DRA field-test evidence and recent high-flow operating data from the pipeline segment. Treated and untreated frictional pressure losses were compared at equivalent flow using flow-corrected hydraulic calculations. DRA performance was evaluated by concentration, pressure saving, percentage drag reduction and pump operating envelope. Performance curves were then used to interpret recent high-flow operating points using publication-safe, internally approved engineering parameters. Results, Observations, Conclusions The latest data indicate approximately 12 barg pressure saving for recent high-throughput operation. At low DRA concentration, recent operation achieved a practical drag-reduction band of approximately 20-30%, with high-flow points around 30-31% drag reduction and about 12 barg pressure saving. Pump and system curve interpretation indicates that DRA injection enabled approximately 15% additional flowrate from the same pump configuration by reducing system resistance and shifting the operating point to a higher feasible flow. These results demonstrate that the high-flow case was enabled by DRA; without friction reduction, the required pressure and power demand would have exceeded the available operating envelope or forced throughput limitation. The same hydraulic benefit can also be used at lower flow to reduce pump loading and save electrical energy. Novel/Additive Information The novelty is the operational framing of DRA as a throughput-enabling and decarbonization lever rather than only a chemical treatment. The paper links field-measured drag reduction to pump configuration, pressure margin, avoided energy demand and CO₂-emissions reduction, while demonstrating a publication-safe method for sharing learning from sensitive production systems.

title: Radiation regimes shape microbial light-harvesting strategies and network organization on glacier surfaces
summary: Glacier cryoconite hosts metabolically active microbial communities despite exposure to solar radiation, which both provides energy and imposes stress. However, how radiation regimes are associated with microbial energy acquisition strategi
content: Glacier cryoconite hosts metabolically active microbial communities despite exposure to solar radiation, which both provides energy and imposes stress. However, how radiation regimes are associated with microbial energy acquisition strategies and ecosystem organization remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 85 cryoconite metagenomes, including 47 from Arctic glaciers and 38 from Tibetan Plateau glaciers, representing contrasting long-term radiation environments. Arctic communities show greater representation of rhodopsin-based phototrophic pathways, whereas Tibetan Plateau communities show higher potential for photosynthetic pathways. These differences are associated with distinct community structures and interaction networks. Tibetan Plateau microbiomes exhibit higher network complexity, with phototrophic taxa as highly connected network nodes, while Arctic networks are simpler and centered on rhodopsin-containing heterotrophs. Functional trait analyses further indicate higher biomass production potential in Tibetan Plateau communities. Together, our results reveal that radiation regimes are associated with divergent microbial energy acquisition strategies, with consequences for community organization and ecosystem metabolic potential in glacier cryoconite ecosystems. Arctic and Tibetan glacier cryoconite microbial communities differ in energy strategies, network organization, and metabolic potential, with rhodopsin-based phototrophy favored in the Arctic and photosynthesis in Tibet, as shown by comparative metagenomic analyses.

title: Autonomous LNG Plant Startup Pre-Cooldown: Scaling Secure AI Closed-Loop Automation for Enhanced Production and Carbon Emission Reduction
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract The objective of this work is to demonstrate the successful deployment of a secure, AI-driven closed-loop automation system for LNG plant pre-cooldown. The scope encompasses the transition from a data-driven advisory model to a ful
content: Abstract The objective of this work is to demonstrate the successful deployment of a secure, AI-driven closed-loop automation system for LNG plant pre-cooldown. The scope encompasses the transition from a data-driven advisory model to a fully autonomous system that executes real-time valve adjustments. It focuses on achieving critical outcomes in enabling autonomous, real-time adjustments through AI-driven recommendations, minimizing startup duration variability, maximizing additional production hours and reducing greenhouse gas emissions through optimized thermodynamic control. The methodology utilized twenty-five years of historical startup data, which was cleaned and profiled to train supervised machine learning models that predict Main Cryogenic Heat Exchanger (MCHE) temperature profiles and valve responses. These predictive models were integrated with an advanced optimization layer to define precise control sequences that satisfy safe operating envelopes. A cyber-resilient IT-OT architecture was engineered, employing network segmentation and protocol gateways to bridge the plant network and the AI engine securely. The process followed a phased validation: initial deployment as a "live advisory" to calibrate model accuracy, followed by the activation of a closed-loop controller that executes autonomous valve adjustments with human-in-the-loop safeguards. The system was successfully deployed across eight LNG train startups at Malaysia LNG plant. Quantitative results confirm a 16% average reduction in pre-cooldown duration compared to the live-advisory baseline. This acceleration directly translates into increased production availability and the reduction of operators' workloads, which allows operators to focus on strategic overview and process safety —enhancing both safety and efficiency. Observations revealed that the closed-loop implementation successfully standardized the pre-cooldown sequence across all eight production runs, delivering near-identical, optimized cooling trajectories. Critically, the tighter control of the Main Cryogenic Heat Exchanger (MCHE) cooling curve led to a 22% reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by minimizing flaring events during the transition to stable operations. The study concludes that autonomous closed-loop systems are superior in achieving repeatable, high-efficiency startups. Furthermore, the integration of a secure IT-OT framework addresses the industry's primary barrier to AI adoption: cybersecurity in critical infrastructure. This paper provides a documented case study of an AI system moving beyond "recommendations" into "autonomous execution" in a critical energy facility. It introduces a novel, hybrid methodology combining Supervised Machine Learning with prescriptive optimization logic. This innovation highlights the transformative power of closed-loop, AI-driven automation, reinforcing the organization's leadership in operational excellence and its commitment to setting new standards for ind

title: Powering Kuwait's Energy Transition: A Cost and Energy Optimised CO2 Transport Network from Multiple Emitters
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract The development of large-scale Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) projects requires safe, reliable, and cost-effective transportation of captured CO2 from multiple emission sources to utilization or storage locations. T
content: Abstract The development of large-scale Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) projects requires safe, reliable, and cost-effective transportation of captured CO2 from multiple emission sources to utilization or storage locations. This paper presents the development and optimization of an integrated CO2 transportation network for North Kuwait, designed to transport approximately 1.85 Mtpa of captured CO2 from six geographically dispersed sour gas processing facilities to a common injection location for Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) and geological storage. The study evaluates alternative transport concepts and identifies the most cost- and energy-efficient network architecture. Three transportation concepts were developed and assessed: (1) dense-phase transport with compression at each emitter, (2) gas-phase transport with final boosting at the injection location, and (3) a hybrid gas-dense phase concept utilizing centralized booster compression. Hydraulic simulations were performed using PIPESIM to determine pipeline sizing, pressure profiles, flow velocities, and turndown performance. CO2 thermodynamic behavior was modeled using the GERG-2008 equation of state to accurately predict density, compressibility, and phase behavior across the operating envelope. Compression, pumping, dehydration, and pipeline pressure rating requirements were optimized for each concept. The alternatives were compared using techno-economic criteria including CAPEX, energy demand, operability, reliability, HSSE considerations, and implementation complexity. Dense-phase transport demonstrated excellent hydraulic performance but required extensive compression infrastructure at each emitter, resulting in the highest capital cost and energy demand. Gas-phase transport reduced source-side compression requirements but required significantly larger pipeline diameters, reducing its overall economic attractiveness. The hybrid gas-dense phase concept combined gas-phase gathering with centralized compression to dense-phase conditions and downstream dense-phase pumping for final injection pressure. This approach minimized compression complexity at individual facilities while retaining the hydraulic advantages of dense-phase transmission. The selected concept achieved approximately 19% CAPEX reduction and 20% energy savings relative to the dense-phase alternative. The study demonstrates that centralized boosting combined with downstream dense-phase pumping can provide a cost- and energy-optimized solution for medium-distance, multi-emitter CO2 transportation networks. By integrating hydraulic modelling, GERG-2008 thermodynamic analysis, and techno-economic evaluation, the work provides a practical and scalable framework for future onshore CCUS developments in Kuwait, the GCC region, and other industrial clusters pursuing large-scale decarbonization initiatives.

Which are traditionally addressed by costly workovers with high GHG emissions, contradicting regional low carbon commitments. title: Evaluation of Iron-Based Chemical Looping Oxidation for CO2Isolation from Refinery Residues, Petroleum Coke, and Off-Gases at Middle East Refining Scale
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This work evaluates an iron-based chemical looping oxidation process for CO2 isolation from refinery residues, petroleum coke, and off-gases, characterizing capture rate, product purity, and energy load against post-combustion amin
content: Abstract This work evaluates an iron-based chemical looping oxidation process for CO2 isolation from refinery residues, petroleum coke, and off-gases, characterizing capture rate, product purity, and energy load against post-combustion amine and oxy-fuel benchmarks. Bench and pilot scale chemical looping units were operated on natural gas, syngas, tail gas, coal, and refuse-derive fuel (RDF) using an iron-based oxygen carrier, with performance benchmarked on a steam-and-hydrogen coproduction basis. Capture rate exceeded 95%, with product purity within specification for pipeline transport and enhanced oil recovery (EOR) injection after supplemental purification. Net thermal efficiency for steam-and-power coproduction reached 38 to 42%, with significantly less capital equipment and fewer consumables than incumbent capture configurations. Syngas, tail gas, biomass, and RDF were utilized directly in the process without prior gasification, and petroleum coke was evaluated through characterization and validated process modeling, broadening the addressable feedstock envelope relative to oxy-fuel, gasification, steam methane reforming (SMR), or autothermal reforming (ATR) routes. Modeled specific CO2 isolation and purification cost was less than $35 per tonne CO2, compared with $160 to $210 per tonne for retrofit monoethanolamine (MEA) capture on equivalent units. Oxygen carrier circulation and attrition were stable over thousands of redox cycles, and NOx emissions are inherently low owing to the absence of N2 in the fuel reactor. Integration analysis indicated delivered CO2 cost reductions relative to retrofit alternatives ranging from approximately 50% for high-pressure, pipeline-quality CO2-EOR to greater than 80% for low-pressure applications such as local geological injection. Given U.S. commercial activity and extensive testing of similar feedstocks, iron-based chemical looping is ready for Middle East development and deployment.

title: Unlocking Carbon Credits from Waste-To-Energy: A Practical MRV and Policy Framework for the UAE
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Municipal solid waste generation in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) continues to increase with rapid urbanization and economic development, placing significant pressure on landfills and contributing to methane emissions. At the same
content: Abstract Municipal solid waste generation in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) continues to increase with rapid urbanization and economic development, placing significant pressure on landfills and contributing to methane emissions. At the same time, the UAE is advancing its Net Zero 2050 Strategy and has introduced the National Carbon Credit Registry (NRCC) to verify and trade domestic emission reductions. Waste-to-Energy (WtE) projects in the UAE already divert significant quantities of waste from landfills and generate renewable electricity, yet their emission-reduction potential is not fully reflected in current waste-management policies or carbon-market regulations. This disconnect prevents WtE projects from registering carbon credits and limits opportunities to monetize their climate benefits. This study develops a policy framework to integrate WtE projects into the NRCC by analysing regulatory gaps, evaluating the technological and environmental performance of an operational WtE facility in the UAE, and modelling national scenarios for energy generation, methane avoidance, and carbon-credit revenue. A simplified MRV (Measurement, Reporting, and Verification) approach is proposed to enable consistent quantification of avoided landfill emissions and fossil CO2 from WtE operations, including future deployment of CCS technologies. Importantly, the study introduces a practical incentive-based waste-segregation system tailored to the UAE context. Drawing on international lessons from Japan, Sweden, and South Korea, the framework recommends smart-bin technologies, household reward schemes, digital tracking systems, and community-level incentives to improve segregation behavior and enhance WtE feedstock quality. These measures strengthen the accuracy of MRV data, increase diversion from landfills, and prepare the waste sector for participation in carbon-crediting mechanisms. The findings demonstrate that aligning waste-management policy, behavioral incentives, and carbon-credit regulations can unlock significant environmental and economic value. Integrating WtE into the NRCC—and improving segregation upstream—positions municipal waste as a measurable climate-action pathway that supports the UAE's Circular Economy and Net Zero objectives.

title: Transforming Marginal Field Development Through a Fit-For-Purpose Not Normally Manned Production Platform with Integrated Wellhead Facilities
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Marginal offshore field developments face significant challenges due to limited recoverable reserves, lower production profiles, and strong sensitivity to capital expenditure (CAPEX). To achieve economic viability, development stra
content: Abstract Marginal offshore field developments face significant challenges due to limited recoverable reserves, lower production profiles, and strong sensitivity to capital expenditure (CAPEX). To achieve economic viability, development strategies must balance cost efficiency, operational reliability, safety, and environmental performance. This paper presents a lean offshore development approach that combines remote operations, compact facility design, and low-carbon solutions to unlock the value of marginal resources while maintaining robust operational standards. The development concept is centered on a Not Normally Manned (NNM) production platform integrating production, wellhead, and utility facilities within a single facility. This approach enables significant simplification of top-side facilities, including the elimination of living quarters and a dedicated control room, as well as full integration of the wellhead facilities, thereby reducing the need for a separate wellhead platform and associated subsea structures. The concept emphasizes strict cost control through equipment minimization, reduced structural footprint, simplified operations, and limited intervention requirements. Key design innovations were selectively implemented to establish a cost-effective and reliable operating model without compromising safety or regulatory compliance. A major enabler of autonomous operations was the implementation of a Digital Microwave Radio (DMR) telecommunications system, providing reliable remote monitoring and control. Justification-based equipment selection ensured high- reliability systems capable of meeting targeted Reliability, Availability, and Maintainability (RAM) performance. Facility simplification was further achieved through modularized design aligned with regional heavy-lift vessel capacity and a lean process configuration incorporating ejectors for gas recovery. Environmental performance was enhanced through a zero-routine-flaring philosophy utilizing surplus gas reinjection and nitrogen-purged flare headers, substantially reducing greenhouse gas emissions while enhancing productivity. Design optimization and value engineering initiatives delivered an overall CAPEX reduction of approximately 10%, equivalent to about USD 23 million. Furthermore, shared resources and remote operations reduced operating expenditure by approximately USD 8 million annually. The adoption of surplus gas reinjection and nitrogen purging in flare systems is estimated to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 65,000 tCO2e per year, supporting both regulatory compliance and corporate sustainability objectives. The successful integration of lean facility design, autonomous NNM operations, and low-carbon technologies demonstrates a practical and transferable model for future marginal offshore developments. The approach provides a viable pathway to improve project economics while enabling safer, lower-carbon, and remotely operated production facilities,

title: A Case Study on Design Strategies and Overcoming Challenges in a 100.8 MW Wind Energy Project in India
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Objectives / Scope This paper discusses the development of a 100.8 MW captive onshore wind project designed to supply renewable electricity to refinery operations in western and central India. The case study follows the project fro
content: Abstract Objectives / Scope This paper discusses the development of a 100.8 MW captive onshore wind project designed to supply renewable electricity to refinery operations in western and central India. The case study follows the project from early site screening to commissioning readiness, with attention to the engineering decisions that shaped wind measurement, layout planning, foundation design, logistics, grid connection and construction sequencing. Rather than presenting the project only as a feasibility exercise, the paper focuses on how the design was adapted to real site conditions, including land availability, road access, monsoon constraints, utility interfaces, local coordination and execution risk. The project is also examined as part of industrial decarbonization, where large energy consumers need renewable power that is technically reliable, commercially viable and practical to deliver on the ground. Methods, Procedures, Process The project was developed through an integrated review of wind resource, land suitability, grid access, constructability, regulatory requirements and local sensitivities. Wind conditions were studied using 120 m meteorological masts, long-term correlation and energy-yield modelling. Turbine locations were then refined in WindPRO to manage wake losses while still allowing practical road access, cable routing, crane movement, environmental buffers and safe erection. Foundation designs were prepared using turbine-wise geotechnical findings rather than applying one uniform design across all locations. Logistics planning included route surveys, strengthening checks and movement strategies for long blades and other oversized components. Electrical planning covered pooling substations, transformers, protection systems, SCADA, forecasting, scheduling and coordination with the utility network. Results, Observations, Conclusions The project is expected to deliver a capacity utilization factor of about 32-34%, with annual generation in the range of 280-310 GWh. Layout optimization kept modelled wake losses within about 5-8%, while internal electrical and evacuation losses were treated separately in the energy estimate. The project is expected to avoid about 290,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions each year. The main observation from the case is that a captive wind project of this scale cannot be managed through sequential engineering alone. Wind assessment, layout design, foundation engineering, transport planning, grid-interface work and stakeholder engagement have to progress together. Early route checks, reserve micrositing options, monsoon-aware planning and interim evacuation arrangements helped reduce execution risk and protected the overall project schedule. title: Umm Al Dalkh Zero Flaring Project: Eliminating Routine Flaring Through Produced Gas Recovery and Compression
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Routine gas flaring is one of the most visible sources of emissions in upstream oil and gas operations. Although flare systems remain essential for process safety, emergency depressurization and operational upset management, contin
content: Abstract Routine gas flaring is one of the most visible sources of emissions in upstream oil and gas operations. Although flare systems remain essential for process safety, emergency depressurization and operational upset management, continuous routine flaring results in avoidable greenhouse gas emissions and the loss of recoverable hydrocarbon resources. The Umm Al Dalkh Zero Flaring Project was initiated by ADNOC Offshore to eliminate continuous flaring at the Umm Al Dalkh field and support ADNOC's sustainability direction, ADNOC's Zero Flaring strategy, the UAE Environmental Vision 2030 and the UAE Net Zero by 2050 strategic ambition. Since the start of production at Umm Al Dalkh in the 1980s, produced gas that could not be handled by the existing facilities was flared. At the time of original field development, the technical and economic basis for complete produced gas recovery was limited. With stronger decarbonization drivers, higher maturity of compression solutions and improved business justification, the opportunity was revisited and converted into a practical brownfield project. The selected solution is based on recovery and compression of produced gas that would otherwise be sent to flare. The project includes development of a deck extension to accommodate a new compressor package and associated piping, structural, electrical, instrumentation and control interfaces. The recovered gas is routed back into the process system, thereby eliminating routine flaring while retaining the flare system for safety-related services. The project has eliminated routine flaring capacity of approximately 6.5 MMSCFD and is estimated to avoid approximately 200,000 to 215,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent emissions per year. Beyond the environmental benefit, the project improves resource utilization, reduces carbon intensity, strengthens asset sustainability performance and provides a replicable model for similar zero-flaring initiatives across mature offshore facilities. This paper presents the background, problem definition, selected solution, execution methodology, challenges, mitigation actions, environmental results and key lessons learned from the Umm Al Dalkh Zero Flaring Project.

title: Integrated Flare Energy Reduction and Emissions Mitigation at Oman LNG: Low-Capital Operational and Digital Solutions
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities are under increasing pressure to lower greenhouse gas emissions while preserving the safety margins required for continuous, high-reliability operation. Flaring will remain necessary for proce
content: Abstract Liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities are under increasing pressure to lower greenhouse gas emissions while preserving the safety margins required for continuous, high-reliability operation. Flaring will remain necessary for process protection during abnormal or emergency conditions; however, routine or avoidable flaring represents lost hydrocarbon value, unnecessary fuel consumption, and additional carbon emissions. Within the Oman LNG complex, flare management was therefore treated not as a single environmental project, but as an operating discipline linked to energy efficiency, production planning, marine coordination, and Oman LNG's broader Net Zero Emissions roadmap. This paper describes an integrated flare energy-reduction program built around practical changes that could be implemented with existing assets and internal technical capability. Implemented or operationally established initiatives include fuel-gas-to-nitrogen flare purge optimization, comprehensive flare quantification, nitrogen monitoring and consumption, warm ship handling improvements, and Cold Gas Recovery. The Direct Cooldown Method is presented as a trial-demonstrated concept with optimization ongoing. Engineering calculations based on restriction-orifice design flows estimated that substitution of continuous fuel-gas flare purging with nitrogen reduced fuel-gas consumption by approximately 7.05 t/d, equivalent to more than 2,500 t/year of avoided hydrocarbon consumption. Digital quantification improved identification of individual flare contributors, event duration, cause classification and emissions reporting. Warm ship handling improvements delivered an observed operational result: zero cooldown-related flare events in 2022 and 2023 despite 20 cooldown activities in 2023 compared with 17 in 2019. The Direct Cooldown Method eliminated the conventional gas-up stage, corresponding to approximately 12,000 MMBtu of avoided gas-up energy and a calculated gross emissions-reduction potential of approximately 793 tCO2e per applicable operation. The trial also identified an important limitation: elevated nitrogen concentration in the ship vapor return prevented the intended fuel-gas-system recycling and resulted in approximately 500 t of flaring. Further optimization is therefore required before the gross emissions-reduction potential can be considered a net achieved benefit. Cold Gas Recovery has been completed and implemented, with an estimated annual reduction potential of approximately 3,303 tCO2e/year based on the recovery of shutdown-related cold gas through the BOG/fuel-gas system. Overall, the case study shows that low-capital engineering, operational and digital interventions can materially reduce routine and avoidable flaring while preserving the safety function and availability of the flare system.

title: From AIS Data to Emissions Reduction: Assessing Decarbonisation Strategies for Offshore Wind Installation Vessels
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper examines how different vessel decarbonisation pathways can reduce CO2 emissions from vessels supporting construction of offshore wind farm (OWF) infrastructure. Although electricity generated via offshore wind already ha
content: Abstract This paper examines how different vessel decarbonisation pathways can reduce CO2 emissions from vessels supporting construction of offshore wind farm (OWF) infrastructure. Although electricity generated via offshore wind already has one of the lowest lifecycle carbon footprints of all electricity sources, vessel operations during construction remain a notable contributor, accounting for approximately 6% of total lifecycle GHG emissions depending on site distance from port (Ørsted 2026). This study assesses how three key vessel types, hereafter referred to as the Study Vessel Types (Jack-Up Installation Vessels, Offshore Construction Vessels, and Cable Lay Vessels), operational, and design constraints influence the feasibility and effectiveness of different decarbonisation strategies. The analysis applies a modelling approach using real-world vessel activity data from a representative OWF installation campaign. Automatic Identification System (AIS)-derived operational profiles are integrated with vessel-specific characteristics, including type, size, and engine configuration. Multiple decarbonisation pathways are evaluated, including shore power connection, methanol fuel, hydrogen fuel, and hybrid propulsion. Fuel consumption and associated CO2 emissions are calculated across a range of operating states to quantify the impact of each pathway under realistic operating conditions. Results indicate that decarbonisation potential varies significantly across vessel classes due to differences in operational patterns and energy requirements. Offshore Construction Vessels spend a significant portion of their time in port, making them well suited for shore- based charging, creating the opportunity to achieve comparatively high emissions reductions. In contrast Cable Laying Vessels, and Jack-Up Installation Vessels operate for extended periods offshore and require substantial energy for dynamic positioning and construction activities, making alternative fuels and hybrid systems more suitable decarbonisation pathways. Analysis further suggests that different vessel categories contribute unequally to total vessel emissions, and their distinct decarbonisation pathways lead to varying overall emissions reduction outcomes. Consequently, no single solution is sufficient across the fleet; instead, a tailored combination of technologies is required to maximise system-level emissions reductions. This paper provides a data-driven, operationally grounded comparison of vessel decarbonisation pathways based on real-world OWF installation activity. It offers new insights into how vessel-specific constraints and operational profiles shape decarbonisation outcomes, highlighting the importance of differentiated strategies and improving the robustness of emissions modelling in carbon lifecycle assessments.

title: Sustainable hybrid activated carbon from banana peel and olive pomace for efficient removal of structurally diverse dyes
summary: Introduction Agricultural-waste-derived activated carbons offer a sustainable alternative to conventional adsorbents; however, most studies rely on single biomass precursors and evaluate adsorption using only one model pollutant. Methods In
content: Introduction Agricultural-waste-derived activated carbons offer a sustainable alternative to conventional adsorbents; however, most studies rely on single biomass precursors and evaluate adsorption using only one model pollutant. Methods In this study, a hybrid activated carbon (HAC) derived from banana peel and olive pomace was developed and evaluated for the removal of four structurally distinct dyes: methylene blue (MB), methyl orange (MO), crystal violet (CV), and Eriochrome Black T (EBT). The effects of adsorbent dosage, pH, and contact time were investigated, followed by adsorption isotherm, kinetic, and regeneration analyses. Results An adsorbent dosage of 12 g/L and pH 2 provided the most favorable adsorption conditions. The hybrid activated carbon was found to have a high removal efficiency of 97.71% for MB, 98.41% for MO, 98.70% for CV, and 98.95% for EBT, respectively, under the optimized conditions to remove different dyes with different chemical structures. The equilibrium data were generally better described by the Langmuir model, while the adsorption kinetics showed stronger agreement with the pseudo-second-order model. HAC exhibited maximum adsorption capacities of 130.34, 99.70, 112.42, and 114.52 mg/g for MO, MB, CV, and EBT, respectively, with hybridization enhancing the adsorption capacities toward MO and EBT compared with the individual activated carbons. Regeneration experiments showed that HAC retained adsorption functionality after ten cycles, although removal efficiencies decreased to approximately 42%–56%. Discussion The results in this study validate the potential of olive pomace and banana peel-based hybrid activated carbon as a waste derived, reusable material for the removal of dyes from contaminated wastewater, thereby valorizing agricultural waste and promoting sustainable resource utilization.

title: Driving Decarbonisation at Scale: PETRONAS Upstream Energy Efficiency Strategy Through Multi-Pronged Solutions to Address Hard-To-Abate Combustion Emissions
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract As flaring and venting emissions continue to decline across the oil and gas industry, combustion emissions are emerging as the dominant contributor to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Within Upstream, combustion emissions are projec
content: Abstract As flaring and venting emissions continue to decline across the oil and gas industry, combustion emissions are emerging as the dominant contributor to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Within Upstream, combustion emissions are projected to contribute more than 50% of operational emissions by 2030, necessitating the need for combustion decarbonisation approaches that can reduce emissions without compromising production reliability and energy security. Recognising that turbomachinery systems account for over 95% of Upstream facility energy consumption, an in-house Energy Landscape Assessment (ELA) framework has been developed aligned with ISO 50001 principles to systematically identify energy efficiency and electrification opportunities across its asset portfolio. The assessment identified significant opportunities for Gas Turbine Generator (GTG) power optimisation across more than twenty (20) Upstream facilities, where generally GTG often run redundantly for reliability, operate inefficiently at low loads, increasing fuel use and emissions. This paper outlines PETRONAS's multi-pronged solutions to optimise GTG operations, enabling scalable decarbonisation, improving energy efficiency, and delivering significant OPEX savings through reduced GTG utilisation. The multi-pronged solution comprises five (5) scalable GTG Power Optimisation, namely Risk-Tolerant Approach, Load Shedding, Predictive Analytics, Power Integration, and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The strategy combines operational, digital, and technology solutions ranging from zero-cost measures to CAPEX-intensive initiatives. Key solutions included transitioning facilities from conservative risk-averse operating philosophies toward quantified risk-tolerant approach, implementing load shedding to maintain power system resilience, integrating predictive analytics tool to provide earlier equipment failure warning, enabling inter- and intra-platform power sharing through power integration, and assessing BESS deployment as a future enabler to reduce spinning reserve and as back-up power. Implementation of three solutioning from Risk-Tolerant Approach, Load Shedding, and Power Integration—across eight (8) Upstream facilities (Facility A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H) successfully increased GTG loading closer to optimum operating efficiency while maintaining safe and reliable operations. The programme delivered realised value creation of approximately RM28 million per year through fuel gas savings and reduced OPEX maintenance expenditure, while achieving GHG reductions of approximately 102,000 tCO₂e per year. The results demonstrate that a facility-specific and calculated risk approach can unlock substantial environmental and economic benefits without major production impacts.
