title: GIS-Based Offshore Wind Electrification Assessment for UAE Offshore Oil and Gas Platforms
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This study evaluates the technical and environmental potential for transforming UAE offshore oil and gas platforms from gas turbine-dependent facilities into lower-carbon energy hubs through offshore wind-powered electrification. T
content: Abstract This study evaluates the technical and environmental potential for transforming UAE offshore oil and gas platforms from gas turbine-dependent facilities into lower-carbon energy hubs through offshore wind-powered electrification. The study combines Geographic Information System (GIS)-based spatial assessment with offshore wind resource and energy production analysis. ArcGIS Pro was used to integrate ERA5 wind data, Global Wind Atlas datasets, OpenStreetMap platform locations, MarineRegions EEZ boundaries, and Marine Protected Area datasets to identify suitable offshore wind development zones. Environmental and spatial constraints were applied to screen candidate locations. Three potential offshore wind farm sites were selected and evaluated using hourly ERA5 wind data at a 100 m hub height for 2025. A hypothetical 300 MW offshore wind farm comprising twenty Vestas V236-15 MW turbines was modeled to estimate annual energy production, capacity factors, wake losses, and potential carbon dioxide (CO2) emission reductions associated with replacing gas turbine-generated electricity on offshore platforms. GIS screening identified multiple technically feasible offshore wind development areas within the UAE EEZ characterized by average wind speeds of approximately 5–6 m/s at a 100 m hub height. Among the three candidate sites, the highest-performing location achieved a gross annual energy production of 457.6 GWh/year and a net annual energy production of 411.8 GWh/year after accounting for wake losses, corresponding to a gross capacity factor of 17.4% and a net capacity factor of approximately 15.7%. Using an assumed displaced-electricity emission factor of 0.40 tCO2/MWh, the proposed wind farm demonstrated the potential to reduce approximately 164,700 tCO2 annually. For load matching, a representative two-platform shallow-water jacket cluster was assigned an average demand of approximately 48 MW as a screening assumption. The findings indicate that offshore wind electrification can contribute meaningfully to offshore operational decarbonization despite the UAE's moderate wind regime, particularly when integrated with existing offshore energy infrastructure. This study presents one of the first GIS-based assessments of offshore wind-powered electrification of UAE offshore oil and gas platforms using site-specific hourly wind data, energy production modeling, and carbon reduction analysis. The research provides a practical framework for identifying suitable offshore wind deployment zones and quantifying their contribution to offshore emissions reduction and energy transition objectives in the UAE.

title: From Field Carbon Intensity to Product Carbon Value: An Integrated Framework for Value-Driven Upstream Decarbonization
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper presents an integrated framework that links facility-level carbon intensity (CI), quantified under ISO 14064, with product-level carbon footprint (CFP) assessment using ISO 14040, ISO 14044, and ISO 14067-compliant Life
content: Abstract This paper presents an integrated framework that links facility-level carbon intensity (CI), quantified under ISO 14064, with product-level carbon footprint (CFP) assessment using ISO 14040, ISO 14044, and ISO 14067-compliant Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). The framework enables upstream decarbonization initiatives to be translated into measurable product-level carbon performance and commercial value. The emergence of market-shaping regulations, including the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, FuelEU Maritime, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), and the European Union Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), has increased the importance of product-level carbon intensity as a determinant of market access, regulatory compliance, and competitiveness. At the same time, growing demand for lower-carbon fuels and chemicals has increased the value of verified CFP information as a differentiator in emerging energy markets. The proposed framework comprises three key components: (1) market intelligence screening to identify products exposed to carbon-related regulatory and commercial drivers, (2) upstream network carbon intensity assessment using actual field-level operational data, and (3) ISO-compliant LCA modeling and CFP quantification on a cradle-to-grave basis. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on generic industry-average or statistical datasets, the framework incorporates asset-specific operational data to improve the representativeness, transparency, and decision relevance of product carbon assessments. The framework is applied to four product value chains: crude oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG), methanol, and ammonia. Results demonstrated that actual upstream operational data consistently exhibited lower carbon intensity than corresponding ecoinvent baseline datasets, resulting in improved product-level carbon performance. The findings further showed that upstream decarbonization initiatives can generate measurable reductions in CFP, improve compliance margins against emerging regulatory requirements, and enhance the competitiveness of conventionally produced hydrocarbons and energy products in increasingly carbon-constrained markets. Ultimately, the framework repositions upstream decarbonization from a compliance-driven activity into a value-driven strategy by providing a transparent link between facility-level emissions performance and product-level carbon outcomes. This enables producers to quantify, verify, and communicate the carbon advantages of their products while supporting low-carbon certification, market differentiation, and future commercial opportunities.

title: Deep Decarbonization of Refineries: A Techno-Commercial Framework for SMR Integration and Low-Carbon Hydrogen Production
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper assesses the potential of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) to enable deep decarbonization of India's refining and petrochemical sectors, in line with the national net-zero 2070 commitment. It focuses on integrating SMRs wit
content: Abstract This paper assesses the potential of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) to enable deep decarbonization of India's refining and petrochemical sectors, in line with the national net-zero 2070 commitment. It focuses on integrating SMRs within refinery ecosystems to deliver reliable low-carbon baseload power, high-grade process heat, and scalable pathways for low-carbon hydrogen production. A structured techno-commercial framework evaluates SMR-based systems against fossil configurations a refinery already operates — captive coal-fired power, CFBC cogeneration, and natural gas-based steam methane reforming — with renewable-integrated configurations considered as alternatives. A representative Indian refinery (10–15 MMTPA) is modelled on a basis of 200 MWe, 400 t/h of steam at 300°C, and 240 t/d of hydrogen. Key metrics are levelized cost of energy (LCOE), combined cost of energy (CCOE), hydrogen production cost, lifecycle emissions, and operational reliability, with integration pathways — nuclear-assisted steam generation, baseload supply, and large-scale electrolysis — assessed under sensitivities on carbon pricing (USD 0–100/ton CO2, extended to USD 500/ton CO2 for hydrogen), capital cost, capacity factor, and delivered electricity price. Modular SMR deployment can reliably meet refinery energy demand of 150–250 MW at capacity factors exceeding 90%. For power alone, the reactor delivers USD 94.07/MWh against USD 87.68/MWh for coal at USD 25/ton CO2, the two crossing near USD 31.6/ton CO2 on the internal petroleum coke reference and USD 59.1/ton CO2 on railed domestic coal; exporting steam alongside 143.99 MWe net lowers the cost of useful energy by about 54% to USD 43.67/MWh-eq, breaking even against CFBC cogeneration near USD 40.9/ton CO2. Nuclear-powered electrolysis yields USD 3.56/kg by low-temperature electrolysis and USD 3.79/kg by high-temperature steam electrolysis once electrolyser stack replacement over the 30-year life is funded, marginally above the USD 2.5–3.5/kg range, with potential for cost reduction through scale and localization. Grey hydrogen remains at USD 1.82/kg, within the USD 1.5–2.5/kg range, and renewable-based green hydrogen at USD 3–6/kg depending on intermittency and storage; parity with grey hydrogen is therefore set by delivered electricity price, at about USD 18/MWh for low-temperature electrolysis, rather than by carbon price. Compared to fossil-based systems, SMRs substantially reduce lifecycle emissions, avoiding an estimated 2.0–2.1 million tonnes of CO2 annually at a single site, while also avoiding the intermittency challenges associated with renewable energy and reducing reliance on backup infrastructure. Under carbon pricing of USD 50–100/ton CO2, SMR-based configurations become clearly more competitive against fossil alternatives, positioning SMRs as a technically viable and economically resilient solution for continuous industrial decarbonization. This study presents a first-of-its-kind integrated evalu

title: From Basin Screening to Injection Feasibility: An Integrated FSM-PSM-Dynamic-Geomechanical Workflow for Saline Aquifer CO2 Storage Lead Maturation Applied in Offshore Peninsular Malaysia
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS) is increasingly recognized as a critical solution for managing CO2 emissions from gas fields with high CO2 content, as well as from other industrial and energy-related sources. While de
content: Abstract Carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS) is increasingly recognized as a critical solution for managing CO2 emissions from gas fields with high CO2 content, as well as from other industrial and energy-related sources. While depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs have traditionally been considered as attractive CO2 storage targets due to their known trap configuration, available subsurface data, and proven containment history, they may be constrained by limited storage capacity, potential well integrity risks, and injectivity limitations. In contrast, saline aquifers offer significantly larger regional storage potential, making them a strategic option for long-term CO2 storage development in Malaysia and worldwide. However, saline aquifer storage sites are commonly associated with greater subsurface uncertainty such as limited well control, poorly constrained reservoir continuity, and higher uncertainty in pressure propagation and plume migration behavior. These challenges require an exploration type evaluation approach supported by basin to subregional scale characterization and modelling. The key challenge in saline aquifer CO2 storage is not only to evaluate storage volume and characterize the reservoir, but to confirm that the site can be safely and practically developed. Existing CO2 storage projects show that: reservoir injectivity and pressure management can be major challenging factors. For example, Snøhvit faced reduced injection performance due to pressure build-up issues, while there were geomechanical and pressure-related challenges in Salah project. Other projects such as Gorgon, Quest, Aquistore, and Decatur also demonstrate the importance of the correct prediction of reservoir injectivity. Therefore, evaluation of CO2 storage leads should integrate reservoir and seal characterization together with pressure management evaluation, plume migration, and geomechanics. It must assess injectivity, pressure build-up, pressure management requirements, geomechanical limits, containment, and long-term plume migration risk, as these factors may highly control the practical storage capacity and development feasibility of the lead.

title: Real-Time Drilling Prognosis for ROP Optimization and Energy Efficiency in Automated Rig Operations
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Driven by the continuous demand for improved drilling performance and operational optimization, automated drilling rigs increasingly rely on real‑time prediction tools to maintain consistent performance and support short‑horizon op
content: Abstract Driven by the continuous demand for improved drilling performance and operational optimization, automated drilling rigs increasingly rely on real‑time prediction tools to maintain consistent performance and support short‑horizon operational decisions. In this study, a commercial real‑time prognosis system was deployed on an automated rig to evaluate its ability to generate short‑horizon forecasts of key drilling parameters during the 8½″ section of Well B. A benchmarking analysis was also performed against the offset Well A to compare drilling performance and better understand the mechanical response observed in Well B. Building on these field observations, a simplified toy prediction model was developed using multivariate regression to estimate rate of penetration (ROP) and to quantify fuel consumption and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions per meter drilled. Unlike the commercial prognosis system, which focuses on mechanical response, the simplified model introduces an additional sustainability-oriented perspective using the same drilling dataset. By integrating mechanical and environmental indicators, the proposed module demonstrates how lightweight analytical tools can complement existing real‑time capabilities on automated rigs.

title: Clean Firm Power for the AI Age: Geothermal Pathways to Data Center Decarbonization Across the Energy Trilemma
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract The evolving development and deployment of Artificial Intelligence (‘AI’) is driving unprecedented 24/7 data center energy demand. A single generative AI query consumes roughly ten times the electricity of a conventional internet s
content: Abstract The evolving development and deployment of Artificial Intelligence (‘AI’) is driving unprecedented 24/7 data center energy demand. A single generative AI query consumes roughly ten times the electricity of a conventional internet search, and one planned US data center has requested 1.4 GW of continuous power. This will exceed the total demand of some small states. These loads reframe the energy trilemma, highlighting the need to simultaneously deliver reliability, low carbon impact, and cost-effective energy, and expose the limitations of intermittent renewables for mission-critical digital infrastructure. Geothermal energy, with capacity factors exceeding 70–90% and very low lifecycle emissions, offers a reliable "clean firm" power and thermal management solutions. This study examines how the United States, UAE, and Saudi Arabia deploy geothermal solutions to decarbonize data centers while advancing all three trilemma pillars. The methodology adopts a three-case comparative analysis. In the United States, we assess Utah's Operation Gigawatt, aiming to double capacity from ∼4 GW, and Ormat Technologies’ long-term Power Purchase Agreements (‘PPAs’), including contracts supplying up to 150 MW of geothermal electricity to hyperscale operators. In the UAE, we evaluated ADNOC's G2COOL geothermal district cooling pilot at Masdar City, using ∼90°C water from ∼2.6 km depth to provide ∼10% of cooling demand with ∼50% lower electricity consumption. In Saudi Arabia, we analyzed KAPSARC resource mapping (Alsuwailem et. al, 2024) and KAUST's 2024 pilot at Thuwal targeting geothermal cooling applications. Each case is systematically assessed against trilemma metrics of reliability, carbon impact, and cost-effectiveness. This study evaluates geothermal applications for power generation and thermal management across three stages of market maturity. The United States case demonstrates reliability through baseload geothermal electricity for hyperscale computing; the UAE delivers carbon impact reduction through operational district cooling in extreme climates; and Saudi Arabia explores cost-effectiveness through early-stage geothermal-exchange systems optimizing cooling-intensive demand. The assessment identifies distinct contributions to reliability, carbon impact, and cost-effectiveness. For reliability, geothermal provides continuous baseload power and long-term PPAs that reduce supply volatility. For carbon impact, geothermal systems emit approximately 90% lower lifecycle CO2 than combined-cycle gas (≈40 against ≈500 gCO2e/kWh) and up to ∼99% lower operational CO2 against the same baseline while materially reducing cooling-related emissions in high-demand regions (IPCC 2011). For cost-effectiveness, for the right application, geothermal cooling and geo-exchange solutions can reduce electricity consumption by up to ∼50%, particularly in markets where cooling accounts for 65–70% of power demand. title: Gamifying Carbon Economics: Building Workforce Carbon Literacy Through Simulation-Based Learning
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Organizations increasingly face the challenge of building new capabilities across diverse workforces while maintaining high levels of engagement and accessibility. Sustainability-related decision making is one example, requiring em
content: Abstract Organizations increasingly face the challenge of building new capabilities across diverse workforces while maintaining high levels of engagement and accessibility. Sustainability-related decision making is one example, requiring employees across technical and non-technical functions to understand how day-to-day choices influence long-term business outcomes. Traditional training approaches often communicate concepts effectively but struggle to create the practical intuition needed for confident decision making. This paper explores whether a gamified, simulation-based learning experience can serve as a scalable mechanism for workforce development by enabling employees to learn through experimentation rather than instruction. To address this challenge, we designed and delivered a fully digital global learning initiative centered on a simulated carbon marketplace spanning a 25-year planning horizon. Participants worked individually or in small teams to develop simple automated strategies that made annual decisions between purchasing carbon credits, investing in emissions reduction measures, or accepting financial penalties. The challenge was intentionally designed to be accessible to employees regardless of coding experience through guided onboarding sessions, sample strategies, reference materials, office hours, and the use of enterprise AI tools as participation enablers rather than prerequisites. Competition, real-time feedback, and iterative experimentation created an environment where participants could learn by observing the consequences of their decisions in a safe and engaging setting. The initiative attracted participation from approximately 20% of the target population, representing a broad cross-section of job families, seniority levels, and geographic locations. Participation extended beyond traditional technical roles to include professionals from product management, delivery, finance, change management, and organizational leadership. Activity logs recorded more than 600 practice simulations, nearly 290 tournament submissions, and 176 unique strategies advancing to final evaluation. Evidence of learning emerged through iterative strategy refinement, active engagement during support sessions, sustained participation outside normal working hours, and the emergence of multiple successful problem-solving approaches rather than a single dominant solution. These patterns suggest that employees were not simply competing, but actively developing and testing new mental models in response to complex trade-offs. The most significant outcome was not the identification of an optimal strategy, but the creation of a highly inclusive learning environment that reduced barriers to participation and enabled knowledge development across a diverse workforce. By combining simulation, gamification, and accessible digital tools, the initiative demonstrated how organizations can cultivate workforce capability, encourage experimentation, and accelerate l

title: Permanent Magnet Motors: A Game-Changer for Reliable and Long-Lasting Electrical Submersible Pumps
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper presents a pilot implementation proposal for Permanent Magnet Motor (PMM)-driven Electrical Submersible Pumps (ESPs) in the mature and marginal ADNOC Offshore Umm Al Dalkh (UAD) field to evaluate the benefits of replacin
content: Abstract This paper presents a pilot implementation proposal for Permanent Magnet Motor (PMM)-driven Electrical Submersible Pumps (ESPs) in the mature and marginal ADNOC Offshore Umm Al Dalkh (UAD) field to evaluate the benefits of replacing conventional Induction Motors (IM). PMM technology is positioned as a key enabler for energy-efficient Artificial Lift, reduced energy intensity (kWh/bbl), long-lasting ESP performance, low-carbon asset transformation and ADNOC's Net Zero ambitions. The paper examines the potential of PMMs to improve reliability, extend ESP run life, reduce energy costs, reduce downtime & workover frequency, lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and accelerate the transition toward more sustainable hydrocarbon production. In addition, critical safety and operational considerations for brownfield retrofit and greenfield applications are assessed. More than 90% of producing oil wells require some form of artificial lift system (ALS) during their lifecycle, with ESPs being one of the most versatile and widely deployed methods. However, conventional IM-driven ESPs are often affected by thermal stress, equipment failures, costly workovers and production impact. Building on more than 20 years of ESP operating experience, this paper evaluates PMM technology as a practical alternative for improving energy performance and sustainability. In the subject offshore field, where approximately 30 ESPs (IM motor ratings of 200-300 HP) operate with an average run life of 4-5 years, PMM deployment offers the potential to lower energy consumption, extend run life, reduce intervention frequency and enhance production reliability.[1] A pilot implementation framework is proposed, together with risk assessment, success criteria and industry benchmarking to support technology adoption. The paper further evaluates the role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) in enabling predictive maintenance, performance optimization and digital surveillance of PMM-driven ESPs. The findings indicate that PMM-driven ESPs can serve as a key enabler for energy-efficient artificial lift, sustainable operations, low-carbon asset transformation and decarbonization of upstream facilities, positioning this paper as a technical reference for the deployment of PMM-driven ESPs in the Oil and Gas industry.[13]

title: A Novel Model for Predicting Carbon Sequestration and Gas Recovery of CCUS-EGR in Gas Reservoirs
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Under the background of net-zero emissions, CCUS-EGR (carbon capture, utilization and storage & enhanced gas recovery) has become an important technology to enhance gas recovery and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. However, it's st
content: Abstract Under the background of net-zero emissions, CCUS-EGR (carbon capture, utilization and storage & enhanced gas recovery) has become an important technology to enhance gas recovery and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. However, it's still unclear how much gas recovery can be improved and how much CO2 (carbon dioxide) can be sequestered in gas reservoirs through CCUS-EGR. Therefore, it's neccesary to establish a theoretical model to quantitatively evaluate the stimulation performance and carbon sequestration capacity of CCUS-EGR. Firstly, a novel model for predicting gas recovery and carbon sequestration of CCUS-EGR was proposed. In this model, a key parameter, CO2 sweep area, could be analytically and efficiently determined by establishing material balance equations and simplifying the distribution characteristics of gas components, which was usually calculated through time-consuming numerical simulation in previous research. Then, the new model was applied to the X pilot area in Ordos Basin to evaluate the stimulation performance and carbon sequestration capacity of CCUS-EGR. Finally, sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate how key parameters influence recovery factor and CO2 storage of CCUS-EGR. The following conclusions were drawn: (a) The recovery increment of CCUS-EGR was comprehensively influenced by four key factors, including sweep efficiency of pressure drop, depletion efficiency in depletion development stage, CO2 sweep efficiency and CO2 displacement efficiency; (b) Carbon sequestration capacity of CCUS-EGR was jointly determined by reservoir pore volume, gas recovery and formation pressure after CO2 injection; (c) In the tight gas reservoir at the X pilot area, sweep efficiency of pressure drop, depletion efficiency in depletion development stage, CO2 sweep efficiency and CO2 displacement efficiency would reach 51.4%, 70.3%, 61.6% and 87.3% respectively, and the recovery increment of CCUS-EGR was estimated to be 5.4%; (d) CCUS-EGR was expected to approximately increase natural gas production by 7.5×107 cubic meters and storage CO2 by 4.82×105 tons in the pilot area. This research innovatively constructed a new model for predicting gas recovery and carbon sequestration of CCUS-EGR in gas reservoirs. It could quantitatively evaluate the potential of production stimulation and carbon sequestration of CCUS-EGR in the X pilot area. The research outcomes provide a solid theoretical and practical reference for a large-scale application of CCUS-EGR technology in gas reservoirs in China.

title: Unlocking Waste Heat Recovery in Oman's Oil and Gas Industry Using ORC – Two Case Studies and a Techno-Economic Framework
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Meeting Oman's commitment to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 7% relative to the Business-as-usual scenario by 2030 (Environment Authority Oman, 2022) requires significant improvements in industrial energy efficiency, particularl
content: Abstract Meeting Oman's commitment to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 7% relative to the Business-as-usual scenario by 2030 (Environment Authority Oman, 2022) requires significant improvements in industrial energy efficiency, particularly in the oil and gas sector. In response, national initiatives have been established to reduce gas consumption in energy-intensive industries, with identified gas-saving potential reaching up to 5 MMSCMD. This paper evaluates the role of waste heat recovery using Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) technology as a practical solution to reduce fuel gas consumption, improve energy efficiency and decarbonize oil and gas operations. While ORC technology is commercially proven, project feasibility remains highly dependent on site-specific conditions and requirements and requires a structured techno-economic evaluation framework to unlock value. Detailed techno-economic assessments were performed focusing on two representative case studies: Open-cycle gas turbine exhaust at a remote oil and gas facility, generating electricity for internal use and exporting surplus power to the grid.Cooling water loop heat recovery, capturing low-grade waste heat traditionally rejected to atmosphere/sea water and converting it into electricity with partial heat recycling into the process. While the evaluated ORC projects demonstrated strong technical feasibility, economic attractiveness was achieved by implementing a combination of measures, including securing power offtakers, optimizing ORC system configuration, integrating multiple waste heat sources, applying realistic energy pricing escalation and recognizing the value of continuous, non-intermittent low-carbon power generation.

title: Emissions Reduction Through the Nigerian Gas Flare Commercialisation Programme - The Approach and Technology
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Routine gas flaring is still a major cause of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and energy waste, since it releases large amounts of carbon dioxide (CO2) and at the same time destroys natural gas that could have been used for generati
content: Abstract Routine gas flaring is still a major cause of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and energy waste, since it releases large amounts of carbon dioxide (CO2) and at the same time destroys natural gas that could have been used for generating electricity, for industrial development and meeting domestic energy needs (World Bank 2024; IEA 2024; IPCC 2022). In Nigeria, over 12.7 trillion standard cubic feet (Tscf) of associated gas have been flared, leading to about 702 million metric tonnes of CO2 emissions and considerable economic losses (NUPRC 2024). The Nigerian Gas Flare Commercialisation Programme (NGFCP) was established to address this problem by promoting the commercialisation of flare gas through market mechanisms and involving the private sector. This paper presents an integrated techno-commercial and portfolio conversion optimisation approach to monetising flare gas under the NGFCP. It brings together engineering characterisation, thermodynamic simulation, technology selection, price determination, techno-economic evaluation, commercial structuring, and project maturation in a single decision-support framework. The methodology assesses flare sites based on gas composition, flare volume, production stability, infrastructure accessibility and market proximity to optimise the adoption of compressed natural gas (CNG), Mini-Liquefied Natural Gas (Mini-LNG), Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) recovery, gas-to-liquids (GTL), distributed gas-to-power and hybrid technologies in flare monetisation. The results show that gas composition, the amount of natural gas liquids (NGL), production stability, gas market price, and infrastructure availability are the main factors determining technology choice and project feasibility. The results also show that combining engineering validation with a systematic approach to commercial sequencing greatly improves technology selection, strengthens investment readiness, and increases execution certainty while reducing project risk. The proposed portfolio conversion optimisation approach offers a scalable method for prioritising projects aimed at monetising flare gas, thereby supporting regular flare reduction, improved energy recovery, greater investment confidence, and Nigeria's goals for decarbonisation, energy security, and sustainable development (World Bank 2024; IEA 2024).

title: Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Technology for Sustainable Power Production: Opportunities and Deployment in the Oil & Gas Sector
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) are emerging as a high-efficiency, low-emission option for distributed and industrial power generation. For oil and gas facilities—particularly offshore and remote assets—power is traditionally suppli
content: Abstract Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) are emerging as a high-efficiency, low-emission option for distributed and industrial power generation. For oil and gas facilities—particularly offshore and remote assets—power is traditionally supplied by gas turbines or diesel generators, which carry a significant fuel and carbon penalty. This paper assesses SOFC fundamentals, compares performance against conventional technologies, and proposes deployment architectures for upstream and midstream operations. A comparative benchmark indicates that SOFC electrical efficiency of ~60% can reduce net fuel consumption by ~25–30% versus simple-cycle gas turbines once balance-of-plant loads are accounted for, with near-zero NOx due to non-combustion electrochemistry. SOFC fuel flexibility enables utilization of natural gas, hydrogen, and conditioned associated/flare gas, and the high-quality waste heat supports combined heat and power (CHP) for further emissions reduction. Key integration challenges—fuel cleanup, thermal management, redundancy, and lifecycle cost—are discussed with mitigation measures suitable for petroleum industry applications. The analysis concludes that a staged, modular deployment strategy allows operators to capture near-term fuel and emissions savings while establishing a technically robust pathway toward hydrogen-ready, carbon-capture-compatible power systems.

title: The Technical and Strategic Architecture of MENA NOC Decarbonization, Coupling Sub-10 kg CO2e Per BOE Upstream Operations with a Gigatonne-Scale CCUS–Hydrogen Backbone
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract MENA National Oil Companies (NOCs) operate under a dual mandate: maximize near-term hydrocarbon revenues to fund economic diversification while delivering verifiable decarbonization. The literature has largely treated this mandate
content: Abstract MENA National Oil Companies (NOCs) operate under a dual mandate: maximize near-term hydrocarbon revenues to fund economic diversification while delivering verifiable decarbonization. The literature has largely treated this mandate as a strategic narrative; this paper treats it as an engineering problem. Anchored on the asset bases of Saudi Aramco, ADNOC, QatarEnergy, and Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC), the study quantifies (i) the reservoir- and production-engineering drivers behind sub-10 kg CO2e/boe upstream carbon intensity, and (ii) the regional techno-economic envelope for a gigatonne-scale CCUS–hydrogen backbone built on an estimated 169 Gt of GCC geological storage capacity (≈41 Gt in depleted reservoirs and ≈119 Gt in saline aquifers) and approximately 1,300 Mtpa of aggregate point-source emissions. The analytical framework combines three layers: an asset-level decomposition of upstream Scope 1+2 carbon intensity across eight operational drivers; a bottom-up CCUS levelized-cost model spanning capture, transport, and storage, calibrated against the Bachu volumetric framework; and scenario stress-testing across Brent price, implicit carbon price, and IEA demand pathways. The results, supported by proprietary analytics benchmarking six global producers on breakeven price and carbon intensity, show that MENA NOCs occupy a globally singular position in the cost-carbon competitive quadrant, sub-USD 20/bbl upstream breakevens paired with sub-10 kg CO2e/boe carbon intensity, produced by deliberate engineering choices in reservoir management, methane control, and field electrification, not inherited from favorable geology alone. Integrated GCC CCUS hubs can deliver all-in abatement at USD 30–60/t for high-concentration sources and USD 90–140/t for hard-to-abate industry, materially below Atlantic-basin benchmarks. With a cumulative global oil supply deficit approaching 9.7 MMbbl/d by 2040 and regional CCUS capacity scaling from roughly 4 MTPA today toward more than 30 MTPA by 2030, a trajectory now subject to near-term geopolitical repricing as the region is positioned as the lowest-cost marginal supplier of both molecules and abatement. The primary remaining barrier is commercial-regulatory rather than technical: bankable transport-and-storage business models, pore-space title, and long-term liability transfer.

title: Reducing Energy and CO2 Emissions in a Refinery, Through a SuperESCO Approach
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Industrial energy efficiency remains one of the most cost-effective pathways for reducing greenhouse gas emissions within the oil and gas sector. Despite the technical maturity of many energy conservation measures (ECMs), implement
content: Abstract Industrial energy efficiency remains one of the most cost-effective pathways for reducing greenhouse gas emissions within the oil and gas sector. Despite the technical maturity of many energy conservation measures (ECMs), implementation across refinery and petrochemical facilities continues to be constrained by capital allocation priorities, fragmented project ownership, performance risk, and limited internal engineering resources. These barriers frequently result in economically attractive projects remaining unimplemented despite favorable investment returns. To address these challenges, OQ Alternative Energy (OQAE) has developed and implemented Oman's first large-scale SuperESCO project for industrial facilities. Unlike conventional engineering procurement approaches, the SuperESCO model centralizes project development, technical due diligence, financing, procurement, implementation, and long-term performance assurance under a single delivery organization using Energy Performance Contracts (EnPCs). This approach transfers technical and performance risks away from refinery operations while enabling implementation without upfront capital expenditure by the facility owner. The project commenced with comprehensive Investment Grade Audits (IGAs) across refinery and associated industrial facilities within the Sohar industrial complex. Detailed engineering assessments identified a portfolio of energy conservation measures including chilled water optimization, HVAC control improvements, air handling unit optimization, ventilation system upgrades, LED lighting retrofits, digital energy monitoring platform, and advanced building automation. Projected annual electricity savings exceed 22 GWh, representing approximately 27% reduction in baseline building energy consumption, together with significant reductions in operational expenditure and carbon emissions. These projections are based on detailed engineering assessments and will be validated through post-implementation Measurement and Verification (M&V) using the International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol (IPMVP). As implementation progresses, early observations indicate that the SuperESCO delivery model provides substantial advantages beyond energy reduction alone. These include accelerated project delivery, improved procurement efficiency, standardized technical solutions, enhanced governance, and stronger alignment between commercial incentives and operational performance. This paper presents the project development methodology, engineering approach, commercial framework, and early implementation experience from Oman's first refinery-based SuperESCO project. It further discusses how this model may provide a scalable framework for deploying industrial energy efficiency projects throughout the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), supporting regional decarbonization objectives while maintaining operational reliability and competitiveness.

title: Electrifying Artificial Lift in a Remote West African Brownfield: Pilot Design, Power Scenarios, and Quantified Emissions Impact
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This study reassesses artificial lift strategy for a remote onshore brownfield in West Africa historically dominated by gas lift (GL). The question addressed is whether moving away from GL can materially increase drawdown and oil r
content: Abstract This study reassesses artificial lift strategy for a remote onshore brownfield in West Africa historically dominated by gas lift (GL). The question addressed is whether moving away from GL can materially increase drawdown and oil rate at late life while providing a credible, quantified pathway to lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions under diesel and grid power. The evolution of a candidate well is followed from GL, through hydraulic solutions like jet pump (JP) and hydraulic piston pump (HPP), to an electric submersible pump (ESP). Converting from other artificial lift methods to ESPs is common in the industry, but few operators have evaluated the emissions benefits of the same. Inflow and outflow models were calibrated for the candidate well, with sensitivities on reservoir pressure, productivity index (0.7–2.5 stb/d/psi), water cut (60–95%) and free-gas handling, to cover a range of well and reservoir performance scenarios, in the absence of direct measurements of certain key parameters such as reservoir pressure. ESP designs were engineered with gas-handler and separator configurations, motor derating, and a variable speed drive (VSD) strategy suited to high water cut and high gas volume fraction (GVF) conditions. For the baseline GL, JP and HPP cases and the proposed ESP cases, lift energy and Scope 1 emissions were estimated using IPCC Tier 1 stationary combustion methodology, taking the specific fuel consumption of each generating set from its certified fuel-consumption table at the load factor actually carried, with boundaries set by the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard. The International Energy Agency (IEA) emission factors database was used for Scope 2 emissions from imported grid electricity. Modelled diesel-powered ESPs increased oil rate from 91.9 bopd (GL) to 228.0 bopd, an uplift of approximately 150%, sustained at 76% water cut. Lift-related emissions depended strongly on the power source: absolute emissions fell from 696 tCO2e/yr (GL) to 239 tCO2e/yr (ESP–diesel) and 76 tCO2e/yr (ESP–grid), reductions of 66% and 89% respectively. Emissions intensity per 1,000 barrels of oil improved from 20.74 tCO2e (GL) to 2.88 tCO2e (ESP–diesel) and 0.92 tCO2e (ESP–grid) giving improvements of 86% and 96% respectively. These gains reflect both the higher lift capability and production efficiency of the ESP relative to compression-driven GL, and the comparatively low grid emission factor (0.24 kg CO2e/kWh) available in the host country. For remote, gas-constrained brownfields with rising water cut, ESPs can unlock meaningful production uplift alongside large, standards-aligned emissions reductions under both power scenarios. Because the intensity gain is driven by simultaneous rate uplift and lower specific lift energy, the case is compelling even before grid electrification. A staged pilot is outlined with KPIs on production, reliability and run life, interventions and emissions. Deployment-ready ESP engineering for a remote West African

title: Nutraceutical-rich oil from passion fruit by-products of beverage processing by green extraction
summary: Processing passion fruit beverages generates substantial agro-industrial by-products that are rich in bioactive compounds. Valorizing these by-products through green extraction offers a sustainable route to transform them into high-value oi
content: Processing passion fruit beverages generates substantial agro-industrial by-products that are rich in bioactive compounds. Valorizing these by-products through green extraction offers a sustainable route to transform them into high-value oils while supporting responsible food-waste reduction. The present study evaluated two sustainable compressed gas extraction alternatives, supercritical fluid carbon dioxide (SF-CO₂) and liquefied dimethyl ether (LDME), alongside conventional cold pressing and solvent extraction, focusing on the retention of nutraceutical compounds in the crude oils to identify the most effective recovery method. LDME gave the highest oil yield (27.36%), together with low acid and peroxide values and high total phenolic content and antioxidant activity (DPPH, FRAP and ABTS). The oils contained total tocopherols, phytosterols and policosanols ranging from 303.92 to 468.34 mg/kg, 370.02 to 673.67 mg/100 g, and 212.10 to 258.37 mg/100 g, respectively, and the LDME-extracted puree oil showed the highest carotenoid content. Principal component analysis revealed a strong association between the SF-CO 2 and LDME methods and these bioactive compounds, indicating the potential of the resulting oils as sources of lipophilic nutraceuticals for functional-food applications.

title: Advancing Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) Plant Decarbonisation Through Extra High Voltage (EHV) Electrification, Digital Control, and Commissioning Excellence
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This project is a strategic initiative advancing the Company's energy transition agenda by decarbonising power supply to Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) facilities through integration with grid‑based renewable energy. By replacing conv
content: Abstract This project is a strategic initiative advancing the Company's energy transition agenda by decarbonising power supply to Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) facilities through integration with grid‑based renewable energy. By replacing conventional Gas Turbine Generators (GTGs) with a 275kV Extra High Voltage (EHV) grid connection delivering up to 90 MW, the project directly accelerates Net‑Zero Carbon (NZC) ambitions through significant reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and carbon intensity produced by the conventional Gas Turbine Generators (GTGs) by reduced direct combustion of fuel gas and reduce GHG emissions (CO2e) from the combustion in PLANT which generates a GHG index of 0.916 tCO2e/MWh. Beyond emissions reduction, it delivers substantial operational and economic value through optimized fuel gas utilisation, reduced reliance on carbon‑intensive generation, and enhanced energy efficiency. The transition strengthens system reliability and resilience via diversified power sources, while enabling a seamless and sustainable conversion within a brownfield environment—positioning the facility as a benchmark low‑carbon LNG operation. The project adopts an integrated power system engineering approach covering engineering design, procurement, construction, installation, and commissioning of 275 kV EHV substations and its utilities, transformers, switchgear, protection relays, and Energy Network Management Control Systems (ENMCS). Key processes include integration with existing facilities, grid‑plant synchronization, protection coordination, dynamic load transfer, and stability validation under multiple operating scenarios. Execution is anchored on a risk‑based commissioning methodology, strengthened by the Smooth Start‑Up Program (SSP) and Operations Readiness Assurance (ORA) framework to ensure disciplined sequencing, operational readiness, and safe transition. Digital monitoring, real‑time control, and advanced simulations further optimize system performance, enhance energy efficiency, and minimize emissions, aligning execution with Net Zero Carbon (NZC) and sustainability objectives. The project delivers significant environmental, operational, and strategic impact. Through systematic displacement of few gas‑based generation with imported grid power, implemented via controlled synchronization and phased load ramp‑up, it achieves substantial reductions in fuel gas consumption, flaring, and reduce CO2 emissions. This transition lowers overall carbon intensity while improving energy efficiency and stability of operations. Operationally, it enhances reliability, optimizes fuel gas utilisation for higher‑value use, and improves energy resilience.
