title: Resource Optimization and Waste Reduction
summary: This chapter explores how AI is transforming resource optimization, waste reduction, and environmental sustainability by enabling organizations to make more efficient, data-driven decisions across ESH Management Systems. It begins by examin
content: This chapter explores how AI is transforming resource optimization, waste reduction, and environmental sustainability by enabling organizations to make more efficient, data-driven decisions across ESH Management Systems. It begins by examining the complementary relationship between resource optimization and waste reduction, demonstrating how organizations can improve operational performance by minimizing the consumption of materials, energy, water, labor, and capital while reducing waste generation at its source. This chapter highlights the application of AI-enabled smart energy grids, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, predictive analytics, and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems to optimize water management, energy consumption, and infrastructure resilience. A detailed case study of Singapore’s Public Utilities Board (PUB) illustrates how integrated water, wastewater, and energy systems can support circular resource management and long-term sustainability. This chapter also examines industrial process optimization as a strategy for reducing emissions through AI-supported digital twins, predictive modeling, and process control, while aligning operational improvements with internationally recognized climate mitigation pathways. Finally, it explores recycling and sustainability simulations, demonstrating how digital twins, material flow analysis (MFA), and Machine Learning enables organizations to evaluate waste diversion, circular economy initiatives, carbon reduction strategies, and resource recovery before implementation. Collectively, these technologies enable organizations to transition from reactive environmental compliance to predictive, system-wide optimization, improving operational efficiency, reducing environmental impacts, strengthening regulatory performance, and advancing long-term organizational resilience and sustainability within a modern Environmental Management System (EMS).

title: Effects of Bioproducts on Tomato Performance across Two Cultivation Cycles under Reduced Mineral Fertilization
summary: Abstract The overuse of mineral fertilizers represents significant environmental and economic concerns, highlighting the necessity of sustainable nutrient management. This study evaluated the biostimulant potential of bioproducts (BPs) from
content: Abstract The overuse of mineral fertilizers represents significant environmental and economic concerns, highlighting the necessity of sustainable nutrient management. This study evaluated the biostimulant potential of bioproducts (BPs) from solid anaerobic digestate in greenhouse tomato cultivation to maintain productivity with reduced fertilization. Trials were conducted over two cycles, with soil application of BPs, combined with 100 or 60% of standard mineral fertilization (MF). Reducing MF by 40% resulted in a decrease in marketable yield; however, the combination of BPs with 60% MF compensated for this reduction, achieving yields comparable to the control in both growing cycles. Pigment content decreased under reduced MF, but BP-treated plants exhibited higher protein accumulation and increased enzymatic activities involved in nitrogen assimilation, suggesting enhanced nitrogen use efficiency. Overall, BPs acted as effective plant biostimulants, enabling a 40% reduction in mineral fertilizer input without compromising total yield or fruit quality, supporting a more sustainable tomato production.

title: Climate Crisis in Contemporary Bangladeshi Architecture
summary: Bangladesh, responsible for just 0.56% of global emissions, ranks among the most climate-vulnerable nations. Farhan Karim traces how contemporary architects like Marina Tabassum and Saif Ul Haque exemplify Bangladesh’s shift from postcoloni
content: Bangladesh, responsible for just 0.56% of global emissions, ranks among the most climate-vulnerable nations. Farhan Karim traces how contemporary architects like Marina Tabassum and Saif Ul Haque exemplify Bangladesh’s shift from postcolonial climate-conscious design to crisis-driven innovation. These are exemplified by Tabassum’s modular Khudi Bari (modular house mounted on stilts) and Haque’s “amphibian” school, which responds to flooding with affordable, adaptive structures. Their work critiques Western-centric sustainability norms, echoing modernist-era South Asian architects such as Charles Correa, who advocated for context over carbon-heavy glass towers. This emerging architecture, rather than relying on formulaic technical fixes, addresses the climate crisis by transforming systemic failures into adaptable practices that orient themselves to community needs in an increasingly uncertain environment.

title: Advancing building decarbonization via electrified thermal management: A VRF heat recovery system with domestic hot water integration
summary: The building sector is responsible for a substantial share of global greenhouse gas emissions, making electrification with high-efficiency technologies a critical pathway toward achieving net-zero targets. Heat pump systems with heat recove
content: The building sector is responsible for a substantial share of global greenhouse gas emissions, making electrification with high-efficiency technologies a critical pathway toward achieving net-zero targets. Heat pump systems with heat recovery capability offer significant opportunities to reduce both energy consumption and carbon emissions by reutilizing waste heat within building thermal systems. This study evaluates a heat recovery–enabled Variable Refrigerant Flow (VRF) system integrated with a domestic hot water (DHW) loop through a hydraulic heat exchanger (VRF-Hy), designed to support fully electrified space conditioning and water heating. A quasi-steady system-level evaluation framework is developed and coupled with whole-building energy simulations using the DOE mid-rise apartment prototype model to quantify energy and decarbonization performance. The framework is applied to six representative U.S. climate locations, Miami (1 A), Tucson (2B), San Diego (3 C), New York (4 A), Seattle (4 C), and Denver (5B), to compare climate-dependent performance under a consistent building and control framework. Results show that integrating the DHW loop provides a stable heat sink, substantially increasing the frequency and magnitude of simultaneous heating and cooling operation and thereby maximizing heat recovery potential. Compared to a conventional baseline system, the proposed VRF-Hy configuration achieves simulated total annual site energy savings ranging from 31.1% to 50.4% and reduces equivalent CO 2 emissions by 31.0–50.3%, while completely eliminating on-site fossil fuel combustion. These findings suggest that heat recovery–enabled VRF systems with DHW integration offer a potential framework for building electrification and decarbonization. Unlike prior VRF-HR studies focused on component-level performance, this work provides a simulation-based system-level assessment of electrification and decarbonization impacts for the multifamily building prototype across multiple U.S. climate zones using a consistent whole-building modeling framework.

title: Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Framework-Confined Carbon Dots toward Efficient Red Room-Temperature Phosphorescence via Resonance Energy Transfer
summary: Abstract Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) materials are promising for information encryption and anticounterfeiting. However, realizing long-wavelength RTP of carbon dots (CDs) is challenging owing to unstable triplet states and stron
content: Abstract Room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) materials are promising for information encryption and anticounterfeiting. However, realizing long-wavelength RTP of carbon dots (CDs) is challenging owing to unstable triplet states and strong nonradiative decay. Herein, we construct a hydrogen-bonded organic framework (HOF) through molecular self-assembly and realize the in situ generation of CDs within the HOF matrix. By further incorporating Rhodamine B (RhB) into the HOF, a donor–acceptor resonance energy transfer (RET) system is established, enabling efficient red RTP emission. In this system, the HOF matrix provides a confined environment for the CDs and RhB. Meanwhile, the hydrogen-bonded network restricts excited-state molecular motions and suppresses nonradiative relaxation. The optimized CDs-RhB@HOF composite exhibits outstanding red phosphorescence centered at 600 nm, achieving a high PLQY of 34.20% (versus 0.71% for CDs@HOF) and a prolonged lifetime of 458 ms. The composite material has been successfully applied to multilevel anticounterfeiting encryption.

title: Platform Synthesis for the Rapid Construction of V-Shaped and Cruciform Push–Pull Compounds
summary: Abstract We report the modular synthesis of cruciform push–pull compounds from V-shaped di- and trisubstituted thiophenes obtained from commercially available 2,3-dibromothiophene (DBT) via sequential couplings using the concept of “platfor
content: Abstract We report the modular synthesis of cruciform push–pull compounds from V-shaped di- and trisubstituted thiophenes obtained from commercially available 2,3-dibromothiophene (DBT) via sequential couplings using the concept of “platform synthesis”. Orthogonal C2/C3 functionalization with EDOT-and naphthothiophene-based molecular modules yielded a library of 8 V-shaped, sterically hindered π-conjugated derivatives. Coupling in C5 with electron-deficient benzothiadiazole units, to complete the “platform” synthetic sequence, afforded two different “cruciform-like” push–pull luminophores emitting in the deep red region of the visible spectrum. Photophysical and electrochemical studies, supported by calculations, revealed that the substitution pattern on DBT is crucial in tuning both emission efficiency and the bathochromic shifts, inducing aggregation-induced enhanced emission (AIEE) in one derivative. This work highlights the versatility of platform synthesis in the realization of relevant materials for optoelectronic applications.

title: Fire asymmetries across global borders reveal distinct ecological governance and cooperation priorities
summary: Abstract International borders divide governance systems but often cut across continuous ecosystems, creating potential mismatches in fire management. We analyze 277 terrestrial international border pairs using a 21-year satellite fire reco
content: Abstract International borders divide governance systems but often cut across continuous ecosystems, creating potential mismatches in fire management. We analyze 277 terrestrial international border pairs using a 21-year satellite fire record and integrate fire burden, relative cross-border asymmetry, ecological value, institutional challenge and cooperation challenge. Border fire burden broadly reproduces global fire geography, with the highest activity concentrated in major fire-prone regions, but our analysis shows that management implications differ markedly among borders. Among 128 active-fire pairs, fire burden and proportional asymmetry are weakly negatively associated and identify partly distinct priorities. Ecological value further reshapes priority geographies, while institutional and cooperation constraints define different governance contexts. Multivariate analysis separates these borders into operational profiles with contrasting management needs. Here, we show that transboundary fire priority cannot be inferred from fire activity alone but emerges from distinct combinations of fire, ecological and governance conditions, requiring border-specific approaches to monitoring, conservation and cooperation.

title: Peatland climate-methane feedbacks in warming periods were governed by pH and hydrology
summary: Abstract Methane is emitted naturally from peatlands, but controls on those emissions and their response to global warming remain debated. Previous research attempted to assess this by exploring how methane cycling responded to past warming
content: Abstract Methane is emitted naturally from peatlands, but controls on those emissions and their response to global warming remain debated. Previous research attempted to assess this by exploring how methane cycling responded to past warming events, with lipid biomarker signatures for methanotrophy (the 13 C-depletion of bacterially-derived hopanoids, δ 13 C hop ) revealing changes to the methane cycle during the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM). However, the lack of modern analogues has hindered interpretation of those changes. We present new δ 13 C hop data from a suite of tropical peatlands, including the discovery of exceptionally 13 C-depleted hopanoids, with values approaching those of the PETM. Across all sites, δ 13 C hop decreases with increasing pH, likely co-occurring with a shift from predominantly hydrogenotrophic to acetoclastic methanogenesis pathways. Modern sites with the lowest δ 13 C hop have elevated methane emissions, higher Type I to Type II methanotroph ratios, and higher methanogen proportions, linking hopanoid isotopic depletion to enhanced methane production and flux. These insights allow re-evaluation of geological records, with low PETM δ 13 C hop also indicating intensified peatland methane emissions. Such processes evidently acted as positive feedbacks in the past and could do so in the future – not only as a direct response to warming but indirectly via changes to peatland hydrology and geochemistry.

title: Treating Waste with Waste: Recent Advances in Greenhouse Gas Capture Using Waste-Derived Porous Materials
summary: Abstract Solid-waste-derived porous materials represent economical and sustainable adsorbents for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS), enabling simultaneous industrial emission mitigation and high-value valorization of solid was
content: Abstract Solid-waste-derived porous materials represent economical and sustainable adsorbents for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS), enabling simultaneous industrial emission mitigation and high-value valorization of solid wastes. Nevertheless, comprehensive review articles dedicated to systematically summarizing and discussing such materials are scarce. In this work, four major categories of solid-waste-based adsorbents for greenhouse gas capture are systematically reviewed: porous carbons fabricated via high-temperature carbonization of plastics and biomass; covalently cross-linked porous polymers synthesized under mild conditions; coal-gangue-derived silica-aluminous porous materials; and multifunctional adsorbents produced from diverse agricultural and industrial solid wastes. This review elaborates the synthetic routes, pore-structure regulation strategies, adsorption performances, and inherent limitations of adsorbents derived from various waste feedstocks, covering a broad spectrum of agro-industrial solid wastes including plastics, biomass, coal gangue, gasification slag, rice husks, new-energy-related solid residues, carbide slag, metallurgical slags, mine tailings, and textile-printing-dyeing sludge. Current studies predominantly conduct performance evaluations using an oversimplified simulated flue gas. Insufficient data are available concerning antipoisoning capability and long-term cyclic stability of these adsorbents. Moreover, existing material systems exhibit poor adaptability to waste feedstocks with variable compositions, while pilot-scale demonstrations and full life-cycle assessments are largely absent. These bottlenecks hinder the industrial translation of waste-derived adsorbents. Future research priorities encompass collaborative conversion technologies for mixed solid wastes, structural modification for antipoisoning performance, development of multimechanism composite adsorbents, and mechanistic insights into adsorption processes via combined in situ characterization and theoretical simulation. This Review systematically recapitulates advances in diverse waste-originated adsorbents and offers theoretical references for large-scale industrial deployment of low-cost solid-waste-based CCUS technologies.

title: Green Software Tracker for Web Applications Using AI
source: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
summary: Web applications consume computing resources such as CPU, memory, and network bandwidth during request processing. High resource consumption can increase energy usage and contribute to carbon emissions. This research proposes a Green Softwa
content: Web applications consume computing resources such as CPU, memory, and network bandwidth during request processing. High resource consumption can increase energy usage and contribute to carbon emissions. This research proposes a Green Software Tracker for Web Applications Using AI to monitor resource utilization and estimate the environmental impact of web applications. The proposed system uses Python and the psutil library to collect process-level CPU and memory data at defined intervals. It aims to estimate energy consumption using a documented estimation method and calculate associated carbon emissions using an appropriate electricity emission factor. A dashboard is planned to display resource usage, estimated emissions, a Green Score, and recommendations for improving software efficiency. The current recommendation approach is rule-based. Further implementation and experimental evaluation are required to validate the estimation method and assess the system's performance

title: Unveiling ESG ratings: corporate perspectives and institutionalisation dynamics
source: Sustainability Accounting Management and Policy Journal
summary: Purpose Environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings have become a central mechanism for assessing, benchmarking and signalling corporate sustainability performance to financial investors. Yet, their widespread use persists despite on
content: Purpose Environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings have become a central mechanism for assessing, benchmarking and signalling corporate sustainability performance to financial investors. Yet, their widespread use persists despite ongoing criticism of their capacity to accurately reflect firms’ social and environmental contributions. This paper aims to examine this paradox from the perspective of rated companies, exploring why firms continue to engage with ESG ratings despite criticism of their effectiveness, even as investors remain their primary users. Drawing on institutional theory, the authors adopt this underexplored perspective and investigate how ESG ratings become institutionalised within organisations. Design/methodology/approach Based on abductive thematic analysis of 45 semi-structured interviews with sustainability executives from listed European firms, the authors develop a framework distinguishing between substantive and symbolic forms of ESG rating institutionalisation. Findings ESG rating adoption is shaped by institutional pressures and unfolds along a continuum. At one end, firms substantively integrate sustainability considerations into core operations; at the other, ESG ratings are used symbolically to secure external recognition and legitimacy. This study also highlights the risk of deinstitutionalisation if the limitations of ESG ratings remain unaddressed. Practical implications This study offers managers, investors and policymakers insights into navigating ESG pressures and strengthening the credibility of ESG frameworks while providing a diagnostic lens to distinguish symbolic compliance from substantive integration. Social implications While the potential deinstitutionalisation of ESG ratings could erode credibility, accountability and investor trust, substantive adoption could benefit transparency, stakeholder oversight and the diffusion of sustainability norms. Addressing their limitations is therefore crucial for maintaining credibility in the financial sector and directing capital towards companies with meaningful sustainability practices. Originality/value This study extends research on corporate responses to ESG ratings by drawing on institutional theory and developing a conceptual framework of symbolic and substantive institutionalisation from the perspective of rated companies. Specifically, it shifts the explanatory focus beyond firms’ strategic orientations by showing that corporate responses are also shaped by the institutional characteristics and structural limitations of ESG rating systems, thereby advancing the concept of ESG ratings’ deinstitutionalisation.

title: Financing Healthcare Sustainability Through Responsible Banking: A Policy Framework for Bangladesh
summary: Bangladesh's health system faces a dual sustainability crisis. On the financing side, public health expenditure has remained below one per cent of GDP for two decades, while out-of-pocket payments account for roughly two-thirds of total hea
content: Bangladesh's health system faces a dual sustainability crisis. On the financing side, public health expenditure has remained below one per cent of GDP for two decades, while out-of-pocket payments account for roughly two-thirds of total health spending — among the highest ratios in South Asia — pushing households into poverty and stalling progress toward Universal Health Coverage. On the environmental side, healthcare is a globally carbon-intensive sector whose facilities, energy use and supply chains contribute materially to emissions even as the sector's mission is to protect health. This paper argues that responsible banking — the alignment of lending and investment with sustainability objectives under frameworks such as the UN Principles for Responsible Banking, and, domestically, Bangladesh Bank's Sustainable Finance Policy — offers an underused channel for addressing both dimensions simultaneously. Using a review of national budget documents, central-bank circulars, capital-market records and international benchmarks from 2016 to 2025, the paper maps the instruments through which responsible finance can mobilise capital for resilient, low-carbon and financially inclusive healthcare: green and social bonds, sustainability-linked loans, concessional green refinancing, blended finance and health micro-insurance. It finds that Bangladesh has built credible sustainable-finance rails — including four concessional refinancing funds and a pioneering green-bond framework — but has yet to direct them deliberately at the health sector. The paper concludes with a set of policy recommendations to bridge the health-financing gap through responsible banking while safeguarding against greenwashing and inequitable access. Medicine Today 2026, Vol.38 (2): 319-323

title: Sustainable Federated Continual Learning for environmental monitoring: a systematic review
summary: Introduction The use of distributed sensing infrastructures is increasingly becoming a key approach to environmental monitoring that is required to be mobile, flexible and adaptable to non-stationary conditions, preserve data privacy and co
content: Introduction The use of distributed sensing infrastructures is increasingly becoming a key approach to environmental monitoring that is required to be mobile, flexible and adaptable to non-stationary conditions, preserve data privacy and consume as few resources as possible. The decentralized training paradigm provided by Federated Learning together with the ability of adapting sequentially over time without forgetting from Continual Learning has resulted in a concept of Federated Continual Learning (FCL) which offers a promising approach for privacy preserving environmental sensing systems that are capable of learning over time without forgetting. This systematic review provides an in-depth synthesis of the latest research, progress, environmental applications, sustainability, trustworthiness and future directions of Federated Continual Learning (FCL) for environmental monitoring. Methods A total of 90 peer-reviewed publications were identified by conducting a systematic literature search using pre-defined inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality assessment, bibliometric analysis and qualitative evidence synthesis with the framework of PRISMA 2020. Results The synthesized evidence suggests that Federated Learning has come of age in terms of optimization, communication complexity, robustness, and personalization, but Federated Continual Learning is still in its infancy with few applications in the real world. Typically, sustainability, trustworthiness, privacy, fairness, personalization and explainability are explored separately and not in parallel. Although most applications have been single-shot Federated Learning systems, without genuine continual adaptation, isolated examples include some applications from air quality to water quality, agriculture to disaster monitoring and remote sensing. Seven cross-cutting research gaps are identified: disjointed integration of research directions, few deployments in the real world, absence of standardized evaluation, unsolved multi-objective optimization, poor scaling in the long term, weak sustainability-trustworthiness coupling, and poor cross-domain generalization. Discussion It is not just about the evolution of single algorithmic breakthroughs anymore, but actual realization of Federated Continual Learning systems that can effectively assist in continual adaptation while ensuring communication efficiency, sustainability, trustworthiness, scalability and long-term deployment under real environmental conditions.

title: Promise and pitfalls of acetogenic Clostridium species for hydrogen and carbon dioxide-driven gas fermentation
summary: Gas fermentation using anaerobic acetogenic bacteria represents a promising carbon capture and utilization strategy for converting C1 gases into valuable bioproducts. Among acetogens, Clostridium species have attracted significant attention
content: Gas fermentation using anaerobic acetogenic bacteria represents a promising carbon capture and utilization strategy for converting C1 gases into valuable bioproducts. Among acetogens, Clostridium species have attracted significant attention due to their ability to produce native C2–C6 acids and alcohols through their versatile metabolism. While industrial applications have primarily focused on CO- and syngas-based fermentation, a large fraction of anthropogenic emissions originates from industrial sectors generating CO 2 -rich gas streams with limited or negligible CO content. CO 2 - fermentation, powered by renewable H 2 , offers a potential route for the valorization of these emissions and the development of carbon-negative bioprocesses. However, research on CO 2 /H 2 -driven gas fermentation by Clostridial acetogens remains limited compared with CO- and syngas-based systems, and a comprehensive overview of their potential is still lacking. This mini-review summarizes the current state of research, highlighting the best laboratory-scale performances achieved for native product formation and discussing the key metabolic constraints affecting growth and productivity. Furthermore, it provides a framework for selecting suitable host species and operating conditions tailored to specific target molecules, while exploring recent advances in strain development and process optimization that may support the future scale-up of CO 2 /H 2 -driven gas fermentation and its application in sustainable biomanufacturing.

title: Nipa Palm (Nypa fruticans) Utilization: Implications for Blue Carbon and the Sustainable Bioeconomy – A Systematic Review
summary: Background Nypa fruticans (nipa palm) provides ecological and economic benefits in tropical mangrove ecosystems but remains underrepresented in blue carbon inventories and bioeconomy policy. This review assessed its uses, carbon sequestrati
content: Background Nypa fruticans (nipa palm) provides ecological and economic benefits in tropical mangrove ecosystems but remains underrepresented in blue carbon inventories and bioeconomy policy. This review assessed its uses, carbon sequestration potential relative to other mangroves, and contribution to a sustainable bioeconomy. Methods A systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. Scopus was searched for “Nypa fruticans,” “Nipa Palm,” and “Nipah.” English-language, open-access journal articles published from 2016 to 2026 were screened in six stages using predefined criteria. Data were extracted into a structured database and analysed using bibliometric analysis and qualitative synthesis. Results Of 454 records identified, 175 studies were included. Research mainly originated from Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand, with publication output increasing after 2019. Eight themes emerged: bioenergy; food and functional products; health and pharmaceutical products; materials; livelihoods and value chains; cultural ecosystem services; blue carbon and ecosystem support; and sustainability risks, including invasiveness. Mean carbon fraction was 42.48% (range 41.45–43.50%), while reported carbon stocks ranged from 7.26 to 38.10 Mg C ha −1 , below values reported for Rhizophora apiculata and Bruguiera gymnorrhiza. Nipa may contribute to carbon storage in degraded coastal areas and dense stands, while bioethanol from its sap may achieve a net-negative carbon balance. Estimated annual net income from nipa-sap bioethanol was IDR 6.1–42.0 million ha −1 . Its phytochemicals indicate antidiabetic, antimicrobial, and neuroprotective potential. Conclusions Nypa fruticans is a multifunctional coastal resource, but economic uses must be balanced against ecological trade-offs, including invasiveness outside its native range. REDD+ and Nationally Determined Contributions carbon accounting should consider nipa-specific values; soil carbon in nipa-dominated stands requires further study. Product innovation and adaptive coastal management could support a sustainable bioeconomy.

title: Beyond the Green Image: A Visual-Documentary Framework for Evaluating Nature-Positive Evidence in Architecture
summary: As architecture increasingly adopts biodiversity and nature-positive terminology, visually prominent greenness is often treated as evidence of ecological value. This chapter develops a visual-documentary framework that separates architectur
content: As architecture increasingly adopts biodiversity and nature-positive terminology, visually prominent greenness is often treated as evidence of ecological value. This chapter develops a visual-documentary framework that separates architectural visibility from ecological verifiability. Twelve international buildings comprising 16 ecological subsystems were examined through criterion-based purposive sampling. Visual Greenness Prominence was assessed independently from nine ecological criteria, while evidence level, source quality, baseline status and evidence architecture were coded separately. The analysis shows that high visual greenness is neither necessary nor sufficient for strong verified ecological response. The principal gap occurred between ecological provision and demonstrated outcome: habitat provision, heterogeneity and natural-process integration were common, but none of the subsystems demonstrated the full combination of broad quantified biodiversity improvement, a defensible baseline or counterfactual, and evidence sufficient to establish baseline- or counterfactual-relative positive biodiversity change. The framework therefore calibrates ecological claims to the quality and completeness of the evidence supporting them.

title: CARBON COMPLIANCE AND EXPORT COMPETITIVENESS OF LITHIUM BATTERIES BASED ON SPATIOTEMPORAL ELECTRICITY-CARBON ACCOUNTING: A CASE STUDY OF EVE ENERGY’S JINGMEN BASE
source: World journal of economics and business research.
summary: Against the backdrop of increasing regulatory attention to lifecycle emissions and product-level traceability, lithium-ion battery exporters need credible carbon footprint information. This study takes the Jingmen base of EVE Energy as a ca
content: Against the backdrop of increasing regulatory attention to lifecycle emissions and product-level traceability, lithium-ion battery exporters need credible carbon footprint information. This study takes the Jingmen base of EVE Energy as a case to analyze how the temporal and spatial resolution of electricity carbon factors affects the visibility of green electricity benefits. The study comprehensively reviews the rooftop photovoltaic and energy storage investments, Hubei grid factors, and third-party verification records reported in the case. The case report shows that the rooftop photovoltaic installed capacity is 92.30 MW, with electricity generation of 104,602.54 MWh, and an estimated emission reduction of 59,654 t CO₂e; after recalculation using refined factors, the carbon emission intensity associated with electricity consumption for energy storage cell production changes from 5.5214 to 3.4477 kg CO₂e/kWh, and the accounting granularity is reported to have improved by 25%. The analysis distinguishes the visibility of carbon accounting from independently verified actual emission reductions, and summarizes the roles of hourly matching, localized grid factors, third-party verification, and digital product records. These measures help improve the auditability of electricity-related performance and enhance export compliance readiness, providing a reference for carbon management optimization for lithium battery exporters.

title: Nature as Rights Holder
summary: The Constitution of Ecuador has made a groundbreaking recognition by acknowledging Nature as a rights holder, challenging existing legal and political perspectives. The document explores the evolution of human perspectives on nature, rangin
content: The Constitution of Ecuador has made a groundbreaking recognition by acknowledging Nature as a rights holder, challenging existing legal and political perspectives. The document explores the evolution of human perspectives on nature, ranging from providential and romantic views to utilitarian and ecological perspectives. The ecological perspective, considering nature as a living being with interconnected systems, is emphasized as a solution to address the environmental crisis and climate collapse caused by the utilitarian view. The essay discusses Ecuador’s legal development regarding Nature as a subject with rights, with the Constitutional Court gradually recognizing nature’s rights and addressing violations. The Constitutional Court of Ecuador has declared specific ecosystems and entities, such as forests, rivers and animals, as rights holders, emphasizing the importance of its recognition, historical context, and systemic perspectives. The essay concludes with a reflection on whether nature, as a subject of rights, can have intellectual property rights. Three positions are discussed: the negationist position (exclusive human ownership), the integrationist position (adapting property rights for nature), and the ecological position (incompatibility of nature’s rights with property rights). The essay advocates for recognizing nature as part of the “commons” rather than within the property regime, emphasizing the need to appreciate, value, and legally protect Nature. From this perspective, one of the most radical ways to mitigate climate change is to prohibit all extractive activities that have the effect of increasing carbon emissions –as has happened in the case of the popular consultation in Ecuador to prohibit oil exploitation in the Ecuadorian Amazon (Yasní ITT). This prohibition is consubstantial with the declaration of subjects of rights.

title: BioExergoEconomics: A Unified Thermodynamic–Environmental Framework Integrating Exergy Analysis, Circular Economy, Life Cycle Assessment and Biological Resource Recovery
summary: The integration of thermodynamic efficiency, environmental mitigation, and circular resource recovery remains a fundamental challenge in the sustainability assessment of agro-industrial systems. Conventional methodologies—such as Exergoecon
content: The integration of thermodynamic efficiency, environmental mitigation, and circular resource recovery remains a fundamental challenge in the sustainability assessment of agro-industrial systems. Conventional methodologies—such as Exergoeconomics, Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), and Circular Economy (CE) indicators—typically operate in methodological isolation, limiting their ability to quantify trade-offs between energy-intensive biological recovery and environmental mitigation. To address this gap, this study proposes BioExergoEconomics, a novel unified framework that structurally integrates physical exergy analysis, Exergoeconomic cost allocation, carbon and water footprints, and biological resource recovery into a single F-P-R-I-B functional model. The principal contribution is the formulation of the BioExergoEconomics Index (BEC Index), a dimensionless metric that uniquely synthesizes exergy efficiency, circular resource recovery, biological recovery, carbon mitigation, water conservation, and economic performance. The framework is validated through a comparative case study of beef production (1 kg functional unit). Although biological processing increases electricity demand by 47.8%, this localized energy investment reduces upstream agricultural burdens, resulting in a 17.6% net reduction in energy and exergy demand, a 99.4% reduction in freshwater footprint, and a 51.1% decrease in carbon emissions. With a BEC Index of 0.55, the framework demonstrates that electrical exergy investments in biological nodes can drive systemic sustainability.

title: Renewable_Energy_Decarbonization_Study_Dataset
summary: This dataset accompanies the study “A Quarter-Century of Carbon-Emissions Reduction Research in the United States.” It comprises bibliographic data from 3,457 publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus between 200
content: This dataset accompanies the study “A Quarter-Century of Carbon-Emissions Reduction Research in the United States.” It comprises bibliographic data from 3,457 publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus between 2000 and 2025.The data support bibliometric analyses using VOSviewer, Biblioshiny, and CiteSpace, examining publication trends, institutional contributions, thematic clusters, keyword co-occurrence, and emerging research directions in US carbon-emissions reduction research.The dataset is shared to promote research transparency, reproducibility, and further investigations into the evolution and future priorities of carbon-emissions reduction research.

title: Linking green entrepreneurship to green innovation: the mediating role of green entrepreneurial self-efficacy
source: African Journal of Economic and Management Studies
summary: Purpose In line with the United Nations 2030 Agenda, environmental sustainability has become a prominent concept in academic discourse. Due to its vast natural resources, Africa is well-positioned to become a global leader in green business
content: Purpose In line with the United Nations 2030 Agenda, environmental sustainability has become a prominent concept in academic discourse. Due to its vast natural resources, Africa is well-positioned to become a global leader in green business. However, with a growing small and medium-sized enterprise (SME)population in Africa, empirical evidence on SME sustainability efforts remains limited. For this reason, this research examined the mediation effect of green entrepreneurial self-efficacy on the relationship between green entrepreneurship and green innovation in Zimbabwean manufacturing SMEs. Design/methodology/approach The data were analysed using SmartPLS 4 from a randomly selected sample of 370 managers. Findings The results showed that while green entrepreneurship strongly influenced green innovation, green entrepreneurial self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between the two variables. Originality/value The study contributes context-specific evidence from an African economy, addressing the limited representation of developing markets in green innovation research. In environments characterised by institutional constraints and resource scarcity, identifying self-efficacy as an enabling mechanism provides novel insight into how firms can stimulate green innovation despite structural limitations. The findings, therefore, enrich both theory and practice by integrating strategic and psychological perspectives within the African economic context.

title: Rebreathing assisted dual fuel combustion (Re-DFC) to enhance low carbon fuel utilization
summary: Several transportation and industrial sectors, including marine propulsion, heavy-duty transportation, and stationary power generation, face challenges in decarbonization due to their high energy demand and reliance on liquid fuels. Dual-fu
content: Several transportation and industrial sectors, including marine propulsion, heavy-duty transportation, and stationary power generation, face challenges in decarbonization due to their high energy demand and reliance on liquid fuels. Dual-fuel combustion facilitates the transition to low-carbon fuels by utilizing a low-reactivity fuel, such as methanol, introduced through port fuel injection, while a small quantity of high-reactivity fuel, such as diesel, is directly injected to initiate ignition. This approach enables improved control over combustion phasing, high thermal efficiency, and partial replacement of conventional diesel fuel. However, a major limitation of dual-fuel operation occurs at low loads, where reduced in-cylinder temperatures lead to poor combustion efficiency and incomplete oxidation of the premixed charge. As a result, unburned fuel emissions increase, and a larger fraction of diesel fuel is required to maintain stable combustion, limiting the utilization of the low-carbon fuel. This study investigates a rebreathing-assisted dual-fuel combustion strategy to enhance methanol utilization compared to conventional dual-fuel combustion. Experiments were performed on a 6.7 L Cummins ISB heavy-duty engine configured for single-cylinder methanol–diesel dual-fuel combustion. The engine was operated at a low-load condition of 4 bar IMEP, representative of typical low-load operation. The rebreathing strategy recirculates a portion of the exhaust gases back into the cylinder using a modified cam. Results show that rebreathing assistance significantly improves combustion efficiency and reduces unburned emissions while maintaining NO x emissions in dual-fuel combustion. The strategy also improves gross indicated thermal efficiency, and after accounting for additional pumping losses, the net efficiency remains comparable to conventional diesel operation at moderate rebreathing levels. Most notably, methanol utilization increases substantially, with the methanol mass fraction reaching 84%. This increased substitution of diesel fuel with methanol results in an estimated 10%–15% reduction in CO 2 emissions. These results demonstrate the potential of rebreathing assistance to improve low-load dual-fuel combustion and increase the utilization of low-carbon fuels.

title: THE HIDDEN ENVIRONMENTAL COST OF DAM CONSTRUCTION
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Dams are among the most significant infrastructure developments undertaken by modern societies. They provide drinking water, irrigation, hydroelectricity, flood regulation, industrial water supply and opportunities for regional economic dev
content: Dams are among the most significant infrastructure developments undertaken by modern societies. They provide drinking water, irrigation, hydroelectricity, flood regulation, industrial water supply and opportunities for regional economic development. However, their construction and operation can also generate substantial environmental, geological, ecological, economic and social consequences that are not always adequately represented in conventional project evaluations. The environmental footprint of a dam begins long before its reservoir is filled. Mountain excavation, quarrying, deforestation, construction of access roads, extraction of sand and aggregates, cement and steel production, and transportation of construction materials can significantly disturb surrounding landscapes. Following construction, reservoir submergence, altered river flows, sediment retention, barriers to fish migration, biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions and community displacement may create additional long-term consequences. This article examines the environmental and social implications of dam development throughout its lifecycle, from resource extraction and construction to reservoir operation, maintenance and eventual decommissioning. It evaluates the interconnected effects of geological disturbance, forest destruction, habitat fragmentation, river ecosystem disruption, material consumption, carbon emissions, hydrological changes and human displacement. The article also proposes an integrated environmental accountability framework incorporating lifecycle assessment, ecological monitoring, social-impact evaluation, economic analysis and transparent public disclosure. Particular attention is given to the importance of comparing large dam projects with alternative approaches to water conservation, energy generation and flood management. The central argument is that infrastructure development should not be evaluated exclusively through electricity generation, water storage, construction expenditure or financial returns. It must also demonstrate ecological responsibility, social justice, engineering safety, economic viability and long-term environmental sustainability.

title: Developing and Evaluating a Real-World Calculus Pedagogy for Sustainable Business Management Students
summary: This study developed and evaluated a real-world calculus pedagogy for Sustainable Business Management students. The purpose was to determine whether contextualized calculus instruction, built around sustainable business problems such as mar
content: This study developed and evaluated a real-world calculus pedagogy for Sustainable Business Management students. The purpose was to determine whether contextualized calculus instruction, built around sustainable business problems such as marginal cost, revenue optimization, carbon-cost trade-offs, inventory control and break-even analysis, improves students' conceptual understanding, engagement and perceived ability to apply calculus in sustainability-oriented managerial decisions. A quasi-experimental mixed-methods design was adopted. The population comprised 320 undergraduate Business Management students enrolled in a business mathematics course at a higher learning institution. From this population, 180 students were selected through stratified random sampling and assigned to a control group (n = 90) and an experimental group (n = 90). Quantitative data were collected through a calculus achievement test, a learning engagement scale, a perceived business applicability scale and a sustainability decision-making confidence scale. Qualitative data were collected through short reflective responses from 24 purposively selected students in the experimental group. The intervention lasted eight teaching weeks. The results showed that the experimental group improved from a pre-test mean of 49.76 to a post-test mean of 70.21, while the control group improved from 47.46 to 55.96. The difference in learning gain was statistically significant, with a large effect size. The experimental group also reported higher engagement, perceived applicability and sustainability decision-making confidence. The study concludes that a real-world calculus pedagogy can make calculus more meaningful for business students by connecting abstract mathematical ideas to practical sustainability decisions. It recommends that business mathematics courses should be redesigned around authentic managerial cases, technology-supported modelling and reflective decision-making tasks.

title: Humic acid urea improved grain yield and farmer’s profits while mitigating the carbon footprint of wheat production
summary: Enhancing crop yield and reducing active nitrogen (N) loss are crucial for the efficient utilization of N fertilizer and the decrease of agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Humic acid urea (HAU), an efficient N fertilizer produced
content: Enhancing crop yield and reducing active nitrogen (N) loss are crucial for the efficient utilization of N fertilizer and the decrease of agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Humic acid urea (HAU), an efficient N fertilizer produced via in-situ incorporating small amounts of humic acid into urea production, has reached to 1 Tg of physical quantity of annual production in China for its efficiency enhanced via the comprehensive regulation on fertilizer-crop-soil systems. Therefore, we hypothesized that HAU would increase yield and reduce the carbon footprint relative to CU, and tested it in a winter wheat experiment at two N rates (225 and 180 kg ha⁻ 1 ) in the North China Plain. The results showed that the application of HAU resulted in a significantly higher grain yield by 7.0–23.3% than CU, and thus significantly increased farmer’s profits by 8.8–29.8%. HAU production resulted in more GHG emission than CU production by 6.9 kg CO 2 -eq Mg −1 ; however, the GHG emission from the field was significantly reduced (10.1–23.3%) by reducing gaseous N loss. In the whole life cycle, HAU resulted in lower GHG emissions (1.9–14.4%) in the winter wheat agroecosystem. HAU application also contributed to higher C fixation and ecosystem economic benefit. HAU at 180 kg ha −1 achieved a comparable yield and farmer’s profit with CU at 225 kg N ha −1 , while reduced GHG emission by 14.4%. Applicating HAU is an advantageous N management strategy for maintaining wheat yield with the lowest C footprint.

title: Data for: Battery charging or battery swapping? Business model choices for electric heavy-duty truck fleets under cost and carbon constraints
summary: This dataset supports the article entitled “Battery charging or battery swapping? Business model choices for electric heavy-duty truck fleets under cost and carbon constraints”. It contains the input parameters and calculated results used t
content: This dataset supports the article entitled “Battery charging or battery swapping? Business model choices for electric heavy-duty truck fleets under cost and carbon constraints”. It contains the input parameters and calculated results used to compare battery-electric heavy-duty trucks, three battery-swapping business models, and liquefied natural gas heavy-duty trucks. The data cover vehicle and battery specifications, freight-service operating conditions, annual mileages ranging from 32,000 to 160,000 km, electricity tariffs, battery-swapping charges, maintenance costs, carbon-emission parameters, electricity-grid composition, and policy incentives. Four freight-service scenarios are considered: urban delivery, port logistics, collection and distribution, and regional line-haul. The dataset also includes five battery-capacity configurations, technology-improvement pathways involving battery-cell prices, energy consumption, battery energy density and vehicle lightweighting, and three policy settings. Dynamic total cost of ownership and well-to-wheel carbon-emission-cost results are provided for the corresponding scenarios. Monetary values are reported in RMB, distances in kilometres, and battery capacities and electricity consumption in kWh. Input data were compiled from vehicle manufacturers, publicly available policy documents, energy-price sources, and published literature, as documented in the article.

title: Evidence-graded regulatory mechanisms of methanogenesis in model archaea
summary: Methanogenesis is an archaeal energy metabolism that often operates near the thermodynamic limits of ATP conservation. Its rate therefore depends not only on pathway chemistry but also on regulatory processes that allocate enzymes, electron
content: Methanogenesis is an archaeal energy metabolism that often operates near the thermodynamic limits of ATP conservation. Its rate therefore depends not only on pathway chemistry but also on regulatory processes that allocate enzymes, electron carriers, and substrates as environmental conditions change. Here, we evaluate experimentally supported transcriptional, signal-transduction and post-transcriptional mechanisms in methanogenic archaea, classifying evidence as direct biochemical or promoter interaction, genetic dependence, expression association or hypothesis. Molecularly resolved links include AmzR ligand-dependent promoter binding, HdrR activation of hdrBCA , MreA binding to selected promoters, NrpR control of nitrogen genes, and cysteine-dependent MsvR promoter binding. In contrast, H 2 -responsive transcription and the proposed MsmS/RdmS phosphorelays remain incompletely connected to their proximal signals or downstream targets. RNA stability, RNA processing and regulatory small RNAs provide an additional layer of control, and single-cell imaging reveals temporally ordered yet heterogeneous expression states. However, most mechanistic evidence derives from a small number of Methanosarcina and Methanococcus models. These studies provide a framework for testing how regulation shapes cellular methane-production rates, but its quantitative contribution to community methane production and net atmospheric emissions remains unresolved.

title: Editorial: Generative AI and consumer search for green products
summary: Generative AI and consumer search for green productsGreen products, also known as eco-friendly products, environmentally friendly products or sustainable products, are "goods or services that minimize their impact on the environment at each
content: Generative AI and consumer search for green productsGreen products, also known as eco-friendly products, environmentally friendly products or sustainable products, are "goods or services that minimize their impact on the environment at each phase of their life cycle" (Albino et al., 2009, p. 84).Thus, encouraging the purchase and consumption of green products is essential for future sustainability (Pathak et al., 2024).However, consumers often struggle to identify green products and assess their multidimensional, complex environmental performance.For instance, a product may have lower carbon dioxide emissions but higher water use or recyclable packaging but poor durability.Various terms and claims have been used for green products, such as "eco-friendly", "sustainable", "natural", "carbon neutral", "biodegradable" and "responsibly sourced".They are often vague or inconsistently defined.Eco-labels can help to some extent; however, their proliferation and variation may also create confusion (Moon et al., 2017).Despite valuing sustainability information, consumers may find labels difficult to understand and use (Grunert et al., 2014).Consequently, consumers may find that the cost of searching outweighs the perceived benefits of choosing eco-friendly products, discouraging them from purchasing such options.Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can help solve the information problem and reduce the costs and complexity of searching for green products.Conventional search engines require consumers to gather evidence from ranked web pages, weigh trade-offs and assess credibility before acting.GenAI simplifies this by providing fluent, synthesized recommendations that condense what was once an effortful comparison into a single conversational exchange (Grewal et al., 2024).Comparative evidence shows that consumers evaluate products differently and often decide more readily when consulting a GenAI chatbot than when using a search engine, because synthesized answers shape consideration sets and perceived effort in ways that a page of links does not (Kim and Priluck, 2025).GenAI allows consumers to ask questions in everyday language, request comparisons and seek explanations of technical information (Mariani et al., 2023).This is particularly helpful in the context of green purchasing, where consumers are often confused about technical concepts (e.g. the distinction between recyclable and compostable packaging).Shoppers might ask an AI system to compare green products based on specified criteria, rather than searching separately for sustainability information on certifications, packaging, energy use and repairability.GenAI can also help consumers scrutinize environmental claims and distinguish between verified data, corporate statements and third-party assessments.There is, however, growing concern that GenAI can amplify greenwashing, which occurs when businesses make environmental claims that are false or misleading (ACCC, 2023).Greenwashing forms inclu

title: Behaviour of concrete made with waste porcelain and silica fume
summary: The demand for natural aggregates has increased with the fast-expanding construction activities and urban development. Meanwhile, significant amounts of waste porcelain, which are the result of construction, demolition, and production, are
content: The demand for natural aggregates has increased with the fast-expanding construction activities and urban development. Meanwhile, significant amounts of waste porcelain, which are the result of construction, demolition, and production, are readily dumped in landfills even though they can be reused. The utilisation of waste aggregates in concrete, however, may be challenging because their physical and mechanical properties differ from those of natural aggregates. Producing concrete with potential environmental benefits by utilising waste materials, while, maintaining its desirable characteristics is an essential issue. This research mainly examined the combined effect of substituting the coarse natural aggregate (NA) with discarded tiles waste porcelain (WP) at multiple ratios, including 30%, 50% and 100%, along with cement partial replacement with silica fume (SF) at 0%, 10% and 20%. Ten concrete mixes, the first of which is control, were tested in terms of fresh-concrete consistency and hardened characteristics, including mechanical strengths, impact energy and abrasion resistance. For every mix, the same experimental programme was employed. The concrete mixes were designed to achieve a target mean 28-day compressive strength of 40 MPa. The absolute-volume method was utilised in the calculation of mixture proportions while maintaining a constant total mix volume, in addition to keeping a water-binder (w/b) ratio at 0.45, but the batch water was adjusted based on the moisture states and absorption of each aggregate fraction, and no superplasticiser was added. The results generally showed that the incorporation of WP individually as well as in combination with SF adversely affects concrete slump values, especially with high dosage replacements. The same adverse effect was noticed on concrete strengths when only WP substituted NA at all levels; the decline in strengths was statistically significant, especially at the 100% replacement level. The 10% SF inclusion slightly enhanced concrete strengths; further increasing of SF dosage to 20% resulted in extra strength gain and surpassing the control in M8 with (3.76%) in compressive strength and (1.08%) in splitting tensile; however, the difference was not statistically significant ( p > 0.05). A statistically significant improvement was observed ( p < 0.05) in the M8 results, with an increase of 8.28% in flexural strength, 18.91% in impact energy resistance, and 30.61% less weight loss in abrasion. Beyond this point, when WP replacement levels increased, keeping 20% SF, the results showed a declining trend. In conclusion, the combined effect using 30% WP and 20% SF revealed a promising approach for producing a waste-material-based concrete for application that requires relatively higher mechanical characteristics and favourable impact resistance and abrasion resistance. However, careful consideration must be given to the used materials’ properties and production quality control.

title: Genetic transformation and fluorescent protein expression in the biomaterial-producing fungus Fomes fomentarius
summary: Abstract Background Fungal-based materials are currently studied as renewable and sustainable alternatives to fossil-based materials used in construction, packaging, textile, and fashion industries. The polypore fungus Fomes fomentarius pro
content: Abstract Background Fungal-based materials are currently studied as renewable and sustainable alternatives to fossil-based materials used in construction, packaging, textile, and fashion industries. The polypore fungus Fomes fomentarius produces a range of lightweight, durable, and flexible materials from diverse plant residual streams. Genetic engineering of this fungus is an important technological objective, both from fundamental perspectives and to optimize performance characteristics of F. fomentarius materials. Results We provide proof of principle that F. fomentarius can be genetically transformed. Hyphae produced high amounts of protoplasts using standard protocols. These protoplasts were transformed using nourseothricin selection and a nourseothricin N-acetyl transferase resistance marker ( natR ). Expression of natR was successful using a F. fomentarius translation elongation factor promoter. Stable, multicopy, and non-targeted integration of exogenous cassettes with recipient genome was confirmed by diagnostic PCR and Southern blotting. Preliminary attempts at genome editing based disruption of a putative ku70 encoding gene were, however, unsuccessful. We validated expression of two fluorescent proteins using a Schizophyllum commune H2B promoter using qRT-PCR and fluorescent microscopy. These data confirm functionality of mCherry and eGFP in F. fomentarius and suggest these proteins can be used for future protein localisation studies. Finally, we report DNase activity in F. fomentarius which we hypothesize may be a significant technical challenge for genetic transformation of this fungus. Conclusion F. fomentarius can be genetically transformed using the promoters, marker, and nourseothricin selection system developed in this study. Expression of both eGFP and mCherry is a significant step towards cell biological and gene functional analyses using fluorescent microscopy. We have laid the foundations for overexpression studies, and, additionally, identified several challenges which need to be overcome for targeted genetic engineering in this important material producing fungus.

title: Cryptocurrency Mining in European Electricity Systems: A Critical Review of Carbon Accounting, Operational Flexibility and Environmental Trade-Offs
summary: Cryptocurrency-energy assessments often conflate electricity use, emissions attribution and avoided system emissions. This targeted, non-exhaustive integrative review separates these quantities and evaluates mining-flexibility claims in Eur
content: Cryptocurrency-energy assessments often conflate electricity use, emissions attribution and avoided system emissions. This targeted, non-exhaustive integrative review separates these quantities and evaluates mining-flexibility claims in European electricity systems. A six-criterion appraisal links principal studies to supported claims and transfer limits. A general electricity-accounting benchmark uses secondary data to compare 2024 production-mix and residual-mix direct CO2 factors for 24 national European Union domains. Their unweighted means are 214.38 and 415.18 g CO2/kWh; the median within-country ratio is 1.95. The two orderings have a Spearman correlation of 0.670 and disagree for 68 of 276 country pairs. The residual factor exceeds the production factor in all 24 countries in both 2024 and a matched 2025 comparison; consumption-weighted contrasts also remain positive. For a fixed hypothetical 1 MW Hungarian load operating throughout leap year 2024, the two accounting descriptors yield 1556.5 and 2798.9 tonnes of attributed direct CO2, a 79.82% accounting difference. These descriptive, non-causal results compare accounting descriptors, which are not freely interchangeable facility reporting options. Conditional procurement scenarios and an explicitly assumed four-hour example distinguish reported emissions, electricity volume and operating schedules. Technical evidence supports curtailment and ancillary-service participation in specified settings, but price responsiveness alone does not establish lower emissions. The applied framework links European disclosure to claim-specific counterfactuals and specifies requirements for joint assessment of heat, methane, water, hardware and health impacts.

title: Editorial: Sustainable innovations in agriculture: economic analysis of climate smart practices
summary: As the primary source of global food, fiber, and energy, agriculture plays an imperative role in human development. However, the sector is under pressure to expand production while simultaneously minimizing climate change impacts and enhanc
content: As the primary source of global food, fiber, and energy, agriculture plays an imperative role in human development. However, the sector is under pressure to expand production while simultaneously minimizing climate change impacts and enhancing adaptive capacity. These pressures demand a fundamental shift toward more sustainable and resilient production systems. Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) has emerged as a robust framework to address these challenges, synchronizing three critical goals: increasing productivity, enhancing resilience to climate shocks, and lowering emissions.However, sustainability must also be financially viable. For farmers, the decision to adopt a CSA practice is ultimately an investment decision. For society, the relevant calculus is broader, because many of the benefits of CSA, such as avoided emissions, improved soil health and biodiversity, accrue as positive externalities that markets do not reward. The gap between private and social returns, together with the costs of information, finance and learning, largely determines whether profitable practices are actually adopted. This Research Topic highlights how CSA innovations can generate measurable economic returns while advancing environmental sustainability and resilience under climate change. Based on this economic evidence, we aim to inform policymakers and investors with evidence-based research materials necessary to scale resilient solutions for a changing world.The distinctive contribution of this Research Topic lies in its explicit economic orientation. The ten articles collected here place economic evaluation at the center, using a notably diverse analytical toolkit: farm-level cost-benefit analysis, benefit-cost ratios from large-scale field demonstrations, net present value and sensitivity analysis, energy-and carbon-adjusted cost assessment, social cost-benefit analysis with externality valuation, real option analysis, treatment-effect and endogenous switching models of welfare impacts, panel econometrics, and a systematic review. The evidence spans South Asia, Sub-Saharan, West and Central Africa, China and Canada, and production systems ranging from cereals and dairy to aromatic plants and insect-based feed. Alltogether, the articles allow us to ask not only whether CSA pays, but for whom, under which institutional conditions, over what time horizon and under what degree of uncertainty.The overarching theme of these articles is the promotion of sustainable and climate-smart agricultural systems that align economic performance with environmental stewardship. Their key goals include: demonstrating the profitability and cost-effectiveness of CSA innovations using metrics such as net returns, benefit-cost ratios and net present values; quantifying the gap between private and social returns once environmental and social externalities are valued; assessing the welfare effects of CSA on rural livelihoods, employment and food security; identifying the adoption costs,

title: Do macroeconomic policies drive environmental sustainability? Empirical insights from India
summary: Although fiscal and monetary instruments are calibrated for economic stabilisation rather than for environmental ends, they act directly upon the volume and composition of the activity that generates environmental pressure, and the literatu
content: Although fiscal and monetary instruments are calibrated for economic stabilisation rather than for environmental ends, they act directly upon the volume and composition of the activity that generates environmental pressure, and the literature has largely assessed their consequences on the implicit assumption that expansions and contractions are reflection of one another. Relaxing that assumption for India over 1971–2021, this study analyse the association through the nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag model in which government expenditure, broad money, foreign direct investment inflows and energy efficiency are decomposed into cumulative increases and decreases, and traces the resulting multipliers across per-capita carbon dioxide emissions, greenhouse gas emissions and the ecological footprint. Fiscal expansion raises environmental pressure, with long-run elasticities of 0.865, 0.585 and 0.450, yet an equivalent contraction lowers it far more sharply, by 2.53 for carbon dioxide and 2.15 for the footprint. Monetary expansion is associated with improvement across indicators, whereas the effect of contraction differs in sign according to the pollutant considered. Deterioration in energy efficiency proves more damaging than an equivalent improvement is beneficial, as the rebound effect implies, while foreign direct investment inflows, though favourable, is economically slight. The findings suggest that monetary policy should account for pollutant-specific and asymmetric environmental effects, while environmental policy should prioritise energy efficiency rather than relying primarily on FDI inflows.

title: Pt Promotion of Zr Catalysts for Furfural-to-γ-Valerolactone Conversion [Dataset]
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The valorization of biomass and its transformation into fuels are highly interesting due to the abundance of biomass and its almost neutral carbon emissions. In this article, we show the production of γ-valerolactone (GVL), a valuable produ
content: The valorization of biomass and its transformation into fuels are highly interesting due to the abundance of biomass and its almost neutral carbon emissions. In this article, we show the production of γ-valerolactone (GVL), a valuable product, from furfural (FF), a compound that can be easily obtained from biomass. This FF to GVL transformation involves a catalytic cascade reaction with two hydrogenation steps. Pt and/or Zr supported on sepiolite catalysts have been prepared and tested in the FF transformation reaction. A physical mixture of a Zr-based and a Pt-based catalyst has reached a yield to GVL of ca. 50% after 16 h at 180 °C. This performance largely exceeds that obtained by each of the single Pt or single Zr metal catalysts independently, showing a strong synergistic effect. These data suggest that each metal (Pt and Zr) plays an important and complementary role in different reaction steps. Furthermore, the physical mixture appears to be much more efficient than bimetallic Pt/Zr catalysts synthesized with the same amount of metals. The role of the type of acidity and the oxidation state of the surface platinum species on the catalytic performance has been discussed. Moreover, this reaction has been carried out in batch and continuous flow reactors, and a comparative study between the two operation modes has been undertaken. A certain correlation between the catalytic results obtained by both operation modes has been found. Description of methods used for collection/generation of data: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of catalysts were collected between 10 and 80 ° at 2θ using an Enraf Nonius FR590 sealed tube diffractometer (Bruker, Delft, The Netherlands) equipped with a monochromatic Cu Kα1 source (40 kV and 30 mA). In order to investigate the Lewis and Brønsted acidity, the adsorption–desorption of pyridine (Py) coupled with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was recorded in a Tensor 27 instrument (Bruker) with a Michelson interferometer. A He–Ne laser was used as an internal reference, and a DTGS infrared detector was also used. 64 accumulations were taken in transmission mode with a spectral resolution of 4 cm–1. The surface of the materials was cleaned by heating at 200 °C for 1 h and under a pressure of 0.1 mbar. Later, the samples were exposed to a pyridine atmosphere (200 mbar of pyridine vapor pressure) for 15 min at 50 °C. Physisorbed pyridine was eliminated by exposing the sample to a vacuum for 15 min after adsorption. The desorption was carried out at 100 and 200 °C, for 15 min each, under a vacuum. The transformation of FF into GVL in one pot was carried out in an autoclave reactor. The reactor has an internal part covered by a Teflon container of 25 mL, which fits with the steel walls. In a typical run, 0.25 mmol of FF was dissolved and mixed with 5 mL of 2-propanol. Later, 0.1 g of the catalyst was added. title: Capitalization effects of digital infrastructure in Chinese cities: agglomeration, accumulation and technovation
summary: Abstract The construction of digital infrastructure requires substantial capital investment from both the government and private sector. A key question arises: to what extent do these investments contribute to economic growth and welfare? T
content: Abstract The construction of digital infrastructure requires substantial capital investment from both the government and private sector. A key question arises: to what extent do these investments contribute to economic growth and welfare? This paper investigates this issue through the lens of the capitalization effect. Specifically, we leverage China’s “Broadband China Pilot Policy” as a quasi-natural experiment in digital infrastructure development and employ panel data from 298 cities between 2010 and 2021. Using a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) approach with two-way fixed effects (TWFE), we empirically establish the presence of a significant capitalization effect. Furthermore, we examine several potential mechanisms associated with the capitalization effect, focusing on population agglomeration, capital accumulation, and technological innovation. The results provide suggestive evidence that these factors are potential channels through which digital infrastructure may affect urban housing markets. To quantify welfare implications, we construct a partial equilibrium framework and integrate an LSTM-based deep learning model for predictive analysis. Furthermore, our partial-equilibrium analysis provides a model-implied monetary assessment of the potential welfare implications of digital infrastructure investment, while acknowledging the limitations of interpreting housing-price capitalization as direct welfare gains. This study provides valuable insights for digital infrastructure investment decisions in developing countries.

title: Amal Bio-Energy: Hydrogen production throughout methane pyrolysis from purified biogas of agricultural wastes, for distributed generation
summary: Abstract Current hydrogen production relies heavily on the carbon-intensive steam-methane reforming (SMR) process, while agriculture remains a leading source of potent methane emissions. Addressing this dual challenge, this project introduc
content: Abstract Current hydrogen production relies heavily on the carbon-intensive steam-methane reforming (SMR) process, while agriculture remains a leading source of potent methane emissions. Addressing this dual challenge, this project introduces a novel prototype for a decentralized, carbon-neutral hydrogen generation system. The process begins with a biodigester that uses agricultural waste to produce biogas, which is then purified to yield biomethane. This biomethane, a renewable source of methane, is subsequently fed into a methane pyrolysis reactor. This method heats the biomethane without combustion, separating it into ultra-clean hydrogen and solid carbon. The entire process, from pyrolysis to hydrogen compression and storage, is designed to be powered by renewable energy, ensuring a zero-emission energy pathway. By integrating agricultural waste valorization with advanced hydrogen production, this prototype offers a powerful solution to multiple systemic issues. It not only mitigates significant methane emissions from farming but also bypasses the need for fossil fuels in hydrogen generation. This in-situ production model facilitates a distributed energy generation framework, democratizing the energy transition and enabling self-sufficiency in agricultural communities. Ultimately, this project presents a scalable and sustainable approach to producing clean hydrogen, fostering a decarbonized future while turning climate liability into a valuable energy and industrial resource.

title: Hydrogen-enriched combustion of CO₂-diluted landfill gas: a Damköhler-number stability framework for power plant life extension
source: Journal of the Brazilian Society of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering
summary: Abstract The CH₄ content of the LFG declines progressively while CO₂ increases, degrading combustion stability until engines can no longer sustain reliable operation below a CH₄ threshold of approximately 40 volume percent (vol.%). This pap
content: Abstract The CH₄ content of the LFG declines progressively while CO₂ increases, degrading combustion stability until engines can no longer sustain reliable operation below a CH₄ threshold of approximately 40 volume percent (vol.%). This paper investigates the combustion physics behind this degradation and evaluates hydrogen enrichment as a mitigation strategy that projects to extend plant operational life by more than a decade beyond the conventional shut-off point, under the assumptions and the empirically calibrated stability mapping. A custom numerical solver was developed in MATLAB and was validated against the canonical coflow diffusion flame benchmark experiments. Parametric simulations systematically varied the CO₂ fraction from 0 to 60 vol.% and the hydrogen (H₂) enrichment level from 0 to 40 vol.%, yielding quantitative maps of adiabatic flame temperature, equivalent flame speed, ignition delay, and radical pool concentrations. Increasing CO₂ from 0 to 60 vol.% reduces Da (Damköhler number) by 83%, doubles ignition delay to 3.16 ms, and depresses the OH radical pool by 49%; 30 vol.% H₂ enrichment fully restores stable operation (Da ≥ 5 in the laminar flame model), projecting, under the stated assumptions and pending engine-level validation, a 14-year plant-life extension and doubling CO₂-equivalent avoidance to 60,700 tonnes. A complementary techno-economic analysis, based on a 30-year discounted cash flow (DCF) model applied to a 1.5-million-tonne reference Brazilian landfill, indicates that the physically-derived H₂ enrichment schedule is projected to double total electricity generation (from 48,200 to 92,100 MWh).
