title: Indeks Pencemaran dan Kondisi Ekologis di Tiga Sungai di Kota Yogyakarta
summary: Dinamika ekologis sungai perkotaan, seperti yang melintasi Kota Yogyakarta, rentan terhadap tekanan antropogenik, namun pemahaman komprehensif mengenai interaksi antara kondisi abiotik, tingkat pencemaran, dan respons keanekaragaman hayati
content: Dinamika ekologis sungai perkotaan, seperti yang melintasi Kota Yogyakarta, rentan terhadap tekanan antropogenik, namun pemahaman komprehensif mengenai interaksi antara kondisi abiotik, tingkat pencemaran, dan respons keanekaragaman hayati pada tiga sungai utamanya (Winongo, Code, dan Gajah Wong) masih terbatas. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis dinamika parameter abiotik dan status Indeks Pencemaran (IP) pada Sungai Winongo, Sungai Code, dan Sungai Gajah Wong serta mengkaji keterkaitan keduanya terhadap sebaran keanekaragaman hayati pada ketiga sungai tersebut. Pengambilan data lapangan menggunakan purposive sampling pada hulu (sebelum area perkotaan), tengah (area permukiman padat), dan hilir (setelah area perkotaan) di masing-masing sungai. Analisis kondisi abiotik mencakup pH, BOD dan DO, yang kemudian digunakan dalam perhitungan Indeks Pencemaran (IP). Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa ketiga sungai tergolong tercemar ringan, dengan nilai IP tertinggi (2,76) ditemukan di hulu Sungai Winongo pada pagi hari dan terendah (1,22) di hilir Sungai Gajah Wong pada waktu yang sama. Perbedaan nilai IP ini secara signifikan memengaruhi sebaran keanekaragaman hayati, yang ditandai dengan dominasi Spirulina sp. dan Tubifex sp. sebagai bioindikator polusi di area dengan tingkat pencemaran yang lebih tinggi. Studi ini menegaskan pentingnya pemantauan berkelanjutan terhadap kualitas air sungai perkotaan serta implikasinya terhadap komunitas biologis.

title: Highly Variable Organic Carbon Burial in Thermokarst Lake Sediments on the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau
summary: Abstract Thermokarst lakes are dynamic carbon sinks and sources in permafrost landscapes, but their organic carbon (OC) burial remains poorly constrained. We analyzed 210 Pb‐dated sediment cores from 12 thermokarst lakes on the Qinghai–Tibe
content: Abstract Thermokarst lakes are dynamic carbon sinks and sources in permafrost landscapes, but their organic carbon (OC) burial remains poorly constrained. We analyzed 210 Pb‐dated sediment cores from 12 thermokarst lakes on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau to quantify sedimentary OC, total nitrogen (TN), C:N stoichiometry, and recent sediment mass accumulation rates (MAR) and OC burial rates (OCBR). Chronology‐dependent comparisons were restricted to sediment intervals with CRS‐derived calendar years of 1900 or later. Across all sediment layers, OC concentrations (1.12–250 g/kg), TN (0.094–26.1 g/kg), and C:N ratios (1.5–188) exhibited pronounced within‐ and among‐lake variability but with no consistent vertical trends shared across lakes. In post‐1900 sediments, MAR (113–21,964 g/m 2 /yr) and OCBR (6.1–1,167 gC/m 2 /yr) also showed substantial within‐core and among‐lake variability. Lake‐level median MAR and OCBR varied from 496 to 5,831 g/m 2 /yr and from 17.8 to 191 gC/m 2 /yr, respectively. MAR and OCBR were positively related in most lakes, but the slopes differed markedly, suggesting that similar increases in sediment accumulation translated into different increments of OC burial among lakes. Across lakes, median MAR decreased with mean annual precipitation (MAP), whereas median OCBR increased with MAP; no significant relationships were detected with mean annual temperature, elevation, lake area, or lake depth. These results show that recent OC burial cannot be inferred from sediment accumulation alone, but reflects differences in both sediment supply and the OC content of deposited material, with postdepositional preservation representing an additional potential influence.

title: PpPKp1 Coordinates Growth and Cold Tolerance by Integrating Energy‐Cytokinin Signalling via Pyruvate Metabolism in Poa pratensis
summary: Plastidial pyruvate kinase (PKp; EC 2.7.1.40), as a core enzyme regulating plant carbon metabolism, has been confirmed to be a key component in plant stress response. However, the specific regulatory network in cold response and the molecul
content: Plastidial pyruvate kinase (PKp; EC 2.7.1.40), as a core enzyme regulating plant carbon metabolism, has been confirmed to be a key component in plant stress response. However, the specific regulatory network in cold response and the molecular mechanism mediating cold tolerance remain elusive. This study reveals that the expression of PpPKp1, a chloroplast-localized plastid pyruvate kinase gene from Poa pratensis var. anceps cv. Qinghai, is significantly induced by low temperature and drought stress. Overexpression of PpPKp1 in Arabidopsis thaliana and Poa pratensis enhanced pyruvate kinase activity and pyruvate content, thereby improving tillering capacity and biomass accumulation under cold conditions, while also promoting root elongation, shoot growth, and maintaining the relative stability of ROS. Conversely, RNAi-mediated suppression of PpPKp1 in P. pratensis elicited contrasting phenotypes and physiological responses. Mechanistic investigations demonstrated that under cold stress, PpPKp1 facilitates energy supply by enhancing glycolytic/TCA cycle flux and simultaneously coordinates arginine biosynthesis with cytokinin signalling transduction. This integrated mechanism of 'energy provision-metabolite synthesis-signal regulation' is closely associated with the maintenance of plant growth and development under cold conditions, balancing resource allocation between stress resistance and growth. Ultimately, it leads to significantly enhanced cold tolerance. Our work unveils for the first time the molecular mechanism by which PpPKp1 regulates plant cold responses through coupling central carbon metabolism and hormone signalling. It provides novel insights into the synergistic network of 'plastid metabolism-systemic stress resistance' in plants, and offers candidate genes and a theoretical basis for the genetic improvement of cold tolerance in crops.

title: Exploring the interface of soil organic matter with phosphorus cycling: A size density fractionation approach
summary: Soil organic matter (SOM) is a key determinant of soil fertility, as it regulates soil physical properties and nutrient cycling. Because SOM generally declines in agricultural soils, the application of organic matter-rich amendments is a co
content: Soil organic matter (SOM) is a key determinant of soil fertility, as it regulates soil physical properties and nutrient cycling. Because SOM generally declines in agricultural soils, the application of organic matter-rich amendments is a common mitigation strategy. However, the processes underlying SOM accrual after the application of these materials remain insufficiently understood and are likely to intersect with both abiotic and biotic processes involving P and other elements. Since SOM and soil P are often studied using separate methodological approaches, we applied a sodium polytungstate (SPT)-based size-density fractionation method adapted to combined SOM and P analyses. We hypothesized that this approach would isolate particulated and mineral-associated fractions relevant to SOM and P cycling, and that long-term application of organic amendments would produce detectable changes in the fractional distribution of C, P, and selected elements, potentially providing insight into the associations involved in SOM accrual. We fractionated Luvisols subjected to long-term fertilization with sewage sludge or household waste compost, as well as to unfertilized controls as follows: Coarse particles (2 mm-50 µm) were separated into fractions CL (< 1.8 g cm-3), CDA (> 1.8 g cm-3), and CDB (≫ 1.8 g cm-3), while fine particles (< 50 µm) were separated into fractions FL (< 2.4 g cm-3), FDA (> 2.4 g cm-3), and FDB (≫ 2.4 g cm-3). Fraction δ15N and total element concentrations were measured, fractional recoveries of C, N, P, Fe, and Ca were calculated relative to whole soils, and dominant organic matter species were characterized using pyrolysis-GC-MS. Compost-amended soils reached 3.5% C and sludge-amended soils 2.2% C, compared with 1.2% in unfertilized soils, despite the sludge treatment receiving only one quarter of the cumulative C inputs of compost over two decades. Recovery of C across fractions was influenced by amendment type. For example, in compost-amended soils, C recovery in the CDA fraction increased significantly. Recoveries of C and P were positively correlated across fractions (R2 = 0.58-0.83), and, in some fractions, were also associated with Ca or Fe recoveries, suggesting a role of P-, Ca- and Fe-mediated associations in SOM accumulation. Our results show that size-density fractionation can provide an exploratory approach for studying the physical fractions where C and P processes co-occur, providing a basis for further investigations.

title: Weathered microplastics reshape gastrointestinal responses to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances during co-exposure
summary: Microplastics (MPs) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants, yet the biological consequences of their co-exposure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the individual and combined e
content: Microplastics (MPs) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants, yet the biological consequences of their co-exposure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the individual and combined effects of weathered polyethylene MPs and three representative PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, and PFBA) using Caco-2 cells and a mouse oral-exposure model, complemented by tissue distribution analysis and multi-omics profiling. PFAS induced concentration-dependent cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cell-cycle disruption, with PFOA showing the greatest cytotoxic potency. Co-exposure with MPs attenuated PFAS-induced acute cytotoxicity, ROS accumulation, and membrane damage in vitro, while aggravating mitochondrial dysfunction and cell-cycle arrest, indicating an endpoint-dependent modulatory effect. In mice, MPs and PFAS were concurrently detected in multiple tissues, and co-exposure altered PFAS tissue burdens and produced organ-specific toxicological responses, including enhanced intestinal oxidative and inflammatory disturbances despite partial attenuation of PFAS-associated metabolic abnormalities. PFOA concentrations showed the strongest associations with hepatic and intestinal injury biomarkers. Multi-omics analyses further revealed pronounced restructuring of the gut microbiota, metabolic reprogramming, and extensive intestinal transcriptional responses under co-exposure, involving Rap1, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, chemokine, Th17-related, and intestinal immune pathways. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that weathered MPs do not simply enhance or reduce PFAS toxicity but reshape PFAS-associated biological responses across cellular, organ, metabolic, microbial, and molecular levels, highlighting the need to consider dynamic interactions among co-occurring emerging contaminants in gastrointestinal health-risk assessment.

title: It is Not the Catalyst: How Angle-of-Attack Engineering Overcomes Diffusion Limits in CNT Forest Growth
summary: Abstract Vertically aligned carbon nanotubes (VACNTs) combine high specific surface area, excellent thermal and electrical conductivities, and tunable directionality, making them attractive for applications including water filtration, energ
content: Abstract Vertically aligned carbon nanotubes (VACNTs) combine high specific surface area, excellent thermal and electrical conductivities, and tunable directionality, making them attractive for applications including water filtration, energy harvesting, biosensing, and thermal interfaces. Maximizing VACNT height is critical to reduce CNT−CNT junction density and increase accessible surface area. While VACNT height is typically optimized through catalyst design and gas composition, reactor-scale fluid dynamics also strongly influence precursor transport. Here, first-order computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations are coupled with growth experiments to clarify how gas-phase transport limits attainable VACNT height and to identify strategies to delay self-limiting growth. Simulations reveal that increasing forest height leads to thickening of the flow boundary-layer (BL) along the substrate. With a Schmidt number near unity, the mass diffusion BL scales similarly, reducing reactant flux to the catalyst and inducing diffusion-limited growth. To mitigate this effect, substrates were modeled at positive angles of attack (10°−30°) relative to incoming flow, which consistently reduced BL thickness across all heights. Guided by these results, substrates were mounted at 15°−25° during in situ CVD growth for durations of 8−26 min. Experiments show that relative height enhancement is most pronounced for shorter forests (up to ∼40%) and decreases for taller ones (∼15%), consistent with BL-mediated limitations. These findings demonstrate that passive geometric control of substrate orientation alleviates transport constraints, increasing VACNT height without altering growth chemistry and shifting optimization from catalyst-centric models to those incorporating reactor-scale transport effects.

title: Heavy metals in road dust across contrasting urban settings and screening assessment of noncarcinogenic risk for adults and children
summary: Abstract Road dust can retain metals from traffic and other urban sources and create repeated contact opportunities in pedestrian environments, yet evidence from smaller settlements remains limited. We compared Cr, Cu, Ni, Pb and Zn in 35 r
content: Abstract Road dust can retain metals from traffic and other urban sources and create repeated contact opportunities in pedestrian environments, yet evidence from smaller settlements remains limited. We compared Cr, Cu, Ni, Pb and Zn in 35 road-dust samples from four towns in north-eastern Poland selected as contrasting urban and transport settings. Pseudo-total concentrations were determined after aqua regia digestion, contamination was assessed using the geoaccumulation index (Igeo), contamination factor (CF) and pollution load index (PLI), and non-carcinogenic hazard was screened for adults and children using the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) framework. Zambrów had the highest median Cu, Zn, Cr and Ni concentrations, while statistically significant among-town differences were confined to Cr, Zn and Cu. Town-mean PLI values were below 1, but three Zambrów sites exceeded 1, indicating localised rather than town-wide multi-metal enrichment. The unrefined total hazard index across the five metals remained below 1 at all locations, reaching maximum values of 0.0238 for adults and 0.214 for children at Z11; among the metal-specific indices, median values were highest for Pb and maximum values for Cr, and ingestion was the dominant pathway. Because each town represented a unique combination of population size, transport function, road-network structure and local environmental conditions, the study could not estimate the independent effects of town size or transport pressure. The results therefore support an exploratory comparison of four case-study towns rather than causal source attribution, broad generalisation or site-specific risk prediction. Within this screening framework, transit-exposed towns and pedestrian-sensitive locations may warrant targeted repeated sampling, with Cu and Zn used as initial screening parameters followed by broader analysis where elevated concentrations persist.

title: Analysing Opportunities and Risks in Utilizing Reverse Osmosis Reject Water for Tomato Cultivation
summary: ABSTRACT Rising global soil salinity has increased freshwater scarcity, driving widespread use of reverse osmosis (RO) systems that generate high total dissolved solids (TDS) wastewater. This study investigated impact of RO reject water (RO
content: ABSTRACT Rising global soil salinity has increased freshwater scarcity, driving widespread use of reverse osmosis (RO) systems that generate high total dissolved solids (TDS) wastewater. This study investigated impact of RO reject water (ROR) at 100 mM of NaCl (ROR100) and 150 mM of NaCl (ROR150) treatments on tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum L) growth and yield. ROR treatments significantly reduced shoot (34.83 g) and root (1.65 g) fresh weights, plant moisture (55.85%) and leaf number (9.28) compared to control. However, plant height and stem thickness remained unaffected. Chlorophyll content increased significantly under salinity. ROR100 enhanced fruit minerals including magnesium (19.36%), phosphorus (107.21%), potassium (28.67%), calcium (23.35%), zinc (24.25%) and lycopene (208.18%). ROR150 treatment increased fruit number but reduced fruit weight and significantly decreased in essential nutrients, indicating ionic imbalance and stress. Overall, the ROR100 improved nutrient enrichment and fruit quality, whereas ROR150 impairs nutrient uptake and may induce stress‐related deficiencies. The integration of moderate ROR generated from water purifiers can be used for tomato cultivation if managed well.

title: Agroforestry development drives a progressive shift from physicochemical to microbially mediated organic matter cycling in tropical soils
summary: Land-use change in tropical soils alters dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry and carbon cycling, however, linkages to microbial functions remain unresolved. We tested whether microbial carbon-degradation potential is associated with DO
content: Land-use change in tropical soils alters dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry and carbon cycling, however, linkages to microbial functions remain unresolved. We tested whether microbial carbon-degradation potential is associated with DOM composition along an Amazonian agroforestry chronosequence (10, 20, and 30 years), using adjacent pasture and primary forest as references. We integrated shotgun metagenomics with high-resolution mass spectrometry to couple carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZymes) profiles to DOM composition. Soil chemistry explained 41.6% of the variability in microbial composition, while land-use type accounted for 28.5% of DOM variability. Seasonality did not affect microbial composition but was a significant source of variation in DOM. Relative to pasture, agroforests showed higher potential for sucrose and α-glucan degradation and a greater abundance of aliphatic DOM, indicating enhanced microbial processing. Older agroforests were enriched in genes targeting lignin and microbial-derived substrates such as peptidoglycan, resembling primary forest, whereas younger agroforests had higher abundances of GH36, GH5, and CE3 genes linked to cellulose and hemicellulose degradation, resembling pasture. Soil pH and available P were marginally associated with microbial-derived compound degradation, while pH, P, and Ca showed a stronger association with plant-derived compound processing. These results suggest that as agroforestry develops, carbon cycling may shift from physicochemical to microbial regulation, while DOM remained related to vegetation inputs and seasonality. Soil management of pH and available P during early establishment could support this transition, but the recovery may take decades.

title: Nonlinear Responses of Chemodiversity to Total Organic Carbon Content in Lake Sediments
summary: Abstract Lake littoral sediments are critical carbon cycle hotspots that bridge terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. The chemodiversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in these sediments reflects ecosystem multifunctionality, particularly
content: Abstract Lake littoral sediments are critical carbon cycle hotspots that bridge terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. The chemodiversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in these sediments reflects ecosystem multifunctionality, particularly regarding carbon storage. However, the relationship between DOM chemodiversity and sediment total organic carbon (TOC) content, a critical quality‐quantity nexus, remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated both linear and threshold models to characterize this relationship across 63 freshwater ecosystems spanning a 31° latitudinal gradient. DOM chemodiversity showed nonlinear responses to sediment TOC content, with critical thresholds identified between 1.0% and 1.8% for alpha diversity, compound abundance, functional traits, and functional diversity, and 1.7% for DOM composition. DOM diversity metrics increased with TOC content before these thresholds and plateaued thereafter, indicating post‐threshold saturation of chemodiversity. Across these transition points, the predominant influence of sediment TOC on DOM chemodiversity declined, while the importance of bacterial compositional dissimilarity increased. Structural equation modeling further suggested that external organic carbon inputs dominated before the thresholds, while in‐lake processes became more important thereafter. Overall, this study challenges the conventional assumption of a positive correlation between chemodiversity and carbon quantity, highlighting the need to incorporate nonlinear dynamics into future carbon cycle models for freshwater ecosystems.

title: DECENTRALIZED FEEDSTOCK FOR THE CIRCULAR BIOECONOMY: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF HOUSEHOLD USED COOKING OIL MANAGEMENT
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: ABSTRACTThe escalating global enforcement of renewable energy mandates in transport haspositioned Used Cooking Oil (UCO) as a critical low-carbon feedstock for producingbiodiesel, hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), and hydroprocessed esters
content: ABSTRACTThe escalating global enforcement of renewable energy mandates in transport haspositioned Used Cooking Oil (UCO) as a critical low-carbon feedstock for producingbiodiesel, hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), and hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids(HEFA). Driven by stringent international sustainability policies and a projected marketexceeding USD 10 billion, securing a stable UCO supply chain has become increasinglyimportant. However, despite the technological maturity of biofuel conversion, systematichousehold UCO collection remains a major reverse logistics bottleneck, as most domesticwaste is still improperly discarded through sinks and drainage systems. This study presentsa comprehensive systematic literature review (SLR) of household UCO collectionstrategies following the PRISMA protocol. A thematic synthesis identifies four pivotaldimensions governing the ecosystem: (1) Supply Chain Optimization, focusing on MixedInteger Linear Programming (MILP) and Robust Optimization to minimize logistics costsand carbon footprints under supply uncertainty; (2) Consumer Behaviour, employing theTheory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to evaluate the intention-behavior gap andpsychological barriers in disposal practices; (3) Policy and Economics, exploring theimpact of subsidies, game theory, and asymmetric information on stakeholder alignment;and (4) Technological Innovation, highlighting Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled smartcollection systems and blockchain for feedstock traceability. The review reveals a criticalresearch gap: limited empirical evidence on household willingness to accept (WTA)incentives in developing economies, particularly Malaysia. This review bridges the gapbetween technical infrastructure design and human compliance, offering a strategicroadmap for policymakers and industry stakeholders to engineer resilient, human-centricUCO collection models within the national recycling ecosystem.Keywords: Circular Bioeconomy, Used Cooking Oil (UCO), Biodiesel feedstocks,Reverse Logistics, Consumer Behaviour, Willingness to Accept (WTA).

title: Elevational variations in fine root production, turnover, and rhizosphere autotrophic soil respiration in subalpine forests
summary: Although aboveground forest biomass and growth decrease with elevation, elevational variation in belowground production has not been well studied. Information on belowground production is necessary to clarify the production and carbon cycli
content: Although aboveground forest biomass and growth decrease with elevation, elevational variation in belowground production has not been well studied. Information on belowground production is necessary to clarify the production and carbon cycling processes of forests in mountainous regions. This study aimed to clarify the elevational variations in fine root biomass, fine root production rate, and rhizosphere autotrophic soil respiration at four elevations (1600, 2000, 2300, and 2500 m above sea level) in central Japan. The fine root production rate was measured using the ingrowth core method. The lower three elevations were characterized by subalpine coniferous forests, whereas light-demanding dwarf pine Pinus pumila and deciduous hardwood Betula ermanii were characteristic of the highest elevation (i.e., treeline ecotone). The aboveground biomass, fine root biomass and fine root production rates were lower at higher elevations. The fine root biomass and fine root production rate per fine root biomass per day during the growing season were also lower at higher elevations, indicating that the lower fine root production rates at high elevations were associated with shorter growing seasons and lower turnover (i.e., fine root production rates per biomass). The rhizosphere autotrophic soil respiration rate per fine root biomass was positively correlated with soil temperature and was higher at higher elevations at all soil temperatures, indicating higher root activities during the growing season at higher elevations. The results of this study will contribute to the understanding of elevational changes in root dynamics in the temperate zone.

title: Long-term spatio-temporal dynamics of sediment-associated heavy metals in a large river system
summary: Abstract Despite the widespread use of geochemical and ecological indices, our understanding of long-term heavy metal dynamics in large river systems is still limited, particularly when it comes to capturing temporal variability and interac
content: Abstract Despite the widespread use of geochemical and ecological indices, our understanding of long-term heavy metal dynamics in large river systems is still limited, particularly when it comes to capturing temporal variability and interactions between multiple elements. In this study, we examine patterns of sediment-associated metal contamination and ecological risk in the Vistula River (Poland), using monitoring data collected between 2015 and 2022 from 23 sites distributed along the entire river course. Concentrations of eight metals (As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Hg, Ni, Pb and Zn) were analysed using a set of commonly applied geochemical and ecotoxicological indices, including Igeo, CF, PLI, PERI and the mean probable effect concentration quotient (mPEC-Q). To better capture changes over time, we also propose a Sediment Contamination Trend Index (SCTI) as a complementary metric that integrates proportional, toxicity-weighted changes in multi-metal contamination. The results show clear spatial variability in sediment contamination, with the highest enrichment observed for Zn, Pb, Cd and Cr. While classical indices indicate moderate to considerable contamination and generally moderate ecological risk, the inclusion of SCTI highlights pronounced year-to-year variability, with alternating periods of increasing and decreasing metal concentrations that are not fully reflected by conventional static approaches. Taken together, the results suggest that combining long-term monitoring data with both established indices and a simple trend-based metric can improve the interpretation of sediment contamination dynamics in large river systems. Such an approach may be particularly useful in supporting environmental monitoring and river basin management under changing environmental conditions.

title: Forested peatland margins as biogeochemical control points of dissolved organic carbon export
summary: Peatlands store large carbon reservoirs, but the landscape controls on their lateral carbon losses remain insufficiently resolved. We investigated dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations and export along a bog–swamp forest–Klyuch Rive
content: Peatlands store large carbon reservoirs, but the landscape controls on their lateral carbon losses remain insufficiently resolved. We investigated dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations and export along a bog–swamp forest–Klyuch River continuum within the Great Vasyugan Mire, Western Siberia. Peat-profile characterization, pore-water chemistry and hydrometeorological monitoring were combined to assess spatial and seasonal DOC patterns. Swamp-forest waters at the thicker-peat site contained more DOC than waters from the open sedge–Sphagnum bog and the shallow-peat forest. The contrast between the two forested sites indicates that forest cover alone is insufficient to explain DOC enrichment. Pore-water DOC varied with peat decomposition and water-table conditions, while bulk peat TOC was a weaker predictor. Riverine DOC concentrations were higher in the forest-draining tributaries than in the main channel. Concentration and export maxima were seasonally separated: DOC concentrations were highest during the warm season, whereas the largest export occurred during spring high flow. These findings identify hydrologically connected swamp-forest margins as important DOC-rich source areas within the studied catchment. They also show why peatland carbon assessments should distinguish carbon availability in pore waters from the hydrological timing of export. Warming, changing precipitation and vegetation shifts may alter these source–transport linkages, but the direction and magnitude of future lateral carbon loss will depend on runoff and retention as well as DOC production.

title: Advances in micromilling: physical effects, sustainability, hybrid processes, and digital intelligence
source: Journal of the Brazilian Society of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering
summary: Abstract Micromilling is a high-precision microfabrication process capable of producing complex geometries and functional surfaces with submicron accuracy across a wide range of engineering materials. Although numerous review studies have a
content: Abstract Micromilling is a high-precision microfabrication process capable of producing complex geometries and functional surfaces with submicron accuracy across a wide range of engineering materials. Although numerous review studies have addressed specific aspects of micromilling, including cutting mechanics, surface integrity, sustainability, hybrid manufacturing, and intelligent production systems, a comprehensive framework integrating these perspectives remains lacking. This study presents a Bibliometric-Systematic Literature Review to identify current developments, emerging trends, industrial applications, and future research directions in micromilling. The analysis reveals significant advances in understanding key physical phenomena, such as minimum chip thickness and Specific Cutting Energy, as well as the growing adoption of hybrid-assisted processes that involve ultrasonic, laser, plasma, and electrochemical technologies. Recent developments in sustainable manufacturing, functional surface texturing, biocompatible applications, and energy-efficient machining are also highlighted. Furthermore, the review demonstrates the increasing role of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Twins in process monitoring, optimization, prediction, and adaptive control. Based on the identified research landscape, an integrated framework is proposed that connects physical mechanisms, sustainability principles, hybrid manufacturing technologies, and digital intelligence. The findings indicate that the future of micromilling lies in the convergence of these domains, enabling more precise, sustainable, adaptive, and industrially scalable microfabrication systems.

title: Ash cover accelerates the mineralization of labile soil organic matter following experimental fire
summary: After fires, the soil surface is covered by ash, which is important to the postfire environment because of its effect on hydrological behavior and its fertilizing properties. Ash effects are difficult to assess in the field but can be studi
content: After fires, the soil surface is covered by ash, which is important to the postfire environment because of its effect on hydrological behavior and its fertilizing properties. Ash effects are difficult to assess in the field but can be studied more readily through manipulative experiments in the laboratory. In this study, a laboratory burn was conducted to replicate the conditions of prescribed burning in the southern Pyrenees (Spain), and to evaluate the effects of ash on soil organic matter (SOM) and nutrients, with particular attention to particulate organic matter (POM) (> 50 μm), which was hypothesized to be more vulnerable to thermal and microbial degradation. Undisturbed soil blocks were covered with plant material and subjected to different burning treatments using a blowtorch. Part of the blocks were analyzed immediately after burning, and the rest, after removing the ash layer from half of them, were kept in a greenhouse for five months. Samples from 0 to 1 and 1–3 cm depths were analyzed for total SOM, POM and N and plant-available (Olsen) P, and POM was analyzed for fiber composition and N, P and K. The results show a large immediate loss of SOM in the surface soil when the blocks were subjected to high intensity burning treatments, with temperatures mainly ranging 400–550 °C. During the following months, only in ash-covered soils, an accelerated mineralization particularly affected POM and, within POM, its most labile components (nonstructural, hemicellulose and cellulose) compared to the more refractory ones (lignin-type), but did not significantly affect nonparticulate organic matter (NPOM). POM mineralization was boosted by nutrients such as P supplied by the ash, both in particulate organic and plant-available forms. Organic mulching and seeding of fast-growing grasses are proposed to help prevent ash-induced POM mineralization in post-fire environments.

title: Off-limits: The ocean as the new battleground in energy transitions
summary: The world’s oceans are emerging as a critical battleground in global debates about transitions away from fossil fuels. There are important implications for marine policy not only because of increasing climate impacts on oceans if fossil fue
content: The world’s oceans are emerging as a critical battleground in global debates about transitions away from fossil fuels. There are important implications for marine policy not only because of increasing climate impacts on oceans if fossil fuel production is not constrained, but because oceans are emerging as a key frontline in debates about energy pathways. As a source of critical transition minerals, a site of energy generation and a route for transporting energy they are assuming an ever more central role. But around the world conflicting and often incompatible state policies come to a head between ocean production and fossil fuel development. Here I explore two particular initiatives to advance this agenda: firstly, a fossil treaty which seeks to prevent expansion, phase out existing capacity and support state capacity to enable a transition away from fossil fuels secondly fossil-free zones as a means to put areas of the sea off limits for fossil fuel exploration and exploitation. I discuss both proposals in turn before reflecting on how issues of justice need to be addressed to reconcile ‘blue justice’ with a just transition away from fossil fuels.

title: Genetic and Physiological Responses of Sunflower to Nitrogen Availability: Implications for Sustainable Agriculture
summary: Sunflower is an important crop for farmers and consumers.A field experiment (RCBD, three biological replicates) at the College of Agriculture -University of Baghdad evaluated two genotypes (Ishaqi1, Ishaqi2) under four nitrogen rates (0, 10
content: Sunflower is an important crop for farmers and consumers.A field experiment (RCBD, three biological replicates) at the College of Agriculture -University of Baghdad evaluated two genotypes (Ishaqi1, Ishaqi2) under four nitrogen rates (0, 100, 200, 300 kg N ha-1).Morphological and yield traits were recorded and expression of gene AY941250 at flowering was measured by RT-qPCR using 18S rRNA for normalization.MIQE-compliant validation of the qPCR assay (primer specificity, efficiency, melt curves, and reference gene assessment) is provided in Methods and Supplementary Materials.Results show that higher N was associated with increased plant growth, yield components and higher AY941250 transcript levels in both genotypes; Ishaqi1 displayed the largest fold increase under the highest N.These findings are associative: they document correlation between N supply and AY941250 expression but do not establish causation.Functional confirmation (e.g., gene knockdown/overexpression and independent qPCR validation) is required to determine the gene's role in nitrogen uptake or use efficiency.

title: Hospital Wastewater as a Clinically Relevant Hotspot of Emerging Contaminants: Multidrug-Resistant Pathogens, Virulence Determinants, and the Challenge of Effluent Treatment
summary: Hospital wastewater (HWW) is a concentrated clinical–environmental interface in which pharmaceutical residues, disinfectants, diagnostic compounds, pathogenic microorganisms, antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, antimicrobial resistance genes
content: Hospital wastewater (HWW) is a concentrated clinical–environmental interface in which pharmaceutical residues, disinfectants, diagnostic compounds, pathogenic microorganisms, antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), virulence determinants, and mobile genetic elements coexist. This review synthesises the evidence on HWW as a reservoir of priority pathogens, from the sink drains and P-traps inside the building—where biofilms of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa have been genomically linked to patient infection—to the effluent that reaches municipal networks. Culture-based, genomic, and metagenomic studies across multiple geographical settings have recovered ESKAPEE organisms, WHO priority pathogens, clinically important antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), and mobile resistance platforms from hospital effluents; fungal (Candidozyma auris, azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus), viral, and protozoan pathogens are recovered far less often but appear to be systematically under-investigated rather than absent. Residual antimicrobials and quaternary ammonium disinfectants sustain selection at concentrations well below therapeutic doses. Conventional treatment reduces bulk organic and microbial load but does not uniformly eliminate micropollutants, viable resistant organisms, ARGs, or mobile elements; membrane bioreactors, activated carbon, ozonation, ultraviolet irradiation, and advanced oxidation perform better, but each performs well against some endpoints and poorly against others. We therefore propose a conceptual endpoint-based framework that separates four complementary domains—chemical, microbiological, genetic, and functional/ecological—and use it as an interpretive tool to show that percentage-removal claims are difficult to interpret unless the endpoint domain is specified. Hospital effluent management should be treated as an infection-prevention problem as much as an environmental one, integrated into One Health antimicrobial-resistance strategies through drain-level source control, molecular surveillance, endpoint-specific performance criteria, and regulation that extends beyond conventional physicochemical compliance.

title: Integrating waterborne GPR and group-aware machine learning to resolve lakebed hydrostratigraphy and potential groundwater–lake connectivity for Lake Vadkerti, Hungary
summary: Abstract. Climate change and increasing anthropogenic pressures have intensified the vulnerability of inland water bodies, altering their hydrological balances, reducing their water levels, and degrading their water quality. One critical is
content: Abstract. Climate change and increasing anthropogenic pressures have intensified the vulnerability of inland water bodies, altering their hydrological balances, reducing their water levels, and degrading their water quality. One critical issue in this context is the limited understanding of lake bed hydrogeology, particularly the extent to which sediments hinder (as aquitards) or permit subsurface leakage. Although sediment sampling provides valuable point-based information, its spatial coverage is limited, emphasizing the need for high-resolution, lake-wide geophysical methods. This study determined whether the bed of Lake Vadkerti, a shallow lake experiencing persistent water level decline, facilitates vertical water loss. An integrated method combining ground-penetrating radar (GPR) and sediment sampling was used to evaluate subsurface sediment structures. A dense grid of GPR profiles was collected, enabling 2D profile interpretation and 3D time-slice visualization. Amplitude polarity, reflector geometry, and attenuation modeling were applied to identify stratified sedimentary layers. The resulting aquitard zoning map revealed heterogeneous lake bed conditions: low-permeability aquitards dominate the central and southern areas, whereas higher-permeability non-aquitards appear along the northeastern and central-western margins, indicating potential zones of groundwater interaction. The performance of four machine learning models—K-nearest neighbors, random forest, extra trees, and gradient boosting—in classifying aquitard zones based on GPR amplitude features was evaluated. The extra trees model demonstrated the most balanced performance across all classes and stronger generalization, with 97 % accuracy and high recall across all classes (aquitard: 100 %, leaky aquitard: 86 %, non-aquitard: 79 %). Moreover, its spatial predictions were consistent with observed hydrostratigraphic patterns. This approach provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the hydrological functioning of lake beds and informing sustainable water management in climatically sensitive freshwater systems.

title: The litter decomposition dynamics under land-type conversion by microbial communities in the Yellow River floodplain
summary: Land-type conversion contributes significantly to litter decomposition, yet microbial feedback mechanisms remain unclear in river-floodplain areas. The distinct roles of bacteria versus fungi in wetland litter decomposition remain a key unr
content: Land-type conversion contributes significantly to litter decomposition, yet microbial feedback mechanisms remain unclear in river-floodplain areas. The distinct roles of bacteria versus fungi in wetland litter decomposition remain a key unresolved issue requiring further investigation. Litter decomposition dynamics and microecological mechanisms of three diverse land-types (riparian higher-beach wetland (RHW), cultivated wetland (CW), mesophytic wetland (MW)) within the Yellow River tidal flat were studied via litter bag method and high-throughput sequencing method for 2 years. Results indicated that land-use conversion induced obvious changes in the dominant microbial community composition, thereby regulating the facilitative role of soil microbiota in wetland litter decomposition processes. Agricultural reclamation on wetland changed microbial habitat and accelerated the litter decomposition 35.7–38.05% and the net release of total carbon 4.15–9.78%. Mesophytization of wetland increased the bacterial species and OTU, and facilitates local carbon retention. Cellulose and lignin content of litter in RHW, CW and MW decreased exponentially over time (R 2 = 0.960, 0.775, 0.896 and 0.959, 0.822, 0.918). C/N ratio (MSE = 15.37%), litter carbon content (8.30%) and soil moisture (6.94%) best predict litter mass loss ( P < 0.01). Furthermore, the DOC, NH 4 + -N, NO 3 - -N etc. content in soil were correlated with microbial Chao1 index and Shannon diversity. Cellulose, lignin DRs were positively related to the DR of nitrogen, fungi Shannon-diversity and bacterial Chao1, with lignin DR being more susceptible to fungi. During the decomposition process, bacteria account for 77.44–84.49% and fungi 0.08–0.22% at kingdom level. Land-use change reduced moisture (r = -0.79) but didn’t significantly increases soil N, both lowering bacterial α-diversity (r = -0.49, -0.76) and accelerating decomposition (r = 0.81) (R 2 = 0.61). Soil N and environment enhance fungal diversity non-significantly. Conclusively, land-use conversion in the Yellow River wetland soil reshapes the microbial engines, mesophytization of natural wetland and anthropogenic reclamation enhance litter decomposition and carbon–nitrogen degradation.

title: Evolution of Air‐Sea Fluxes in Modeled Long‐Lived Mesoscale Eddies in the South Atlantic Ocean
summary: Abstract Mesoscale eddies modify physical and biogeochemical properties, facilitating the exchange of heat and CO 2 between the surface, mixed‐layer and ocean interior. Most state‐of‐the‐art Earth System Models fail to resolve mesoscale pro
content: Abstract Mesoscale eddies modify physical and biogeochemical properties, facilitating the exchange of heat and CO 2 between the surface, mixed‐layer and ocean interior. Most state‐of‐the‐art Earth System Models fail to resolve mesoscale processes (10–100 km) due to computational constraints, thus contributing to uncertainties in current and future projections of ocean heat and CO 2 fluxes. While recent advances have shown progress in understanding regional and seasonal mean characteristics of eddies, their impact on air‐sea fluxes over the eddy life cycle remains poorly understood. We use a high‐resolution (1/12°) ocean physical‐biogeochemical (NEMO‐PISCES) model to investigate the temporal evolution air‐sea heat and CO 2 fluxes in long‐lived (>90 days) eddies in the South Atlantic Ocean. These eddies have varying lifespans, different propagation pathways, regional and seasonal dynamics. Examining these features reveals important nuances in their impact on air‐sea heat and CO 2 fluxes. We find a high occurrence (∼30%) of “abnormal eddies,” defined as cold surface anticyclonic and warm surface cyclonic eddies (CEs), emerging more frequently in longer‐lived eddies, which can weaken or reverse the direction of air‐sea fluxes. Long‐lived anticyclonic eddies sustain heat fluxes to the atmosphere and reduced CO 2 uptake throughout the eddy life cycle. In contrast, CEs in the South‐East Atlantic exhibit declining heat uptake with time, highlighting an asymmetry between eddies of different polarities. This asymmetry extends to other regions of the South Atlantic when considering CO 2 fluxes. Understanding these dynamics is necessary to improve air‐sea flux projections, inform mesoscale parameterizations that influence the carbon‐climate sensitivity of the Southern Ocean.

title: Nitrous oxide dynamics across nitrogen and pH gradients in headwater streams
summary: Abstract. Headwater streams in agricultural landscapes can contribute substantially to nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions, yet the environmental controls on stream N₂O dynamics remain poorly resolved, particularly in systems with low pH. We inve
content: Abstract. Headwater streams in agricultural landscapes can contribute substantially to nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions, yet the environmental controls on stream N₂O dynamics remain poorly resolved, particularly in systems with low pH. We investigated 72 Danish headwater streams spanning broad gradients in pH (5.0 - 8.8), land use, and soil type to identify the main drivers of N₂O variability. Nitrate (NO₃⁻) was the strongest predictor of N₂O saturation, and its positive association with N₂O intensified under acidic conditions according to linear mixed models. Ammonium, dissolved organic carbon, and stream depth also showed significant but weaker positive relationships with N₂O. Spatial differences among streams explained considerably more variation than seasonal or regional patterns, underscoring the dominance of local factors. Streams with pH < 6 consistently exhibited higher N₂O saturation, and generalized additive modelling indicated a marked decline in N₂O levels beginning near pH 6. Despite generally high N₂O saturation, approximately 9 % of observations displayed undersaturation, which occurred mainly in streams with low NO₃⁻ concentrations and across all seasons. Our results indicate that acidic, weakly buffered catchments may enhance in‑stream N₂O accumulation even at moderate nitrogen levels. These findings highlight the need to consider pH‑related controls when assessing N₂O dynamics in freshwater networks and when designing mitigation strategies for agricultural landscapes.

title: SLAMS‐2.0: A Stochastic, Lagrangian Particle‐Resolving Modeling Framework for Investigating the Biological Carbon Pump
source: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
summary: Abstract Sinking biogenic particles drive the ocean biological carbon pump (BCP), yet the processes governing their formation, transformation, and fate remain poorly constrained and are difficult to represent with existing modeling framewor
content: Abstract Sinking biogenic particles drive the ocean biological carbon pump (BCP), yet the processes governing their formation, transformation, and fate remain poorly constrained and are difficult to represent with existing modeling frameworks. Traditional approaches either resolve particle populations as bulk distributions or simulate individual particles at high computational cost, limiting their ability to capture both particle‐scale processes and emergent particulate fluxes. Here we present SLAMS‐2.0, a stochastic, particle‐resolving Lagrangian framework that bridges particle‐based and population‐based approaches by explicitly simulating individual, heterogeneous particles and their probabilistic interactions while efficiently capturing the evolving particle population across the full size spectrum through a “superparticle” formulation. The model combines this approach with observation‐informed BCP process representations, allowing particle composition, microstructure, and interactions to emerge dynamically from first‐principles fractal scaling and stochastic encounter dynamics. SLAMS‐2.0 is evaluated at six open‐ocean time‐series sites spanning contrasting biogeographical regimes against a wide range of observations, including particulate organic carbon (POC) and biogenic mineral fluxes, particle abundances, and size distributions. We show that carbon packaging, porosity, mineral ballast, and aggregation efficiency—rather than particle size or sinking velocity alone—govern POC flux transfer to depth, with large, porous, ballast‐rich aggregates driving deep‐ocean POC flux. SLAMS‐2.0 provides a framework for investigating how particle physicochemical attributes and interactions shape emergent carbon fluxes, with applications to both observational process studies and the development of improved biogeochemical model representations.

title: Niosomal in situ gel enhances the ocular bioavailability of kaempferol and improves therapeutic efficacy in dry eye disease
summary: Abstract Background Conventional dry eye formulations frequently demonstrate low bioavailability and necessitate high dosing frequency, resulting in poor patient compliance. This is largely due to the ocular physiological barrier. Aim of th
content: Abstract Background Conventional dry eye formulations frequently demonstrate low bioavailability and necessitate high dosing frequency, resulting in poor patient compliance. This is largely due to the ocular physiological barrier. Aim of the study We developed a novel ophthalmic formulation, kaempferol-loaded niosomal in situ gel (KAE-NIO-ISG), to improve the treatment of dry eye disease by increasing the ocular bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Materials and methods KAE-NIO-ISG was prepared by thin-film hydration and incorporated into an ion-sensitive in situ gel. Results The optimized KAE-NIO-ISG exhibited nanoscale characteristics particle size (PS) 177.27± 1.26 nm; polydispersity index (PDI) 0.21±0.03. The viscosity increased markedly upon dilution with simulated tear fluid (from 27.24±0.49 cP to 238.71±1.75 cP), indicating effective in situ gelation. Approximately 60% of the kaempferol（KAE） was released after 72 h, which is substantially greater than that of the KAE suspension (16.62±5.74%). The formulation demonstrated robust storage stability, no cytotoxicity in Human corneal epithelial cells (HCE-2) or Rat conjunctival epithelial cells (rPCEC), and excellent ocular tolerance. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed that compared with the KAE suspension, KAE-NIO-ISG increased AUC 0-180 min values in the rabbit cornea and conjunctiva by 23.52-fold and 3.98-fold, respectively. In vivo pharmacodynamics revealed dose-dependent efficacy, with the high-dose group achieving effects comparable to those of cyclosporine A (CsA). Conclusions In summary, KAE-NIO-ISG is a well-tolerated, efficient therapeutic approach for dry eye disease that significantly enhances ocular bioavailability and therapeutic outcomes.

title: Acceleration of the global methane growth rate over two decades: comparison with shared socioeconomic pathways and implications for future modeling
summary: Abstract The Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are a set of four harmonized greenhouse gas emission and concentration trajectories, representative of scenarios from the literature, that would result in radiative forcings of 2.6,
content: Abstract The Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are a set of four harmonized greenhouse gas emission and concentration trajectories, representative of scenarios from the literature, that would result in radiative forcings of 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, and 8.5 Wm − 2 by the year 2100. The RCPs show a particularly large range of methane (CH 4 ) trajectories early in the first quarter of the century, with vastly different implications for near-future climate warming. Using observation-constrained global atmospheric methane estimates from NASA’s Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) model, we estimate that atmospheric methane has been consistently accelerating from 2001 through 2024, driven by microbial emissions; only RCP8.5 (associated with a radiative forcing of 8.5 Wm − 2 ) models an acceleration during this time. A continuation of this acceleration would produce average concentrations between 2360 ppb and 2600 ppb (95% confidence) by midcentury, closest to RCP8.5. Thus, scenarios that include methane trajectories between the sharp acceleration of RCP8.5 and the much smaller and more stable growth of RCPs 4.5 and 6 should be resolved. Continued atmospheric monitoring and further investigation of the microbial processes that may be causing this increase, including both agriculture and wetland climate feedbacks, are necessary to produce realistic predictions and mitigation scenarios.

title: Bryophyte functional traits regulate root and soil microbial responses to reduced snow cover in boreal forests
summary: Boreal forests store substantial soil carbon yet are experiencing climate change characterized by reduced snowpack and increased soil freeze-thaw cycles. Mosses, particularly Sphagnum spp. and Pleurozium schreberi, dominate boreal forest fl
content: Boreal forests store substantial soil carbon yet are experiencing climate change characterized by reduced snowpack and increased soil freeze-thaw cycles. Mosses, particularly Sphagnum spp. and Pleurozium schreberi, dominate boreal forest floors, contributing to soil insulation and moisture retention, but their role in buffering belowground carbon processes under reduced snow cover remains poorly understood. This study examined functional traits of these moss types and their capacity to mitigate snow-cover loss effects on root biomass, soil microbial biomass, and microbial diversity and community composition. Thirty-six experimental plots were established across three mature black spruce stands in Nord-du-Québec, Canada, with treatments varying in moss type, moss presence, and snow cover. Sphagnum spp. colonies under snow were denser with greater water absorption capacity than those without snow. Root biomass was significantly lower under Sphagnum spp. with reduced snow, with no such difference observed in P. schreberi across treatments. Soil bacterial diversity was stable across treatments, though community composition shifted; Actinobacteria were more abundant under reduced snow in P. schreberi plots, and Acidobacteriota were more abundant in Sphagnum spp. plots with snow. Soil fungal diversity decreased significantly under reduced snow in P. schreberi plots but remained stable in Sphagnum spp. plots. Microbial biomass increased in Sphagnum spp. plots with snow by late summer. These findings suggest that as snow cover declines, forest floors dominated by Sphagnum spp. may shift from stable carbon sinks to disturbance-sensitive systems, while P. schreberi-dominated floors may offer greater resistance, at the cost of reduced thermal protection and long-term carbon accumulation.

title: The open uncertainty window in ocean biogeochemical responses to fossil carbon emissions
summary: Abstract. Automated parameter optimisation can effectively reduce model-data mismatch and provide information about ocean biogeochemistry parameter sensitivities, but to what extent it reduces uncertainty in responses to climate change is n
content: Abstract. Automated parameter optimisation can effectively reduce model-data mismatch and provide information about ocean biogeochemistry parameter sensitivities, but to what extent it reduces uncertainty in responses to climate change is not well understood. To explore the robustness of simulated ocean biogeochemical responses to a “business-as-usual” RCP 8.5-equivalent fossil CO2 emission scenario until year 2300, six biogeochemical parameters are optimised against contemporary oxygen, phosphate, and nitrate fields in three different physical configurations of the UVic ESCM. The phytoplankton maximum growth rate parameter value and the nitrogen-to-oxygen molar ratio of organic matter remineralisation were found to be robust across the calibration ensemble, with the former varying less than 1.6 % across the calibrated ensemble and the latter varying less than 4 %. While each calibrated model performs nearly equivalently in terms of optimal total misfit (a result of the model calibration objective), significant differences in biogeochemical fluxes and rates (e.g., global net primary and particulate organic carbon; POC) remain. Application of CO2 emissions to the calibrated models to the year 2300 produces model responses that start diverging in global average trends in the early 2000s. Models with more sluggish pre-industrial circulations respond less to climate warming in terms of physical changes, but more in their primary production (as these models have been tuned to have weaker limitation on production). Models that have larger changes in circulation metrics due to anthropogenic CO2 emissions, in particular the Southern Ocean overturning, demonstrate larger changes in shallow (130 m) and deep (2 km) POC fluxes (due to stronger parametric control on particle flux). Suboxic volume trends are smaller in models with larger changes to the physical circulation metrics owing to compensation between model tuning favouring strong biological oxygen consumption in their vigorous pre-industrial state and these models’ having a greater physical sensitivity to warming. By the year 2300, the resulting model responses vary by a factor 2.8 in net primary production, 5 in shallow POC fluxes, 1.7 in deep POC fluxes, 1.5 in nitrogen fixation and 1.2 in suboxic volume, but the model spread in absolute values relative to the pre-industrial remains largely unchanged, demonstrating the utility of constraining the pre-industrial ocean state in diverse model ensembles for robust projections of ocean change. These results demonstrate the potential to reduce, but not to close the open uncertainty window in ocean biogeochemical responses to CO2 emissions.

title: Changes in elemental composition and cell wall phenolics in maize leaves under water deficit: Implications for drought performance
summary: Leaves are a primary organ of interest for studying drought tolerance in maize because they integrate the main physiological and biochemical responses that determine carbon gain, water loss, and growth under water deficit. However, the asso
content: Leaves are a primary organ of interest for studying drought tolerance in maize because they integrate the main physiological and biochemical responses that determine carbon gain, water loss, and growth under water deficit. However, the association of elemental traits and cell wall-bound phenolics in leaves under drought conditions in real field conditions remains poorly understood. We evaluated 15 diverse Mediterranean maize inbred lines over two years under well-watered and water-deficient field conditions. Drought stress significantly reduced plant height and biomass yield, decreased leaf nitrogen concentration and δ15N, and increased the C ratio. At the cell wall level, water deficit increased p-coumaric acid, ferulic acid, and diferulates, while lignin content.,Attending to the differential response of inbreds evaluated, drought-sensitive lines showed larger increases in hydroxycinnamates and diferulate cross-linking, together with greater reductions in nitrogen. In contrast, tolerant lines-maintained biomass with smaller declines in nitrogen and more limited wall dimerization. These findings suggest that increased wall fortification reflects a defensive, growth-limiting response, rather than an advance under drought conditions. Nitrogen homeostasis and restrained cell wall cross-linking emerge as distinctive traits of drought-resilient genotypes.

title: Persistent influx of atmospheric microplastics and nanoplastics to Mount Everest driven by large scale circulation
summary: The Third Pole receives long-range transported pollutants, yet atmospheric micro- and nanoplastics inputs remain poorly constrained. Here we report year-long monitoring on the northern slope of Mount Everest using dry, wet, and total deposi
content: The Third Pole receives long-range transported pollutants, yet atmospheric micro- and nanoplastics inputs remain poorly constrained. Here we report year-long monitoring on the northern slope of Mount Everest using dry, wet, and total deposition sampling. Microplastic deposition fluxes at Qomolangma Station (64.0 n m−2 d−1) significantly exceed those at Everest Base Camp (23.0 n m−2 d−1), reflecting topographic and anthropogenic differences. Deposited microplastics are dominated by fragments, mainly polyamide, polyethylene terephthalate, and polyethylene. Nanoplastic concentrations across five representative months are higher at Qomolangma Station than at Everest Base Camp and include polyethylene, polyethylene terephthalate, polyvinyl chloride, and polypropylene. Monsoon periods enhance wet deposition via short-range transport, whereas non-monsoon periods receive long-range continental inputs. Upscaling suggests an annual atmospheric input of 56.4 tons of microplastic to the Tibetan Plateau above 4000 m. These results identify the atmosphere as an efficient pathway for plastic delivery to the Third Pole, with potential ecological risks despite low ambient concentrations. Microplastic deposition fluxes at Qomolangma Station exceed those at Everest Base Camp, reflecting topographic and anthropogenic differences, with an estimated annual atmospheric input of 56 tons to the Tibetan Plateau above 4000 m, based on year-long monitoring on Mount Everest’s northern slope.

title: Optimizing within-event nitrogen fertigation timing enhances winter wheat productivity by coordinating soil N distribution with root development
summary: Under drip fertigation, the timing of nitrogen (N) application within a single irrigation event is a key determinant of water and N distribution and crop uptake, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. A three‐yea
content: Under drip fertigation, the timing of nitrogen (N) application within a single irrigation event is a key determinant of water and N distribution and crop uptake, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. A three‐year lysimeter experiment with winter wheat was conducted on the North China Plain from 2021 to 2024. Three within-event N application timings were evaluated: application at the beginning (T1), middle (T2), or end (T3) of the irrigation cycle, under two irrigation regimes: full irrigation (W1) and deficit irrigation (W2). The study assessed how fertigation timing affected N distribution, root growth, canopy development, grain yield, and resource use efficiency under different water regimes. The results showed that T2 and T3 mainly accumulated nitrate and ammonium-N in the 0–20 cm topsoil layer, whereas T1 promoted nitrate movement into the 40–100 cm deep layer, particularly under full irrigation. T2 and T3 significantly increased root length density and root surface area density in the topsoil, reduced mean root diameter, and produced a ”fine‐root, high‐density” architecture, that spatially coincided with the surface N enrichment. This spatial coordination promoted canopy development and nutrient uptake, increasing grain yield by 13.4%–19.5%, water use efficiency by 8.9%–11.7%, and the partial factor productivity of N and phosphorus (P) by 16.4%–19.0% and 11.5%–19.5%, respectively. Structural equation modeling further confirmed that, by aligning surface N enrichment with dense root distribution, T2 and T3 strengthened the pathways from soil N availability to root growth, nutrient uptake, and yield formation. Overall, W1T2 and W1T3 established a spatially coordinated root–N distribution that improved crop acquisition of water, N, and P, thereby achieving high yield and efficient water‐fertilizer use. These findings provide a theoretical basis for managing drip fertigation in winter wheat grown in water‐sufficient regions.

title: An Updated Model for ϵ Eridani b and Prospects for Imaging with the Roman Coronagraph
summary: Abstract ϵ Eridani b, the nearest known Jupiter analog, has its orbit and mass constrained from radial velocity (RV) and absolute astrometry, and its atmosphere from JWST/NIRCam imaging upper limits in A. Sanghi et al. Here we follow up tha
content: Abstract ϵ Eridani b, the nearest known Jupiter analog, has its orbit and mass constrained from radial velocity (RV) and absolute astrometry, and its atmosphere from JWST/NIRCam imaging upper limits in A. Sanghi et al. Here we follow up that work with a self-consistent model of ϵ Eridani b that treats all available data within a single Bayesian framework. We extend the RV data with new measurements, update the treatment of the astrometry data with a new model, and include the NIRCam observations with a grid of evolutionary and atmospheric models. We find a mass of 0.91 ± 0.04 M Jup and an orbit consistent with previous work. The imaging data helps constrain planet effective temperature, atmospheric metallicity, and surface gravity. The constraints are dependent on model assumptions: for an atmosphere in chemical equilibrium, an otherwise low statistically significant feature in one of the epochs is recovered as the planet at high confidence. When assuming chemical disequilibrium, the posteriors exhibit a bimodal distribution, with one mode consistent with zero flux and the other coinciding with the flux of the tentative feature. Consistent with previous work, the clear atmosphere models are found to be viable at very enhanced metallicity, whereas the cloudy models yield more moderate values. Applying these models to the Roman Coronagraph, we find that the predicted reflected-light fluxes place every cloudy atmosphere our fit allows within the instrument’s expected sensitivity. A nondetection would be very constraining: a final contrast sensitivity of 2 × 10 −9 would rule out all cloudy atmospheres under our model assumptions.

title: Carbon storage dynamics in temperate peatlands over the past centuries
summary: Peatlands store ~613 Pg of carbon, are a net carbon sink, and could contribute to the carbon dioxide removals that are needed to mitigate climate change. Peatlands are therefore a key ecosystem that should be studied and protected. The acro
content: Peatlands store ~613 Pg of carbon, are a net carbon sink, and could contribute to the carbon dioxide removals that are needed to mitigate climate change. Peatlands are therefore a key ecosystem that should be studied and protected. The acrotelm effect, which describes how apparent accumulation rates increase at the top of the core even if net accumulation rate is constant through time, has complicated research into recent carbon storage dynamics in peatlands. This thesis aims to improve understanding of carbon storage dynamics in temperate peatlands over recent centuries, by employing methods including both conventional and novel ways of applying radiocarbon dating, X-ray fluorescence to study geochemical signals and anthropogenic pollution, and thermal decomposition analysis to study the composition and stability of peat under different conditions. Four sites across Northern Ireland and Scotland were selected, covering three raised bogs and one blanket bog. Three cores were collected from each site and high-quality age-depth models covering at least the last 500 years were constructed for ten peat cores. Age-accumulated mass models were considered to reduce the bend in age-depth models at the acrotelm-catotelm boundary. X-ray fluorescence and loss-on-ignition were deployed to investigate the peat for anthropogenic pollution. Elements that could indicate pollution were identified and their potential sources were discussed. The composition and stability of peat were investigated using ramped pyrolysis/oxidation and thermogravimetric mass spectrometry. Carbon released at specific temperature fractions was radiocarbon dated and compared to other radiocarbon dates of the same depth. The molecules that made up the peaks in gas release were identified, and that information was combined with information in the literature to consider what compounds were decomposing at a given temperature. Radiocarbon dating was also applied to determine the growth rate of an individual shoot of Sphagnum magellanicum, collected from East Falkland, offering an alternative method to measure growth rates for non-vascular plants. Age-depth modelling was applied to model the growth rate along the whole shoot. Finally, carbon sequestration was estimated for all five sites and compared between each other and with the wider literature.

title: Soil nitrogen dynamics in riparian zones of two pristine Arctic rivers
summary: Abstract Riparian zones act as protective buffers, filtering land-to-river nutrient inputs through retention and nitrogen (N) gas losses. While rapid Arctic warming and permafrost thaw may enhance terrestrial nutrient inputs to aquatic syst
content: Abstract Riparian zones act as protective buffers, filtering land-to-river nutrient inputs through retention and nitrogen (N) gas losses. While rapid Arctic warming and permafrost thaw may enhance terrestrial nutrient inputs to aquatic systems, comprehensive assessments of N cycling in Arctic riparian soils are lacking. Conventionally, these zones are considered inactive due to N limitation of Arctic soils and low temperatures, leaving their N cycling unexplored. To address this, we investigated N pools and turnover processes in riparian zones of two Arctic rivers in Finland and Greenland. We combined measurements of the extractable N pool and in-situ nitrous oxide (N 2 O) flux with 15 N-labeling techniques to quantify gross mineralization, nitrification, potential denitrification, and potential dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA). Our findings reveal that mineral N cycling in high-latitude riparian zones is more active than previously assumed. Despite low temperatures and low to intermediate soil organic carbon content, we found high gross N mineralization rates, alongside detectable rates of gross nitrification and potential DNRA. We attribute the unexpectedly high N activity in C-poor soils to low C/N ratios, which create a stoichiometric imbalance, thereby enhancing N mineralization. The presence or absence of vegetation largely determined the dominance and magnitude of these pathways. While dense vascular plant cover was associated with higher extractable N pools and gross mineralization rate, low nitrification rates and elevated DNRA potential indicated a tight N cycle. Conversely, sparsely vegetated patches with cryptogamic biocrusts acted as N 2 O hotspots. In bare sandy soils adjacent to the river, we found high gross nitrification rate and detectable N 2 O losses, possibly driven by riverine organic N inputs. Taken together, this research shows that Arctic riparian zones may play an important role in reducing terrestrial N inputs to the rivers, which should be considered when studying the fate of N in the rapidly changing Arctic.

title: Interfacial and Aqueous‐Phase Oxidation of Salicylic Acid by ·OH Radicals
summary: Abstract Salicylic acid (SA, C 7 H 6 O 3 ) is an aromatic compound widely used in medicine and industry. Its low solubility and partial dissociation in water affect its environmental persistence and transport via atmospheric aerosols, leadi
content: Abstract Salicylic acid (SA, C 7 H 6 O 3 ) is an aromatic compound widely used in medicine and industry. Its low solubility and partial dissociation in water affect its environmental persistence and transport via atmospheric aerosols, leading to its increasing detection in seawater and sea spray aerosols. Recent European Union regulations have heightened interest in its chemical transformations in natural systems. This study investigated the degradation of SA initiated by ·OH radicals either (1) spontaneously generated at the air–water interface of SA aerosols at 25°C, or (2) in the bulk aqueous phase, where they were produced by UV photolysis ( λ > 300 nm) of H 2 O 2 or NO 3 − at 25°C. Aerosols were generated by nebulization, stabilized through alkaline deprotonation (pH 8.2), oxidized in a flow tube, collected onto filters and analyzed via ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography coupled with high‐resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC‐HRMS), and at the bulk‐phase products at pH 4.5 were identified also by UHPLC‐HRMS. At the air–water interface, spontaneous dark oxidation yielded maleic acid, catechol, and dihydroxybenzoic acids within a 90‐s timescale. The bulk‐phase chemistry under simulated solar irradiation produced a consistent suite of products; notably, H 2 O 2 /UV and NO 3 − /UV systems also generated trihydroxylated derivatives, triggering a temporary toxic activation window flagged by REACH Annex III regulations. These results demonstrate that SA undergoes radical‐mediated oxidation in both phases through highly spatially decoupled mechanisms, highlighting its complex role in atmospheric multiphase chemistry.

title: Compost from urban biowaste shapes the bacterial community and its functional traits in the rhizosphere of tomato plants
summary: Industrial compost derived from urban biowaste is a sustainable biofertilizer made from food waste and plant matter. It has long been used as a fertilizer in agriculture and horticulture for its rich nutrient content. However, the compositi
content: Industrial compost derived from urban biowaste is a sustainable biofertilizer made from food waste and plant matter. It has long been used as a fertilizer in agriculture and horticulture for its rich nutrient content. However, the composition of the microbiota in industrial biowaste compost has been studied only partially, and the effects of this bacterial community on soil, rhizosphere, and plant root communities have received limited attention. In this study, we conducted community and functional analyses to examine how the microbiota in biowaste compost influences bacterial diversity, community composition, and metabolic potential in tomato plants, compared with plants fertilized with conventional, unsustainable chemical fertilizer. Source contribution analysis tracking bacterial taxa indicated a significant contribution of compost-derived taxa to the soil, rhizosphere, and roots. The community analysis revealed distinct clustering by fertilizer type, with biowaste compost promoting a unique, more diverse rhizosphere community, enriched in Firmicutes species. Functional analysis highlighted increased microbial pathways in the rhizosphere treated with biowaste compost, including enzymes for cellulolytic and xylanolytic activity, nitrogenase, phytase, and 1-ACC deaminase. Overall, food-derived industrial biowaste compost enhances bacterial diversity and the predicted functional and plant growth-promoting potential in the rhizosphere of tomato plants, underscoring its potential as a sustainable biofertilizer that supports soil health, microbial biodiversity, and crop productivity.

title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension
summary: The sequential occurrence of leaf unfolding, flowering, fruiting, foliar senescence and other life-cycle events constitutes a full cycle of plant phenology. Temporal shifts in the seasonal timing of these phenophases have been regarded as k
content: The sequential occurrence of leaf unfolding, flowering, fruiting, foliar senescence and other life-cycle events constitutes a full cycle of plant phenology. Temporal shifts in the seasonal timing of these phenophases have been regarded as key evidence of global environmental change. Most previous studies, however, have focused on the timing of individual phenophases. Little is known about the relationships between changes in timing across sequential phenophases. Here, using in-situ phenological records of major European tree species between 1980 and 2017, we show strong positive associations between consecutive phenophases. In particular, the statistical relationship between the timing of consecutive phenophases is comparable to that of temperature for spring phenological events and substantially exceeds the relationship with climatic factors for late-season phenological events. However, the associations themselves have shifted across years, with a significant decrease in the association between the timing of fruit ripening and autumnal coloration, corresponding to the largest extension of interphase duration. Current process-based phenological models largely overlook associations between consecutive phenological events and their interplay with climate change, potentially leading to biased projections of phenological changes and ecosystem adaptation to future climate change. Seasonal events in temperate deciduous trees, from leaf-out to leaf fall, follow a fixed annual sequence.
