title: Depth-resolved carbon-pool composition and climate-scenario sensitivity across contrasting peatland sites in the Altai Mountains
summary: Peatland carbon stability reflects the vertical distribution of organic-carbon fractions and their response to changing hydrothermal conditions. We quantified soil organic carbon (SOC), particulate organic carbon (POC), mineral-associated o
content: Peatland carbon stability reflects the vertical distribution of organic-carbon fractions and their response to changing hydrothermal conditions. We quantified soil organic carbon (SOC), particulate organic carbon (POC), mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), measured carbon stability index (CSI), soil properties, and extracellular enzyme activities across five depth intervals within the upper 0–80 cm profiles of three contrasting Altai peatland sites. At D1, SOC and POC followed a non-monotonic profile, with maxima of 304.42 and 211.17 g kg⁻¹ at 0–10 cm and a secondary maximum at 20–40 cm. At D2, SOC remained within 104.14–117.36 g kg⁻¹ and POC within 11.42–19.09 g kg⁻¹, while MAOC constituted 75.47–94.40% of SOC. At D3, SOC decreased from 147.61 to 148.09 g kg⁻¹ in the upper 20 cm to 93.12 g kg⁻¹ at 60–80 cm; measured CSI reached 23.68 at 20–40 cm. Principal components 1 and 2 explained 41.9% and 14.3% of standardized variance. PC1 contrasted pH, electrical conductivity, bulk density, and moisture with LAP, NAG, and POC, whereas PC2 contrasted total phosphorus with N/P, total nitrogen, and SOC. Under SSP5–8.5, simulated SOC changed by − 23.29%, + 5.11%, and − 2.11% from 2025 to 2100 at D1, D2, and D3, respectively; corresponding SSP2–4.5 changes were − 13.45%, + 16.79%, and + 5.43%. These results provide depth-resolved carbon-pool profiles and quantitative site-specific scenario trajectories for Altai peatlands.

title: Two-step carbonation of recycled aggregate concrete incorporating calcium-rich wastes for enhanced CO2 sequestration
summary: This study develops a two-step carbonation approach to maximize CO 2 sequestration in recycled aggregate concrete incorporating calcium-rich waste materials as partial replacements for cement. In the first phase, different combinations of f
content: This study develops a two-step carbonation approach to maximize CO 2 sequestration in recycled aggregate concrete incorporating calcium-rich waste materials as partial replacements for cement. In the first phase, different combinations of fine and coarse aggregate types (i.e., natural aggregates, recycled aggregates, and pre-carbonated recycled aggregates) were integrated in carbonation-cured concrete while measuring CO 2 sequestration potential and compressive strength. The Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) and a sensitivity analysis were used to identify the mix comprising natural fine aggregates and pre-carbonated recycled coarse aggregates as optimal based on CO 2 storage capacity and compressive strength. Subsequently, the second phase investigated the synergistic impact of accelerated carbonation curing and partial cement replacement by calcium carbide residue (CCR) and waste paper ash (WPA) at levels of 5%, 10%, and 20% by binder mass on the properties of the optimum concrete mix from the first phase. Performance evaluation involved CO 2 sequestration potential, compressive strength, water absorption, and volume of permeable voids. Results showed that the two-step carbonation approach achieved an estimated gross CO 2 reduction by up to 70 g/kg while maintaining performance requirements for masonry unit applications. Maximum CO 2 sequestration potential and superior properties were attained in concrete with 20% and 5% WPA replacement, respectively, with 8-hour carbonation curing. The proposed approach provides routes to reduce cement demand and upcycle recycled aggregates and calcium-rich wastes while producing concrete with enhanced CO 2 sequestration potential, supporting decarbonization and circular economy efforts in the construction sector.

title: Optimization of biogas production from Phragmites australis co-digested with poultry manure: Impacts of pretreatments and microbial dynamics
summary: This research examined the anaerobic co-digestion of Phragmites australis and poultry manure in batch reactors and evaluated the impact of combined pretreatment methods. Two substrate variants were analyzed: Sample A (mechanical pretreatmen
content: This research examined the anaerobic co-digestion of Phragmites australis and poultry manure in batch reactors and evaluated the impact of combined pretreatment methods. Two substrate variants were analyzed: Sample A (mechanical pretreatment only) and Sample B (integrated mechanical-thermal-chemical pretreatment) with poultry manure. We assessed key physicochemical characteristics of the substrates using standardized techniques, both before and after digestion. Water displacement was used to quantitatively collect the produced biogas, and the biogas composition was determined using the Gas Chromatography Mass Spectrometry/Electron Ionization (GC-MS/EI) model. We optimized process parameters using Response Surface Methodology (RSM) and used high-throughput next-generation sequencing (NGS) to identify the digester microbiota. Initial biogas production occurred between days 2 and 5 for both substrates, with cumulative biogas yields of 1.0745 and 1.0908 m³/kg VS for samples A and B, respectively. Based on these yields, sample B showed 47.46% greater methane content than sample A. The RSM model exhibited excellent predictive capability (R² = 0.9097) for sample B. The digester microbiota showed that the abundant and predominant phyla across all samples are Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteriota, Chloroflexi, Verrucomicrobiota, Desulfobacterota, Synergistota, and Spirochaetota. Major functional groups implicated include hydrolytic, acidogenic, acetoclastic, syntrophic, carbon-degrading, and sulfur-cycling bacteria . All four stages of digestion were characterized by different enzymes, including cellulase, Endoglucanase, Exoglucanase, β-glucosidase, Xylanase, Amylase, Protease, Lipase, Hexokinase, Phosphofructokinase, Pyruvate kinase, Lactate dehydrogenase, Alcohol dehydrogenase, Hydrogenase, Acetyl-CoA synthase, Formate dehydrogenase, Carbon monoxide dehydrogenase (CODH), Electron-transfer flavoproteins, Methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR), Formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase, and coenzyme F420-dependent hydrogenase. The study concluded that a combination of pretreatment methods can increase both biogas yield and the methane content of biogas produced from digested materials.

title: Lessons From CABBI : Advancing Vegetative Oil Production in C 4 Crops Through a Vertically Integrated DBTL Framework
summary: ABSTRACT The global demand for renewable liquid fuels and biobased chemicals has intensified interest in engineering high‐biomass C 4 grasses to accumulate triacylglycerol (TAG) in vegetative tissues. Achieving this goal requires coordinate
content: ABSTRACT The global demand for renewable liquid fuels and biobased chemicals has intensified interest in engineering high‐biomass C 4 grasses to accumulate triacylglycerol (TAG) in vegetative tissues. Achieving this goal requires coordinated solutions across molecular biology, crop science, chemical engineering, and life cycle assessment, disciplines that rarely operate within a single research program. The Center for Advanced Bioenergy and Bioproducts Innovation (CABBI) was established to provide this integration through a Design–Build–Test–Learn (DBTL) framework applied to three C 4 feedstocks: saccharum ( Saccharum spp. hybrids), sorghum ( Sorghum bicolor ), and miscanthus ( Miscanthus × giganteus ). Through iterative DBTL cycles, CABBI has produced transgenic saccharum and sorghum lines with substantially elevated levels of vegetative TAG, with multi‐location field trials having confirmed stable trait heritability and lipid yields. We have also leveraged our integration to develop a dual system biorefinery that co‐recovers vegetative lipids with fermentable sugars at levels sufficient to achieve industrial ethanol titres. Importantly, this fully integrated cross‐disciplinary data integration model has highlighted the key constraints currently preventing TAG‐rich vegetative oil from achieving commercial viability as: (i) active lipid turnover, (ii) photosynthetic trade‐offs, (iii) spatial misexpression, and (iv) bioprocessing challenges. CABBI uses emerging technologies, including biofoundry‐enabled construct screening, precision genome editing, and machine‐learning‐assisted regulatory design, to further accelerate DBTL cycles. More broadly, this work illustrates how integrative centre‐scale research that unites diverse expertise can accelerate discovery and translation, positioning these systems to expand agricultural markets and contribute to a more secure and resilient bioeconomy.

title: EVALUATING YEAST-BASED INOCULANT FORMULATIONS FOR SOIL PHOSPHORUS AVAILABILITY AND MICROBIAL ACTIVITY IN LETTUCE CROPS – INTERSECTIONS OF AGRONOMIC EFFICIENCY, FAMILY FARMING, PUBLIC POLICIES, AND CLIMATE JUSTICE
source: Veredas do Direito Direito Ambiental e Desenvolvimento Sustentável
summary: Yeast-based inoculant formulation to ensure soil phosphorus (P) and microbial productivity in tropical lettuce plants is tested in this research, promoting agronomic efficiency and family farming resilience and climate justice. In field tri
content: Yeast-based inoculant formulation to ensure soil phosphorus (P) and microbial productivity in tropical lettuce plants is tested in this research, promoting agronomic efficiency and family farming resilience and climate justice. In field trials using Chromic Ferralsol, we conducted elite soil yeasts with industrial Kraft lignin residue under low mineral fertilization. The data was cleaned and refined using the Z-loo algorithm to control environmental noise. Some formulations produced commercial output equivalent to the full mineral fertilization and minimized soil P depletion and water eutrophication risks. In addition to agronomic benefits, low-cost bioformulations reduce farmer reliance on imported fertilizers and increase the socioeconomic independence of family farmers who produce over 60% of all vegetables in the country. These findings are consistent with Brazilian public policy frameworks like the Family Farming Law (Law 11,326/2006), PL 1787/2025 and ABC+ Plan to protect diffuse rights to an ecologically balanced environment (Art. 225, Federal Constitution) and advance UN Sustainable Development Goals and IPCC climate justice frameworks.

title: Agroforestry's ecological promise: A global meta-analysis reveals context dependence, temporal decline, and policy implications
summary: Balancing the demand for agricultural production with the maintenance of ecosystem services, climate mitigation and adaptation, and biodiversity conservation will be a major challenge of this century. Crop production in agroforestry systems
content: Balancing the demand for agricultural production with the maintenance of ecosystem services, climate mitigation and adaptation, and biodiversity conservation will be a major challenge of this century. Crop production in agroforestry systems is being widely practiced with the expectation that it can simultaneously meet all of these goals. This study conducts a global meta-analysis of peer-reviewed literature on agroforestry outcomes. By synthesizing 1328 matched data pairs from 42 studies across 14 countries, using indicators that encompass biodiversity, soil properties, and carbon-related metrics, we find that agroforestry has a positive impact, improving overall environmental performance by 13.0%. After accounting for the influence of the replaced land-use type, agroforestry shows a 44.5% improvement in environmental performance relative to monoculture plantations. However, in contrast to reference native forests, its effect on environmental performance is not significant (RR = −0.02, 95%CIs = −0.12 to 0.09). Furthermore, the likelihood of agroforestry systems delivering simultaneous benefits across the assessed ecological indicators declined with increasing implementation duration. These findings demonstrate that the ecological value of agroforestry is fundamentally context-dependent, underscoring the necessity of incorporating baseline land-use history into policy design and environmental assessment frameworks for sustainable land management.

title: HOB: A Holistically Optimized Bidding Strategy under Heterogeneous Bidding Environments
source: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
summary: Optimizing a single advertising campaign across heterogeneous channels is a central challenge in industrial autobidding. Auction mechanisms vary across channels in ranking rules (pure eCPM vs. UE-augmented scoring), pricing formats (first-
content: Optimizing a single advertising campaign across heterogeneous channels is a central challenge in industrial autobidding. Auction mechanisms vary across channels in ranking rules (pure eCPM vs. UE-augmented scoring), pricing formats (first- vs. second-price), and bidding conventions (uniform vs. non-uniform), while advertisers impose shared campaign-level constraints. We propose HOB, which makes marginal cost (MC) computable and alignable across heterogeneous channels, especially for first-price auctions (FPA) with organic-paid coexistence, where existing bidding formulations do not yield a practical aligned MC form. At the global level, HOB derives channel-specific MC forms and coordinates disparate channels through a shared MC target. At the local level, HOB models free-win probability and winning-price uncertainty with a zero-inflated exponential distribution, yielding an efficient surplus-optimal bidding strategy for non-uniform first-price auctions. We show that any interior optimum satisfies MC equalization across channels. Experiments on a controlled offline benchmark, industrial log replay, and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate that HOB consistently delivers significant performance gains. Deployed on a large-scale commercial DSP, HOB delivers a 3.0% lift in GMV while maintaining return on advertising spend (ROAS) constraints.

title: SenseFlow: A Physics-Informed and Self-Ensembling Iterative Framework for Power Flow Estimation
source: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
summary: Power flow estimation plays a vital role in ensuring the stability and reliability of electrical power systems, particularly in the context of growing network complexities and renewable energy integration. However, existing studies often fa
content: Power flow estimation plays a vital role in ensuring the stability and reliability of electrical power systems, particularly in the context of growing network complexities and renewable energy integration. However, existing studies often fail to adequately address the unique characteristics of power systems, such as the sparsity of network connections and the critical importance of the unique Slack node, which poses significant challenges in achieving high-accuracy estimations. In this paper, we present SenseFlow, a novel physics-informed and self-ensembling iterative framework that integrates two main designs, the Physics-Informed Power Flow Network (FlowNet) and Self-Ensembling Iterative Estimation (SeIter), to carefully address the unique properties of the power system and thereby enhance the power flow estimation. Specifically, SenseFlow enforces the FlowNet to gradually predict high-precision voltage magnitudes and phase angles through the iterative SeIter process. On the one hand, FlowNet employs the Virtual Node Attention and Slack-Gated Feed-Forward modules to facilitate efficient global-local communication in the face of network sparsity and amplify the influence of the Slack node on angle predictions, respectively. On the other hand, SeIter maintains an exponential moving average of FlowNet's parameters to create a robust ensemble model that refines power state predictions throughout the iterative fitting process. Experimental results demonstrate that SenseFlow outperforms existing methods, providing a promising solution for high-accuracy power flow estimation across diverse grid configurations.

title: Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series
source: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free prediction intervals for fixed forecasters, but its standard calibration procedure is often inefficient for time series data, where forecast errors are temporally dependent and change acr
content: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free prediction intervals for fixed forecasters, but its standard calibration procedure is often inefficient for time series data, where forecast errors are temporally dependent and change across time and operating conditions. Recent time series CP methods improve local calibration using recent, weighted, or localized residuals. Yet local calibration can remain indirect, since broad residual weighting or additional adaptation procedures may dilute the evidence most relevant to the current prediction. This motivates a simple retrieval and correction strategy that selects similar past residuals as local evidence and then corrects the coverage error left by retrieval. In this paper, we propose Retrieval--Corrected Conformal Prediction (RCCP), a retrieval-augmented calibration method for time series prediction intervals. RCCP builds an asymmetric interval from retrieved one-sided residuals and calibrates its normalized retrieval error with a scalar conformal correction. Thus, retrieval provides local residual evidence, while conformal correction determines the final scale needed for coverage. We provide a coverage-gap bound based on the stability of the normalized retrieval error distribution. Across standard benchmarks and backbone forecasters, RCCP attains the target coverage in every setting and achieves the lowest Winkler scores, with fewer severe misses. RCCP also achieves low calibration and inference overhead, showing that retrieval-corrected calibration is an effective and scalable approach to uncertainty quantification in time series forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/jinsaaang/rccp.

title: Economic and institutional drivers of renewable energy adoption: A cross-country panel analysis
summary: This article identifies the economic and institutional factors driving cross-country differences in renewable energy adoption, focusing on solar and wind power. Unlike previous studies that either compare the share of renewable energy sourc
content: This article identifies the economic and institutional factors driving cross-country differences in renewable energy adoption, focusing on solar and wind power. Unlike previous studies that either compare the share of renewable energy sources or analyze individual support policies, we propose the Renewable Deployment Gap Index (RDGI), an indicator which captures the gap between actual renewable deployment and the level expected under given resource, macroeconomic, and regulatory conditions. The empirical analysis is based on a panel dataset of countries spanning 2010–2023. The methodology includes country- and year-fixed effects models, a dynamic specification with a lagged dependent variable, and a counterfactual scenario in which regulatory quality is improved to the level of leading countries. The results indicate that the most persistent barrier is fossil fuel inertia in the electricity sector: a higher share of fossil-fuel-based generation is statistically associated with a lower share of renewables (excluding hydropower) and a lower share of solar and wind generation specifically. The Regulatory Indicators for Sustainable Energy (RISE) tool exhibits stronger explanatory power across countries than within-country short-term dynamics. The counterfactual analysis suggests that if countries below the 90th percentile of the RISE distribution were to raise their regulatory quality to the level of top performers, the expected share of solar and wind generation would increase by approximately 11.9 percentage points on average. These findings underscore the importance of grid access reforms, competitive auctions, long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), streamlined permitting procedures, and mechanisms to mitigate investment risk.

title: Predicting wind turbine aerodynamic loads using laser-scanned blade geometry with validation based on operational and structural data
summary: Abstract. Aeroelastic wind turbine models are key tools in lifetime extension studies, but their application is often hindered by high uncertainty in aerodynamic load predictions. Manufacturers typically do not disclose blade geometry, whic
content: Abstract. Aeroelastic wind turbine models are key tools in lifetime extension studies, but their application is often hindered by high uncertainty in aerodynamic load predictions. Manufacturers typically do not disclose blade geometry, which drives aerodynamic loading and is therefore an essential input. Furthermore, model outputs are often only compared with Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) data, which contains limited information on structural loading. The present work addresses these challenges by using experimental measurements to develop and validate an aeroelastic model of a utility-scale wind turbine. Results from the terrestrial laser scanning of a wind turbine blade are processed with a new methodology based on consensus algorithms to derive spanwise chord, twist, and airfoil distributions, which are used as OpenFAST inputs. Simulation results are compared with structural health monitoring measurements of tower bending moments at two elevations, in addition to SCADA data. Moreover, rotor thrust and torque are estimated from the tower measurements and used as additional comparison metrics. The simulations show good agreement with the experimental data, supporting the proposed methodology. A parametric study investigates how several uncertainties in the model inputs affect the predicted aerodynamic loads. The results highlight the usefulness of laser scanning for improving conﬁdence in aerodynamic model inputs, as well as the value of tower load measurements as a complementary validation source to SCADA data. Therefore, the paper proposes and validates a new strategy to obtain a highly reliable model for load estimation, using a quite unique set of diverse measurements and new data processing approaches.

title: Electrical Resistivity as a Supplementary Site Characterisation Tool Within an Integrated Geotechnical Investigation Framework for Calcareous Desert Deposits
summary: Calcareous desert deposits present significant challenges for geotechnical site characterisation because of their heterogeneous composition, variable carbonate cementation, and complex mechanical behaviour. This study investigates the pract
content: Calcareous desert deposits present significant challenges for geotechnical site characterisation because of their heterogeneous composition, variable carbonate cementation, and complex mechanical behaviour. This study investigates the practical engineering value of electrical resistivity as a supplementary site characterisation tool within an integrated geotechnical investigation framework at the Shagaya area , Kuwait. An integrated geotechnical–geophysical investigation was conducted to evaluate the engineering significance of electrical resistivity in characterising heterogeneous calcareous desert deposits. The results indicate that the site is predominantly underlain by medium-dense to very dense calcareous sandy deposits exhibiting substantial variability in density, fines content, carbonate cementation, penetration resistance, and foundation stiffness. Standard penetration test (SPT) N-values ranged from 10 to 84, CPT cone resistance values ranged from 15 to 27.5 MPa, and PLT-derived modulus of subgrade reaction (Ks) values ranged from 24.3 to 210.3 MN/m3, demonstrating considerable spatial variability in engineering behaviour. Electrical resistivity values ranged from 57.2 to 271.9 Ω·m and consistently reflected variations in density, carbonate cementation, and foundation stiffness identified from conventional geotechnical testing. Higher resistivity values generally corresponded to denser, more strongly cemented deposits, whereas lower values were associated with finer-grained or less cemented materials. Unlike previous studies that focused on developing empirical resistivity-based correlations, this research evaluates electrical resistivity as a complementary investigation tool integrated with conventional geotechnical methods. Rather than developing site-specific predictive relationships, resistivity measurements were interpreted alongside borehole, laboratory, SPT, CPT, and PLT data to improve the understanding of subsurface variability. Instead, resistivity measurements are interpreted alongside borehole, laboratory, SPT, CPT, and PLT data to improve the understanding of subsurface variability and support engineering judgement. The proposed integrated geotechnical–geophysical framework enhances site characterisation, reduces uncertainty, and provides practical guidance for foundation investigations in heterogeneous calcareous deposits and large-scale renewable energy infrastructure projects in arid environments.

title: Green Hydrogen will Only Reach Cost Parity Once Electrolyzers are Engineered to Survive Cheap, Intermittent Renewable Electricity
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper examines why falling renewable electricity costs have not yet translated into cost-parity green hydrogen. It defines the technical requirements for electrolyzers operating directly on low-cost, intermittent solar and win
content: Abstract This paper examines why falling renewable electricity costs have not yet translated into cost-parity green hydrogen. It defines the technical requirements for electrolyzers operating directly on low-cost, intermittent solar and wind power and evaluates how conventional alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) and proton exchange membrane (PEM) systems perform under variable-load and repeated on/off cycling conditions. The paper combines techno-economic framing, literature-based engineering analysis, and novel decoupled water electrolysis (DWE) performance data. It reviews the role of electricity in the levelized cost of hydrogen and evaluates published evidence on alkaline and PEM behavior under partial load, dynamic input, shutdown, restart, and idle conditions. Key degradation and performance mechanisms assessed include shunt currents, gas crossover, reverse-current corrosion, catalyst dissolution, membrane thinning, and transient gas-composition instability. The analysis shows that access to cheap renewable electricity is necessary but insufficient for low-cost green hydrogen production. The lowest-cost electricity is typically intermittent, behind the meter, curtailed, or directly linked to renewable generation. Conventional electrolyzers were designed for stable baseload electricity. Due to inherent engineering limitations, they struggle under intermittency. Under variable load, AWE suffers from shunt current losses and gas crossover, severely reducing efficiency and limiting safe operation at low loads. PEM can follow load but incurs accelerated catalyst degradation (Ir/Pt dissolution) and membrane degradation (ROS-driven thinning), shortening system lifetime. Under repeated ON/OFF cycling, AWE experiences reverse-current-driven electrode corrosion and phase degradation, rapidly degrading performance. PEM suffers from small gas crossover during idle periods; unlike during normal operation, these gases are not swept away and can accumulate during shutdown, accelerating corrosion of both the electrocatalysts and the membrane. These findings are compared with performance data from a membraneless DWE architecture that temporally separates hydrogen and oxygen evolution. The reported results show specific energy consumption near 50 kWh/kg H2 over more than 10,000 cycles, normalized electrode performance through more than 50,000 accelerated cycles, and set-level current efficiency above 95% at 10% load and approaching 99% at higher loads. Calculated set specific energy consumption remained approximately 47 to 51 kWh/kg H2 from 10 to 100% load. These development-scale results support the architecture's ability to operate efficiently under variable power but do not establish field lifetime or project-level cost parity. The paper concludes that competitive renewable hydrogen requires electrolyzer architectures designed from the outset for efficient partial-load operation, frequent cycling tolerance, intrinsic gas separation, and durability under th

title: Minimising Marine Footprint: How the TRACS-16 Integrated System Decarbonises Subsea Recovery
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Subsea pipeline and flowline decommissioning has traditionally treated cutting and recovery as two discrete operations, each with its own tooling spread, ROV configuration and vessel deck time. This sequential approach introduces d
content: Abstract Subsea pipeline and flowline decommissioning has traditionally treated cutting and recovery as two discrete operations, each with its own tooling spread, ROV configuration and vessel deck time. This sequential approach introduces downtime, re-rigging delays and additional handling steps that increase vessel-active days and, with them, fuel consumption and Scope 3 emissions. This paper presents the TRACS (Twin Recovery & Cut System), an integrated subsea tool that combines cutting and recovery into a single ROV-deployed operation and reports its performance on a deepwater flowline decommissioning campaign in the Exmouth Basin, offshore Western Australia, delivered for client Cyan Renewables in support of operator Woodside Energy. Across a 15 km scope of hydrate-bearing flexible pipeline at 900 m water depth and spanning multiple pipe diameters, a TRACS-16/C1-16 spread cut and recovered just over 10 km of pipe, completing 1,051 clean cuts with no tool-attributable downtime. Cutting was executed across 44 active days within a 144-day charter, recovering approximately 300 m of pipeline to the subsea basket per active day at a mean cycle time of 31 minutes and, when accounting for servicing and blade changes, a rate of 29 cut-and-recover cycles per 24 hours. By batching cut sections into a subsea basket rather than returning to surface after every cut, the campaign saved more than 30 vessel days relative to a conventional per-cut recovery workflow, an estimated 1,400–2,300 tonnes CO2e based on the deployed vessel's published specifications. The paper discusses how reduced vessel-active days lower marine footprint and identifies basket transit as the dominant remaining inefficiency.

title: Industrial Waste Heat Recovery Using Innovative and Efficient MVR Technology
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Industrial decarbonization requires reliable alternatives to fossil-fired process steam, while refineries and chemical plants reject substantial quantities of low- and medium-temperature heat. Open-loop heat pumps based on mechanic
content: Abstract Industrial decarbonization requires reliable alternatives to fossil-fired process steam, while refineries and chemical plants reject substantial quantities of low- and medium-temperature heat. Open-loop heat pumps based on mechanical vapor recompression can recover this energy by generating water vapor at reduced pressure and compressing it to a useful steam-header level without an intermediate refrigerant cycle. This paper presents two industrial use cases. At a large European refinery, five process streams with inlet temperatures of 124-204 degrees C and a combined nominal cooling duty of approximately 68 MW were evaluated under strict host-process constraints. Preferred configurations generate 34 t/h of steam at 12 bar(a) and approximately 8-74.5 t/h at 2.5 bar(a), with calculated COP values of 3.15-3.44 and 5.52-6.63, respectively. Raising the common flash pressure reduces compressor stages, electrical demand, footprint, and investment cost. A full-scale industrial installation at BASF in Ludwigshafen, Germany, currently under construction, upgrades waste heat recovered from 1,900 t/h of steam cracker process water at 76 °C. The system employs an eleven-stage open-loop MVR compressor train to generate up to 60 t/h of steam at 5.8 bar(a), corresponding to approximately 47 MW of thermal output with a COP of up to 3.4, including auxiliary losses. The plant is designed to operate with a turndown ratio of 58%, enabling flexible adaptation to varying process conditions. When powered by renewable electricity, it is expected to reduce CO2 emissions by up to 100,000 metric tons per year. Together, these projects demonstrate the technical feasibility, operational flexibility, and industrial scalability of large-scale open-loop MVR systems for industrial waste heat recovery and steam generation.

title: Liquid Nitrogen Fracturing: Leveraging Thermal Stress to Boost Stimulation Performance in Geothermal Reservoirs
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract As an important renewable energy resource, geothermal energy is playing a vital role in the sustainable supply of clean energy. Hydraulic fracturing is a commonly used stimulation method to extract geothermal energy stored in hot d
content: Abstract As an important renewable energy resource, geothermal energy is playing a vital role in the sustainable supply of clean energy. Hydraulic fracturing is a commonly used stimulation method to extract geothermal energy stored in hot dry rock (HDR) reservoirs. However, some key challenges are met in HDR stimulation by using conventional fracturing, especially in generally forming 2D planar fracture patterns and requiring high breakdown pressure. A novel non-aqueous stimulation method, namely liquid nitrogen (LN2) fracturing is regarded as one of the possible solutions to solve the above issues. When LN2 is injected into the high-temperature reservoir formation, a large temperature difference between the reservoir rocks and fracturing fluid can exert a sharp thermal gradient that induces numerous thermally-induced fractures near the cooling surface/borehole. An innovative thermo-hydro-mechanical-damage (THMD) coupling method considering the rock heterogeneity based on phase-field regularized cohesive zone model (PF-CZM) is used to study the fracture propagation process. The fracturing performances in terms of the fracture patterns and damage ratio are investigated as a function of reservoir and engineering conditions. The coupling thermal-hydraulic effect on the propagation behavior of induced fracture and the resulting fracture patterns are illustrated. Results indicate that thermal stress plays an important role in forming large-scale fracture networks and reducing fracture initiation pressure in HDR stimulation by using LN2 fracturing. LN2 fracturing tends to generate complex thermally-induced fractures near the cooling surface, particularly under conditions of higher rock heterogeneity and greater thermal conductivity along fracture planes. Quantitatively, the damage ratio decreases by 59.3% as the heterogeneity index increases from 2 to 40. Moreover, when the injection temperature increases from -170 °C to 80 °C, the damage ratio drops by 92.6%, further demonstrating that maintaining low bottom hole temperatures is crucial for enhancing the stimulation efficiency of LN2 fracturing. However, due to the stress shadow effect, the propagation of thermally-induced fractures can interfere with one another, suggesting that fracture complexity has an upper limit. Therefore, optimizing injection parameters by considering both reservoir geological characteristics and economic constraints is essential to achieve a practical balance between stimulation effectiveness and cost efficiency. The key findings of this study are expected to provide an efficient numerical simulation approach and valuable theoretical guidance for optimizing LN2 fracturing in HDR reservoirs, thereby supporting the design and field implementation of cryogenic stimulation strategies.

title: Beyond P50: Bridging Renewable Energy Yield Assessment and Integrated Plant Operability Through Hybrid Modelling of Green Hydrogen and Derivative Facilities
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Renewable energy yield assessments explore exceedance levels to understand the clean-energy generation capability of large-scale renewable power plants (typically P50 or P90 for project financing). Although resource seasonality, un
content: Abstract Renewable energy yield assessments explore exceedance levels to understand the clean-energy generation capability of large-scale renewable power plants (typically P50 or P90 for project financing). Although resource seasonality, uncertainty and interannual variability are considered in conventional renewable projects, for project financing, the annual energy production figures tend to dominate the bankability assessment of projects. In green hydrogen projects, the renewable energy yields have a direct contribution to the overall bankability assessment of the facility. However, the intricacies of imbalances and system stability play a much larger role when the product is molecules rather than electrons. Therefore, although the traditional energy yield practice is sound for power projects, green hydrogen requires a more comprehensive and holistic assessment of the system and interdependencies to establish reassurance regarding the security of supply. This paper sets out why the practice took hold, what the annual figure conceals once a variable resource feeds a chemical plant, and how the gap can be closed. The contribution is an operability-driven hybrid modelling framework that couples renewable generation profiles, electrolyser part-load behaviour, synthesis-loop flexibility limits, utility demand and delivery obligations on a single hourly time base. The renewable resource assessment enters as a timeseries of 8,7601 hours rather than as an annual scalar. The paper presents the structure of the modelling framework itself rather than results for a specific development. Facility configurations, resource profiles and commercial obligations differ so widely between projects that scenario-specific numbers would not transfer, what transfers is the method and the metrics it produces. Published work supports the scale of the error being corrected: assuming fixed electrolyser efficiency overestimates hydrogen production by 5 to 24% under variable operation and understates the optimal plant size (Virah-Sawmy et al. 2024), while increasing ammonia synthesis-loop turndown flexibility to a level achievable with existing technology has been shown to cut the hydrogen storage requirement by up to 84% and the levelised cost of ammonia by 21 to 22% (Tully et al. 2025). A limited reproducible analysis demonstrates the method. It is built from public reanalysis and agency cost data for a generic coastal site, demonstrates the method across scenarios that reallocate flexibility between the renewable system, the buffer and the process is shown to provide an outline of how results may be portrayed and discussed. Five operability metrics are proposed to sit alongside P50 and P90 in the development deliverable set. The conclusion is deliberately narrow: renewable energy yield assessments should be regarded as one input to integrated optimisation, rather than the primary basis of design.

title: Simulation-Based Logistics Modelling for Offshore Wind Port Readiness and Project Delivery
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Simulation-based logistics modelling can improve port readiness, project sequencing and delivery confidence for large-scale fixed and floating offshore wind. The scope covers port functional requirements, fabrication-to-installatio
content: Abstract Simulation-based logistics modelling can improve port readiness, project sequencing and delivery confidence for large-scale fixed and floating offshore wind. The scope covers port functional requirements, fabrication-to-installation interfaces, integration capacity, wet storage, vessel movements, weather windows, tow-out strategies and multi-project scheduling, with transferable lessons for emerging energy markets. A proof-of-concept simulation model was developed to assess simultaneous offshore wind delivery across three ScotWind and one INTOG representative projects. The methodology defined port functional requirements for fixed and floating wind, screened 162 Scottish east coast ports, applied a Red-Amber-Green assessment to shortlisted ports and translated port capability into simulation logic. Twenty-five scenarios tested spread, hub, split integration and super-port strategies, examining port allocation, weather limits, wet storage, integration and commissioning berths, vessel sequencing and installation timing. The modelling demonstrates that floating offshore wind requires a different logistics model from fixed-bottom delivery rather than simply a larger version of the same approach. Large assembly hubs, wet storage, tow-out sequencing, integration berths, fabrication flow, vessel scheduling and weather-dependent offshore installation have to be planned as one connected operational system. Spread, hub and split integration strategies were broadly viable, while the super-port strategy became constrained under adverse weather and limited integration berth availability. Increasing integration and commissioning-capable berths improved feasibility, whereas reducing integration times alone had limited impact unless the wider supply chain could also accelerate. Larger wet storage areas further away were preferable to smaller, closer locations where capacity was constrained. The findings are relevant to the Middle East, where established port infrastructure already supports mature markets such as oil and gas and LNG, while the region scales renewable energy, clean industrial infrastructure and potential offshore or coastal energy projects. As ports increasingly seek to serve a broader mix of users and markets, their readiness cannot be judged only by land availability or headline quay capacity; it depends on how existing and future demand, port infrastructure, vessel movements, component flows, storage requirements, weather windows, workforce capability and project sequencing interact. The modelling can also simulate the additional vessel movements required during offshore wind construction alongside existing marine traffic. This helps assess potential congestion, berth availability, navigational constraints and competition for port resources across multiple sectors. For NOCs, developers, ports and public stakeholders, simulation-based logistics modelling can support multiple sectors concurrently, identify operational constraints and com

title: Powering Decarbonization: A Scalable Solar-Grid Strategy for Energy-Intensive Onshore Oil Assets
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper documents an actual field-level study conducted for an onshore oil field to assess the feasibility and impact of integrating utility-scale solar power into an existing high-reliability oilfield electrica
content: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper documents an actual field-level study conducted for an onshore oil field to assess the feasibility and impact of integrating utility-scale solar power into an existing high-reliability oilfield electrical network. The objective was to reduce power cost per barrel, lower operational emissions, improve long-term energy cost predictability, and establish a scalable decarbonization model applicable to energy-intensive onshore oil operations. Methods, Procedures, Process The study was executed using field-specific data, including real electrical load profiles, existing 220 kV grid architecture, and available land parcels within operating facilities. The methodology combined detailed load analysis, grid interconnection and protection studies, energy-yield modelling, and levelized cost of electricity benchmarking against prevailing grid tariffs. Multiple solar photovoltaic configurations, including PV-only and solar PV with battery energy storage, were technically and economically evaluated. A long-term power purchase agreement structure was assessed to minimize capital exposure while ensuring operational reliability and performance accountability. Results, Observations, Conclusions The field study identified an optimal configuration comprising a 116 MWp utility-scale solar PV plant synchronized with the field's 33 kV electrical network, supplying approximately 270 GWh of renewable electricity annually. The results indicate annual cost saving of approximately USD 9.6 million, equating to a 7-10% reduction in electricity expenditure and a measurable lifting-cost reduction of about USD 0.106 per barrel. The solution enables avoidance of more than 140,000 tons of CO2 emissions per year under a fixed long-term tariff, reducing exposure to electricity price escalation. Operational assessment confirmed that the hybrid solar-grid configuration maintains uninterrupted supply to critical production loads, with no adverse impact on system stability, protection coordination, or power quality. Comparative evaluation demonstrated that while battery energy storage improves dispatch flexibility, a solar-only configuration provides the most cost-effective and lowest- risk decarbonization pathway for the load profile. The study validates the technical viability of large-scale renewable integration within an operating oilfield environment. Novel/Additive Information This paper presents a field-validated case study demonstrating how utility-scale solar power can be integrated into a live onshore oilfield electrical system while delivering measurable cost-per- barrel reduction and emissions avoidance. By linking renewable deployment directly to operational and economic performance at field level, the study provides a practical, replicable framework for decarbonizing power supply across similar upstream assets.

title: Bridging the Educational Gap with Virtual Reality (VR): Virtual Labs for the Next Generation
source: International Journal of Technology in Education and Science
summary: This research addresses the systemic educational inequality in Thailand, where a severe shortage of physical science laboratories in rural areas hinders the development of 21st-century scientific literacy. Using the ADDIE model, the study d
content: This research addresses the systemic educational inequality in Thailand, where a severe shortage of physical science laboratories in rural areas hinders the development of 21st-century scientific literacy. Using the ADDIE model, the study developed a virtual world technology innovation, the AR SciLab platform, to serve as a high-quality, risk-free learning infrastructure. The innovation comprises a database of eight career-oriented experiments (e.g., biodiesel production and essential oil extraction), 3D immersive VR environments built on Unreal Engine 5, and bilingual instructional media. Tested with 500 primary and secondary students and 10 teachers across diverse regions, the results showed significant academic improvement, with 70.8% of students achieving a relative gain score of at least 50%. Qualitative data revealed that the metaverse environment effectively bypassed geographical resource gaps and increased student motivation through “learning by doing.” Despite technical challenges such as “VR sickness,” the study demonstrates that virtual labs provide a scalable, equitable solution for marginalized schools, supporting the “Thailand Zero Dropout” initiative by ensuring that a student’s location no longer dictates the quality of their scientific education.

title: Respons Campuran Asbuton–Gondorukem terhadap Variasi Suhu Pencampuran: Stabilitas Marshall dan Kekuatan Sisa setelah Perendaman
summary: The use of Asbuton as a local asphaltic material combined with bio-based additives requires appropriate processing conditions to obtain consistent mixture performance. This study aims to evaluate the response of Asbuton–gondorukem asphalt m
content: The use of Asbuton as a local asphaltic material combined with bio-based additives requires appropriate processing conditions to obtain consistent mixture performance. This study aims to evaluate the response of Asbuton–gondorukem asphalt mixtures to different mixing temperatures based on Marshall stability and retained strength after immersion. The mixtures were prepared at mixing temperatures of 60°C, 90°C, and 120°C, with immersion durations of 0, 1, 2, and 3 days. A total of 36 specimens were prepared, consisting of three specimens for each combination of mixing temperature and immersion duration. Marshall stability was analyzed descriptively by comparing the average stability values and the Retained Strength Index (IKS), calculated as the ratio of stability after 3 days of immersion to the initial stability. The results showed that the highest initial stability was obtained at 120°C, reaching 4,204.25 N, whereas after 3 days of immersion the highest stability was obtained at 90°C, reaching 4,034.57 N. The IKS values were 126.32%, 130.53%, and 84.11% for mixing temperatures of 60°C, 90°C, and 120°C, respectively. The results indicate that the mixing temperature associated with the highest initial stability did not necessarily produce the highest stability after conditioning. The 90°C condition was therefore identified as the most prospective condition for further investigation within the temperature range studied, rather than being established as the optimum mixing temperature. Further research is required using additional performance parameters, including volumetric properties, flow, Marshall Quotient, moisture susceptibility, and durability.

title: Mobile Solar-Diesel Hybrid Power Solution for Jet Pumps in Abu Dhabi: Field Deployment of a Containerized Energy-As-A-Service Model for Off-Grid Oilfield Production
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper presents the design, field deployment, and operational evaluation of a mobile solar-diesel hybrid power system used to supply electricity to temporary jet pumps in off-grid wellsite locations in Abu Dhabi, UAE deployed b
content: Abstract This paper presents the design, field deployment, and operational evaluation of a mobile solar-diesel hybrid power system used to supply electricity to temporary jet pumps in off-grid wellsite locations in Abu Dhabi, UAE deployed by an onshore oil and gas operator in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The pilot was developed to demonstrate whether a containerized renewable-power solution could reduce diesel dependence while maintaining the continuity, power quality, and operational flexibility required by artificial-lift applications that were previously powered by traditional diesel generators. The deployed architecture combined a mobile solar container with inverters, integrated power electronics, a hybrid control system, diesel generation sized to the pump load with prime and backup configurations, fuel monitoring, and a remote monitoring platform. The solution was delivered under an energy-as-a-service model, allowing the operator to obtain a complete power-generation service without assuming responsibility for the hybrid plant's day-to-day operation and maintenance. The pilot covered several well locations in the UAE with different deployment and approval conditions. One unit achieved sustained hybrid operation with 16% solar contribution and 100% availability during its operating period using the original unchanged diesel generator setup, while the second unit achieved a 21% solar contribution with availability of at least 99.9% over more than twelve months of continuous operation, also with the original diesel generator setup. A third location operated initially with a correctly sized diesel generator achieved a 21% solar contribution with availability of at least 99.9% over more than six months of continuous operation. Based on the well-level energy data available through 31st July 2026, the three locations delivered approximately 961 MWh in aggregate, with approximately 140 MWh attributable to solar generation at the two sites where photovoltaic was deployed and no solar-attributable outage was recorded, which is equivalent to approximately 63,000 liters of diesel saved. The field experience demonstrates that the technical integration of mobile solar with diesel generation can provide reliable power to artificial-lift loads while reducing fuel consumption, generator operating hours, acoustic impact, and maintenance burden. The principal limitation on higher solar penetration during the pilot was not the hybrid technology itself, but operational administration complexity. The pilot also identified the importance of correctly sizing diesel generators before mobilization, resolving electrical interfaces with variable-speed-drive equipment, and establishing documentation and permit requirements before equipment reaches site. The results support further deployment of containerized solar-diesel systems for temporary wellsite power, with battery energy storage and power-conversion equipment offering a pathway toward substantially higher r

title: A provenance-tracked State-day panel of India’s power system built from official public reports, 2018–2026
summary: Abstract India publishes daily information on electricity demand, scheduling, generation and prices, but as thousands of report files whose layouts change, spread across the grid operator, the Central Electricity Authority and the meteorolo
content: Abstract India publishes daily information on electricity demand, scheduling, generation and prices, but as thousands of report files whose layouts change, spread across the grid operator, the Central Electricity Authority and the meteorological department. We describe a State-day panel for 34 Indian State control areas from 2018-04-01 to 2026-08-31 (104,550 State-days, 107 variables). It joins, from official sources only, energy met and shortages, scheduled and actual drawal with over- and under-drawal, conventional generation by fuel, renewable generation, bid-area exchange prices and deviation charge rates, system frequency stress, carbon intensity and weather. Each of the 9,614 source files it uses is recorded with its URL, retrieval time and SHA-256 hash, and the panel can be rebuilt deterministically from the raw files. Each variable carries an availability delay, based on measured publication times where available, so forecasting studies can respect what was known each day. Technical validation reproduces the sources’ own totals exactly and agrees with an independent copy of the generation data within 1% on 100.0% of 75,485 State-days.

title: TCERA: Environmental Resonant Energy Harvesting Theory / Teoría de Cosecha Energética Resonante Ambiental
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Abstract & Metadata for Zenodo Submission Project Title: TCERA: Environmental Resonant Energy Harvesting Theory (Teoría de Cosecha Energética Resonante Ambiental) Title (English/Spanish) TCERA: Continuous Multi-Spectral Environmental Energy
content: Abstract & Metadata for Zenodo Submission Project Title: TCERA: Environmental Resonant Energy Harvesting Theory (Teoría de Cosecha Energética Resonante Ambiental) Title (English/Spanish) TCERA: Continuous Multi-Spectral Environmental Energy Harvesting via Monolithic Layered Metamaterials and Quantum Tunneling Description / Abstract (English) This package contains the foundational technical compendium and executive summary for the Environmental Resonant Energy Harvesting Theory (TCERA). TCERA is a comprehensive theoretical and architectural framework designed to extract electrical power continuously ($24/7$) from ambient electromagnetic and thermal radiation without violating thermodynamic principles. By unifying three functional strata—Phase I (optical and thermal infrared harvesting via metallic nanoantenas and Metal-Insulator-Metal [MIM] quantum tunneling diodes), Phase II (non-Hermitian quantum metamaterials operating near exceptional points for ambient radiofrequency collection), and Phase III (zero-threshold sub-threshold logic and distributed solid-state energy management)—the TCERA architecture forms a monolithic "smart skin" collector. This documentation presents the mathematical formulation of the total transduction power ($P_{\text{TCERA}}$), analyzes bottleneck resolutions (such as hBN-Graphene nano-patches and resonant tunneling diodes), and establishes an experimental laboratory blueprint. Open Access & Common Good Declaration: In accordance with the foundational principles of TCERA, this work is permanently released into the global public domain as open-access knowledge. Its primary objective is to eradicate energy poverty, dismantle corporate energy monopolies, and ensure that electrical energy remains an entirely free, decentralized, and accessible resource for all humanity. Commercial patenting or exclusive proprietary restrictions over this core architecture are strictly prohibited. title: Metamaterial-based square ring–hourglass resonator for broadband and polarization-independent graphene solar absorption with machine-learning-assisted optimization for renewable mining applications
summary: Solar absorbers are promising technologies for renewable energy harvesting due to their simple and practical implementation. Their absorption performance strongly depends on the constituent materials and the geometry of the resonant structu
content: Solar absorbers are promising technologies for renewable energy harvesting due to their simple and practical implementation. Their absorption performance strongly depends on the constituent materials and the geometry of the resonant structures, which can be tailored to achieve enhanced and broadband absorption. The current work is developed as a Square Ring with Hourglass Resonator Broadband Absorber (SRHRBA) structure, and the total performance is 93.63% for overall absorption at 2800 nm. With the graphene layer, it achieves more than 97% within 1000 nm, and the absorption under the AM 1.5 situation explored 96.4%. The geometry designs for lithography, the resonance development, the parametric ‘nm’ analysis, and the Random Forest model under the ML section, used with a 0.25 test size, are included in the current SRHRBA work. The incidence angles of 0 – 80-degree variation are included to show the polarization–independent development and the comparison with the related references also presented. With perfect absorption, the current SRHRBA can be used for thermal conversion involving domestic hot water, pool and space heating, industrial process heating, and photothermal catalysis.

title: The Effect of Circular Economy Practices on Sustainable Tourism Development Among Tourism and Hospitality Enterprises Around Simien Mountains National Park in Ethiopia
summary: Abstract Circular economy practices have become increasingly important for promoting sustainable tourism by reducing resource consumption, minimizing waste, strengthening local resource use, and encouraging innovative tourism products and s
content: Abstract Circular economy practices have become increasingly important for promoting sustainable tourism by reducing resource consumption, minimizing waste, strengthening local resource use, and encouraging innovative tourism products and services. However, tourism and hospitality enterprises in developing destinations often face challenges in adopting circular practices due to limited infrastructure, financial resources, technical capacity, and institutional support. This study examined the relationship between circular economy practices and sustainable tourism development among tourism and hospitality enterprises around Simien Mountains National Park, Ethiopia. A cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from tourism and hospitality enterprises using a structured questionnaire. A total of 305 usable questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression analysis. The study examined six dimensions of circular economy practices: resource reduction and efficiency, reuse practices, recycling and waste recovery, sustainable procurement, renewable energy and resource conservation, and circular product and service innovation. The findings revealed that the overall regression model was statistically significant, F(6, 298) = 68.236, p < .001, with the six circular economy practices jointly explaining 57.9% of the variation in sustainable tourism development. Circular product and service innovation (β = .552, p < .001), sustainable procurement (β = .303, p < .001), reuse practices (β = .261, p < .001), and resource reduction and efficiency (β = .102, p = .041) were positively and significantly associated with sustainable tourism development. In contrast, recycling and waste recovery (β = −.143, p = .032) and renewable energy and resource conservation (β = −.238, p = .001) showed statistically significant negative associations within the fitted model. These findings suggest that circular economy practices are important predictors of sustainable tourism development, although their relationships differ across dimensions and may reflect contextual implementation conditions. The study provides practical implications for tourism and hospitality enterprises, local government, park authorities, and other stakeholders to strengthen circular product and service innovation, sustainable procurement, resource efficiency, reuse systems, recycling infrastructure, and renewable-energy initiatives. The findings can contribute to the development of more resource-efficient, environmentally responsible, economically viable, and resilient tourism practices around Simien Mountains National Park..

title: Performance of packed-bed thermal energy storage using recycled aggregate: From a lab-scale prototype to a 1 MWh module
summary: Recycled aggregate (RA) is produced during construction and demolition activities, but its reuse is limited by residual mortar content and the energy-intensive thermal treatment required. Using RA as a filler in packed-bed thermal energy st
content: Recycled aggregate (RA) is produced during construction and demolition activities, but its reuse is limited by residual mortar content and the energy-intensive thermal treatment required. Using RA as a filler in packed-bed thermal energy storage (PBTES) offers a dual function: acting as a sensible heat-storage medium and supporting RA thermal treatment, which enhances material recovery and circularity. This study explores a concept of concrete circularity-renewable energy symbiosis through a case study of RA-PBTES with dual functions. Laboratory experiments assessed the thermal response, pressure drop, cyclic repeatability, and structural behaviour of RA-PBTES under repeated heating and cooling. Results showed RA maintained stable thermocline development, good heat storage, and acceptable hydraulic resistance, though some thermal ratcheting occurred at 250°C, emphasising the need to consider particle movement and bed structure for long-term design. Repeated thermal cycling made RA particles more brittle, suggesting benefits for crushing and residual mortar removal. To explore scalability, a one-dimensional heat-transfer model based on the Schumann formulation was developed and validated, accurately predicting temperature and thermocline development obtained from the experiments. Applying this model to a 1 MWh storage module assessed large-scale thermal performance, fan energy, and system behaviour, revealing trade-offs among heat transfer, resistance, energy use, and material utilisation. The use of waste-derived RA further offers potential sustainability benefits through material reuse and subsequent thermal upgrading.

title: On the motion of a catamaran-type wave energy converter under periodic external forcing
summary: Abstract Wave energy is one of the most promising renewable energy sources, and the catamaran-type point-absorption wave energy converter (PAWEC) is a widely studied prototype because of its compact size and its ability to absorb wave energ
content: Abstract Wave energy is one of the most promising renewable energy sources, and the catamaran-type point-absorption wave energy converter (PAWEC) is a widely studied prototype because of its compact size and its ability to absorb wave energy from all directions. The dynamics of such a device, however, are described by a system of high-dimensional nonlinear non-autonomous vibration equations under $T$-periodic excitation, and whether the system possesses a stable periodic response has not been rigorously established in general. In this paper, the radiation damping is represented by an equivalent constant-coefficient linear damping model commonly used in engineering practice, and the PTO system is modeled as a linear spring acting in parallel with a nonlinear damper whose damping coefficient is proportional to a power of the relative velocity. Using the coincidence degree theory of Mawhin, we prove that the resulting system admits a unique $T$-periodic solution, and we further prove that the solution of the Cauchy problem with arbitrary initial values converges asymptotically to this periodic solution. Numerical simulations for a catamaran-type PAWEC confirm the theoretical results and illustrate the global attractivity of the periodic response.

title: Hydrokinetic energy recovery using a controllable-pitch propeller on a kite-assisted ship: Propeller performance mapping and a notional route case study
summary: To enhance the efficiency of wind-assisted ships, the propeller may operate as a turbine. Because harvesting efficiency is strongly dependent on blade pitch, this study maps the propulsive and generative performance of a controllable pitch
content: To enhance the efficiency of wind-assisted ships, the propeller may operate as a turbine. Because harvesting efficiency is strongly dependent on blade pitch, this study maps the propulsive and generative performance of a controllable pitch propeller (CPP) by simulating the Potsdam Propeller Test Case (PPTC) across a wide range of blade and advance angles. The power coefficient ( C P ) reaches 0.22 at design pitch, but achieves a global maximum of 0.44 at a 215° reversed pitch. The VORTEX ship performance model utilised this map to evaluate a notional merchant vessel with a 160 m 2 kite on a transatlantic route. Only mechanical shaft energy was considered, electrical losses are neglected. Results indicate hydrokinetic energy harvesting delivers minimal benefits over wind-assist alone at transit speeds of 18 kts and above. However, effectiveness scales rapidly during slow-steaming; at 15 kts , harvesting provides a 7.3% relative improvement over kite-assist alone (raising the absolute voyage energy reduction from 9.3% to 10.0%). System performance is sensitive to wind conditions, ship speed, kite size, and propeller type; notably, fixed-pitch propellers recover three to eight times less energy than CPPs. While maximising energy recovery requires CPPs capable of full blade inversion, conventional CPPs still capture the majority of the available generative benefit.

title: From Problematic Residues to Valuable Streams: Analytical Characterization and Valorization of Secondary Fractions from Agricultural-Waste Thermochemical Conversion
summary: Agricultural residues are increasingly used as feedstocks for renewable heat and power generation, but their thermochemical conversion also produces secondary fractions that are often treated as problematic wastes. Condensates, tars, aqueou
content: Agricultural residues are increasingly used as feedstocks for renewable heat and power generation, but their thermochemical conversion also produces secondary fractions that are often treated as problematic wastes. Condensates, tars, aqueous phases, bio-oil-derived liquids, chars, and ash-rich residues may cause corrosion, fouling, toxicity, microbial inhibition, or additional treatment costs. However, these streams may also contain recoverable chemicals, catalytic feedstocks, biodegradable carbon sources, or functional carbonaceous materials. This narrative review examines secondary fractions generated during the torrefaction, pyrolysis, gasification, and hydrothermal processing of agricultural waste as streams that can be analytically characterized and potentially valorized, rather than simply treated as unavoidable residues. Particular attention is given to the role of chromatographic, spectroscopic, elemental, thermal, and bulk physicochemical analyses in determining whether a fraction is suitable for separation, purification, catalytic upgrading, biological transformation, energy recovery, or controlled disposal. The review also highlights key research gaps, including inconsistent terminology, feedstock variability, excessive reliance on model compounds, insufficient quantitative chromatographic data, limited integration of chemical analysis with biological testing, and the scarcity of techno-economic and life-cycle assessments. An analytical-to-valorization decision framework is proposed to support more complete circular waste-to-energy systems.

title: Consume better, integrate more renewables: a critical framework for assessing energy synergy
summary: The combination of renewable energy and energy efficiency is often described as synergistic, although its benefits are evaluated using indicators and references that are not always equivalent. This article develops a critical framework for
content: The combination of renewable energy and energy efficiency is often described as synergistic, although its benefits are evaluated using indicators and references that are not always equivalent. This article develops a critical framework for assessing that interaction through a targeted integrative review of verified scientific literature and technical documents, emphasizing recent publications. The synthesis compares mechanisms, analytical boundaries, operating conditions, and the scope of the evidence without estimating an aggregate effect or conducting a bibliometric analysis. The findings distinguish reduced energy per service, electricity supply substitution, temporal flexibility, and consumer responses. Based on this differentiation, the Integrated Energy Synergy Model (MISE, its Spanish acronym) is reformulated as a conceptual proposal connecting renewables, efficiency, enablers, optimization decisions, and sustainability outcomes. A comparison is proposed between a reference and standalone efficiency, standalone renewables, and joint implementation scenarios, maintaining service equivalence and assessment conditions. The framework identifies favorable, zero, or unfavorable interactions for each indicator and avoids interpreting reduced electricity purchases as automatic evidence of total savings. The discussion explains why consumption timing, rebound, financing, and implementation constraints condition benefits. It concludes that synergy should be treated as a testable hypothesis rather than an inherent attribute of technological combination. MISE requires empirical validation or calibrated simulations before local benefits can be estimated or specific configurations recommended.

title: Turning sunlight into electricity: how does solar power work?
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This project explores the fundamental principles of solar energy and its crucial role in the ongoing global energy transition, with a specific focus on Australia's renewable landscape. It breaks down the mechanical and technological differe
content: This project explores the fundamental principles of solar energy and its crucial role in the ongoing global energy transition, with a specific focus on Australia's renewable landscape. It breaks down the mechanical and technological differences between Solar Photovoltaic (PV) cells and Solar Thermal systems (including small-scale and concentrated solar thermal). Furthermore, the document highlights real-world case studies of large-scale clean energy developments—such as the Aldoga Solar Farm in Queensland and the Goulburn River Hybrid project in New South Wales—analyzing their socioeconomic impacts, local job creation, and regional grid stabilization. This work serves as a comprehensive overview of how modern solar technologies operate and contribute to community sustainability.

title: Petrocultures and the Energy Cycle: From Researcher to Politician and Back Again
summary: This paper explores the intersection between scholarly inquiry and political practice within the global energy transition. Drawing from the author’s experience as both a researcher in the energy humanities and the Climate Critic for the Gre
content: This paper explores the intersection between scholarly inquiry and political practice within the global energy transition. Drawing from the author’s experience as both a researcher in the energy humanities and the Climate Critic for the Green Party of Canada, it investigates how academic ideas about petrocultures can inform, challenge, or fail to influence political action. The analysis begins from the recognition that energy systems are not merely technical infrastructures but cultural and social formations that shape subjectivities, values, and imaginaries. Building on reflections from the Petrocultures Research Group and the After Oil project, the paper shows how collective and interdisciplinary research can reimagine both the content and the form of knowledge production on energy. These experiences reveal the persistence of fossil-fueled cultural logics within current narratives of renewable transition, where new energy regimes often reproduce the same extractive and unequal structures of petrocapitalism. The findings highlight how the shift to renewables risks becoming a “renewable normal” that conceals the continuity of fossil modernity behind the promise of green innovation. The discussion calls for an energy transition that is also a social and cultural transformation, linking decarbonization to equity, care, and collective responsibility. The conclusion emphasizes that a just and sustainable energy future depends on reimagining not only how energy is produced but also how societies understand and live with it.

title: The sectoral blind spot of green bonds in the European green transition
summary: Abstract As sustainable finance becomes the central engine of the European green transition, how green-bond proceeds map onto distinct environmental objectives remains poorly understood. This study provides cross-sectional econometric evide
content: Abstract As sustainable finance becomes the central engine of the European green transition, how green-bond proceeds map onto distinct environmental objectives remains poorly understood. This study provides cross-sectional econometric evidence on the macro-financial and environmental correlates of green-bond issuance across the EU-27. Defining market penetration as the green-bond share of total national corporate and sovereign issuance, we use four-year averages (2021–2024) to combine bivariate correlation with ordinary least squares regression. We find that issuance is associated with the share of renewable energy and environmental health but shows no detectable association with circular material use, ecosystem vitality, environmental taxation, or climate-change performance (R² = 0.44; renewable energy, p = 0.002; GDP per capita, p = 0.019; climate performance, p = 0.50). A concentration analysis further shows that participation broadened until 2021 and narrowed again in 2024 (Gini 0.85 in 2014, 0.48 in 2021, 0.79 in 2024) rather than rising steadily. These findings point to a critical policy challenge, as capital appears to follow institutional capacity and structural measurability rather than holistic climate ambition, creating a sectoral blind spot. To broaden the environmental reach of green bonds, we identify the standardisation of metrics for underfunded sectors – through the EU Taxonomy and the European Green Bond Standard – as the most direct policy lever.

title: Editorial: Adaptive building envelopes and renewable energy strategies
summary: Achieving climate-neutral building operation remains a major challenge for the building sector, 10 requiring reductions in energy consumption, improvements in resource efficiency, and greater 11 integration of renewable energy technologies.
content: Achieving climate-neutral building operation remains a major challenge for the building sector, 10 requiring reductions in energy consumption, improvements in resource efficiency, and greater 11 integration of renewable energy technologies.
