title: Os pilares do ganho de escala na agricultura circular
source: Anais ... Encontro Nacional de Engenharia de Produção/Anais do Encontro Nacional de Engenharia de Produção
summary: 1. Introdução Sendo um dos setores econômicos com maior produção de biomassa e um grande potencial para a Economia Circular (EC) e a bioeconomia, a agricultura contribui para o estabelecimento de mercados verdes, o crescimento de iniciativa
content: 1. Introdução Sendo um dos setores econômicos com maior produção de biomassa e um grande potencial para a Economia Circular (EC) e a bioeconomia, a agricultura contribui para o estabelecimento de mercados verdes, o crescimento de iniciativas de valorização de biomassa e a descarbonização da economia mundial.Além dos ganhos de mercado e de sustentabilidade, as iniciativas de EC no setor agrícola são vias para o atingimento dos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS) da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU), a exemplo de ODS 2 "Fome zero", ODS 11 "Cidades e Comunidades Sustentáveis", ODS 12 "Consumo e Produção Responsáveis" e ODS 13 "Combate às Alterações Climáticas", e a mitigação das mudanças do clima (Duque-Acevedo et al., 2020; Holden et al., 2023).Apesar da reconhecida potencialidade, no geral, as práticas de EC no meio agrícola ainda se restringem à pequena escala, sendo observadas em pequenos negócios e comunidades rurais.Para que os benefícios da EC sejam plenamente alcançados, é necessário ampliar a escala de influência dessas práticas, o que requer a articulação de diferentes atores em múltiplas frentes de atuação (Shawky; Gibbons; Selim, 2025).O processo de ganhar relevância em contextos meso e macroeconômicos se baseia na coexistência de avanços tecnológicos e alterações nas práticas sociais, de forma a gerar impactos sólidos e duradouros, podendo ser compreendido como uma transição sociotécnica.Na prática, isso se reflete em modelos de negócio que, ganhando relevância no mercado, se tornam acessíveis a públicos diversos e influenciam padrões pré-existentes em suas áreas de atuação.Essas interações mercadológicas e sociotécnicas são tidas na literatura como caminhos de transição ou escalabilidade, para que soluções de nicho sejam incorporadas ao contexto amplo (Johnston; Baker, 2005; Moore; Riddell; Vocisano, 2015; Siegel; van Leeuwen, 2025).Velasco-Muñoz et al. (2021) apontaram a necessidade dos esforços científicos para aumentar a eficiência e diminuir as externalidades negativas da agricultura através de práticas de EC, mas salientaram o protagonismo do entendimento sobre como essas práticas operam e como poderiam ser implementadas no setor.Assim, entende-se que é fundamental, para a implementação, em larga escala, das soluções circulares nas cadeias agrícolas, que a comunidade científica compreenda o estágio de maturidade da literatura especializada, a fim de esclarecer o cenário global do desenvolvimento dessas iniciativas, apontar fatores que favoreçam sua aplicação no setor agrícola e identificar potenciais campos de investigação minuciosa.Embora estudos anteriores tenham apontado a necessidade de circularizar a agricultura, poucos sintetizaram sistematicamente os fatores que viabilizam a transição XLVI ENCONTRO NACIONAL DE ENGENHARIA DE PRODUÇÃO "Engenharia de Produção para a Transição Sustentável: Modelagem de Dados e Inovação" São Paulo/SP, 20 a 23 de outubro de 2026. 2 sociotécnica para implementar essas práticas em larg

title: ABORDAGENS BASEADAS EM MODELOS MATEMÁTICOS PARA ALOCAÇÃO E DIMENSIONAMENTO DE GERAÇÃO DISTRIBUÍDA
source: Anais ... Encontro Nacional de Engenharia de Produção/Anais do Encontro Nacional de Engenharia de Produção
summary: O presente artigo introduz um modelo de Programação Quadrática Inteira Mista (PQIM), onde as potências ativa e reativa serão representadas na forma de corrente, assim como as potências das demandas pelas cargas.Três variações do modelo PQIM
content: O presente artigo introduz um modelo de Programação Quadrática Inteira Mista (PQIM), onde as potências ativa e reativa serão representadas na forma de corrente, assim como as potências das demandas pelas cargas.Três variações do modelo PQIM para geração distribuída são propostas.A primeira variação considera apenas o problema de redução de perdas, ou seja, não há alocação e dimensionamento de unidades de geração distribuída (GD).A segunda variação recebe uma rede já reconfigurada para decidir onde alocar as unidades de GD.A terceira variação otimiza simultaneamente a reconfiguração, alocação e dimensionamento das unidades de GD.Os modelos são testados em dois sistemas com 33 e 135 barras, respectivamente.Os resultados indicam que as abordagens propostas são satisfatórias na redução de perdas no sistema de 33 barras e uma das abordagens apresentou redução de perdas, considerando variações no fator de penetração da carga dentro do sistema de 135 barras.

title: "Indian Energy Generation Observatory: A Multi-Source Dataset of Energy Generation, Power Supply, Renewable Energy, and Outages"
summary: "The Indian Energy Generation Observatory is a multi-source dataset developed to provide a comprehensive view of India's electricity generation, power supply, renewable energy availability, and generating-unit outages. It integrates data fr
content: "The Indian Energy Generation Observatory is a multi-source dataset developed to provide a comprehensive view of India's electricity generation, power supply, renewable energy availability, and generating-unit outages. It integrates data from official sources, including the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) and Grid Controller of India (Grid-India), covering conventional and renewable energy sources across different temporal and geographical levels. The dataset consists of multiple structured tables containing daily generation records, generating-unit performance, outage events, grid-level generation, state-wise power supply, renewable energy availability, and grid disturbances. It provides data in CSV, Excel, and Apache Parquet formats to support accessibility and efficient computational analysis. The dataset is designed to facilitate research in energy analytics, power system reliability, renewable energy integration, electricity demand and supply assessment, and energy infrastructure planning. By consolidating information from multiple authoritative sources into a unified and documented collection, the Indian Energy Generation Observatory provides a useful resource for researchers, analysts, policymakers, and stakeholders studying the Indian power sector."

title: Peran Moderasi Eco-Efficiency pada Pengaruh Environmental Management Accounting dan Green Accounting Practices terhadap Environmental Performance Hotel di Bali
source: MENAWAN Jurnal Riset dan Publikasi Ilmu Ekonomi
summary: The hospitality industry plays a vital role in Bali's economy; however, its operational activities also pose environmental challenges that require sustainable management. This study aims to examine the effects of Environmental Management Ac
content: The hospitality industry plays a vital role in Bali's economy; however, its operational activities also pose environmental challenges that require sustainable management. This study aims to examine the effects of Environmental Management Accounting (EMA) and Green Accounting Practices (GAP) on Environmental Performance (EP), with Eco-Efficiency (EF) serving as a moderating variable, among four- and five-star hotels operated by Marriott and Hilton in Bali. A quantitative research approach was employed using a census sampling technique involving 132 respondents comprising Accounting Managers, Sales and Marketing Managers, and Operations Managers. Primary data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings reveal that EMA and GAP have positive and significant effects on EP, with path coefficients of 0.391 and 0.379, respectively. Furthermore, EF positively and significantly affects EP, with a coefficient of 0.241. Moderation analysis confirms that EF strengthens the effect of EMA on EP (interaction coefficient 0.211) and the effect of GAP on EP (0.165). All relationships are statistically significant (p < 0.05), while the proposed model explains 46.8% of the variance in environmental performance. These findings highlight the importance of integrating environmental management accounting, green accounting practices, and resource efficiency to enhance environmental performance. This study provides practical implications for hotel management in developing measurable sustainability strategies, optimizing resource utilization, and balancing economic objectives with long-term environmental conservation.

title: Cost-Based Price Floors, Soft Budgets and Capacity Adjustment in China’s Solar Photovoltaic Industry
summary: Persistent overcapacity in photovoltaic (PV) manufacturing raises a question for the economic sustainability of renewable energy supply chains: does protecting producers’ margins help or hinder capacity adjustment? We evaluate cost-based pr
content: Persistent overcapacity in photovoltaic (PV) manufacturing raises a question for the economic sustainability of renewable energy supply chains: does protecting producers’ margins help or hinder capacity adjustment? We evaluate cost-based price floors with an agent-based model of China’s PV module industry that features adaptive pricing, market-share-driven investment, credit guarantees and local government rescues. The model is driven by observed polysilicon prices and reproduces eight of ten moments from public company data within a pre-registered tolerance, although it captures only part of the 2024 price decline. Policy effects are paired comparisons across 200 random seeds. A floor at each firm’s own average total cost lowers utilisation by 5.8 percentage points and welfare by 1.1% over ten years and, in the main specification, slows exit even under hard budgets; its welfare loss grows when products are more substitutable and turns into a gain only when demand is much less price-sensitive, R&D responds strongly to profits or share pressure is very high. An industry-reference floor stabilises prices but cuts capacity exit by 75%; its 1.8% welfare gain falls to 0.5% when surviving firms are not valued as additional variety. An admission standard for new capacity raises utilisation and, while demand plateaus, welfare. Protecting margins is a poor substitute for policies that change the returns to expansion.

title: Beyond Project Delivery: Reimagining Aid Governance for Sustainable Community Development in Nigeria
source: European Conference on Management, Leadership and Governance (ECMLG)
summary: The uncertainty surrounding foreign-assisted projects and programmes, despite the influx of development aid, stems from governance and institutional policies, which have undermined efforts to achieve sustainable development in developing co
content: The uncertainty surrounding foreign-assisted projects and programmes, despite the influx of development aid, stems from governance and institutional policies, which have undermined efforts to achieve sustainable development in developing countries like Nigeria. World Bank-assisted projects have played a significant role in achieving sustainable community development in areas such as healthcare services, education, infrastructure, social services, and poverty alleviation. The benefits of foreign aid have been influenced by unfavourable policies, resulting in the discontinuity of projects and programmes after donor exit. This study examines how foreign aid governance can be reinvented through World Bank-assisted projects and programmes, thereby providing a framework to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of foreign aid in achieving sustainable community development. Good Governance Theory (GGT) was adopted as the theoretical framework, focusing on the basic principles of transparency, accountability, responsiveness, participation, and institutional effectiveness. The study employed a qualitative research design, drawing on secondary data from government policy documents, World Bank project reports, and academic journals on foreign-aided projects and programmes, and analysed the collected data thematically. Findings revealed that sustainable community development outcomes are driven by good institutional mechanisms, inclusive participation, effective resource management, inter-agency collaboration, and that the lack of these inhibits the sustainability of community projects. The study contributes to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 16 and 17 by strengthening local governance institutions and policies, and institutionalising community partnership and participation across the phases of community projects and programmes. Thus, enhancing transparency and accountability mechanisms, and ensuring policy continuity among political administrators. The study concludes that sustainable community development should prioritise good governance and local ownership, rather than merely meeting project and programme implementation targets. The study recommends that the government, development agencies, and international organisations adopt a governance-based framework for the design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of foreign-aided projects to ensure sustainable community development.

title: A Conjectural Equilibrium Model for Public Goods: Dynamics and Policy Implications
summary: ABSTRACT We provide a dynamic conjectural equilibrium model where, at each date, heterogeneous and uncertain individuals decide whether to contribute or not to a public good. The model frames the contribution problem within a novel perspect
content: ABSTRACT We provide a dynamic conjectural equilibrium model where, at each date, heterogeneous and uncertain individuals decide whether to contribute or not to a public good. The model frames the contribution problem within a novel perspective, keeping various classical public good issues together. The results show that a unique conjectural equilibrium exists for given structural parameters; however, it is compatible with an infinity of possible equilibrium conjectures. Various policies can be used to increase the provision of the good, including (i) the enlargement of the exogenous provision of public goods, (ii) a fight against corruption and inefficiencies in the public sector, (iii) positive (negative) incentives to contribute (or not contribute), and (iv) actions supporting social capital. However, significant dynamical effects must be considered: the interaction between uncertainty and the conjectures makes any given policy differ in both impact and feasibility, since the system might eventually stop at a position different from the projected one. This can help explain the varied observable impacts of the same policy across different real‐world contexts. Nevertheless, policies (iii) and (iv) proved to be effective and more feasible.

title: LIGHTING QUALITY ASSESSMENT OF A HERITAGE LIBRARY: A CASE STUDY OF MONTGOMERY HALL, QUAID-E-AZAM LIBRARY, LAHORE
summary: Heritage buildings adapted for contemporary library use often face difficulties in providing adequate and uniform lighting while preserving their architectural character. This study evaluates the lighting quality of Montgomery Hall, a histo
content: Heritage buildings adapted for contemporary library use often face difficulties in providing adequate and uniform lighting while preserving their architectural character. This study evaluates the lighting quality of Montgomery Hall, a historic Neo-Classical reading space within the Quaid-e-Azam Library, Lahore, with particular emphasis on illuminance, visual comfort, and compliance with recommended lighting requirements. A case-study methodology was adopted using field measurements, architectural documentation, a user questionnaire, and lighting assessment modelling. The study area was divided into a 3 m × 3 m measurement grid, and illuminance was measured at 20 points at a desk height of 0.75 m during daytime operating hours. Measured values were compared with recommended illuminance levels for reading, bookshelf, and circulation areas. A questionnaire survey was conducted to assess users’ perceptions of lighting quality, satisfaction, visual comfort, and reading conditions. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS. The field assessment revealed spatial variation in illuminance. Areas adjacent to the large arched windows received higher daylight levels, whereas central and interior zones, particularly bookshelf areas, experienced lower illumination. Glare and excessive brightness were observed near window-adjacent seating. Questionnaire analysis indicated significant relationships between lighting-related variables and perceived visual comfort and satisfaction, with regression models statistically significant at p < 0.001. The findings indicate a performance gap between the existing lighting environment and contemporary library requirements. Conservation-sensitive interventions, including improved luminaire distribution, glare control, optimised daylight integration, and energy-efficient lighting controls, are recommended to enhance visual comfort and lighting uniformity while preserving the heritage character of Montgomery Hall.

title: Submolecular Selenium Enables Low‐Pressure and Recyclable All‐Solid‐State Li–Se Batteries
summary: ABSTRACT All‐solid‐state lithium‐selenium (Li–Se) batteries offer high energy density and intrinsic safety, but their practical deployment is hindered by sluggish solid‐state redox kinetics, large volume fluctuations, and unstable solid‐sol
content: ABSTRACT All‐solid‐state lithium‐selenium (Li–Se) batteries offer high energy density and intrinsic safety, but their practical deployment is hindered by sluggish solid‐state redox kinetics, large volume fluctuations, and unstable solid‐solid interfaces, particularly under low stack pressure. Here we report a submolecular Se x cathode by converting crystalline cyclo‐Se 8 into amorphous single‐atom and short‐chain Se (Se x , x < 4) species anchored on graphene (Se x @G), which increases the electronic conductivity from 6.3 × 10 −5 to 13 S cm −1 and Li + diffusivity from 1.7 × 10 −14 to 2.0 × 10 −11 cm 2 s −1 . Meanwhile, a Li 2 O‐nanoshell‐modified sulfide solid electrolyte is designed to stabilize the interface against both Li metal and Se cathode. As a result, all‐solid‐state Li–Se batteries deliver the theoretical capacity of 673 mAh g −1 at 0.1 C and retain 86% capacity over 2800 cycles at 3 C under 8 MPa, with stable operation down to −30°C. All‐solid‐state Li–Se pouch cells further achieve an energy density of 420 Wh kg −1 and 94% capacity retention after 300 cycles under 2.5 MPa. Post‐mortem analysis reveals that the submolecular Se x species are not only structurally preserved but also recyclable after electrochemical cycling within the solid‐state reaction environment. This work establishes submolecular chalcogen chemistry as a new design paradigm for low‐pressure, recyclable, and high‐energy all‐solid‐state batteries.

title: Desain Buck-Boost Converter MPPT Berbasis Feedforward Neural Network (ANN) pada Sistem Photovoltaic
summary: The development of renewable energy technology has encouraged the utilization of photovoltaic (PV) systems as an alternative energy source. However, variations in irradiance and temperature cause changes in PV output power, making it diffic
content: The development of renewable energy technology has encouraged the utilization of photovoltaic (PV) systems as an alternative energy source. However, variations in irradiance and temperature cause changes in PV output power, making it difficult to maintain the Maximum Power Point (MPP). This study aims to design and analyze a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) system based on an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) integrated with a buck-boost converter for a PV system. The system was simulated using MATLAB/Simulink with a 100 Wp PV module and a Feedforward Neural Network (FNN) trained using the Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) algorithm. The FNN uses irradiance and temperature as inputs and generates the duty cycle as the converter control output. Testing was conducted under 16 conditions with irradiance levels of 300–1000 W/m² and temperatures of 25–40°C. The training results achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.92, with a duty cycle ranging from 0.40 to 0.45. The highest PV power was 99.84 W at 1000 W/m² and 25°C, with an output power of 92.85 W and an efficiency of 93.00%. The results demonstrate that the FNN-based MPPT system can adjust the duty cycle according to changes in PV conditions.

title: Optimal Control‐Limit Structure of Nonperiodic Inspection and Delayed Replacement Policies for Stochastic Degradation Systems
summary: ABSTRACT For many engineering systems, continuous condition monitoring is often infeasible due to technical and cost constraints, and system condition information is only available at inspection times. Delayed replacement, implemented after
content: ABSTRACT For many engineering systems, continuous condition monitoring is often infeasible due to technical and cost constraints, and system condition information is only available at inspection times. Delayed replacement, implemented after a certain waiting time, can help reduce inspection costs. Motivated by this, we study an optimal inspection and maintenance problem aimed at minimizing the long‐run average cost rate, in which system degradation can only be revealed through inspections. At each inspection epoch, the decision maker chooses whether to schedule a nonperiodic inspection, implement a delayed replacement, or perform an immediate replacement to mitigate the risk of failure. By formulating the problem as an average‐cost semi‐Markov decision process, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal average cost rate and characterize an optimal stationary policy. Furthermore, the optimal policy is shown to exhibit a control‐limit structure, under which the optimal waiting times across different actions follow an ordered pattern. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate that the proposed policy consistently outperforms commonly used benchmark strategies. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis further reveals a clear separation of roles: degradation dynamics primarily influence the length of optimal waiting times, whereas cost parameters govern the partition of inspection and replacement action regions.

title: Spatiotemporal graph neural network-based multi-node coordinated scheduling optimization for renewable energy power systems
source: Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy
summary: The large-scale integration of wind and photovoltaic generation turns power-system dispatch into a strongly coupled spatiotemporal decision problem. Conventional optimization models become computationally demanding as system scale and uncer
content: The large-scale integration of wind and photovoltaic generation turns power-system dispatch into a strongly coupled spatiotemporal decision problem. Conventional optimization models become computationally demanding as system scale and uncertainty grow, whereas existing data-driven dispatch models usually rely on fixed topologies and cannot ensure physically admissible decisions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a physics-constrained spatiotemporal graph cooperative dispatch network (PC-STGCD) for multi-node coordinated scheduling of renewable-dominated power systems. First, an adaptive coupling graph fuses impedance-based electrical distance with similarity learned from node embeddings, so that weather-driven correlations among electrically remote stations can be identified. Second, a dual-branch encoder combines multi-head graph attention with multi-scale gated dilated convolution to jointly capture spatial cooperation and renewable fluctuations over different horizons. Third, power balance, ramping, branch-capacity, and storage-energy constraints are embedded into training as differentiable penalties, and a warm-started projection layer maps the network output onto the linearized feasible region during inference. On the modified IEEE 118-bus system, PC-STGCD reduces the operating cost by 6.94% and the renewable curtailment rate by 47.9% relative to the strongest baseline, limits the constraint violation rate to 0.43%, and produces a dispatch decision within 0.36 s; these improvements are statistically significant over five independent runs and persist under N−1 and N−2 contingencies without retraining. Validation on 1 year of measured data from a 236-node provincial grid yields an average cost saving of 5.84% and a 43.3% reduction in curtailment, demonstrating the potential of the proposed method for online cooperative dispatch of renewable-rich networks.

title: Organizational Rootedness, Territorial Dynamic Capabilities and Environmental Priorities: Evidence From European Regional Firms
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines organizational rootedness as the degree of territorial integration that differentiates environmental priorities in regional firms. Although its constitutive function in shaping environmental engagement is recogn
content: ABSTRACT This study examines organizational rootedness as the degree of territorial integration that differentiates environmental priorities in regional firms. Although its constitutive function in shaping environmental engagement is recognized, its ordering function in determining which initiatives become more salient is less clear. We examine whether higher‐ and lower‐rooted regional firm patterns prioritize environmental initiatives differently, how their priorities vary under social and economic pressures, and how these pressures are associated with eco‐innovation orientation in higher‐rooted patterns. The conceptual framework integrates organizational embeddedness with territorial dynamic capabilities: the first conceptualizes the different degrees of firms' territorial integration, whereas the second explains how this integration supports readaptation processes and eco‐innovative development under pressures. Using a novel database from 145 EU regions, we identify distinct priorities in environmental initiatives, reordered under contextual pressures. Furthermore, in higher‐rooted patterns, eco‐innovation orientation tends to be stronger under economic than social pressures. The findings suggest that managers should treat environmental sustainability as a territorially ordered portfolio of initiatives.

title: Can the Crippled Giant Walk Again? Evaluating Nigeria’s Rising State Credentials in Environmental Resource Governance
source: European Conference on Management, Leadership and Governance (ECMLG)
summary: Nigeria, often referred to as the “Giant of Africa”, has long been perceived as an emerging power with evident regional influence, a perception that stems from its foreign policy adopted by successive administrations since independence. How
content: Nigeria, often referred to as the “Giant of Africa”, has long been perceived as an emerging power with evident regional influence, a perception that stems from its foreign policy adopted by successive administrations since independence. However, internal challenges have transformed the accolade into a “crippled giant” in literature. Drawing on secondary sources, this paper assesses Nigeria's credentials as a rising state in an emerging multipolar world, where traditional Western hegemony is contested by rising Asian powers, the expansion of the BRICS, and shifting global alliances. The analysis reveals that Nigeria has substantial credentials, including its youthful demographic, enormous military capabilities, growing soft power projection, rapid technological expansion, particularly in fintech, and abundant natural resources, including oil, lithium, and sand. However, unlike traditional credentials of rising states that emphasise military and economic capabilities in existing international relations scholarship, this paper argues that strategic natural resource endowment and environmental governance constitute an additional pivotal credential of rising states, as the ability to harness these resources can translate into economic prosperity. Nevertheless, these credentials remain under-optimised due to structural and institutional challenges, environmental security issues, corruption, and policy inconsistency, which undermine Nigeria’s capacity. The paper concludes that for Nigeria to realistically join the league of rising states, transformational leadership must be embraced, accompanied by domestic reforms in governance, security, and economic diversification beyond oil. Until such conversion is pragmatically embraced, the crippled giant is unlikely to walk again on the global stage, and as a result, Nigeria’s potentials will remain unrealised.

title: Built in Minutes, Checked by Script: Instructor-Made Interactive Chemistry Study Guides with Generative AI
summary: Interactive study guides, with practice problems that change every time, help on request and small simulations, are valuable and slow to build; few instructors have time to make one for every unit. I describe a workflow that lets one instru
content: Interactive study guides, with practice problems that change every time, help on request and small simulations, are valuable and slow to build; few instructors have time to make one for every unit. I describe a workflow that lets one instructor, a chemist with no programming background, build such guides with a generative AI coding assistant in about ten minutes each, plus about half an hour of polishing, and deliver them through GitHub Pages to Canvas or D2L Brightspace. Twenty pages for General Chemistry I, a course for non-science majors, biochemistry and Organic Chemistry I illustrate it; seventeen were built with this workflow over about a month. Each guide is a single web page that runs in any current browser, needs no account and sends nothing to a server. The guides share a design: a roadmap of the topic, sections in teaching order, problems whose numbers change each time, feedback on wrong answers, and small virtual instruments such as a titration, a calorimeter and a thin-layer plate; nine offer three levels of help. The biochemistry and organic guides take their values from named textbooks, and a check of every page, which ran about 1.6 million generated problems and recomputed each answer independently, found no wrong answer key but did find faults that reading had missed: named mistakes accepted as correct, correct answers rejected, an answer given away, and physically impossible setups; all were fixed and the check run again. No learning outcomes are claimed; evaluation is future work.

title: Green Financial Innovations and Sustainable Economic Development: Evidence from Emerging Economies
summary: Green financial innovations have the potential for mobilizing financial resources towards environmental and inclusive sustainable development. Green financial innovation includes green bonds, climate resilient financial products, fintech-ba
content: Green financial innovations have the potential for mobilizing financial resources towards environmental and inclusive sustainable development. Green financial innovation includes green bonds, climate resilient financial products, fintech-based environmental, social, and governance platforms. These platforms facilitate the allocation of capital towards green and sustainable investment, which provisions the transition to promote environmentally sustainable practices and sustainable economic development (SED). The financial development and access to financial services contribute to improving resource allocation, mobilizing savings, facilitating investment, and expanding access to financial opportunities. Since the emerging economies are facing the dual challenge of environmental pressures and SED, the fundamental objective of this research is to explore the role of green financial innovation, financial development, information, and communication technology (ICT and renewable energy consumption (REC) on SED in selected emerging economies. This study concentrated on panel data ranging from 1990 to 2022 to investigate sustainable economic development in selected countries. The Generalized Method of Movements (GMM) is used for empirical analysis as it provides remedial measure for presence of serial correlation and endogeneity. Based on empirics, green financial innovation has positive and significant effect on SED in emerging countries. Moreover, it is observed that financial development, REC, ICT, international tourism, trade openness, and foreign direct investment exert positive and significant impact on SED. However, this research identified that natural resource abundance and aging population dependency variables have negative and significant effect on SED. Concluding, this research suggested that financial institutions should devised regulatory frameworks and hybrid models to support green finance through innovative financial products, digital banking, fintech solutions, and services. Likewise, central banks should prioritize strategies that enhance financial development, increase the availability of green financial resources, and ensure efficient mechanisms for directing capital towards renewable tech-driven industries.

title: Active Symmetry Support Control for Grid-Following/Grid-Forming Hybrid Renewable Energy Stations Considering Transient Synchronization Stability
summary: An active symmetry support control method based on model predictive control and incorporating transient synchronization security boundaries is developed for a grid-following (GFL)/grid-gorming (GFM) hybrid renewable-energy station comprisin
content: An active symmetry support control method based on model predictive control and incorporating transient synchronization security boundaries is developed for a grid-following (GFL)/grid-gorming (GFM) hybrid renewable-energy station comprising GFL wind energy and GFM energy storage. The control objective is to suppress disturbance-induced departures from the dynamic balance between generation-side support and grid/load demand, which are referred to here as power asymmetry rather than phase-domain three-phase imbalance, and to restore a power-symmetric operating state through coordinated active- and reactive-power support. Reduced-order transient synchronization models are established separately for the GFL phase-locked loop and the GFM virtual synchronous generator without explicitly constructing a transient coupling model between the two converter types. For the GFM converter, damping energy is incorporated into the fault-stage transient-energy balance. The resulting transient-energy functions and critical-energy criteria are used to determine the synchronization-stability boundaries, which are then mapped into dynamically updated P-Q feasible regions. A frequency–voltage prediction model combining a system frequency-response model and a point-of-common-coupling voltage-sensitivity model is then established. The GFL/GFM transient-energy constraints, dynamic P-Q security regions, power-regulation capability limits, and command-direction constraints are embedded in the receding-horizon optimization to coordinate active- and reactive-power support while preserving transient synchronization security. Local linearization of the transient-energy constraints and second-order-cone reformulation of the dynamic P-Q regions are adopted to improve online computational efficiency. Simulation results show that, compared with MPC without transient synchronization security boundaries, the proposed strategy limits power-angle excursions, enhances active- and reactive-power support, and mitigates frequency and voltage deviations. A sensitivity analysis is further conducted to examine how uncertainties in grid impedance, inertia, damping, and filter inductance affect the calculated critical energies and P-Q security regions. The results highlight the distinct effects of these parameters on the critical-energy thresholds and dynamic energy margins.

title: Stabilizing hydrogen bonds and engineering multi-component hetero-solvation architecture for dendrite-free zinc metal anodes
summary: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are promising candidates for renewable grid energy storage, but their development is limited by non-uniform zinc deposition, hydrogen evolution reactions (HERs), and byproduct growth at the zinc anode inte
content: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are promising candidates for renewable grid energy storage, but their development is limited by non-uniform zinc deposition, hydrogen evolution reactions (HERs), and byproduct growth at the zinc anode interface. Herein, a dual-regulation strategy integrating bulk solvation reorganization with interfacial dynamic electrostatic shielding is developed by introducing a trace amount of 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium iodide (BMIMI, BI) into a Zn(OTf) 2 aqueous electrolyte. Multi-dimensional microscopic spectra and quantitative molecular dynamics simulations confirm that the co-incorporation of BMIM + cations and I − anions establishes a diversified I − -H 2 O-OTf − hetero-primary solvation sheath, disrupting the chemical degradation pathways caused by free water aggregation. Due to its electrostatic adsorption energy advantage on multiple crystal planes, BMIM + preferentially occupies active sites to form a dynamic cation shielding field. This forces Zn 2+ to diffuse away smoothly from local tip protrusions and induces lateral planar epitaxial growth along the dense (002) preferred crystal plane. Consequently, the electrolyte shows stability within the fundamental potential window during cyclic voltammetry tests, and the interfacial desolvation energy barrier decreases from 51.29 to 23.28 kJ mol −1 . This affords the Zn//Cu battery a stable Coulombic efficiency of 99.74%, and the Zn//Zn symmetric battery achieves a lifespan exceeding 7500 h under variable loads and high areal capacities. In full-cell applications, the cell maintains a capacity retention of 84.07% after 5000 cycles at a high current density of 2 A g −1 . Combined with ex-situ distribution of relaxation times and dynamic impedance evolution, this strategy confirms the feasibility of the system for industrial-grade variable-load energy storage scenarios.

title: Low temperature equilibrium conditions for H2, CO, CO2, CH4 mixtures ('Syngas') aiming for separation by flash distillation
summary: The need for clean energy has grown due to dramatic increases in global emissions and increasing environmental concerns. This has driven a worldwide trend toward developing sustainable energy solutions while reducing carbon footprints. Biom
content: The need for clean energy has grown due to dramatic increases in global emissions and increasing environmental concerns. This has driven a worldwide trend toward developing sustainable energy solutions while reducing carbon footprints. Biomass has emerged as one of the most promising renewable sources, including crops, agricultural residuals, animal residues, solid waste, wood, and sewage. These materials are converted to biofuels through various processes, commonly producing syngas containing hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide. Separating these components is crucial since hydrogen offers excellent clean energy potential, methane provides a cleaner fossil fuel alternative, and capturing carbon dioxide reduces greenhouse gas emissions. However, common separation methods like flash distillation require equilibrium data unavailable in literature for four-component syngas mixtures. We employed a thermodynamic method supporting any number of components and phases at given conditions. The method combines stability testing with Helmholtz energy minimization, implemented through MATLAB code. Five syngas compositions were investigated across 70-290 K temperature ranges, with pressure determined algorithmically. Results demonstrate separation achieving up to 99% hydrogen purity and 98% carbon dioxide purity while retaining most mass. This approach provides reliable equilibrium data for syngas separation processes, enabling effective clean energy production and carbon capture from biomass-derived fuels.

title: Stage-Resolved Dynamics of Antibiotic Resistance Genes and Mobile Genetic Elements in Full-Scale Anaerobic Digestion Systems
summary: Abstract Anaerobic digestion (AD) has the potential to reduce antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) during waste treatment, yet evidence from full-scale plants remains limited and the relative importance of o
content: Abstract Anaerobic digestion (AD) has the potential to reduce antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) during waste treatment, yet evidence from full-scale plants remains limited and the relative importance of operational and physicochemical drivers is poorly resolved. Here, we profiled stage-resolved resistome and mobilome dynamics across substrates, digestates, and post-digestion storages from ten Swedish farm-scale AD plants (42 samples). High-throughput qPCR (ResistoMap) was combined with absolute 16S rRNA gene quantification and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to quantify ARG/MGE abundances and characterise bacterial community structure. ARGs and MGEs showed heterogeneous changes during digestion and subsequent storage, with both increases and decreases across plants. Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) suggested that higher pH and free ammonia were associated with decreasing trends in ARG and MGE relative abundance. Stage-resolved correlation networks revealed a dominant ARG-MGE association backbone that remained largely conserved from substrates to digestates and storage, whereas host-ARG and host-MGE associations were extensively restructured across processing stages. Collectively, these results show that stage-resolved, network-informed analyses offer a more informative framework than pooled, static approaches for evaluating resistance persistence and potential environmental risks associated with digestate application.

title: The k-th power expectile periodogram for time series analysis
summary: Abstract This paper introduces the k-th power expectile periodogram (KEP) as a generalization of the quantile periodogram (QP) and expectile periodogram (EP) for time series analysis. Constructed from trigonometric k-th power expectile regr
content: Abstract This paper introduces the k-th power expectile periodogram (KEP) as a generalization of the quantile periodogram (QP) and expectile periodogram (EP) for time series analysis. Constructed from trigonometric k-th power expectile regression (KER), the KEP provides a flexible tool to balance robustness and efficiency. The KEP retains the key properties of the ordinary periodogram as a frequency-domain representation of serial dependence in time series, while offering a more comprehensive understanding by examining the data across the entire range of expectile levels with power 1 < k ≤ 2. Simulations demonstrate the capability of the KEP in detecting hidden periodicities, while maintaining robustness against outliers. We establish the asymptotic theory and investigate the relationship between the KEP and the so-called k-th power expectile spectrum (KES). Finally, we leverage the inherent two-dimensional property of the KEP to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify the epilepsy electroencephalogram (EEG) data, where the proposed estimator outperforms competitive estimators.

title: HiResCastNet: A 3D Deep Learning Model for Probabilistic Regional High‐Resolution Subseasonal Forecasting Through Downscaling
source: Journal of Geophysical Research Machine Learning and Computation
summary: Abstract High‐resolution subseasonal forecasts, spanning two to 6 weeks, play a vital role in bridging the gap between short‐range forecasts and seasonal predictions. They provide crucial information for decision‐making in disaster and haza
content: Abstract High‐resolution subseasonal forecasts, spanning two to 6 weeks, play a vital role in bridging the gap between short‐range forecasts and seasonal predictions. They provide crucial information for decision‐making in disaster and hazard preparedness, early warning systems, water resource management, and renewable energy. However, generating subseasonal forecasts at high spatial and temporal resolutions remains a significant challenge. Global subseasonal forecasting systems such as European Center for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) typically provide outputs at a coarse spatial resolution of about 31 km and a temporal resolution of 12 hr, which limits their usefulness for regional‐scale planning and impact assessments. Our three‐dimensional (3D) high‐resolution regional subseasonal forecasts are generated by dynamically downscaling the ECMWF subseasonal forecasts using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, producing outputs at a spatial resolution of 4 km and a temporal resolution of 3 hr. Yet, the dynamical downscaling model is computationally very demanding, especially when using multiple ensemble members. To address this limitation, we introduce HiResCastNet, a data‐driven, probabilistic downscaling framework combining Swin‐transformer and a diffusion model, which serves as an efficient surrogate for the traditional downscaling system. HiResCastNet takes spatio‐temporal coarse resolution forecasts from ECMWF subseasonal system as inputs, and generates 3D high‐resolution forecasts at 4 km spatial resolution and 3‐hourly intervals. Our results suggest that HiResCastNet significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining strong agreement with WRF physical model. It reproduces the dynamical behavior across variables such as wind and temperature and handles the downscaling of multiple ensemble members efficiently, which highlights its potential for operational use.

title: PyPacity: A Python framework for dynamic line rating
summary: Dynamic line rating (DLR) exploits the dependence of overhead-conductor ampacity on weather conditions to make better use of transmission capacity. IEEE Std 738 and CIGRE TB 601 define the reference thermal models, but provide equations rat
content: Dynamic line rating (DLR) exploits the dependence of overhead-conductor ampacity on weather conditions to make better use of transmission capacity. IEEE Std 738 and CIGRE TB 601 define the reference thermal models, but provide equations rather than software, so users must implement and verify them independently. PyPacity is an open-source Python library implementing the steady-state and transient methods of both standards behind a common interface, validated against their benchmark cases. Ampacity calculations can be embedded in larger workflows driven by measured or forecast weather data, from single-point studies to long time series.

title: BQEB: A Reproducibility-First Architecture for Modular Energy AI Benchmarking
source: International Journal of Global Innovations and Solutions (IJGIS)
summary: Reproducibility in applied energy AI research depends on more than a public dataset or a published benchmark: it depends on whether the software producing a benchmark’s numbers can be independently re-run, whether artifacts are versioned an
content: Reproducibility in applied energy AI research depends on more than a public dataset or a published benchmark: it depends on whether the software producing a benchmark’s numbers can be independently re-run, whether artifacts are versioned and checksummed, and whether governance practices are documented well enough that a discrepancy can be found rather than concealed. This paper presents the BQEB Reproducibility Architecture, a modular research-artifact framework for energy AI research, now formally released as an independent, citable artifact (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22291930). The architecture comprises four layers: a Research Artifact Layer connecting manuscripts, datasets, models, and experiments; a Reproducibility Layer built on deterministic execution, checksummed artifacts, and an evidence registry; a Benchmark Evolution Layer supporting extensions and comparative studies; and a Scientific Lineage Layer maintaining citation tracking, version management, and DOI separation across related artifacts. BQEB ForecastBench (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21735978), previously published standalone, is the first validated benchmark implementation developed within the BQEB Reproducibility Architecture—built using the framework, not identical to it. Within-environment deterministic execution has been verified through 15 real executions (3 seeds × 5 repeats, independently re-confirmed twice); checksummed-artifact verification has been executed against this program’s own engineering files, with real tamper-detection confirmed. Cross-environment reproducibility, statistical significance of model comparisons, and extensibility beyond this architecture’s first module remain explicitly disclosed as pending or future work, not claimed as validated. Where internal audit identified an unresolved issue—a numerical discrepancy between two published versions of the same benchmark result—we document it as a governance case rather than resolving it here. The contribution is the architecture itself: how a research program’s artifacts can be structured, checksummed, and tracked for independent verification, at the evidence tier this paper actually supports.

title: NES2Go: A Multi-Objective Dispatch and Decision Support Framework for Integrating Small Modular Reactors in Industrial Clusters
summary: This article presents Nuclear Energy Systems to Go (NES2Go), an hourly dispatch and multi-objective ranking model for assessing the integration of small modular reactors (SMRs) in industrial clusters across process heat, electricity and cog
content: This article presents Nuclear Energy Systems to Go (NES2Go), an hourly dispatch and multi-objective ranking model for assessing the integration of small modular reactors (SMRs) in industrial clusters across process heat, electricity and cogeneration operation. A harmonised database of SMR technologies is developed, covering technical, physical and operational characteristics from publicly available sources. The framework complements Renewable Energy Sources to Go (RES2Go), an open platform for matching energy demand and supply in European industry hubs. NES2Go compares economic performance, spatial footprint and annual fissile material requirement, with unmet heat retained as an additional objective in thermal modes. Annual grid export is reported descriptively and does not enter the ranking. Electricity reliability remains an acceptance criterion; unmet electricity is not an objective. Greenhouse gas emissions are reported alongside the ranking rather than entered as an objective. NES2Go simulates hourly SMR operation under varying industrial demand, renewable generation and storage configurations, with process heat demand resolved by temperature level to assess the thermodynamic compatibility of processes and reactors. Cogeneration mode represents the production of electricity and useful heat from the same reactor thermal output. The framework was tested in the port of Antwerp (Belgium) for process heat, electricity and cogeneration. The case study illustrated how temperature compatibility and operating mode constrain the ability of SMRs to supply industrial electricity and process heat. In cogeneration mode, fleets based on 19 designs passed screening and supplied approximately 31–77% of estimated heat demand, findings that apply to the case study for the port of Antwerp. NES2Go can be rolled out to other industrial clusters or individual companies using their demand profiles and assumptions. NES2Go is implemented in Python, providing a transparent and reproducible decision support tool for analysing the role of SMRs in future low emission industrial systems.

title: Pm-Kusum and India's Sustainable Energy Transition: A Critical Review of Solarising Agriculture, Energy Security And Rural Sustainability
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Abstract India’s transition towards sustainable energy is closely connected with the transformation of agricultural energy use. Irrigation has traditionally depended on subsidised electricity and diesel, enabling agricultural expansion but
content: Abstract India’s transition towards sustainable energy is closely connected with the transformation of agricultural energy use. Irrigation has traditionally depended on subsidised electricity and diesel, enabling agricultural expansion but also contributing to rising public expenditure, fossil-fuel consumption and pressure on groundwater resources. The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyaan (PM-KUSUM), introduced in 2019, represents a major national policy initiative that seeks to address these interconnected challenges through decentralised renewable-energy generation and solarisation of agricultural pumps. Unlike conventional renewable-energy programmes that primarily focus on electricity generation, PM-KUSUM places farmers at the centre of the energy transition by enabling them to use, generate and, under specified arrangements, sell renewable electricity. This chapter critically reviews the PM-KUSUM scheme through the perspectives of sustainable energy transition, agricultural economics and the water–energy nexus. The review synthesises relevant peer-reviewed literature, systematic review evidence and official policy documents to examine the scheme’s potential benefits, implementation challenges and sustainability implications. The analysis shows that solarisation can reduce dependence on diesel, improve daytime electricity availability, create opportunities for supplementary farm income and contribute to decentralised renewable-energy generation. However, solar irrigation is not automatically sustainable. Where the marginal cost of pumping approaches zero, inappropriate incentives can encourage excessive groundwater extraction. Evidence from India indicates that the outcomes of solar irrigation vary according to groundwater conditions, cropping patterns, tariff structures and the design of electricity buyback mechanisms. The chapter argues that the long-term success of PM-KUSUM depends on moving beyond pump installation towards integrated management of energy, water and agricultural resources. A conceptual framework is proposed in which policy design, financial accessibility, technological reliability, farmer participation, electricity-market incentives and groundwater governance jointly determine sustainable outcomes. The chapter concludes that PM-KUSUM has considerable potential to support India’s sustainable energy transition, provided future implementation is more inclusive, region-specific and closely aligned with groundwater conservation and efficient agricultural water use.

title: Green Intelligence 5.0: Designing a Net-Positive Digital Future through Artificial Intelligence, Environmental Sustainability, and Human Well-being
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a general-purpose layer across education, healthcare, agriculture, energy, manufacturing and governance. It can strengthen climate-risk mapping, renewable-energy forecasting, precision irrig
content: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a general-purpose layer across education, healthcare, agriculture, energy, manufacturing and governance. It can strengthen climate-risk mapping, renewable-energy forecasting, precision irrigation, biodiversity monitoring, waste sorting and early-warning systems. Yet AI is not immaterial: computation depends on electricity, cooling, water, hardware, minerals, networks and labour, while rapid equipment turnover adds to electronic waste. This paper asks how AI can be designed so that its verified benefits for people and the planet outweigh its lifecycle burdens. Using an integrative evidence-synthesis and conceptual framework approach, the paper proposes Green Intelligence 5.0, a six-pillar architecture integrating ecological responsibility, responsible AI, circular infrastructure, inclusion, human well-being and accountable governance. Three practical contributions are introduced: the GROW-AI operating model, a 30-point Green Intelligence Scorecard, and a Net-Positive-by-Design decision rule. Recent global indicators illustrate the scale of the challenge: the International Energy Agency estimated data-centre electricity use at about 415 TWh in 2024 and projects approximately 945 TWh by 2030 in its base case; the Global E-waste Monitor reported 62 billion kg of e-waste in 2022, with 22.3% documented as formally collected and recycled. These figures are presented as sourced contextual indicators, not as original measurements by the authors. The framework is mapped to SDGs 3, 4, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 16, with an India-focused proposition: “AI for All, Green by Design.” The paper concludes that digital progress should be assessed by net human and planetary value—not computational scale alone.

title: Motivating Consumers in the Protein Transition: Promoting Individual Change in a Collective Problem
summary: The protein transition, the societal shift towards more plant-based diets, is an important way to mitigate climate change. Like any sustainability transition, the protein transition requires technological innovations, changes in formal and
content: The protein transition, the societal shift towards more plant-based diets, is an important way to mitigate climate change. Like any sustainability transition, the protein transition requires technological innovations, changes in formal and informal rules and lasting consumer behavior change. However, consumer engagement, as well as individual behavior change, is not self-evident. Climate change is a collective problem, and as it is caused by collective behavior it also requires collective behavior change. When the collective dimension of the problem is not acknowledged, the scale of the problem may lead to low individual response efficacy beliefs because people believe that their individual behavior change is insignificant. Feeling part of a collective, cooperate with others, and collectively achieve goals may be able to motivate individual consumers in the collective problem of climate change. The current dissertation set out to study how consumers perceive their own role and that of other actors in the protein transition, and how consumers can be motivated to engage with this collective transition. In particular, we studied whether the ability to act as a collective, also known as collective agency, can be harnessed to promote consumer engagement with the protein transition. The studies showed a positive association between feeling connected to others and the perceived effect of individual behavior, as well as a positive association between the feeling of working together and the perceived effect of individual behavior. Additionally, the studies showed that emphasizing a change in collective behavior by means of trending or dynamic norm interventions can promote pro-environmental choices and positively affect norm perceptions. However, the current dissertation also identified some challenges when harnessing the collective to promote consumer engagement with the protein transition and possibly also other sustainability transitions. The feeling of being part of a collective appears difficult to activate through communication that can be used on a larger scale, such as slogans or campaigns. Also, observations in daily life regarding the shift towards more plant-based diets may affect the credibility of communication about collective efforts in the protein transition. All in all, the current dissertation highlights the opportunity of harnessing the collective to promote consumer engagement with the protein transition, identifies challenges with this approach and supports the development of interventions to accelerate the protein transition.

title: Transition to a much warmer climate for the global ocean and Antarctic Ice Sheet coupled system, and its reversibility
summary: Abstract. In Antarctica, two plausible tipping points have been suggested: an ocean tipping point involving a cold-to-warm transition of ice shelf cavities, and an ice sheet tipping point associated with the marine ice sheet instability. Th
content: Abstract. In Antarctica, two plausible tipping points have been suggested: an ocean tipping point involving a cold-to-warm transition of ice shelf cavities, and an ice sheet tipping point associated with the marine ice sheet instability. This study explores the existence of such tipping points at the scale of Antarctica, using a coupled ocean–ice-sheet model. We first apply and then remove an abrupt perturbation to the ocean, instantaneously switching the atmospheric forcing to high-end 23rd century conditions, which shifts all ice shelf cavities of Antarctica to warm conditions. Our findings reveal that Antarctic continental shelf waters rapidly warm, leading to a regime shift with increased ice shelf melt rates, significant ice shelf thinning, and retreat of ice sheet grounding lines. The ocean conditions reverse over a few years when the atmospheric perturbation ceases, while the ice sheet’s response is much slower. Some regions of East Antarctica show signs of ice sheet reversibility over several centuries. In contrast, we identify 14 ice streams, primarily in the Ross, Amundsen, Filchner, Ronne, and Dronning Maud Land basins, that still undergo irreversible retreat several centuries after the removal of the perturbation.

title: Agent-based simulation of shared autonomous electric vehicle fleets: application to Montreal Olympic Park
summary: Abstract Many cities now offer shared vehicle fleets as an alternative mode of daily transportation. These fleets can be further enhanced through the use of autonomous or electric autonomous vehicles, which reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emiss
content: Abstract Many cities now offer shared vehicle fleets as an alternative mode of daily transportation. These fleets can be further enhanced through the use of autonomous or electric autonomous vehicles, which reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, lower staffing requirements, enable automated charging, and provide smoother operation. This paper proposes an agent-based simulation framework to model a fleet of shared electric autonomous vehicles (SEAVs) providing one-way, short-distance trips. A case study is conducted for Montreal’s Olympic Park, encompassing five strategically located stations. By varying key fleet parameters, 105 scenarios are generated and analyzed. Results indicate that a fleet of 20 vehicles with a 50 km range and 30 parking spots can meet demand across all tested customer arrival frequencies, achieving service performance rates of 90% or higher. Vehicle range is shown to have minimal impact on performance compared to fleet size and demand probability. Additionally, reducing the number of parking spots decreases the number of rejected customers but increases the number of empty trips.

title: Delivering ~100,000 tCO2e/year Through an Integrated Energy Management Programme Across ADNOC Offshore Assets — 2025 Portfolio Verification and Lessons Learned
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract ADNOC Offshore's 2025 energy-management portfolio delivered 97,011 tCO2e/year of independently verified greenhouse-gas (GHG) abatement across 13 initiatives spanning six operating areas: Upper Zakum, Lower Zakum, SARB, Zirku, Das I
content: Abstract ADNOC Offshore's 2025 energy-management portfolio delivered 97,011 tCO2e/year of independently verified greenhouse-gas (GHG) abatement across 13 initiatives spanning six operating areas: Upper Zakum, Lower Zakum, SARB, Zirku, Das Island and Ettouk Island. Unlike the majority of decarbonization case studies, which report projected abatement estimated at the project-sanction stage, this paper presents verified end-of-year performance measured against pre-committed, asset-specific baselines. The interventions are organized into four engineering families: gas-turbine and generation heat-rate improvement; process reconfiguration to eliminate parasitic loads; end-use auxiliary load reduction; and replacement of diesel-based power generation with grid power. Each initiative was tracked against an asset-specific energy-performance indicator and converted to abatement using asset-specific fuel-gas emission factors. The results demonstrate that disciplined, predominantly low-capital interventions on existing offshore infrastructure can translate national net-zero commitments into auditable, year-on-year decarbonization at national-oil-company (NOC) scale. Two transferable lessons emerge: modest heat-rate improvements on existing gas-turbine generators are the workhorse of mature-asset decarbonization, and parasitic loads are systematically under-investigated relative to their abatement potential and low cost of mitigation. Recognized abatement is projected to exceed 130,000 tCO2e/year by 2030 as the 2025 initiatives reach steady-state operation and proven mechanisms are extended to additional assets.

title: Policies for Microfinance and Climate Justice
summary: Climate change is a global phenomenon with disproportionate regional impacts, particularly affecting low-income countries that contribute the least to greenhouse gas emissions. Vulnerable communities, including women, children, and marginal
content: Climate change is a global phenomenon with disproportionate regional impacts, particularly affecting low-income countries that contribute the least to greenhouse gas emissions. Vulnerable communities, including women, children, and marginalized groups, face heightened risks due to existing socio-economic inequalities. The adverse effects of climate change, such as water scarcity and extreme weather events, exacerbate these vulnerabilities, making climate justice a pressing issue. This chapter explores the intersection of climate change, gender inequality, and poverty, emphasizing the need for inclusive adaptation strategies. The chapter’s general objective is to analyze the role of microfinance in advancing climate justice by enhancing the adaptive capacity of marginalized groups, particularly women, through financial mechanisms tailored to climate resilience. It explores how microfinance institutions (MFIs) can support climate adaptation and mitigation efforts while addressing social inequalities exacerbated by climate change. The chapter employs a literature review approach, synthesizing existing academic literature, policy documents on climate change adaptation, gender inequality, and microfinance. It analyzes case studies from countries like Bangladesh, Kenya, and Peru, where MFIs have integrated climate considerations into their operations. The chapter also reviews policy frameworks and initiatives that promote green microfinance and climate resilience. The findings suggest that microfinance can play a crucial role in climate change adaptation by providing financial resources to vulnerable communities. Green microfinance, which integrates environmental considerations, has shown promise in promoting sustainable practices and reducing vulnerability. However, challenges such as high implementation costs and limited awareness among MFIs remain. Policy interventions, including regulatory measures and financial incentives, are essential to mainstream climate finance and enhance the adaptive capacity of vulnerable populations. The chapter concludes that empowering women through microfinance is key to achieving climate justice and building resilient communities.

title: Stabilizing a fragile antibiotic order: reconstructing the development of EU policy on antimicrobial resistance
summary: Displaying findings from a discourse and dispositif analysis, this article traces the emergence and evolution of European Union antimicrobial resistance (AMR) regulation, addressing a significant gap in medical sociology and social science
content: Displaying findings from a discourse and dispositif analysis, this article traces the emergence and evolution of European Union antimicrobial resistance (AMR) regulation, addressing a significant gap in medical sociology and social science research. We understand antibiotics as infrastructure. Hence, we understand AMR as a phenomenon of infrastructural destabilization of a techno-social order and its political regulation as an endeavour to reestablish stability. The EU’s biopolitical regulatory dilemma — balancing its public health mandate versus economic imperatives and the individual’s right to access antibiotics — reflects deeper tensions between free trade market policies, extractive prosperity models, and the pursuit of technological control. While early regulatory steps were taken, the EU’s approach remains hesitant and fragmented, as the cultural symbolism of antibiotics as a “miracle weapon” and productivity factor obstructs recognition of AMR as a socially produced consequence. Ultimately, EU measures have prioritized status quo containment over structural reform, perpetuating an unstable antibiotic order.

title: Pre-symptomatic crop intelligence: a closed-loop framework for anticipatory, confidence-aware decision-making in site-specific crop protection
summary: Abstract Purpose Symptom-triggered crop protection acts only after damage is committed, and the intervention window has narrowed. This review reframes pre-symptomatic sensing from a detection problem into a closed decision loop, establishin
content: Abstract Purpose Symptom-triggered crop protection acts only after damage is committed, and the intervention window has narrowed. This review reframes pre-symptomatic sensing from a detection problem into a closed decision loop, establishing the physiological lead time of a signal, set against its detection confidence and the latency of the response it can trigger, as the organizing principle for anticipatory, site-specific decision-making. Methods A systematic-narrative synthesis was conducted across major bibliographic databases through June 2026. Studies reporting pre-symptomatic capability under field or realistic conditions were retained and coded onto a coupled lead-time × confidence × actionability framework spanning sensing, inference, and actuation. Results Optical modalities were found to dominate the evidence base, while electrophysiological and volatile signals extended achievable lead time. Single modalities were insufficient to separate biotic from abiotic stress, motivating heterogeneous fusion. Edge inference and temporal onset forecasting remained immature, detection confidence was rarely quantified, and the sensing-to-actuation loop was seldom closed. Reported performance degraded sharply from laboratory to field, particularly in perennial and smallholder systems. Conclusions A unifying Pre-Symptomatic Crop Intelligence framework is proposed, governed by the principle that system value is bounded by the weakest of lead time, detection confidence, and response latency; priorities identified include lead-time-labeled benchmarks, uncertainty-aware inference, field-robust fusion, and economic evaluation for perennial crops.

title: Guest Editorial: Spinach in Your Teeth: How the Hyper-Transparency of Methane Emissions Data Will Impact the Oil and Gas Industry
summary: This guest editorial addresses how the methane data landscape is changing as new organizations expand emissions monitoring efforts and seek to put the information to work. The truth of the matter is that there is much about the oil and gas
content: This guest editorial addresses how the methane data landscape is changing as new organizations expand emissions monitoring efforts and seek to put the information to work. The truth of the matter is that there is much about the oil and gas industry’s methane emissions that isn’t especially new. We’ve been hearing for years that methane is considered the second-most-harmful greenhouse gas overall after CO2, that methane is 28–80 times more potent than CO2 as a greenhouse gas, and that the oil and gas sector continues to be responsible for a large fraction of the world’s methane emissions. Despite an impressive amount of attention being paid to this topic throughout the SPE and the industry over the past decade, the International Energy Agency estimates that the oil and gas sector (upstream and downstream combined) emitted over 81 million metric tons of methane in 2025, which translates to over 21% of the total methane emissions that can be attributed to human activity during that timeframe. But let’s be honest: As confronting as these numbers might be, many oil and gas industry insiders were largely aware of them already. And many of the technologies being used to track methane aren’t all that new, either. Satellites have been used to monitor and measure methane emissions around the world for at least 10 years. It has also been possible for quite some time to augment intelligence from satellites with data sets from other collection methods and technologies— including aircraft, drones, ground-based systems, and continuous monitors—to create a joined-up, detailed understanding of what is happening with regard to methane emissions almost everywhere in the world. However, as technologically impressive as they are, most of these capabilities also don’t come as a total surprise to the oil and gas industry. But a change is underway that will very likely prove to be materially important to the sector, and that will definitely be worthy of its attention.

content: As mudanças climáticas deixaram de ser exclusivamente uma pauta de conformidade ambiental para se consolidarem como um dos maiores vetores de risco e disrupção operacional do século XXI (Wang
