Based on panel data from 31 provinces in China (2012–2023), this study constructs a dual-methodological framework integrating the Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to investigate the spatiotemporal evolution, transmission mechanisms, and causal recipes of this relationship. The empirical results reveal four key findings. First, green manufacturing transformation exhibits a steady upward trend but follows a distinct “East-High, West-Low” spatial gradient. Second, the digital economy exerts a significant positive impact on local green transformation and generates positive spatial spillovers to neighboring regions, though the spillover effect is weaker than the direct effect due to administrative barriers; technological innovation and environmental regulation are identified as two pivotal transmission channels. Third, a “Northeast Paradox” is observed: while the digital economy promotes green growth in most regions, it shows a significant negative interaction effect in the Northeast, attributed to the “lock-in effect” of rigid industrial structures. Fourth, fsQCA identifies four sufficient pathways leading to high green efficiency: “Digital-Talent Driven,” “Digital-Innovation Driven”, “Internal-Capability Driven”, and “Comprehensive Synergy”. Notably, a substitution effect exists between talent support and R&D intensity, offering flexible transformation strategies for resource-constrained regions. By moving beyond linear effect analysis, this study provides a multidimensional analytical roadmap to support the design of differentiated, context-sensitive green transformation policies.

title: Decarbonisation dynamics through electrification: Sectoral pathways for Colombia
source: International Journal of Sustainable Energy Planning and Management
summary: Electrification facilitates decarbonisation; however, its effectiveness depends on the way public policies shape demand-side technological substitution across end-use sectors. In Colombia, despite efforts to integrate renewable energy sourc
content: Electrification facilitates decarbonisation; however, its effectiveness depends on the way public policies shape demand-side technological substitution across end-use sectors. In Colombia, despite efforts to integrate renewable energy sources into the electricity mix, the energy transition remains constrained by insufficient policy coordination across transport, residential, tertiary, and industrial sectors, placing the country at risk of failing to meet its CO2 emissions reduction targets. While existing studies propose multiple transition pathways – largely focused on developed economies – demand-side dynamics and behavioural responses to policy-driven technological substitution remain marginal in analyses of developing countries. To examine these dynamics, a sectoral energy transition model for Colombia is developed using a system dynamics approach that captures feedback between public policy, consumer behaviour, and long-term energy demand. Results indicate that a transformation of the Colombian energy matrix by 2050 is achievable from the demand side, provided electrification policies prioritise transport, residential, and tertiary sectors. Residential electrification rises from 47% in 2024 to over 92% by 2050, while clean technologies exceed 80% of the transport fleet. Economy-wide electrification increases electricity demand by a factor of 3.5, requiring a 4.3-fold expansion of fully renewable electricity generation capacity.

title: Metakaolin-based concrete for marine structures: Performances, chloride binding, and perspectives
summary: Abstract Metakaolin (MK) contains highly reactive alumina, which could be a proper supplementary cementitious material to design low-carbon and durable concrete in marine structures. This review critically examines the characteristics of MK
content: Abstract Metakaolin (MK) contains highly reactive alumina, which could be a proper supplementary cementitious material to design low-carbon and durable concrete in marine structures. This review critically examines the characteristics of MK and its effects on cement hydration, mechanical properties, durability, and the chloride-binding capacity. The relatively fine particle size and high volume of reactive contents of silica and alumina enable MK to provide proper filler effects and pozzolanic reactions, forming additional C-A-S-H gels to refine the pore structure of the cementitious matrix. For ternary-blended system, MK could react with calcite to form hemicarboaluminate (Hc) and monocarboaluminate (Mc), while the synergistic use of MK and calcite can enable cement replacement levels of approximately 40-50 wt% while maintaining comparable strength. Appropriate MK incorporation (5 wt% to 10 wt%) can reduce water absorption by up to 38.82% and, in some studies, the carbonation depth could be reduced by 46.1%. Furthermore, MK enhances chloride resistance through physical pore refinement and adsorption, while Hc and Mc promote chemical chloride binding and Friedel’s salt formation. These mechanisms demonstrate the potential of MK for durable and low-carbon marine concrete.

title: Axiom-Free Invariants of the Cut-Set Lattice in the Chrysene Formalism: Admissible Maximal Chains, Obstruction Functionals, and Disjoint Optima on Hamiltonian Paths
summary: This paper characterizes the combinatorial and redox invariants governing the stepwise linearization of the chrysene skeleton, defining the cleavage poset of a chain-forming cut set — whose maximal chains represent the cleavage orderings —
content: This paper characterizes the combinatorial and redox invariants governing the stepwise linearization of the chrysene skeleton, defining the cleavage poset of a chain-forming cut set — whose maximal chains represent the cleavage orderings — to establish how substituent placement and ring-opening sequence determine synthetic pathway properties. Two functionals on this poset structure the analysis: an activation index that counts cleavage steps at unhydrogenated carbons, and the oxidation number, which acts as a path-independent state function that fixes total redox demand directly from the endpoint structures. Because the chrysene skeleton has an automorphism group of order 2, its two K-regions lie in a single symmetry orbit that is preserved under 6,12-disubstitution, meaning that ring opening at positions 11–12 and 5–6 represents a single experimental equivalence class. Of the 27 chain-forming cut sets, 24 admit a clean ordering, while the remaining sets are characterized precisely as those in which every bond joins two ring-fusion carbons. Across all cut sets and clean orderings, the activation index has an exact lower bound of 2, which is attained on the poset. Evaluating where the substituted carbons land along the product chain reveals a structural trade-off between activation count and terminal substituent placement. Exactly 1 of the 7 realized substituent patterns places a substituted carbon at a chain terminus as required for the target 1-yl membrane lipid, and every cut set realizing this terminal pattern carries an activation index of 3. Consequently, minimizing the activation index and delivering the terminal-linkage product are optimized by disjoint families of cut sets separated by 1 step, confirming that the 3-step sequence is optimal for the target lipid architecture. Extending the enumeration across all 5 four-ring cata-condensed isomers — including the branched isomer — shows that all 5 share the minimum activation index of 2 and the clean cut-set count of 24, while chrysene uniquely minimizes the total number of clean orderings. Finally, because the oxidation number is a state function, reaching the target ether lipid chain requires 52 reducing equivalents per dimer independently of mechanism, confirming the route-based material ledger directly from the molecular endpoints.

title: Copper-modified nickel membrane reactor for electrochemical hydrogenation in low-conductivity water
summary: Electrochemical hydrogenation (ECH) for wastewater treatment is often limited by its reliance on high-conductivity media, restricting applications such as nitrate-contaminated groundwater remediation. Here we show that a copper-modified ele
content: Electrochemical hydrogenation (ECH) for wastewater treatment is often limited by its reliance on high-conductivity media, restricting applications such as nitrate-contaminated groundwater remediation. Here we show that a copper-modified electrochemical nickel membrane reactor (Cu/eNMR) can remove nitrate from deionized water. For water containing 50 mg/L NO3−-N, Cu/eNMR achieves 90.5% nitrate removal at 5 mA/cm2 within 3 h, with an energy consumption of 0.139 kWh/g-N, compared with 12.8% removal and 8.6 kWh/g-N for a conventional reactor using the same cathode. Mechanistic analysis reveals that nitrate hydrogenation is enabled by direct electron transfer to the reaction chamber, coupled with directional K+ migration that maintains charge neutrality, while interfacial charge-transfer resistance governs electron-flow direction. The membrane configuration also suppresses anodic side reactions, including active chlorine formation, chlorinated by-products, organic polymerization and metal-induced anode deactivation. Solar-powered treatment of real groundwater further demonstrates practical applicability, while life-cycle analysis indicates reduced greenhouse-gas emissions compared with conventional electrochemical and biological treatments. This architecture broadens the feasible application of ECH to low-conductivity water treatment. Electrochemical hydrogenation is promising for water remediation yet limited by high energy use in poorly conductive media. Here, the authors report a copper-modified nickel membrane reactor for energy-efficient nitrate removal from low-conductivity water.

title: Research on Stabilization Strategies for Inter-Enterprise Cooperative Carbon Reduction Behavior under Incentive-Based Environmental Regulation
source: Polish Journal of Environmental Studies Politics Economics and Industry
summary: To effectively mitigate the free-riding phenomenon prevailing in inter-enterprise collaborative carbon emission reduction behavior, this paper establishes an evolutionary game model for cooperative carbon emission reduction based on the spa
content: To effectively mitigate the free-riding phenomenon prevailing in inter-enterprise collaborative carbon emission reduction behavior, this paper establishes an evolutionary game model for cooperative carbon emission reduction based on the spatial public goods game. By introducing incentive-based environmental regulations, the equilibrium solution of the game model is derived and analyzed. Numerical simulations are conducted to examine the impact of three types of incentive-based environmental regulations on the strategic choices of inter-enterprise cooperative carbon emission reduction in China. The research conclusions are presented as follows: (1) when two enterprises both opt for cooperation in carbon reduction, each party can obtain higher benefits compared with adopting non-cooperative strategies. In addition, when the synergistic benefits of cooperative emission reduction exceed the sum of the benefits from one enterprise cooperating while the other does not, and when this sum surpasses the sum of non-cooperative emission reduction benefits and external effects, the optimal choice for both enterprises is to adopt a cooperative emission reduction pattern; (2) incentive-based environmental regulation acts as an implicit incremental cost. Among these, an increase in carbon tax rates will inhibit enterprises from carrying out collaborative emission reduction activities. On the contrary, an increase in carbon emission trading prices and input subsidy coefficients can effectively incentivize enterprises to implement joint carbon emission reduction. This study reveals the dynamic evolutionary path and degree of influence of enterprises’ cooperative carbon reduction under incentive-based environmental regulation, providing theoretical foundations and practical references for facilitating inter-enterprise collaboration on carbon reduction initiatives.

title: Household affordability of sanitary landfilling is governed by cost allocation rather than metropolitan economic capacity
summary: Abstract Open dumping remains a dominant municipal solid waste disposal practice globally, including in megacities whose populations and economic output rival that of small countries. Sanitary landfilling is a common transition away from op
content: Abstract Open dumping remains a dominant municipal solid waste disposal practice globally, including in megacities whose populations and economic output rival that of small countries. Sanitary landfilling is a common transition away from open dumping, yet system-level feasibility does not translate into household affordability. Here we quantify this divergence using an integrated city-scale framework that combines spatial landfill siting, engineering-based net-present-value modeling, and satellite-derived metropolitan gross domestic product. Applying this framework across six developing megacities with over 100 million residents, we find that all cities possess surplus land meeting screening-level suitability criteria. Required cost-recovery tipping fees range from 54–130 US dollars per tonne, with 5 th –95 th -percentile intervals of ±25%–30% under joint parameter uncertainty. Under full household cost recovery, these fees imply annual disposal costs equivalent to 1.2%–2.0% of the minimum wage, whereas associated revenue requirements represent only 0.26%–1.04% of metropolitan gross domestic product. Across cities, household affordability is uncorrelated with metropolitan economic capacity. Landfill depth is the dominant engineering control on affordability, particularly in high-rainfall systems, but cost allocation exerts greater leverage than any design parameter. Thus, technically and macroscopically feasible landfills may remain difficult to sustain through direct household cost recovery without cross-subsidization and public financing.

title: Questions raised by sinking seaweed: A Life Cycle Assessment of Macroalgae Cultivation and Sinking for Carbon Dioxide Removal
summary: Abstract Purpose: Among the portfolio of emerging marine carbon dioxide removal approaches, macroalgae cultivation and sinking (MCS) has attracted growing scientific, commercial, and policy interest; yet its environmental implications remai
content: Abstract Purpose: Among the portfolio of emerging marine carbon dioxide removal approaches, macroalgae cultivation and sinking (MCS) has attracted growing scientific, commercial, and policy interest; yet its environmental implications remain poorly understood. This study presents the first comprehensive cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment of the ‘grow nearshore, sink offshore’ MCS strategy with Saccharina latissima in Northern Europe. Beyond climate mitigation potential, it identifies environmental trade-offs and hotspots across three areas of protection, and evaluates key parameters influencing environmental performance. Methods: An attributional cradle-to-grave LCA was conducted, covering the complete MCS product system from onshore hatchery operations and nearshore cultivation to offshore transportation and deep-sea deposition. A functional unit of one tonne of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) stored for > 100 years via the intentional deep-sea deposition of cultivated macroalgae below the deep-ocean carbon sequestration horizon (> 1 000 m) was adopted. Using ReCiPe 2016, environmental impacts were assessed across climate change, ecosystem quality, human health, and natural resource scarcity, accounting for carbon (C) and nutrient uptake and leakage. Contribution analyses were performed to identify environmental hotspots, while the influence of seven key parameters (biomass yield, transportation distance, C/nutrient leakage, line seeding method, longline material, future background conditions, and LCIA method family) were examined via sensitivity analyses. Results and discussion: Under the modelled conditions, MCS achieves a net climate benefit of 227 kg CO 2 -eq/t of CO 2 stored. This is, however, accompanied by net adverse impacts on ecosystem quality (2.03 x 10 − 6 species.yr), human health (1.40 x 10 − 3 DALYs), and natural resource scarcity (83.9 USD 2013). Offshore transportation, C/nutrient leakage, cultivation infrastructure, and hatchery electricity consumption emerge as the main environmental hotspots. Climate change impacts are the most susceptible to sensitivity, with the largest effects caused by biomass yield and sequestration durability variability, with a 50% reduction in yield or increase in C/nutrient leakage, shifting MCS from net carbon removal technology to net-emitter. Alternative longline materials, future background conditions, and LCIA method families also each substantially affect the environmental outcomes. Conclusions: Although MCS could potentially achieve net carbon removal under the assumed conditions, sequestration efficiency is limited (23%), and its broader environmental trade-offs and remaining uncertainties raise concerns regarding large-scale deployment. Improving biomass yields, reducing transportation, optimising cultivation and deposition infrastructure, and adopting energy-efficient, renewably powered hatchery operations could markedly enhance environmental performance. Nevertheless, further researc

title: Calculation of carbon footprint of forestry tourism and optimization of emission reduction strategies in sustainable supply chain management
summary: This study aims to construct a high-precision and dynamic carbon footprint accounting model and provide feasible emission reduction strategy combinations to address specific issues in the forest tourism supply chain, such as blurred boundar
content: This study aims to construct a high-precision and dynamic carbon footprint accounting model and provide feasible emission reduction strategy combinations to address specific issues in the forest tourism supply chain, such as blurred boundaries in carbon footprint accounting, static lag in emission factors, and divergent emission reduction strategies in balancing environmental, economic, and social benefits. Firstly, this paper determines the lifecycle accounting boundaries based on the ISO 14067 (International Organization for Standardization) standard, covering upstream material supply, midstream scenic area operation, downstream waste disposal, and tourist return. Then, this paper collects and preprocesses multi-source heterogeneous data, including smart meter data and GPS (Global Positioning System) trajectories, to address data silos and noise issues. Next, this paper introduces a triple dynamic correction mechanism based on load factors, grid time series marginal emission factors, and biodynamic parameters to achieve spatiotemporal dynamic perception of carbon footprint. Also, this paper takes the dynamic accounting results as input and constructs a multi-objective optimization model with clean energy substitution rate as the decision variable. Finally, this paper uses NSGA-II (Non dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II) and elite strategy to solve the Pareto front, achieving closed-loop collaboration between accounting accuracy and multi-dimensional objective trading operations. The experimental results show that the average absolute percentage error of the carbon footprint time series prediction method in this paper is 2.01%; the unit emission reduction cost is 40.97 yuan/ton of carbon dioxide equivalent; the tourist satisfaction index reaches 0.87. The method proposed in this paper combines triple dynamic factor correction with three-dimensional NSGA-II multi-objective optimization, significantly improving the accuracy of carbon footprint calculation in the forestry tourism supply chain, and formulating emission reduction strategies that consider environmental, economic, and social benefits.

title: Decoupling the Impact of Key Industrial Operating Conditions on the Stability of CoP Alloy Catalysts for the Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
summary: Abstract Green hydrogen, as a key energy carrier in pursuit of carbon neutrality, has advantages such as high energy density and zero carbon emissions. Transition metal phosphides (TMPs) are considered potential catalysts for producing gree
content: Abstract Green hydrogen, as a key energy carrier in pursuit of carbon neutrality, has advantages such as high energy density and zero carbon emissions. Transition metal phosphides (TMPs) are considered potential catalysts for producing green hydrogen through water electrolysis due to their unique electronic structures and excellent conductivities. However, TMPs face challenges such as activity degradation and unclear stability degradation mechanisms under actual operating conditions. Herein, CoP was selected as a model electrocatalyst to systematically evaluate its durability under decoupled key industrial conditions. The influence of various parameters such as soaking time, temperature, electrolyte concentration, current density, and reverse current on the structure of CoP and the performance of water electrolysis was revealed. Under the specific experimental protocols employed in this study, the results showed that the effect of reverse current was the most significant, leading to changes in structural morphology, driving irreversible structural phase transition of CoP to form CoOOH, and resulting in a large amount of P dissolution, structure collapse, and reconstruction. High electrolyte concentration is the second major factor limiting stability, as the high concentration of OH– adsorbs on the material surface and is difficult to desorb, suppressing charge transfer and slowing down reaction kinetics. In contrast, current density has a relatively minor effect on CoP activity and stability. This work highlights the crucial role of conducting accelerated degradation tests under real working conditions, providing insights and theoretical guidance for designing efficient electrocatalysts for industrial applications.

title: Is there an environmental Kuznets curve in Saudi Arabia? cointegration and decoupling evidence
summary: Introduction This study asks whether the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) describes the relationship between income and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions in Saudi Arabia. Methods A log-quadratic EKC specification, augmented with primary ene
content: Introduction This study asks whether the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) describes the relationship between income and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions in Saudi Arabia. Methods A log-quadratic EKC specification, augmented with primary energy use and the renewable share of primary energy, is estimated on annual data for 1990–2022 (n = 33; 31 effective observations in the dynamic models). The sample ends in 2022 because the harmonised real-income series ends in that year; data for 2023–2024 are used descriptively only. The autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds test provides the decisive evidence. For the specification selected by both the Akaike and Schwarz criteria, ARDL(2,0,0,0,1), the bounds F-statistic is 2.01, below the 10% lower (I(0)) bound of both the asymptotic (2.45) and finite-sample (2.75) critical values. It remains below the I(0) bound in all 162 lag configurations, in the best-fitting configuration free of residual serial correlation, after adding level shifts for 2014 and 2016, and after adding oil rents and trade openness. A Gregory–Hansen test allowing a regime shift also detects no cointegration. Unit-root tests indicate that per-capita emissions are stationary around a shifting mean, whereas income is integrated of order one. Long-run coefficients from the ARDL, nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) and dynamic ordinary least squares (DOLS) models are therefore reported only as exploratory quantities with measures of uncertainty. The income terms are jointly insignificant in every specification, and the Lind–Mehlum slope conditions for an inverted U are not met. The NARDL Wald test does not reject long-run income symmetry (p = 0.62), a result conditional on a long-run framework that the bounds test does not support. Results The data provide no evidence of an inverted-U EKC, but they also do not establish a statistically significant U-shape. Total emissions show relative but not absolute decoupling from gross domestic product (GDP): the Tapio elasticity is 0.34 for 2016–2022, and total emissions rose by 7.9% between 2016 and 2024. The decline in carbon intensity slowed after 2016. Discussion These patterns are described as associations and are not attributed causally to Vision 2030. Code and data that reproduce every table and figure are provided.

title: Physicochemical Controls on Methane Adsorption Capacity of Coal Seams Beneath Red Beds: Roles of Pore Structure and Surface Chemistry
summary: Abstract The abnormal occurrence of coalbed methane (CBM) beneath thick red beds poses a major challenge to gas disaster prevention and safe coal mining. Previous studies have mainly focused on the sealing capacity of red beds and their inf
content: Abstract The abnormal occurrence of coalbed methane (CBM) beneath thick red beds poses a major challenge to gas disaster prevention and safe coal mining. Previous studies have mainly focused on the sealing capacity of red beds and their influence on CBM migration and accumulation, whereas the response of the underlying coal matrix, particularly its methane adsorption behavior, pore structure, and surface chemistry, remains insufficiently understood. Consequently, the mechanisms linking red beds occurrence conditions to variations in the methane storage capacity of underlying coal seams have not yet been fully quantified. Taking the Xutuan Coal Mine in the Huaibei Coalfield as a case study, this work integrates high-pressure methane adsorption–desorption tests, low-pressure N2/CO2 adsorption experiments, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy to reveal the effects of red beds on methane adsorption behavior, pore structure, and chemical composition of coal. The results show that, with increasing red beds thickness and decreasing distance between the coal seam and the red beds, micropore volume generally decreases, whereas the relative abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups increases. Correlation analysis further shows that methane adsorption capacity is positively correlated with micropore volume and negatively correlated with the relative abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups, with correlation coefficients of 1.0 and −1.0, respectively. These results indicate that both micropore structure and surface chemical characteristics are closely related to the variation in methane adsorption capacity. Combined with the geological characteristics of the red beds, the observed micropore variation may be related to stress-related pore compression, whereas the increase in oxygen-containing functional groups reflects changes in the surface chemical structure of the coal matrix. Fe-related oxidation is proposed as a geochemical hypothesis for the observed variation in oxygen-containing functional groups, based on the regional geological background of the red beds. Furthermore, a normalized red beds geometric influence index, k, was proposed to integrate red beds thickness and its spatial relationship with the coal seam. Field gas content exhibits a strong negative correlation with k, indicating that the proposed index can provide a quantitative reference for the relative evaluation of methane occurrence under comparable red beds geological conditions.

title: A socio-technical transition framework for biomass torrefaction at the nexus of energy security and energy justice
summary: The global energy transition necessitates a critical re-evaluation of bioenergy’s role and moving beyond its conventional perception as a mere renewable source, aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 7 (Aff
content: The global energy transition necessitates a critical re-evaluation of bioenergy’s role and moving beyond its conventional perception as a mere renewable source, aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 13 (Climate Action). Biomass torrefaction, a mild thermochemical pretreatment, emerges as a pivotal technology that can fundamentally upgrade biomass into a high-quality solid biofuel. This review examines torrefaction as a socio-technical pathway that may contribute to multidimensional energy security while identifying potential energy justice implications across distributive, procedural, recognitional, and restorative dimensions within the bioenergy sector. This review systematically synthesizes recent advancements in torrefaction science, reactor design, and sustainability assessment. A novel analytical framework is developed to evaluate its role in enhancing energy security across the dimensions of availability, accessibility, affordability, and acceptability. Crucially, this review offers a systematic energy justice-oriented assessment of the torrefaction pathway, critically evaluating its implications across the distributive, procedural, recognitional, and restorative justice dimensions. The analysis reveals that the techno-economic promise of torrefaction is necessary but insufficient for its sustainable integration. Its success depends on active governance that is explicitly coupled with justice-oriented frameworks. This review concludes by proposing an integrated research and policy agenda that prioritizes co-benefit strategies, robust sustainability certification, and community-centric business models to steer the development of torrefaction towards a future of security, low carbon, and equity. Not applicable.

title: A global panel study on urbanization and energy consumption as drivers of black carbon emissions
summary: Black carbon is a short-lived climate pollutant formed during the incomplete burning of fossil fuels. It has turned out to be a significant cause of global warming, climate change and air pollution. This paper examines the impact of urbaniz
content: Black carbon is a short-lived climate pollutant formed during the incomplete burning of fossil fuels. It has turned out to be a significant cause of global warming, climate change and air pollution. This paper examines the impact of urbanization and fossil fuel energy consumption on black carbon emissions across 125 countries from 2005 to 2022 with the help of both panel regression and multiple linear regression model estimated using OLS. The results of the F-test, LM test and Hausman test support the Fixed Effects Model at the p value < 0.01 level. This includes strong country-specific heterogeneity among MLR that indicates countries such as Cote d’Ivoire, Romania, Belarus, Azerbaijan and Namibia, demonstrating a strong positive significance between urbanization and fossil fuel energy consumption on black carbon emissions. In contrast, developed countries such as Iceland, Belgium and Canada, UK, Ireland and many others have negative or weak coefficients, suggesting the positive impact of clean technologies and stricter policies. The novel contribution of this study lies in combining global coverage with heterogeneous country level impact analysis and suggestions for policymakers with evidence-based insights on integrated urban planning and energy efficiency that will help to reduce black carbon emissions and achieve sustainable development goals such as promoting good health and wellbeing (SDG3), fostering sustainable cities (SDG11) and climate action (SDG 13). Not applicable.

title: How to foster a resilient, efficient and clean hydrogen ramp-up – A comparative assessment of EU and US support systems
summary: Achieving climate targets in hard-to-electrify sectors such as energy-intensive industries, aviation and maritime requires rapid uptake of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen despite market uncertainties. However, hydrogen will contribute to
content: Achieving climate targets in hard-to-electrify sectors such as energy-intensive industries, aviation and maritime requires rapid uptake of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen despite market uncertainties. However, hydrogen will contribute to decarbonization only when its production comes with zero or very limited greenhouse gas emissions. Moreover, limited public funding calls for an efficient allocation of support. Public support systems for hydrogen need to address this conundrum of greenhouse gas effectiveness, economic efficiency and resilient market uptake with a suitably designed instrument mix. A key question is how to identify ex-ante gaps and deficiencies in the instrument mix. This paper develops assessment criteria for such support systems, expanding existing assessments beyond supply-side policies and electrolytic hydrogen. The criteria are then applied to the most relevant deployment policies in the European Union, including but not limited to the Hydrogen Bank, and the United States, namely the Inflation Reduction Act and the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The findings indicate that the EU support system is more stringent regarding greenhouse gas effectiveness and economic efficiency than the US support system but poses greater risks to rapid market uptake due to its complexity and limited focus on domestic supply chains. The results are partially validated by recent market developments based on the IEA Hydrogen Projects Database, while the infancy of the market prevents a complete ex-post evaluation. The findings imply that the EU support system could benefit from strengthening domestic manufacturing, while the US should consider establishing a governance mechanism that enables a phaseout of fossil-based hydrogen production.

title: Institutional role in shaping the students’ attitude toward sustainable tourism: integration at the personal, socio-economic level
source: Journal of Teaching in Travel & Tourism
summary: Although tourism has emerged as a driving force of the world economy, its carbon footprint and contribution to world pollution are non-negligible. The anthropause period revealed that a delicate balance between tourism activities and nature
content: Although tourism has emerged as a driving force of the world economy, its carbon footprint and contribution to world pollution are non-negligible. The anthropause period revealed that a delicate balance between tourism activities and nature is essential. Therefore, educating individuals about the environmental impact of their activities has become necessary, as collective action can drive meaningful progress toward sustainability goals. It is argued that implementing changes at the grassroots level and teaching sustainability subjects at the university level can guide youngsters and involve them in the process of change. The study has surveyed undergraduate students enrolled in hospitality and tourism-related programs in Thai universities to understand the implications of sustainability subjects in their curricula. The students were assessed based on integrating sustainable tourism subjects into the curriculum through experiential learning and by educational visits outside the university for real-time exposure. The study has yielded mixed results, revealing both micro and macro-level transformations. It contributes to the literature by emphasizing the need to develop young students into full-fledged environmental custodians for a greener future.

title: Physiological carry-over responses across inter-heatwave intervals in two subtropical tree species
summary: Recurrent heatwaves can induce physiological carry-over effects, but how inter-heatwave intervals influence photosynthesis, oxidative stress, and photochemical performance in trees remains poorly understood. We investigated two subtropical
content: Recurrent heatwaves can induce physiological carry-over effects, but how inter-heatwave intervals influence photosynthesis, oxidative stress, and photochemical performance in trees remains poorly understood. We investigated two subtropical tree species, Schima superba and Phoebe bournei , exposed to a single heatwave or two heatwaves separated by intervals of 7, 15, or 23 days. Leaf gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, antioxidant enzyme activities, and malondialdehyde (MDA) content were measured at a common final sampling date. Under the shortest inter-heatwave interval, net photosynthetic rate declined by 50.8% in S. superba and 32.4% in P. bournei relative to the control, with higher photosynthetic rates observed at longer intervals in both species. However, their carbon–water responses contrasted: water-use efficiency was higher at 23 than at 7 days in S. superba , whereas the opposite pattern occurred in P. bournei ( P < 0.001). Oxidative responses also differed between species. MDA content peaked under the 7-day interval in S. superba but under the 15-day interval in P. bournei , while catalase and peroxidase activities exhibited contrasting interval-associated patterns. Chlorophyll fluorescence parameters varied among treatments, although significant species × interval interactions were not detected. Exploratory association analyses further revealed contrasting relationships between antioxidant activity and photosynthetic performance, including a negative catalase–photosynthesis association in S. superba and a positive peroxidase–photosynthesis association in P. bournei . The findings suggest that inter-heatwave interval length is associated with contrasting physiological responses in subtropical trees, particularly in carbon–water relations, oxidative stress, and antioxidant–photosynthesis associations. These results highlight the value of integrating multiple physiological traits when evaluating potential heatwave carry-over effects. However, the lack of independent greenhouse replication and repeated physiological measurements limits treatment-level inference and prevents direct characterization of recovery kinetics or causal mechanisms. Further replicated experiments are needed to test the proposed physiological response patterns.

title: The Rise of Small Island Developing States in the Indo-Pacific
summary: The Rise of Small Island Developing States in the Indo-Pacific analyses the region, not through the lens of major-power competition but from the perspective of four island states: Solomon Islands and Fiji in the Pacific Ocean and Seychelles
content: The Rise of Small Island Developing States in the Indo-Pacific analyses the region, not through the lens of major-power competition but from the perspective of four island states: Solomon Islands and Fiji in the Pacific Ocean and Seychelles and Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. This book challenges traditional realist conceptions of small states and prevailing dominant narratives that portray Small Island Developing States (SIDS), increasingly referred to as Large Ocean States (LOS), as peripheral actors constrained by limited power and agency. It redirects analytical attention towards island states that remain largely absent from mainstream accounts of international politics despite their growing geopolitical significance. Covering the period 2017–2026, this book combines thematic analysis of foreign policy documents with elite government interviews to examine how these islands have responded to intensifying geopolitical competition. It argues that they enact the roles of ‘pioneer’ and ‘activist-challenger,’ demonstrating that SIDS/LOS retain meaningful agency, even as the international order becomes increasingly contested. This book advances an alternative framework for analysing their foreign policies, highlighting how island states exercise agency through strategies such as manipulation of interdependence, fluid partnerships and issue-specific engagement, together with sources of influence including strategic positioning, collective power, relational resources, narrative shaping and moral suasion. It also challenges the land-centric orientation of International Relations by incorporating ocean space and marine resources as important sources of influence and agency. The Rise of Small Island Developing States in the Indo-Pacific will be of great interest to scholars and students of International Relations, Foreign Policy Analysis and those studying Ocean or Maritime Studies, as well as Small State Studies and Contemporary History.

title: سياسات التحوّل الطاقوي في الموانئ الصناعية وفاعليتها في خفض الانبعاثات الكربونية: دراسة حالة ميناء روتردام (2016 -2025)
summary: يتناول البحث استجابة السياسة العامة للانبعاثات الكربونية في ميناء روتردام من خلال تقويم برنامج تحول الطاقة الذي أطلقته هيئة الميناء عام 2016 ضمن بنية مؤسسية تتوزع فيها صلاحيات التخطيط والتنفيذ والتمويل بين هيئة الميناء والشركات والسلطات الع
content: يتناول البحث استجابة السياسة العامة للانبعاثات الكربونية في ميناء روتردام من خلال تقويم برنامج تحول الطاقة الذي أطلقته هيئة الميناء عام 2016 ضمن بنية مؤسسية تتوزع فيها صلاحيات التخطيط والتنفيذ والتمويل بين هيئة الميناء والشركات والسلطات العامة ومشغلي الشبكات، واعتمد البحث تحليل السياسات العامة وتحليل المساهمة السببية مع تتبع مسار التنفيذ وقراءة التحولات السنوية والقطاعية في مستويات الانبعاثات، وتكشف النتائج عن انخفاض انبعاثات الشركات بنسبة 31٫8٪ خلال مدة الدراسة مع تمركز الجزء الأكبر من الخفض في قطاع توليد الكهرباء، بما يحدد الوزن الفعلي للبرنامج داخل الحصيلة الكلية للانخفاض، فيما اتسع أثره المؤسسي والتنفيذي عبر تطوير البنية المشتركة وحشد الاستثمارات وتسريع مشروعات احتجاز الكربون والهيدروجين والكهرباء والحرارة، ويشير التقويم إلى تقدم في إنشاء البنية المشتركة وتنفيذ مشروعات التحول، مع تحقق التشغيل في نطاقات محددة، وبقاء تقدير مساهمة البرنامج في الخفض الكلي مرتبطًا بالأدلة الخاصة بالمشروعات وبفحص أثر السياسات والأسواق والنشاط الصناعي.

title: National Culture and Corporate Environmental Strategy: Uncertainty Avoidance, Future Orientation, and Green Revenue Target
source: International Journal of Energy Economics and Policy
summary: This study examines whether GLOBE societal-practice measures of national culture predict corporate green revenue target setting, a rare, forward-looking disclosure with a 0.21% base rate in our sample. We estimate logistic regressions on 73
content: This study examines whether GLOBE societal-practice measures of national culture predict corporate green revenue target setting, a rare, forward-looking disclosure with a 0.21% base rate in our sample. We estimate logistic regressions on 73,501 firm-year observations from 10,544 firms headquartered in 48 countries over 2002-2024, using LSEG (Refinitiv) ESG and financial data, GLOBE scores, and World Bank accounts, testing whether uncertainty avoidance and future orientation predict disclosure of a green revenue share target. Contrary to our hypothesis, uncertainty avoidance is significantly and negatively associated with disclosure (β = -3.574, p = .035), while future orientation is positively associated but only at the 10% level (β = 3.538, p = .054). Both results survive a linear probability model, a year-trend control, a random-intercept multilevel logit, and Firth's penalized-likelihood estimator. A formal interaction test shows both cultural effects differ in Japan and South Korea, which together account for 77% of the 155 disclosures observed (joint Wald χ²(2) = 22.01, p < .001); neither coefficient differs from zero once these two countries are excluded. The findings caution against treating GLOBE scores as uniform predictors of environmental target setting: country-specific institutional or regulatory dynamics more plausibly drive the association than any shared cultural mechanism.

title: Functional Reconstitution of Human OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 in Proteoliposomes: Effect of Bicarbonate Gradients and Substrate-specific Stimulation on Transport
summary: The hepatic organic anion transporting polypeptides OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 are critical for the clearance of widely prescribed drugs, hepatotoxins, and endogenous metabolites. However, the thermodynamic driving force governing their transport
content: The hepatic organic anion transporting polypeptides OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 are critical for the clearance of widely prescribed drugs, hepatotoxins, and endogenous metabolites. However, the thermodynamic driving force governing their transport has remained a subject of debate due to the complexity of cellular models. Here, we report a defined, reconstituted proteoliposome system to study the transport kinetics of isolated human OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. Through direct functional assays, real-time counter-ion tracking, and a novel ABCG2-OATP1B1 functional co-reconstitution, we identify an outwardly directed bicarbonate gradient as a thermodynamic driving force for concentrative substrate uptake. In contrast we find no evidence for the proposed role of reduced glutathione efflux as a possible driving force. Targeted mutagenesis experiments revealed that the conserved TM3 residue His115 is needed to couple the bicarbonate gradient to concentrative substrate uptake, mechanistically linking substrate antiport to local pH-sensitive bicarbonate processing. We also investigated the substrate-specific stimulatory effect of the green tea catechin epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) on OATP1B3 transport, confirming that this effect is intrinsic to OATP1B3, substrate specific, and does not need the involvement of other cellular proteins. Our findings define the energetic basis of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 hepatic xenobiotic clearance.

title: Microbial Respiration in Subtropical Urban Soils Depending on Vegetation Type
summary: ABSTRACT Urban vegetation combines invasive and introduced species with native relics, whose litter is the primary source of organic matter inputs in urban soils. Plant litter quality regulates both organic carbon (C) storage and microbial
content: ABSTRACT Urban vegetation combines invasive and introduced species with native relics, whose litter is the primary source of organic matter inputs in urban soils. Plant litter quality regulates both organic carbon (C) storage and microbial activity in urban soils. Here we examined the microbial respiration and organic C stocks in the subtropical urban soils depending on plant litter decomposability. Five urban areas differing in vegetation (deciduous forest, shrubland, grassland, ruderal area, and turfgrass) were used for kinetic analysis of plant litter decomposition over a 12‐week incubation, and CO 2 efflux and microbial biomass C in soil were analyzed. The plant litter decomposability decreased as its C/N ratio increased. The decay constant of potentially mineralized litter components decreased progressively from turfgrass and grassland to shrubland and ruderal area, and finally to forest. Higher litter decomposition was associated with a faster rate of soil microbial respiration per unit of organic C content. Soil organic C stocks were 20%–38% larger in urban forest and areas with ruderal vegetation than in turfgrass. This was caused by the greater biostability of forest litter and lower microbial activity in the soils of semi‐natural areas compared with those of completely transformed and managed urban ecosystems such as turfgrass. Consequently, the decrease in decomposability of plant litter increased organic C stocks and reduced microbial respiration rates, highlighting the importance of vegetation type in managing C storage in urban soils.

title: Fluorinated carbon nanotubes for electrochemical energy storage: from bonding chemistry to structure–property relationships
summary: Fluorination provides an unusually direct means of tuning the bonding, electronic structure, surface chemistry, and interfacial behavior of carbon nanotubes (CNTs). The conversion of sp 2 carbon into fluorinated sp 3 environments produces s
content: Fluorination provides an unusually direct means of tuning the bonding, electronic structure, surface chemistry, and interfacial behavior of carbon nanotubes (CNTs). The conversion of sp 2 carbon into fluorinated sp 3 environments produces semi-ionic and covalent C-F species whose relative abundance depends on the fluorination route, fluorine content, and CNT structure. These changes regulate conductivity, wettability, defect chemistry, thermal stability, and electrochemical reactivity. This review therefore organizes fluorinated carbon nanotubes (FCNTs) through a route-bonding-structure-property-performance framework. Direct gas-phase, atomic, plasma, liquid-phase, and solid-state fluorination routes are compared in terms of fluorination uniformity, bonding configuration, structural preservation, and scalability. The resulting structure-property relationships are then connected to four application roles: active Li/CF x and Na/CF x cathodes, interphase-forming components for alkali-metal batteries, adsorption and electrocatalytic interfaces, and conductive or structural electrode networks. Particular attention is given to the capacity-conductivity trade-off, the spatial distribution of fluorinated domains, and advanced characterization needed to resolve dynamic structural evolution. The review closes by distinguishing established consensus from unresolved questions and by identifying precision fluorination, operando multimodal characterization, standardized descriptors, and scalable manufacturing as priorities for FCNT-based energy storage.

title: Earthquake-driven influx of organic matter enhances authigenic carbonate formation in hadal trenches
summary: Shallow marine carbonates are recognized as key agents in deep carbon cycling. However, the formation and burial of carbonates below the carbonate compensation depth still remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate carbonates from the >
content: Shallow marine carbonates are recognized as key agents in deep carbon cycling. However, the formation and burial of carbonates below the carbonate compensation depth still remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate carbonates from the > 7000 m water-depth Japan Trench hadal zone and find widespread authigenic calcium carbonate buried in these ultra-deep sediments. Stable and radiocarbon isotope depletions in the authigenic carbonates indicate an organic carbon (OC) source, likely primarily delivered by deep-sea landslides. Isotopic modeling suggests that subduction of these OC-derived carbonates can impart negative δ13C signatures to fluids released in the NE Japan subduction zone. The OC-derived carbonate flux in the Japan Trench is estimated to reach ~ 28.6 Tg C Myr–1. We propose that earthquake-driven organic matter influx into the hadal zone may have facilitated sustained carbonate production. Thus, OC-derived authigenic carbonates in hadal trenches represent an underappreciated carbon sink and a potential mechanism for transferring OC into the deep Earth. Earthquake-driven organic matter influx into hadal zones facilitates sustained organic carbon-derived carbonate production. The formation of these authigenic carbonates represents both an underappreciated carbon sink and a potential mechanism for transferring OC into the deep Earth.

title: Is water hyacinth greener on the other side? a perspective on the valorization of invasive-plant biomass surplus
summary: The global expansion of invasive plant species generates vast biomass surpluses that challenge freshwater ecosystems while simultaneously offering opportunities for circular bioeconomy innovation. Pontederia crassipes (Mart.) [formerly know
content: The global expansion of invasive plant species generates vast biomass surpluses that challenge freshwater ecosystems while simultaneously offering opportunities for circular bioeconomy innovation. Pontederia crassipes (Mart.) [formerly known as Eichhornia crassipes (Mart.) Solms] is no exception, representing one of the most abundant invasive plant biomasses worldwide and an underexplored resource with significant potential for circular bioeconomy applications. This perspective explores whether water hyacinth may indeed be “greener on the other side” by evaluating its suitability for biomass valorization in multiple sectors. Agricultural applications remain one of the most promising pathways because water hyacinth nutrient-rich biomass supports composting, anaerobic digestion, mulching, and fertilizer production. Nevertheless, challenges such as metal accumulation require strict site-specific screening to ensure safe use. Beyond agriculture, water hyacinth can be processed through mechanical harvesting, biochemical fractionation, thermochemical conversion, and biological pretreatment, enabling integration into diverse value chains, including bioenergy, biochar, adsorbents, biocomposites, and specialty biochemicals. The presented comparison revealed that water hyacinth biomass may perform comparably or outperform other lignocellulosic feedstocks in textiles, composites, acoustics, and related sectors. Despite their versatility, operational constraints still limit large-scale deployment, including harvest logistics, drying energy, seasonal variability, contaminant accumulation, standardization gaps, and incomplete life-cycle assessment studies. Future perspectives highlight the need for decentralized biomass processing, integrated biorefineries, local building material production, and regenerative agriculture systems that link ecosystem restoration with biomass valorization. Together, these insights position water hyacinth as a viable bioeconomic resource when ecological control, sustainability, and value chain integration are strategically aligned.

title: Innovation, financial development, foreign direct investment, renewable energy, and economic growth in Malaysia: Evidence from an ARDL bounds testing approach
summary: Engineering solutions for sustainable energy systems require supportive innovation ecosystems, efficient financial systems, and sustained investment to achieve long-term economic and environmental objectives. However, limited evidence exist
content: Engineering solutions for sustainable energy systems require supportive innovation ecosystems, efficient financial systems, and sustained investment to achieve long-term economic and environmental objectives. However, limited evidence exists on how these factors jointly relate to economic growth in Malaysia. This study investigates the relationship among innovation, financial development, foreign direct investment (FDI), renewable energy, and real GDP per capita in Malaysia using annual data from 1990 to 2023. The Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach is employed because it accommodates variables integrated at mixed orders and estimates both long-run equilibrium relationships and short-run dynamics. The bounds test confirms cointegration among the variables (F-statistic = 5.84). Long-run ARDL estimates indicate that innovation (β = 0.118, p = 0.002), financial development (β = 0.092, p = 0.032), and renewable energy (β = 0.067, p = 0.028) exhibit statistically significant positive relationships with real GDP per capita. Foreign direct investment also has a positive coefficient (β = 0.031), but the relationship provides only weak evidence at the 10% significance level (p = 0.095). The findings indicate that innovation, financial development, and renewable energy consumption have positive long-run relationships with real GDP per capita. These results provide evidence on the macroeconomic drivers of economic growth in Malaysia and offer policy insights relevant to the country's broader energy transition. However, environmental sustainability is not directly estimated in this study. Beyond macroeconomic policy implications, the findings provide engineering insights for renewable-energy infrastructure planning, smart-grid modernization, energy-storage deployment, and technology investment supporting Malaysia's National Energy Transition Roadmap. The findings provide several evidence-based policy implications. Malaysia should increase investment in research and development and in renewable energy innovation, expand green financial instruments and sustainable infrastructure financing, and accelerate renewable energy deployment through grid modernization and energy storage investment under the National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR). Given the weaker evidence for aggregating FDI, policies should prioritize technology-intensive and clean-energy foreign investment rather than focusing solely on increasing FDI inflows. These findings provide empirical evidence to support renewable energy infrastructure planning and long-term economic growth in Malaysia.

title: Shape design of a morphing elevator to enhance aircraft low speed efficiency of a regional aircraft
summary: Control surface aerodynamics plays a crucial role in aircraft performance, both in cruise and low speed conditions, where fuel consumption and stability are most critical. This study presents an aerodynamic shape design based on numerical o
content: Control surface aerodynamics plays a crucial role in aircraft performance, both in cruise and low speed conditions, where fuel consumption and stability are most critical. This study presents an aerodynamic shape design based on numerical optimization applied to a future green aircraft elevator, to reduce its drag, maintaining required stability and control authority during the low-speed phases. A numerical aerodynamic optimization based on the application of Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) to Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has been performed to identify aerodynamic improvements of the baseline configuration. The methodology integrated parametric shape modifications, by means of Radial Basis Functions (RBFs), assuring a smooth elevator’s deflection maximizing aerofoil’s lift capabilities, improving or keeping baseline’s efficiency. The optimization process was executed under representative low speed conditions (Mach number equal to 0.23, sea level altitude, International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) with temperature difference deviation null – K –), so results are directly applicable to operational flight regimes. Results demonstrate that the optimized elevator can improve aerofoil lift (up to above 9%), reducing drag (up to above 7%), contributing to improve fuel efficiency (up to 10% aerodynamic efficiency improvement), reducing environmental impact. The study highlights the importance of tailoring control surface geometry also for low-speed efficiency, an aspect often overlooked in conventional design practices. This work underscores the potential of aircraft design advanced optimization techniques, offering a pathway toward more sustainable and cost-effective operations. The methodology presented can be extended to other control surfaces and flight regimes, reinforcing the role of aerodynamic optimization in modern aircraft development. The activities here reported have been carried out within the EU-funded research project HERFUSE (Hybrid-Electric Regional FUSelage & Empennages), aimed to develop advanced designs for the fuselage and empennages of Hybrid-Electric Regional (HER) aircraft.

title: Evaluating the full scale potential of urban mobility measures through a multi city cluster analysis of public transport interventions in Europe
summary: Abstract The transition toward sustainable urban mobility requires a better understanding of how measures perform when implemented at scale. While many pilot projects have been tested across European cities, evidence on their full-scale pot
content: Abstract The transition toward sustainable urban mobility requires a better understanding of how measures perform when implemented at scale. While many pilot projects have been tested across European cities, evidence on their full-scale potential remains limited. This study evaluates 78 mobility measures across ten cities through expert-based assessments on five criteria: congestion, road safety, modal share, accessibility, and user satisfaction. Using cluster analysis, supported by Elbow and Silhouette diagnostics, four distinct groups of measures were identified. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was subsequently used to provide a two-dimensional visualization of the resulting cluster structure. The results reveal: (i) digital measures with high anticipated user-related ratings but lower anticipated system-impact ratings, (ii) transformative public transport and infrastructure measures with consistently high performance, (iii) administrative actions with comparatively lower anticipated direct-impact ratings, and (iv) “push” policies characterized by moderate-to-high anticipated system-impact ratings but comparatively lower anticipated user satisfaction. Overall, the findings highlight that large-scale interventions received the highest anticipated impact ratings across multiple dimensions, while the results also suggest differentiated trade-offs between system-oriented and user-oriented outcomes across intervention types.

title: Using Nanotechnology for Electrode Materials in Lithium-Ion Batteries
summary: Nowadays, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely used in portable electronics, electric vehicles, and grid-scale energy storage systems. However, the commercial graphite anode has almost reached its theoretical capacity limit of 372 mAh g⁻
content: Nowadays, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely used in portable electronics, electric vehicles, and grid-scale energy storage systems. However, the commercial graphite anode has almost reached its theoretical capacity limit of 372 mAh g⁻¹, and conventional cathode materials still face problems such as low specific capacity and unstable electrode-electrolyte interfaces, which limit the cycle life and safety of the batteries. Nanotechnology can provide useful ways to deal with these problems, because it shortens the diffusion path of lithium ions, buffers the volume strain during charge and discharge, and stabilizes the interfacial chemistry between electrode and electrolyte. This paper reviews the recent development of nanotechnology in both cathode and anode materials. For cathode materials, elemental doping can stabilize the crystal lattice and improve ion transport, surface coatings can reduce the dissolution of transition metals and side reactions with the electrolyte, and morphology control can further shorten diffusion paths and improve rate capability. For anode materials, carbon coating, porous structures, and one-dimensional nanowires can relieve volume expansion and make the solid-electrolyte interphase more stable. This review also discusses several key challenges, such as nanoparticle agglomeration, side reactions at the interface, and manufacturing cost, and gives some prospects for future multi-scale synergistic design.

title: Implementation Gap in Global Power Capacity Expansion to meet Paris Agreement Climate Targets
summary: Abstract Meeting the Paris Agreement’s climate targets demands an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy. Despite global commitments, significant implementation gaps persist due to economic, policy, and technical uncertainties. Here, w
content: Abstract Meeting the Paris Agreement’s climate targets demands an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy. Despite global commitments, significant implementation gaps persist due to economic, policy, and technical uncertainties. Here, we develop a Global Power Capacity Dynamics Framework, integrating facility-level data, machine learning and transition modeling to assess the feasibility of global power expansion. Analyzing 215,849 power plant units across five status modes (operating, planned, canceled, standby, retired), the framework explicitly incorporates the likelihood of planned capacity realization and the conversion of existing fossil assets. We find that by 2030, only 51% [40%–61%] of announced planned capacity is expected to become operational, while 26% [19%–36%] is likely to be canceled, with fossil fuel projects, especially coal, facing a cancellation rate of about 35%. Global operational capacity is projected to reach 9727 GW [9626–9848], including 178 GW [159–198] of existing fossil units requiring conversion or replacement (e.g., coal-to-gas, fossil-to-biomass). Although renewables dominate the planned pipeline, they are projected to constitute only 52% of the global energy mix by 2030, well below levels needed to meet climate goals. Regional disparities are pronounced: Asia, despite its relatively low cancellation rate, faces the world’s largest implementation gap, requiring an additional 2488 GW of solar and contending with 523 GW of stranded coal capacity to remain on a 1.5 °C pathway. This study provides the first probabilistic, facility-level assessment of global power capacity trajectories, revealing critical shortfalls in planned deployment and underscoring the urgency of aligning capacity expansion with climate targets.

title: Plenty of fish in the farm: Analysing the effect of aquaculture-based tourism on public perceptions of aquaculture
summary: This study explores aquaculture-based tourism as a tool to improve public perceptions of aquaculture, promote sustainable development of marine industries, and advance Blue Growth. Global aquaculture production is rapidly increasing due to
content: This study explores aquaculture-based tourism as a tool to improve public perceptions of aquaculture, promote sustainable development of marine industries, and advance Blue Growth. Global aquaculture production is rapidly increasing due to increased food security demands, protein needs, and declining wild fish stocks. However, the sustainable growth of the aquaculture industry is challenged in policymaking due to public scepticism and environmental concerns. Through 48 semi-structured interviews with visitors to a fish farm-tourism collaboration in Western Rhodes, Greece, this study examines the impact of these tours on public perceptions of aquaculture. Using a mixed methods approach combining quantitative Likert scale rankings and qualitative thematic analysis, this study investigates participants’ knowledge, perceptions, and the benefits and challenges of aquaculture-based tourism. Results show that over 80% of participants improved their views of aquaculture after the tour, influenced by experiential learning through snorkelling and educational talks. Thematic analysis revealed a lack of prior knowledge among participants, the reasonings for respective negative and positive and shifts from little understanding of fish farming to an appreciation of sustainable aquaculture practices. The findings underscore the role of effective communication in bridging public knowledge gaps, improving acceptability of aquaculture, and fostering a social license to operate for marine policymaking. By enhancing environmental awareness and reconnecting individuals with the marine socio-ecological system, aquaculture-based tourism incentivises responsible practices and supports multi-use marine management. This study contributes to limited literature on aquaculture perception research and highlights the potential of educational tourism to reshape attitudes and drive sustainable marine development.

title: Targeting Ferroptosis-Inflammation Crosstalk: A Novel Strategy for the Prevention and Treatment of Myocardial Ischaemia Reperfusion Injury
summary: Abstract Myocardial ischaemia-reperfusion injury (MIRI) is a major cause of residual myocardial damage following coronary revascularisation. Unfortunately, effective mechanism-based pharmacological interventions that can be translated into
content: Abstract Myocardial ischaemia-reperfusion injury (MIRI) is a major cause of residual myocardial damage following coronary revascularisation. Unfortunately, effective mechanism-based pharmacological interventions that can be translated into clinical practice remain limited. Emerging evidence indicates that ferroptosis and inflammation mutually reinforce each other and constitute a critical pathological process responsible for the amplification of myocardial injury during the early phase of reperfusion. Upon myocardial reperfusion, ferroptotic cardiomyocytes release damage-associated molecular patterns and disrupt tissue barriers, thereby activating the innate immune system and initiating inflammatory responses. In turn, inflammation promotes oxidative stress, dysregulation of iron metabolism and lipid peroxidation through the activation of inflammatory signaling pathways and the release of pro-inflammatory mediators, ultimately exacerbating ferroptosis. This reciprocal interaction establishes a self-perpetuating vicious cycle that contributes to the progression of MIRI. Encouragingly, several Western medicines and bioactive compounds derived from traditional Chinese medicine have shown therapeutic potential in modulating MIRI. This review systematically summarizes the molecular mechanisms underlying the bidirectional interaction between ferroptosis and inflammation in MIRI and discusses emerging pharmacological strategies targeting this pathological network. Collectively, the available evidence suggests that future therapeutic approaches to MIRI should extend beyond reperfusion therapy, antioxidant treatment, or anti-inflammatory intervention alone and instead consider combined strategies that simultaneously suppress inflammation and ferroptosis. Such an integrated approach may provide a novel translational framework for early risk assessment, therapeutic response prediction and targeted intervention in patients with MIRI.

title: Farmers’ beliefs about the impacts of a CO2e tax on agriculture and their acceptance of the tax: A randomized survey experiment
summary: Agriculture is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions but has largely been exempt from stringent climate change mitigation policies, often due to concerns about resistance from the sector. With Denmark introducing the world’s first CO 2
content: Agriculture is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions but has largely been exempt from stringent climate change mitigation policies, often due to concerns about resistance from the sector. With Denmark introducing the world’s first CO 2 -equivalent (CO 2 e) tax on agricultural emissions, this paper provides representative evidence of farmers’ beliefs about its impacts and examines whether providing expert-predicted impacts can causally influence these beliefs and acceptance of the tax. Using a randomized survey experiment with 981 Danish farmers, we find a widespread overestimation of the tax’s impacts on production, employment, and land value, with 94–97 % of farmers expecting the impacts to be up to three times larger than expert-predicted estimates. Providing an expert-predicted impact reduces these perception gaps, with effects varying according to the tax’s stringency, size of belief gaps, and farm characteristics such as size and type. However, our results also indicate that, in some cases, belief updating may be muted or even contrary to the information provided, consistent with behavioral theories beyond the Bayesian framework. We also find that the belief revisions can translate into greater acceptance of the tax, although these effects vary with tax stringency, initial belief gaps, and farm characteristics. Our findings suggest that designing acceptable climate policies for agriculture may require not only expert information but also targeted communication and complementary measures that account for farmers’ diverse characteristics and perceptions.

title: The Role of Civil Engineering in Renewable Energy Storage: Contributions and Challenges
summary: Renewable energy generation is characterized by intermittency; consequently, energy storage is a prerequisite for its large-scale utilization. Existing research primarily focuses on power systems and electrochemical materials, often overloo
content: Renewable energy generation is characterized by intermittency; consequently, energy storage is a prerequisite for its large-scale utilization. Existing research primarily focuses on power systems and electrochemical materials, often overlooking the civil engineering aspects of energy storage projects. This paper employs a literature review approach to examine the engineering characteristics of four mainstream technologies, namely pumped hydro storage, compressed air energy storage, battery energy storage stations, and hydrogen energy storage, and summarizes the roles of civil engineering and the typical issues involved. The study reveals that civil engineering encompasses the entire lifecycle of energy storage projects from site selection and design to construction, and that the extent of civil engineering involvement directly impacts project feasibility and long-term operational safety. Specific challenges include lining cracking and hydraulic fracturing risks in pumped hydro storage; surrounding rock degradation and sealing performance in lined-cavern compressed air energy storage; caprock integrity and fault avoidance in salt-cavern hydrogen storage; pollution containment following thermal runaway in battery storage; and the prevention of hydrogen embrittlement in pipelines for hydrogen transport. This study demonstrates that the engineering constraints associated with energy storage technologies are fundamentally civil and geotechnical issues, which should be systematically considered during the evaluation of energy storage solutions.

title: Multiple Pathways for High-Level Development of Construction Industrialization Empowered by Technology-Resource-Economy——A Dynamic QCA Analysis Based on Panel Data of Sichuan Province
source: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
summary: Compared with the traditional construction industry, construction industrialization features low carbon emissions, high efficiency and environmental friendliness, which satisfies China's development requirements in the new era. Nevertheless
content: Compared with the traditional construction industry, construction industrialization features low carbon emissions, high efficiency and environmental friendliness, which satisfies China's development requirements in the new era. Nevertheless, the unbalanced development of construction industrialization in China remains prominent at present. Located in the southwest of China, Sichuan Province needs further improvement in construction industrialization when compared with more developed regions. Therefore, based on practical case analysis of Sichuan Province, this paper sorts out and summarizes six factors affecting the development of construction industrialization. It adopts the fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) method to examine the impacts of different factor configurations on the development level of construction industrialization, and explores effective pathways suitable for the development of construction industrialization in this province.

title: Defining equity: Government and community notions of equity in marine conservation co‐management
summary: Abstract Perceived inequities lie at the core of many conservation conflicts, yet empirical comparisons of how different stakeholders conceptualise equity remain rare. Despite its prominence in global policy frameworks, equity is context‐de
content: Abstract Perceived inequities lie at the core of many conservation conflicts, yet empirical comparisons of how different stakeholders conceptualise equity remain rare. Despite its prominence in global policy frameworks, equity is context‐dependent and understood differently by different actors, making it difficult to define and operationalise. Using an empirical environmental justice lens, we compared the notions of distributional, procedural, and recognitional equity held by coastal residents and government actors in a co‐managed marine protected area in Indonesia. We drew on semi‐structured interviews with 26 coastal residents and three government officials and analysed the protected area's management plan. We identify three key findings. First, both groups shared similar distributional and procedural criteria in principle, but they carried different meanings in practice. Second, recognitional equity was relational and internally derived for residents but externally conferred and legalistic for government actors. Third, misaligned notions of equity generated perceived inequities that undermined local support for conservation. Our findings highlight the central role of recognition in shaping notions of equity and show that agreement in principle does not ensure alignment in practice. Crucially, these divergences influence how coastal residents relate to, engage with, and support marine conservation, with significant implications for conservation legitimacy, stewardship and socio‐ecological outcomes. To foster more equitable and sustainable conservation co‐management, governance approaches must centre local understandings of equity and legitimacy by aligning formal rules with community values, practices and lived relationships with marine environments. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

title: Governing trade, governing carbon: How environmental provisions in RTAs affect carbon inequality within global value chains?
summary: Environmental provisions in regional trade agreements (RTAs) play an important role in aligning trade with environmental objectives and mitigating carbon inequality. Using data covering 80 economies and 50 industries, we apply a multi-regio
content: Environmental provisions in regional trade agreements (RTAs) play an important role in aligning trade with environmental objectives and mitigating carbon inequality. Using data covering 80 economies and 50 industries, we apply a multi-regional input–output model to construct a bilateral measure of carbon inequality from a value-capture perspective and examine whether deeper environmental provisions mitigate it. Three main findings emerge. First, we document pronounced asymmetries between countries’ value added gains and the carbon burdens they bear within global value chains (GVCs). Second, deeper environmental provisions significantly reduce bilateral carbon inequality by curbing pollution-intensive exports and narrowing green-technology gaps between RTA partners. Third, their effectiveness varies systematically across country pairings, industries, and provision types. The mitigating effect is evident in North-North and South-South pairs but weaker in North-South pairs, as the difference is systematically associated with asymmetries in forward and backward GVC participatiotexn. It is particularly pronounced in pollution-intensive manufacturing and for participatory environmental provisions. These findings provide policy-relevant evidence on how trade agreements can be designed to advance both economic integration and global climate governance.

title: Study on the Improvement of Coal Gangue and Soil Composite Matrix by Organic Acid Erosion of Plant Roots
summary: Abstract Coal gangue is a kind of solid waste produced in the process of coal mining and washing, which a large amount of stockpiling poses a serious threat to the environment in Guizhou karst area. Coal gangue contains a certain amount of
content: Abstract Coal gangue is a kind of solid waste produced in the process of coal mining and washing, which a large amount of stockpiling poses a serious threat to the environment in Guizhou karst area.
