Coal gangue contains a certain amount of organic matter, clay minerals and other soil components, which creates favorable conditions for coal gangue preparation. Organic acids secreted by simulated plant roots were used to treat coal gangue, and scanning electron microscope was used to analyze the surface microstructure after acid etching. The result showed that organic acid soak of simulated root system could effectively etch that surface of coal gangue and destroy its compact mineral structure. After acid etching, BET specific surface area increased by 37.81%, average pore size of adsorption and desorption increased by 60.94% and 49.11%, respectively, and pore volume increased greatly, indicating that organic acid could significantly promote the transformation of coal gangue into soil. The pot experiment was carried out with shallot, strawberry, garland chrysanthemum and ryegrass as plants. The results showed that the biomass of different plants was significantly different due to different optimum mixing ratio. Compared with the control group, the water content of strawberry was 81.36g, and the change was obvious. The results show that heavy metals in coal gangue distribute to different parts through plant roots, and the contents in different parts are different. The enrichment in roots of different plants is the highest, and the enrichment in stems and leaves (edible parts) varies with different plants. Ni, Hg and Zn have the strongest mobility among the four plants, while Pb and Cu have the weakest mobility. Through high-throughput sequencing analysis of soil microbial community composition, diversity and species difference analysis under the optimal coal gangue doping conditions for plant growth, coal gangue doping in soil can improve soil microbial community composition, diversity and species difference, promote soil micro-ecological virtuous cycle, and provide theoretical basis and experimental support for coal gangue agricultural resources and soil improvement.

title: Floating Solar Photovoltaics and the Sustainable Development Goals: A Global Review of Technical, Environmental, and Socioeconomic Impacts
source: Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews Energy and Environment
summary: ABSTRACT Floating solar photovoltaics (FSPV) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional ground‐mounted photovoltaic (GPV) systems. By deploying solar panels over water bodies such as lakes and reservoirs, FSPV systems mitigate l
content: ABSTRACT Floating solar photovoltaics (FSPV) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional ground‐mounted photovoltaic (GPV) systems. By deploying solar panels over water bodies such as lakes and reservoirs, FSPV systems mitigate land‐use constraints while enhancing energy performance and contributing to more effective water‐resource management. This paper presents a comprehensive review of FSPV technology, including its operational principles, technological developments, techno‐economic feasibility, environmental impacts, system reliability, and sustainability implications. One of the major advantages of FSPV systems is their enhanced energy generation compared with GPV installations. The presence of water beneath the modules provides a natural cooling effect that lowers the operating temperature of the panels and improves their efficiency. However, the level of performance improvement depends on climatic conditions, installation configuration, and system design. Beyond electricity generation, FSPV systems also provide several ancillary benefits related to water‐resource conservation and management. The coverage of water surfaces reduces evaporation losses and can support water conservation. Despite these benefits, FSPV deployment may also affect aquatic ecosystems and water quality. Therefore, proper site selection and environmental impact assessments are essential to minimize ecological disturbances. From an economic perspective, the initial capital cost of FSPV systems is generally higher than GPV systems because of floating structures, anchoring systems, and specialized installation requirements. Addressing the remaining technical, environmental, economic, and regulatory challenges will require coordinated research, technological standardization, and policy support. Overall, FSPV systems represent an important solution within the energy‐water‐climate nexus and can contribute significantly to global climate goals and sustainable energy development.

title: Hierarchical Design of MXene Architectures for Photothermal Phase-Change Energy Storage: From Nanosheet Synthesis to Ordered 3D Composites
summary: Solar energy is clean and abundant but intermittent, and the mismatch between solar energy supply and demand leads to significant energy waste. Phase-change materials (PCMs) can store solar energy as thermal energy, but conventional PCMs su
content: Solar energy is clean and abundant but intermittent, and the mismatch between solar energy supply and demand leads to significant energy waste. Phase-change materials (PCMs) can store solar energy as thermal energy, but conventional PCMs suffer from leakage, low thermal conductivity, and poor energy conversion ability. MXenes, a family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides/nitrides, possess high electrical and thermal conductivity, large specific surface area, abundant surface functional groups, and high photothermal conversion efficiency. Represented by Ti3C2Tx, MXene achieves efficient photothermal conversion through localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR)-enhanced broadband photon capture, electron-phonon coupling-induced non-radiative relaxation, and interlayer phonon transport, offering new opportunities for photothermal phase-change energy storage. This review focuses on MXene-based photothermal conversion phase-change energy storage materials. It summarizes MXene preparation/etching methods and photothermal conversion mechanisms, discusses the relationship between photothermal energy storage and oxidation resistance in light of practical applications, and analyzes the factors of performance degradation in MXene-based three-dimensional structures. It then reviews ordered structural design strategies and surface modification/composite preparation methods, with emphasis on MXene aerogels and hydrogels and their applications in solar thermal energy storage, thermal management, sensing, supercapacitors, electromagnetic shielding, and batteries. Finally, effective solutions for specific applications and future development directions are proposed. This review aims to provide insights into the rational design and practical application of next-generation MXene-based photothermal phase-change materials.

title: Scalable Gigapascal Strength Bamboo Veneers via Nanocellulose Reinforcement
summary: Carbon neutrality demands materials that deliver both performance and low environmental impact. Carbon fiber and glass fiber rely on fossil feedstocks and energy-intensive processing, while nature bamboo the ecological marvel is limited by
content: Carbon neutrality demands materials that deliver both performance and low environmental impact. Carbon fiber and glass fiber rely on fossil feedstocks and energy-intensive processing, while nature bamboo the ecological marvel is limited by inefficient load transfer within their heterogeneous cell walls. Here we show that this limitation can be overcome by reprogramming the bamboo cell wall through supramolecular nano-reinforcement. Cellulose nanocrystals infiltrate the cell wall and promote the reorganization of the interfacial hydrogen-bonding network within the aligned cellulose framework converting structural discontinuities into a continuous load-bearing scaffold. This enhances interfibrillar stress transfer and homogenizes mechanical response across scales. The resulting material achieves a tensile strength of 0.98 GPa and a Young's modulus of 52.7 GPa, with specific strength rivaling many synthetic fiber materials. These gains are achieved with up to two orders of magnitude lower carbon intensity than that of carbon fiber. This work demonstrates a scalable route to transform abundant biomass into high-performance structural materials, decoupling mechanical performance from carbon intensity.

title: Land degradation compromise drought risk financing across Africa, impacting pastoralist welfare
summary: Drought and land degradation threaten pastoral livelihoods in Africa, particularly in the Horn of Africa (HoA), where livestock losses can undermine household resilience, local economies, and the effectiveness of climate-risk financing mech
content: Drought and land degradation threaten pastoral livelihoods in Africa, particularly in the Horn of Africa (HoA), where livestock losses can undermine household resilience, local economies, and the effectiveness of climate-risk financing mechanisms. Index-Based Livestock Insurance (IBLI) offers an important means of reducing pastoral vulnerability by linking indemnity payouts to satellite-derived forage indices. However, its effectiveness depends on the assumption that vegetation-rainfall relationships and historical ecological baselines remain sufficiently stable over time. Increasing climate variability, land degradation, and other human-induced changes may violate these assumptions, creating basis risk and misaligned payouts for both pastoralists and insurers. We examine the implications of these changing environmental conditions for drought risk management and IBLI performance by integrating about 20 years of satellite-derived vegetation Indices (VIs) and precipitation data with linear and nonlinear modeling and Residual Trend (RESTREND) analysis. Across Africa, ~25% of the land area exhibits significant long-term changes in vegetation productivity, including 19% greening and 6% browning. Our analysis indicates that only 7% of these changes are primarily associated with rainfall variability, whereas 18% are linked to non-climatic factors such as agricultural expansion, bush encroachment, and invasives. These findings demonstrate that vegetation dynamics increasingly reflect interacting climatic, ecological, and anthropogenic processes, rather than rainfall variability alone. Consequently, drought indices based on historical vegetation-precipitation relationships may not adequately represent contemporary forage conditions or pastoral risk, with implications for the accuracy, equity, and financial sustainability of climate-risk financing systems. In IBLI operational regions within the HoA, ~20% of IBLI units (n = 124) exhibit significant changes in vegetation productivity that influence payout trends, highlighting the potential for changing ecological baselines to alter insurance performance and the correspondence between measured index risk and pastoralists’ realized exposure. The results suggest that environmental change can affect not only drought monitoring but also the distribution and reliability of climate-risk protection available to pastoral households. We therefore argue that robust drought-risk management in pastoral systems requires insurance and adaptation frameworks that account for land use/cover changes, shifting climatic baselines and degradation-sensitive vegetation dynamics, incorporate ground-based validation, and periodically reassess index-risk relationships. By linking long-term environmental change to insurance performance and pastoral vulnerability, this framework advances understanding of how ecological change can reshape risk measurement, climate-risk financing, and adaptation decision-making in drought-prone pastoral s

title: Morocco’s Energy Mix in the Context of Global Climate Change: A Socioeconomic Perspective
source: International Journal of Energy Economics and Policy
summary: As global climate challenges intensify, the transition toward low-carbon energy systems has become a central pillar of national sustainability strategies. Morocco, with limited fossil fuel resources and growing energy demand, has embarked o
content: As global climate challenges intensify, the transition toward low-carbon energy systems has become a central pillar of national sustainability strategies. Morocco, with limited fossil fuel resources and growing energy demand, has embarked on an ambitious energy transition aimed at enhancing energy security, promoting renewable energy, and contributing to global climate mitigation efforts. This paper adopts a qualitative descriptive approach based on a structural analysis of secondary data to provide an integrated and analytical reading of Morocco’s energy transition in the context of climate challenges, emphasizing its economic implication. As a results, the country's energy transition strategy has a positive outcome in terms of job creation while dealing with climate change. This is because Morocco's economy is gradually developing alongside the country's energy transition, which has a positive impact on both the labor market and environmental conservation. Consequently, Morocco can fully realize its potential as a hub for renewable energy innovation and green growth.

title: Hydrogen blending amplifies seismic risk to global gas pipelines
summary: Abstract Repurposing existing natural gas pipelines for hydrogen service provides a promising approach for accelerated development of hydrogen economy. Yet hydrogen blending remains an underestimated amplifier of seismic risk to the pipelin
content: Abstract Repurposing existing natural gas pipelines for hydrogen service provides a promising approach for accelerated development of hydrogen economy. Yet hydrogen blending remains an underestimated amplifier of seismic risk to the pipelines. Herein, we assess the seismic hazard exposure, failure risk, and resilience loss on 2,554 operating pipelines, including 1,731 fault-crossing risk points and 476 topological systems, in the world. Results demonstrate that a prolonged hydrogen exposure elevates failure risk of the pipelines, with the failure probability increasing by nearly 40 times at certain sensitive crossings. The risk amplification is primarily driven by accumulated hydrogen damage to the pipelines, rather than by extreme seismic hotspots. Generally, the resilience loss of pipelines is topology-dependent, with main trunklines most affected. The findings exhibit a cross-scale risk spanning from pipe material degradation and structural failure to infrastructure disruption. It is proposed that evaluating the existing pipelines for hydrogen transport must include the seismic risk.

title: Tailoring surface and structural properties of WO3 thin films via mixed-gas plasma deposition for optimized H2 gas sensing performance
summary: Detecting hydrogen at low concentration is essential for the early identification of leaks in hydrogen storage and transportation systems, thereby improving operational safety. In this work, thin films of tungsten trioxide (WO 3 ), a well-k
content: Detecting hydrogen at low concentration is essential for the early identification of leaks in hydrogen storage and transportation systems, thereby improving operational safety. In this work, thin films of tungsten trioxide (WO 3 ), a well-known hydrogen-sensing material, were deposited via DC reactive magnetron sputtering under systematically varied gas environments to elucidate the role of deposition conditions in tailoring film morphology and sensing performance. Introducing mixed Ar/O 2 , Ar/He/O 2 , and He/O 2 sputtering atmospheres with varying gas flow rates at a substrate temperature of 400 °C produced a marked reduction in grain size and film thickness compared with films grown in an equal flow-rate Ar/O 2 plasma. The film synthesized in the Ar/O 2 environment exhibited superior resistance modulation upon H 2 exposure and significantly enhanced sensitivity compared with the other films. Gas sensing characteristics toward H 2 were evaluated at operating temperatures of 100, 150, and 200 °C, and the optimized film was further investigated for low H 2 concentrations down to 25 ppm. These findings demonstrate a strong correlation between microstructure and sensing response and highlight the critical influence of the deposition environment on the morphological and electronic properties of WO 3 thin films, providing a viable strategy for developing next-generation high-performance hydrogen gas sensors.

title: Strategic assessment of hydropower resilience under climate change: an integrated SWOT-PESTEL perspective within the water–energy nexus
summary: ABSTRACT Hydropower is central to renewable-energy transitions and to the Water–Energy Nexus (WEN), but its resilience is increasingly shaped by hydrological variability, competing water demands, aging infrastructure, and changing governanc
content: ABSTRACT Hydropower is central to renewable-energy transitions and to the Water–Energy Nexus (WEN), but its resilience is increasingly shaped by hydrological variability, competing water demands, aging infrastructure, and changing governance conditions. This study develops an evidence-weighted framework that integrates SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) with PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, and Legal) analysis. Twenty-two publicly available institutional reports were examined through 33 structured questions, producing 726 source-question evaluations. Documentary evidence was synthesized into retained SWOT factors and weighted according to source coverage, evidence density, geographic breadth, and recency before being mapped to PESTEL dimensions. Intersectoral water-use conflict and competition, climate change and extreme weather, renewable-energy integration, and adaptive reservoir management emerged as the most strongly supported strategic factors. Technological conditions most strongly reinforced the strengths of hydropower, whereas social, environmental, political, and economic pressures dominated weaknesses and threats. Alternative weighting scenarios produced highly stable rankings (Spearman's rho = 0.976–0.995). The framework provides a transparent and transferable basis for identifying strategic priorities, while its numerical outputs should be recalibrated with basin-specific hydrological, institutional, and stakeholder data.

title: Cross-kingdom quorum sensing: mechanisms driving Candida albicans and Staphylococcus aureus synergistic pathogenesis
summary: Background Co-infection with Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans represents a prevalent, clinically important polymicrobial challenge that can be associated with worse outcomes than monomicrobial infection. Emerging evidence indicate
content: Background Co-infection with Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans represents a prevalent, clinically important polymicrobial challenge that can be associated with worse outcomes than monomicrobial infection. Emerging evidence indicates that their synergistic pathogenicity is shaped by quorum sensing (QS) related and other cross-kingdom interactions.Objective To summarize current evidence on cross-kingdom interactions involving the S. aureus agr quorum-sensing system and the C. albicans farnesol signalling pathway and their contributions to polymicrobial pathogenicity.Design This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on QS-related, metabolic, environmental, structural, and host-mediated mechanisms underlying S. aureus - C. albicans interactions.Results Extracellular pH regulation, ribose metabolism, mixed-biofilm architecture, and farnesol-induced stress adaptation modulate bacterial virulence and antimicrobial tolerance. Furthermore, microbial signalling and host innate immune responses interact bidirectionally to shape infection outcomes. Importantly, direct recognition of a C. albicans-derived quorum-sensing molecule by a defined S. aureus QS receptor has not yet been demonstrated.Conclusions QS-targeted and anti-adhesion/anti-virulence strategies may offer therapeutic opportunities, but their efficacy requires further validation in host-relevant oral and systemic infection models.

title: Thermal Conductive Materials for Lithium-Ion Batteries
source: Academic Journal of Science and Technology
summary: As part of the development of energy, battery storage systems have emerged recently; however, large-scale applications of lithium-ion batteries have shown problems with heat management and safety. A high-thermal-conductivity material is add
tags: Thermal management of electronic devices and systems
content: As part of the development of energy, battery storage systems have emerged recently; however, large-scale applications of lithium-ion batteries have shown problems with heat management and safety. A high-thermal-conductivity material is added to the cooling system of the battery to extend the service life of the equipment and ensure stable, safe operation. This paper compiles available data and analyses the reasons for heat generation in lithium-ion batteries. It compares and contrasts the features of the three kinds of thermal management materials: metal-based, carbon-based and phase-change materials. Metal-based materials have good thermal conductivity and high mechanical strength, but they are relatively heavy; carbon-based materials are light and corrosion-resistant, but their thermal conductivity is anisotropic; phase-change materials absorb heat through latent heat and have the advantage of temperature regulation, but their continuous heat dissipation capacity is limited. The article introduces the current technical bottlenecks of all kinds of materials, forecasts the future development direction of thermal management materials, and concludes that future materials will be customised to some extent. This paper review and analyse battery thermal management materials to provide a basic reference for selecting materials in battery thermal management technology, promote the development of energy storage technology, and support the transition to a low-carbon energy system.

title: Exhibition as pedagogy: teaching energy geographies through Sweden’s transformed world exhibition 2045
source: Journal of Geography in Higher Education
summary: Teaching energy transitions requires students to engage with complex systems, contested futures and inequalities across places, scales and everyday life. This article explores how exhibitions can contribute to critical energy geography educ
content: Teaching energy transitions requires students to engage with complex systems, contested futures and inequalities across places, scales and everyday life. This article explores how exhibitions can contribute to critical energy geography education. Using Sweden’s Transformed World Exhibition 2045, a digital exhibition developed from research on Sweden’s contested transition towards biofuels, we examine the pedagogical potential of exhibitions for geographical inquiry. Through three pedagogical pathways, orienting and unsettling, connecting and tracing, and questioning and reimagining, we show how the exhibition can open energy transitions to questions of representation, temporality, justice, classification, power and possible futures. More broadly, we identify three ways exhibitions can be mobilised in teaching: teachers can invite students to critically read existing exhibitions, asking how particular energy futures are staged and what they leave out; use curated exhibitions as teaching resources for exploring contested energy geographies; or involve students in making exhibitions and counter-exhibitions themselves. Ultimately, we propose counter-exhibitionary pedagogy as an approach that uses exhibition not to present transition as settled, but to make it available for questioning, connection and critique.

title: A Panel Data Study of Economic Development and Carbon Emissions vs. Level of Green Investment
summary: This study examined the relationship between economic development and carbon dioxide emissions across 15 emerging nations from 2000 to 2024, employing a fixed effects panel data set within the STIRPAT framework, then verified the legitimacy
content: This study examined the relationship between economic development and carbon dioxide emissions across 15 emerging nations from 2000 to 2024, employing a fixed effects panel data set within the STIRPAT framework, then verified the legitimacy of the result via a 5-model sequential test. The findings confirm that all 15 sampled nations remain on the upward slope of the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC), with GDP per capita, population, and energy intensity emerging as the three dominant drivers of emissions growth.

title: Leading Systemic Change for Sustainable Higher Education Futures
source: Global Journal of Education Finance and Management
summary: Change is the only constant in life, so every organisation is interested in change. This article provides a coherent, theory-informed, integrated framework for leading the systemic change of higher education (HE) towards sustainable futures
content: Change is the only constant in life, so every organisation is interested in change. This article provides a coherent, theory-informed, integrated framework for leading the systemic change of higher education (HE) towards sustainable futures. Based on the Transformative Change Theory, Institutional Theory, and Systems Thinking, it synthesises how HE systems operate as adaptive complex networks and how resilient reform emerges from multi-level cross-actor processes. To offer practical insights for leaders and policymakers, this discussion navigates five intertwined dimensions: curriculum transformation (ESD and interdisciplinary learning), governance and leadership models, research/knowledge production for sustainability, campus operations/net-zero transitions, and community engagement with societal impact. The article details its three central propositions: HE is a learning system; the fundamental need for boundary-spanning governance/ distributed leadership to create intentional co-alignment between policy, practice and resource deployment, and between SUD goals; legitimacy/funding structure ecosystems co-evolve with reform, as drivers of systemic inertia and key enablers in re-orienting institutional purpose and ongoing iterative learning; and stakeholder co-production, co-design and cross-sector collaborations are necessary to transition scale-ready innovations emerging from pilot projects into systemic transformation outcomes. The analysis avoids prescriptive recommendations yet recognises tensions between central coherence and local autonomy, the long-term investment required, and the necessity for equity and inclusion. The article ends with some specific implications for policy, governance and practice, along with an evaluative framework to help track whether the change achieved through such mechanisms can be construed as durable over time.

title: Substantiating Green Claims: Corporate Liability and the Burden of Proof for Greenwashing under Indonesian Consumer Protection Law
summary: Environmental claims such as “eco-friendly”, “biodegradable” or “carbon neutral” now shape purchasing decisions in Indonesia, yet no Indonesian statute defines greenwashing or sets a standard for substantiating such claims. This article ask
content: Environmental claims such as “eco-friendly”, “biodegradable” or “carbon neutral” now shape purchasing decisions in Indonesia, yet no Indonesian statute defines greenwashing or sets a standard for substantiating such claims. This article asks whether existing Indonesian law can already qualify greenwashing as an unlawful act, under which legal elements, and what burden-of-proof model should govern environmental claims. Using normative legal research with statutory, conceptual, case and comparative approaches, it analyses Law No. 8 of 1999 on Consumer Protection element by element, its interaction with Law No. 1 of 2024 on Electronic Information and Transactions and the e-commerce rules, Indonesian decisions on misleading claims, and greenwashing decisions from the Netherlands, Germany and Australia. Three findings emerge. First, Articles 8(1)(f), 9(1) and 10 of the Consumer Protection Law are legally capable of covering false and unsubstantiated environmental claims without a new statute. Second, enforcement fails less for want of prohibitions than because of the evidentiary structure: consumers must disprove claims built on information held by the company, while administrative sanctions under Article 60 do not reach Articles 8 to 10. Third, Article 28 of the same law, which already reverses the burden of proving fault in compensation claims, provides a doctrinal foundation for a duty of prior substantiation. The article proposes a substantiation model in which business actors must hold verifiable evidence at the time a claim is made, generic claims are presumptively misleading, and sanctions are graduated by the claim’s seriousness.

source: Journal of Advanced Development in Engineering and Science
summary: This study aims to evaluate the technical performance and investment returns of a 5 kWp rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) system for a home office in Thailand. The analysis integrates simulation using PVsyst with actual electricity generation
content: This study aims to evaluate the technical performance and investment returns of a 5 kWp rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) system for a home office in Thailand. The analysis integrates simulation using PVsyst with actual electricity generation data collected over a one-year period. The economic feasibility is assessed using Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and Payback Period (PP). In addition, sensitivity analyses are conducted using both One-at-a-Time (OAT) and two-variable approaches to examine the effects of key parameters, including electricity tariff, solar irradiance, panel degradation rate, and discount rate. The potential for greenhouse gas emission reduction is also evaluated.The results indicate that the system achieves an average Performance Ratio of 0.839 (83.90%) and delivers a net annual electricity output of 7,032 kWh to the grid. The deviation between simulated and measured data is only 0.59%, confirming the reliability of the model. With an initial investment cost of THB 195,000, the project yields an NPV of THB 190,751 and an IRR of 15.38%, which is more than twice the discount rate of 6.82%, along with a payback period of 6.49 years. The two-variable sensitivity analysis shows that the IRR ranges from 11.84% to 19.04%, remaining higher than the discount rate under all scenarios.The installation of a rooftop PV system for a home office offers a significant advantage due to the alignment between daytime electricity consumption and solar generation, enabling full savings at the retail electricity tariff of 4.2 THB/kWh. Over a 25-year project lifetime, the system can reduce cumulative carbon dioxide emissions by 84,888 kgCO2e. In conclusion, the proposed system represents a cost-effective, low-risk investment that supports sustainable development goals.

title: Wind energy acceptance and forest owners’ land-leasing intentions: The role of beliefs and attitudes
summary: The expansion of wind power plays a crucial role in the European Union's decarbonization strategy. However, the social acceptance of wind power projects, particularly among landowners and non-landowners, remains a significant concern. Drawi
content: The expansion of wind power plays a crucial role in the European Union's decarbonization strategy. However, the social acceptance of wind power projects, particularly among landowners and non-landowners, remains a significant concern. Drawing on behavioural insights of the social acceptance literature, this study examines the beliefs, attitudes, and behavioural intentions of these groups towards wind power. We focus on the national context of Finland, where wind energy development has accelerated in recent years. Utilizing survey data from 2,103 respondents, including forest owners and non-forest owners, the study employs Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) and regression models to explore how beliefs shape attitudes, policy support and forest owners' behavioural intentions. The acceptance measures indicate that non-forest owners held more favourable attitudes towards wind power, associating it with environmental benefits and economic opportunities, while forest owners expressed greater concerns about landscape changes, land ownership, and economic impacts. The SEM model reveals that attitudes toward wind power were strongly influenced by beliefs about energy production and local impacts, which, in turn, shaped policy support. Additionally, forest owners’ willingness to lease land for wind turbines was associated with higher income level, owned land area size, and positive attitudes towards wind power. These findings highlight the need for tailored landscape-orientated policies that address explicitly address landowners’ concerns while fostering broader societal support for wind power. Enhancing procedural and distributive justice, improving compensation mechanisms, and integrating participatory planning processes could help accommodate resistance and facilitate a just energy transition.

title: Pathways to future sustainable wastewater management
summary: Wastewater management (WWM) plays a crucial role in protecting the environment and public health while also contributing to sustainable development. WWM currently faces significant challenges driven by ageing infrastructure and urbanisation
content: Wastewater management (WWM) plays a crucial role in protecting the environment and public health while also contributing to sustainable development. WWM currently faces significant challenges driven by ageing infrastructure and urbanisation, as well as uncertainties about future developments related to regulations, climate impact, energy use, and resource recovery. Developing WWM sustainably therefore requires decision support that can account for such challenges and uncertainties while balancing environmental, social, and economic considerations. This thesis addresses three issues: which future conditions WWM should prepare for, what sustainable WWM entails, and how alternative development pathways can be assessed in terms of their sustainability.First, to identify future conditions that WWM should prepare for, a future scenario approach was developed, combining stakeholder participation, expert knowledge, and process modelling. Applied to an existing wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), the approach identified and specified relevant future conditions related to flows, treatment requirements, and environmental and climate impact. Process modelling of quantified future scenarios showed that the WWTP would require substantial upgrades to meet anticipated future demands. Second, to clarify what sustainable WWM entails, a definition of sustainable WWM was formulated by interpreting and synthesising established sustainability frameworks in the context of WWM. The resulting definition consists of eleven sustainability areas, specified by objectives and linked to criteria, providing a structured basis for understanding and assessing sustainable WWM. Third, to compare alternative development pathways, a sustainability assessment method based on multicriteria analysis was developed. The methodological contributions include linear scoring, calculation of weighted score ratios, structured sensitivity analyses, and a monetary-based weighting procedure supported by a compilation of monetary reference values. These contributions aim to increase transparency and help decision-makers understand how scoring and weighting choices affect results. Application of the method to case studies showed that making monetary implications explicit and relating them to reference values facilitates discussion of criterion weighting and trade-offs. Including sensitivity analyses helps evaluate result robustness and account for uncertainties.This thesis provides a coherent framework for sustainable decision-making in WWM, with interconnected components that can be used individually. The thesis supports decision-making under uncertainty and promotes transparent and robust planning of future WWM.

title: Chemical Coordination and Pore Confinement Enabling a Bifunctional Interface for Accelerated Desolvation and Oriented Deposition Toward Stable Zinc Metal Anodes
summary: ABSTRACT Aqueous zinc‐ion batteries show great potential for large‐scale energy storage; however, dendrites formation and corrosion on zinc anodes significantly hinder their practical applications. Uneven Zn deposition leads to dendrite gro
content: ABSTRACT Aqueous zinc‐ion batteries show great potential for large‐scale energy storage; however, dendrites formation and corrosion on zinc anodes significantly hinder their practical applications. Uneven Zn deposition leads to dendrite growth, while H 2 O molecules in solvated Zn 2+ ions exacerbate surface corrosion and the hydrogen evolution reaction. Herein, we propose a Schiff‐base‐covalently‐grafted UiO‐66‐NH 2 metal‐organic framework to construct a bifunctional interface for stable zinc metal anodes. Specifically, the chemical chelation between Schiff base and Zn 2+ accelerates desolvation and suppresses side reactions. Meanwhile, the uniformly distributed Zn 2+ ‐chelated sites and the well‐defined confined pore channels of UiO‐66‐NH 2 scaffold guide a homogeneous Zn 2+ flux and promote Zn(002)‐oriented deposition. As a result, this bifunctional interface enables Zn plating/stripping with a high Coulombic efficiency of 99.8% over 2000 cycles at 5 mA cm −2 /1 mAh cm −2 . Furthermore, it achieves a capacity retention of over 90% after 4000 charge–discharge cycles in a Zn||MnO 2 full cell. This work is expected to open a new avenue for interfacial chemical regulation toward stabilizing zinc metal anodes.

title: Redirecting gypsum scaling in pervaporation desalination via activated alumina granules
summary: Membrane scaling, particularly CaSO4 (gypsum) crystallisation, severely limits the practical application of pervaporation (PV) desalination for high-salinity wastewater treatment. Herein, an online interception strategy using nitric acid-ac
content: Membrane scaling, particularly CaSO4 (gypsum) crystallisation, severely limits the practical application of pervaporation (PV) desalination for high-salinity wastewater treatment. Herein, an online interception strategy using nitric acid-activated alumina granules (AAG) is proposed to redirect gypsum scaling from the membrane surface to a sacrificial medium. By tuning nitric acid activation, the physicochemical properties of AAG were optimised. AAG activated with 7.5% nitric acid exhibits an optimal pore structure (specific surface area of 295.4 m2/g, pore volume of 0.361 cm3/g) and surface positive charge, significantly reducing the heterogeneous nucleation energy barrier for gypsum crystallisation. This enables the transfer of scaling from the membrane surface to AAG, reducing the membrane surface scaling amount by approximately 45%. Combined with the extended XDLVO theory analysis, the dominant mechanism of surface-induced heterogeneous nucleation by AAG was elucidated. Moreover, ultrasonic–EDTA cleaning enables efficient regeneration of AAG, and the strategy is validated using real reverse osmosis concentrate. This work establishes a scaling control paradigm based on crystallisation relocation rather than inhibition, providing mechanistic insight and a scalable approach for fouling mitigation in PV desalination.

title: From global rare earth resources to the EU supply security: An overview on primary and alternative resources and strategic pathways
summary: Abstract The increasing strategic importance of rare earth elements is shaped by geopolitical factors, supply risks, and rising demand from high-technology, energy transition, and defense sectors, rather than geological scarcity. For the Eu
content: Abstract The increasing strategic importance of rare earth elements is shaped by geopolitical factors, supply risks, and rising demand from high-technology, energy transition, and defense sectors, rather than geological scarcity. For the European Union, rare earth elements represent both a critical vulnerability and an essential resource for achieving policy objectives. Therefore, peer-reviewed literature, industry reports, and policy documents published through 2026 were synthesized to assess geological conditions of rare earths global and EU resources, current mining and refining capacities, potential contribution of selected alternative sources, and global diversifying strategies of major rare-earth consuming economies. The findings indicate that alternative sources, such as coal ash, red mud, electronic waste, and deep-sea mining, are unlikely to reduce the EU import dependence in the short to medium term due to combined geological, technological, economic, and environmental constraints. The findings show that the EU’s mining, refining, and stockpiling capacities remain comparatively underdeveloped, whereas major rare earth element-consuming economies, including China, the U.S., and Japan have strengthened supply security through integrated strategies combining domestic production, overseas investments, technological innovation, and stockpiling. To reduce strategic dependence, the EU requires an integrated strategy aligned with the Critical Raw Materials Act, including expanded exploration incentives and refining capacity, strategic partnerships and coordinated stockpiling mechanisms. Such measures are essential to enhance resilience against supply disruptions, strengthen competitiveness, and support the EU’s transition to a sustainable and secure resource future under evolving global market conditions and intensifying geopolitical competition worldwide.

title: Can integrated legal and administrative governance reduce corporate carbon emissions?
summary: Traditional environmental governance often relies on a single regulatory form, necessitating the exploration of more comprehensive integrated governance models. Utilizing the pilot program of procuratorial public interest litigation in Chin
content: Traditional environmental governance often relies on a single regulatory form, necessitating the exploration of more comprehensive integrated governance models. Utilizing the pilot program of procuratorial public interest litigation in China as a quasi-natural experiment, this study investigates the impact of integrated legal and administrative governance on corporate carbon emissions and the underlying mechanisms. The findings demonstrate that this governance model significantly reduces corporate carbon emissions. Mechanism tests reveal that the policy functions by strengthening institutional constraints, incentivizing green investments, mobilizing public environmental supervision, and heightening corporate litigation risks. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that factors such as executives’ environmental experience, industry pollution attributes, regional rule of law levels, and market competition exert differential effects on the policy’s impact. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the policy further enhances firms’ overall ESG performance. These findings confirm that integrating judicial oversight with administrative supervision is a viable pathway for achieving carbon neutrality, offering valuable insights for constructing a multi-stakeholder environmental governance system.

title: Mitochondrial transplantation for kidney disease: evidence, delivery constraints, and translational priorities
summary: Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies multiple forms of renal injury, prompting strategies to restore organellar function rather than target discrete signaling pathways. Mitochondrial transplantation (MTx) has produced short-term functional,
content: Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies multiple forms of renal injury, prompting strategies to restore organellar function rather than target discrete signaling pathways. Mitochondrial transplantation (MTx) has produced short-term functional, histological, or cellular benefits in preclinical models of renal ischemia-reperfusion, toxic and complex acute kidney injury, focal diabetic tubular injury, ex vivo kidney perfusion, and direct renal-cell stress. Interpretation remains difficult because routes, preparations, and follow-up differ, and few studies connect organ benefit to recipient-cell delivery and donor-organelle fate. We posit that renal MTx is most plausible when reversible mitochondrial lesions, viable recipient renal cells, and accessible delivery routes coexist. Acute reperfusion-associated injury currently aligns these conditions most clearly, whereas diffuse chronic disease is less clearly suited to intact-organelle therapy. The immediate task is to determine whether a defined product can reproducibly reach an accessible renal target and alter its trajectory.

title: Valorization of Jackfruit Seed Waste for Composite Film Preparation: Property Enhancement via Bacterial Cellulose Reinforcement
summary: Conventional plastic has become an essential element in the manufacturing of nearly all consumer products. However, it has emerged as a major contributor to environmental pollution and is difficult to biodegrade. This research therefore syn
content: Conventional plastic has become an essential element in the manufacturing of nearly all consumer products. However, it has emerged as a major contributor to environmental pollution and is difficult to biodegrade. This research therefore synthesizes composite films from jackfruit seed (JSF) reinforced with bacterial cellulose (BC) for a sustainable alternative. The structural, physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of Jackfruit Seed Starch-based composite films (JSF/BC) were investigated. The incorporation of BC fiber into the JSF composite film matrix significantly enhanced the water resistance, UV blocking, and thermal stability. By loading BC at 40 wt.%, the mechanical properties, such as tensile strength and elongation, were 0.74 MPa and 10.21%, respectively. JSF/BC composite films had a thermal stability at temperatures up to approximately 270 °C. JSF/BC composite films also exhibited a biodegradability of 72.1 - 100% within 15 days. The experimental results indicate that the composite film offers a green, high-performing alternative to conventional plastics, suitable for packaging and other short-term plastic products.

title: Advances in medical plastic waste treatment methods towards sustainable development
summary: The rapid expansion of healthcare services has led to a substantial increase in medical plastic waste (MPW), posing significant environmental and public health challenges and highlighting the need for sustainable waste management strategies
content: The rapid expansion of healthcare services has led to a substantial increase in medical plastic waste (MPW), posing significant environmental and public health challenges and highlighting the need for sustainable waste management strategies. The present review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in MPW treatment and valorization strategies for sustainable development. Previous reviews have primarily focused on general biomedical waste management or individual treatment technologies. This review critically examines MPW, its classification, major medical polymers, environmental impacts, conventional and advanced treatment technologies, their comparative assessment, emerging recycling approaches, derived value-added products and their characterization, challenges and their potential solutions, and future prospects for sustainable MPW management. Conventional and advanced treatment methods are evaluated with respect to their treatment efficiency, environmental impacts, resource-recovery potential, and limitations. The analysis demonstrates that no single treatment technology is universally suitable for heterogeneous MPW rather, the appropriate pathway depends on polymer composition, contamination level, treatment objective, resource-recovery potential, environmental and economic considerations. Emerging approaches such as catalytic recycling, enzymatic depolymerization and artificial intelligence assisted waste management further expand opportunities for selective recovery. This review also highlights the conversion of MPW into fuels, syngas, carbon-based materials, construction materials, acoustic panels, and composite fillers. Overall, integrated polymer-specific treatment and valorization pathways supported by life cycle and techno-economic assessment are essential for transitioning MPW from conventional disposal toward resource recovery and a circular healthcare system. title: Mechanism‐guided direct regeneration of degraded NCM cathodes: From atomic‐scale degradation to structural and electrochemical recovery
summary: Abstract As a cornerstone technology for clean energy storage, lithium‐ion batteries confront critical challenges of resource scarcity and environmental impacts from decommissioned cells. This study focuses on the regeneration of degraded n
content: Abstract As a cornerstone technology for clean energy storage, lithium‐ion batteries confront critical challenges of resource scarcity and environmental impacts from decommissioned cells. This study focuses on the regeneration of degraded nickel‐cobalt‐manganese (NCM) cathodes exhibiting low capacity of 128.33 mAh g −1 at 0.1 C. Through atomic‐scale scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis, multiscale degradation mechanisms were systematically revealed: progressive phase transformations from layered structure to rock‐salt and spinel configurations driven by lithium vacancy clustering and transition metal migration, oxygen lattice evolution involving irreversible oxygen release, and mechanical degradation through bulk microcrack propagation and dissolution. Based on these mechanistic insights, LiOH·H 2 O compensation and oxygen‐controlled thermal reconstruction are combined to repair degraded NCM cathodes. Advanced STEM characterization verifies three‐dimensional structural restoration, including phase reversion from rock‐salt/spinel intergrowth to reconstructed layered architecture, oxygen vacancy remediation through lattice oxygen reincorporation, and microcrack healing. The regenerated NCM cathodes achieve exceptional electrochemical recovery, delivering a high reversible capacity of 184.78 mAh g −1 at 0.1 C with restored cycling stability. Those findings provide both fundamental insights into phase transformation dynamics and an industrially viable approach for next‐generation battery recycling technology.
