JOURNAL OF THE AIR & WASTE MANAGEMENT ASSOCIATION. Air & Waste Management Association, Pittsburgh, PA, USA, 576-591, (2019).

title: Defending Indigenous Territories Through Law and Collective Power
summary: Law’s capacity to transform unequal power relations depends on how legal action supports community organising and whether this support remains guided by communities’ own priorities and decisions. This matters because energy projects begin t
content: Law’s capacity to transform unequal power relations depends on how legal action supports community organising and whether this support remains guided by communities’ own priorities and decisions. This matters because energy projects begin to transform territories before construction starts: Contracts establish claims over land, permits authorise particular uses, and administrative procedures determine whose participation counts. Indigenous peoples challenging these projects must therefore engage with institutions whose decisions helped make them possible.

title: Intensification and Low-Carbon Performance: A Two-Stage Framework for Evaluating Urban Construction Land Use Efficiency Across 268 Chinese Cities
summary: Evaluating urban construction land use efficiency (UCLUE) from the dual perspectives of intensification and low-carbon performance is critical for sustainable urban development. Previous studies often assess this efficiency from a single pe
content: Evaluating urban construction land use efficiency (UCLUE) from the dual perspectives of intensification and low-carbon performance is critical for sustainable urban development. Previous studies often assess this efficiency from a single perspective, failing to capture potential conflicts and synergies between economic density and emission reduction goals. This study adopts a two-stage super-SBM approach to evaluate UCLUE of 268 Chinese cities from 2001 to 2021, systematically examining both intensification and low-carbon dimensions. Results show that (1) the average efficiency from an intensification perspective remains relatively low and exhibits a fluctuating pattern of initial increase, subsequent decline, and final rebound, with the eastern region ranking highest, followed by the western and central regions. (2) The low-carbon efficiency follows a U-shaped trajectory over the study period, with the eastern region again performing best, followed by the western and central regions. (3) Many cities exhibit relatively low efficiency in both dimensions, with 146 of the 268 cities (54.48%) falling into the Low–Low development mode and only 53 cities (19.78%) achieving the High–High development mode. Furthermore, cities with larger population sizes demonstrate stronger sustainable performance. These findings provide empirical evidence for identifying spatial heterogeneities and formulating differentiated, context-specific land use policies to coordinate urban expansion and carbon reduction.

title: Temperature modulates sediment priming triggered by simulated algal blooms: Insights from sediment microbial fuel cells
summary: Abstract. Mangrove sediments are major blue carbon reservoirs, yet how warming and eutrophication interact to control the stability of sediment organic carbon (SOC) remains uncertain. Here, we combined sediment microbial fuel cell (SMFC) mo
content: Abstract. Mangrove sediments are major blue carbon reservoirs, yet how warming and eutrophication interact to control the stability of sediment organic carbon (SOC) remains uncertain. Here, we combined sediment microbial fuel cell (SMFC) monitoring with (in)organic carbon analyses, and lignin biomarker measurements in 13C-labeled algal-amended subtropical mangrove sediments to investigate temperature-dependent priming of SOC at 25, 30, and 35 ℃. Baseline SOC mineralization exhibited a nonlinear increase across the 25–30 °C thermal range, followed by a distinct decline at 35 °C. In contrast, priming intensity increased progressively with increasing temperature, shifting from weakly negative to strongly positive. This divergence reveals that warming decouples intrinsic SOC mineralization from priming-driven carbon turnover. Mechanistically, algal inputs provided energetic sources that activated opportunistic copiotrophs (Bacteroidota) and restructured anodic interactomes by enriching syntrophic microorganisms (e.g., Anaerolineaceae, Desulfosarcinaceae). Rather than relying on obligate aerobes, late-stage oxidative cleavage of recalcitrant lignin phenols was sustained under anoxic conditions by the active anode, which served as an inexhaustible electron sink via extracellular electron transfer. These findings suggest that warming shifts microbial metabolisms rather than uniformly stimulating carbon mineralization, promoting the priming degradation of otherwise stable SOC. Consequently, warming may disproportionately increase the vulnerability of stabilized SOC in eutrophic mangrove ecosystems by amplifying priming effects relative to baseline mineralization. Incorporating temperature-dependent priming into blue carbon models may improve predictions of coastal carbon storage under future climate change.

title: Effect of Cassava Value Web Participation On the Livelihood of Farming Households in Saki Adp Zone of Oyo State, Nigeria
summary: This study investigates the impact of cassava value web participation on the livelihoods of farming households in the Saki Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) zone of Oyo State, Nigeria. Utilizing a multistage sampling technique, data
content: This study investigates the impact of cassava value web participation on the livelihoods of farming households in the Saki Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) zone of Oyo State, Nigeria. Utilizing a multistage sampling technique, data were collected from 296 cassava farmers through structured questionnaires. The analysis reveals that about 54.70% of the respondents were male, about 38.4% fall between the ages of 51 to 60 years, a significant proportion of respondents are engaged primarily in farming, with limited formal education impacting their adoption of innovative agricultural practices. The most common cropping pattern among the cassava-based farmers was cassava/yam/ Maize mixture with 33.1% concentration of the sampled. The findings indicate that participation in the cassava value web enhances household income and promotes sustainable agricultural practices through resource efficiency and waste reduction. However, challenges such as inadequate processing technology and environmental pollution from cassava waste remain critical concerns. The study underscores the necessity for integrated approaches that enhance value addition and promote sustainable practices within the cassava sector. In conclusion cassava value web presents a significant opportunity for improving the livelihoods of farming households in the Saki ADP zone. The study therefore recommends that implementing training programs that will focus on modern agricultural practices and technologies to improve farmers' skills and knowledge and promote higher productivity should be considered

title: Reduced soil disturbance as a regenerative agriculture practice in organic winter squash production : short-term trade-offs in yield, soil health, and greenhouse gas emissions
summary: A growing body of evidence shows that, over the long term, organic and regenerative agricultural practices, including reduced soil disturbance and cover cropping, can improve soil health, crop productivity, biodiversity, and climate change
content: A growing body of evidence shows that, over the long term, organic and regenerative agricultural practices, including reduced soil disturbance and cover cropping, can improve soil health, crop productivity, biodiversity, and climate change mitigation while lowering fuel and input use. Given these benefits, reduced-disturbance practices have been adopted widely in certain cropping systems but less so in organic vegetable systems, which rely on intensive tillage for weed control. Thus, despite reported long-term benefits, the short-term trade-offs remain unclear, impeding adoption in organic vegetable production. This study evaluated the short-term effects of three regenerative practices on organic winter squash relative to the current standard: Summer Cover Crop (SCC), No-Tillage + Tarp (NTT), Reduced Tillage + Tarp (RTT), and Standard Tillage (ST). Treatments were compared for crop yield, soil health indicators, and greenhouse gas emissions at the UBC Farm in Vancouver, British Columbia, over two field seasons (2024–2025). Across most indicators, NTT, RTT, and SCC did not differ significantly from ST. Yield showed no significant treatment effects, and no differences were observed in any of the soil health indicators measured, including nitrogen availability, aggregate stability, and earthworm abundance. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) fluxes were closely tied to the timing of physical disturbance events, but no significant treatment effects were detected on any individual sampling date. Cumulative CO₂ emissions and yield-scaled CO₂ emissions, however, were significantly higher in NTT than ST during the 2025 production season, reflecting a short-term trade-off consistent with the literature. Across treatments, CO₂ and N₂O emissions were substantially higher than values reported for comparable reduced-tillage vegetable systems, likely reflecting UBC Farm's baseline soil conditions. Although NTT showed elevated CO₂ emissions in the 2025 production season, findings across most indicators suggest that, over the short term, reduced-disturbance practices did not incur trade-offs that would prevent adoption, a necessary first step toward realizing their long-term benefits reported in the literature. Adoption decisions may be guided by practical factors like labour and site-specific goals, while longer-term, regionally grounded research is needed to establish these practices’ full agronomic and climate implications in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Effect of Water Temperature, Contact Time and Particle Size on the Leaching Characteristics of Organic and Inorganic Matter from Sugarcane Trash Briquettes
summary: Global depletion of fossil fuels and the environmental costs of their use motivate renewable alternatives. Sugarcane trash is abundant but rich in potassium, silica, chlorine, and alkali/alkaline earth metals, which drive ash formation, sla
content: Global depletion of fossil fuels and the environmental costs of their use motivate renewable alternatives. Sugarcane trash is abundant but rich in potassium, silica, chlorine, and alkali/alkaline earth metals, which drive ash formation, slagging, fouling, corrosion, and hazardous air pollutants during combustion. This study evaluates water leaching as a pretreatment to reduce problematic inorganic/organic constituents and to improve combustion and emission performance of sugarcane trash briquettes. Raw cane trash (CO 421, Migori County) was collected, size-reduced (1, 5, 10 mm), and leached in ultrapure water at 25, 50, and 100 °C for 20, 40, and 60 min using a 3×3×3 full factorial design (27 runs; triplicates). Post-leach solids were densified via hydraulic press (18 MPa; DIN 54385:2016-08). Elemental and ash-forming species (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Si; Cl, S, P) were quantified by standard methods; leachates were analyzed for pH, EC, TOC, and organic acids. Leaching increased C from 46.27 to 49.73 wt% and eliminated detectable Cl; N and S decreased by 39.5% and 66.7%, respectively. Ash-forming K and Mg in solids fell by 63.09%and 44.00%, while Si declined slightly (≈4.3%) and Ca rose (≈15.9%). Leachates were mildly acidic (pH ≈ 5.5) and contained organic acids totaling 2.91% of TOC. Electrical conductivity trends and performance gains were strongest with smaller particle size, higher temperature, and longer contact time. The optimum temperature, time and size were 50 °C, 60-minute and 1 mm, respectively.

title: Pilot-scale pyrolysis of green coconut husk pellets for biochar production and evaluation in bituminous coal–biochar blends
summary: Coal-fired thermoelectric plants remain important for dispatchable electricity generation and supply stability, but their dependence on fossil carbon results in high greenhouse gas emissions. This study evaluated pilot-scale batch pyrolysis
content: Coal-fired thermoelectric plants remain important for dispatchable electricity generation and supply stability, but their dependence on fossil carbon results in high greenhouse gas emissions. This study evaluated pilot-scale batch pyrolysis of green coconut husk pellets for biochar production and its incorporation into bituminous coal blends as a potential route for partial fossil-coal substitution. Pyrolysis experiments were performed in a pilot-scale pyrolysis unit using 40 kg of pellets at final temperatures of 400 and 500 °C. The products were characterized by proximate analysis, higher heating value (HHV), non-condensable gas composition, and mass and energy balances. Coal–BIO400 blends were prepared with biochar produced at 400 °C (BIO400) at 1, 5, 10, and 20 wt% and characterized for proximate, elemental, inorganic, morphological, surface elemental, and energetic properties. Pyrolysis at 400 °C favored biochar production, with a yield of 34.13%, compared with 28.05% at 500 °C. Although the 500 °C condition increased non-condensable gas yield from 15.93% to 22.57%, the 400 °C condition showed a significantly higher recoverable product-energy ratio, while no statistically significant differences were detected in gross product-energy recovery ratio or biochar energy between the two conditions. BIO400 showed low moisture content, high fixed carbon content, and an HHV of 27.42 MJ·kg⁻¹, corresponding to 96.7% of the bituminous coal HHV. The coal–BIO400 blends retained HHV values of 28.25–28.44 MJ·kg⁻¹, and no statistically significant differences in HHV were detected among BIO400, bituminous coal, and the coal–BIO400 blends under the reported analytical conditions. These results support the evaluation of green coconut husk biochar as a potential component for partial fossil-coal substitution, although combustion, emission, ash behavior, boiler compatibility, and life-cycle assessments are still required.

title: A “cradle-to-grave” life-cycle assessment of biokerosene production through chemical looping gasification for use in jet engine: Comparing second and third generation biomasses
summary: Current biofuels are mainly derived from second and third generation biomasses. When used in chemical looping gasification (CLG), biomasses can be converted to undiluted syngas that is ready for conversion to biofuels, while the energy-inte
content: Current biofuels are mainly derived from second and third generation biomasses. When used in chemical looping gasification (CLG), biomasses can be converted to undiluted syngas that is ready for conversion to biofuels, while the energy-intense air separation needed in conventional gasification is avoided. This work performs a “cradle-to-grave” life-cycle assessment (LCA) for biokerosene production and use in jet engines. The syngas for kerosene synthesis is generated through CLG technology with ilmenite as oxygen carrier and tablets of two types of microalgae and pellets of wheat straw and forest wood as feedstocks. These biomasses are representative precursors of two generations of biofuels. The LCA model covers all steps from biomass cultivation/growth to the final biokerosene combustion in jet engines. The four biomasses and ilmenite originate from inside Spain, and after production and mining they are transported to produce syngas in a CLG plant that is assumed near Zaragoza in Spain. Downstream syngas processing includes catalyzed Water-Gas Shift, Fischer-Tropsch (F-T) synthesis, Dry Reforming and uncatalyzed Pressure Swinging Adsorption and Refining. The syntheses of catalysts and adsorbents are also considered. The biokerosene is finally transported to a nearby airport for use in jet engines. The European Commission’s Environmental Footprint method with sixteen indicators is employed to study the process’s potential life-cycle impacts to climate, atmosphere, ecosystem, biodiversity, human health and natural resource depletion. Among the four biomasses, the microalgae produced from raceway pounds have the highest global warming potential (19.4 kg CO 2 eq. emissions), and this is followed by the microalgae from photobioreactors (16.6 kg CO 2 eq. emissions). Microalgae from the photobioreactor use the least land (only 83.7Pt), while wheat straw occupies the most land (1770Pt) for production of 1 kg biokerosene. Hotspot analyses are done through subprocesses’ contributions, and the most influencing flows and parameters are identified. A series of sensitivity and Monte Carlo analyses are made to study the indicators’ sensitivity and robustness. Finally, a scenario analysis is performed to find options that could be used to lower the life-cycle impacts with microalgae.

title: Effect of C–N Cross-Reactions between Volatiles and NH3 in NO Formation during Coal/Ammonia Co-Firing under Low-Oxygen Dilution
summary: Abstract Coal/NH3 co-firing is one of the feasible technological pathways for the low-carbon transition of coal-fired plants, and reducing NOx emissions is key to promoting its application due to the extremely high nitrogen content in NH3 f
content: Abstract Coal/NH3 co-firing is one of the feasible technological pathways for the low-carbon transition of coal-fired plants, and reducing NOx emissions is key to promoting its application due to the extremely high nitrogen content in NH3 fuel. During co-firing, the gas-phase interaction between coal volatiles and NH3, which mainly involves the C–N cross-reactions between N-containing intermediates and hydrocarbon components, critically regulates NO formation and is strongly dependent on the local oxygen environment. The low-O2 dilution environment achieved in MILD (moderate or intense low-oxygen dilution) combustion favors this interaction and enhances its inhibitory effect on NO formation. However, the underlying mechanism of this influence remains unclear. This study combines experiments with chemical kinetics to elucidate how C–N cross-reactions suppress NO under low-oxygen dilution, in terms of free radical regulation, key reaction enhancement, and dominant pathway competition. Results indicate that C–N cross-reactions significantly inhibit the formation of the free radical pool, and their inhibitory effect is enhanced as the NH3 blending ratio increases. Besides, C–N cross-reactions inhibit the conversion of NH2 → HNO and NH → NO by weakening R95 (NH2 + O = HNO + H) and R112 (NH + O = NO + H), while promoting the conversions of NO → N2 and NNH → N2 by enhancing reactions R107 (NH2 + NO = N2 + H2O) and R121 (NNH = N2 + H). Furthermore, a two-step ROP analysis method was further developed to quantify the probability of occurrence for different fuel-N conversion pathways at the moment of maximum NO production rate, thereby evaluating changes in the contribution of main pathways to NO formation. The removal of C–N cross-reactions increases the probabilities of path a (NH3 → NH2 → HNO → NO) and path c (NH3 → NH2 → NH → NO) from 24.2 and 7.2% to 38.4 and 18.0%, respectively. The decoupling of C–N cross-reactions indicates that NH2 hydrogen abstraction (G1 subset) and N2Hx/CH3 interaction (G5 subset) play a key role in inhibiting NO formation.

title: QINKUAL LiFePO4 Prismatic Cells
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Persistent and Transient Carbon Efficiency in the Provision of Water Services: Evidence From England and Wales
summary: ABSTRACT Assessing the carbon performance of water utilities is essential for the transition towards low‐carbon urban water systems. However, the design of effective policies and managerial actions requires a clear understanding of the unde
content: ABSTRACT Assessing the carbon performance of water utilities is essential for the transition towards low‐carbon urban water systems. However, the design of effective policies and managerial actions requires a clear understanding of the underlying drivers of carbon performance. This study contributes to this objective by proposing and estimating an overall carbon efficiency index (OCEI) that explicitly distinguishes between transient (time‐varying) and persistent (time‐invariant) components of inefficiency. Carbon efficiency is modelled using a four‐error‐component stochastic frontier carbon‐oriented distance function for English and Welsh Water and Sewerage Companies and Water Only Companies over the period 2010–2020. The results show that average OCEI values remain low, at 0.403 for Water and Sewerage Companies and 0.440 for Water Only Companies, indicating substantial scope for reducing carbon emissions. Improvements in OCEI observed up to 2017 are driven almost entirely by transient carbon efficiency, which increases to approximately 0.88 before declining sharply after 2018, highlighting the dominant role of short‐run operational practices in shaping overall carbon performance. In contrast, persistent carbon efficiency remains stable and low throughout the period, with average values close to 0.51 across all utility types, indicating a substantial persistent component of carbon inefficiency throughout the period. These findings provide new evidence on the relative importance of operational versus persistent drivers of carbon efficiency in the water sector and offer policy‐relevant insights for the design of regulatory and managerial strategies aimed at long‐term decarbonization.

title: Dataset for "Comparing UK Construction and Built Environment Sectoral Coverage and Carbon Footprints Across Global MRIO Databases"
summary: This dataset contains the analytical source code, processed data tables, and mapping frameworks supporting the conference paper "Comparing UK Construction and Built Environment Sectoral Coverage and Carbon Footprints Across Global MRIO Data
content: This dataset contains the analytical source code, processed data tables, and mapping frameworks supporting the conference paper "Comparing UK Construction and Built Environment Sectoral Coverage and Carbon Footprints Across Global MRIO Databases". The data focuses on the harmonisation and comparison of 13 global Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) databases, specifically assessing their representation of UK Construction and Built Environment (CBE) sectors. The dataset includes three primary components: 1-Sectoral and Geographical Resolution Data: Comprehensive Excel tables documenting the spatial and sectoral granularity of 13 MRIO databases (including CEDA, EXIOBASE, WIOD, Eora, and others). This includes a harmonisation framework that maps diverse original MRIO classifications into nine functional CBE categories (e.g., Mining, Wood, Cement, Services) to enable cross-database comparison. 2-Carbon Footprint Comparison Data: Calculated monetary emission factors (kgCO₂e/£) for the year 2022, covering specific UK CBE sectors. This data facilitates a direct quantitative comparison across four key databases: UK MRIO, SWC MRIO, EXIOBASE (Industry-by-Industry and Product-by-Product versions), and ADB MRIO. 3-Code: A suite of Jupyter Notebooks (Python) used to parse raw MRIO data, perform currency and unit conversions, calculate carbon footprints, and generate the study's comparative visualizations (Figure 1 and Figure 2).

title: Optimizing the carbon footprint of an offshore upstream asset by maximizing its energy efficiency: An integrated exergetic modeling approach
summary: Le contexte climatique actuel requiert une décarbonation massive des actifs de production d’hydrocarbures. L’objectif de cette étude consiste à élaborer une méthodologie avancée pour l’évaluation quantitative et l’optimisation de la perform
content: Le contexte climatique actuel requiert une décarbonation massive des actifs de production d’hydrocarbures. L’objectif de cette étude consiste à élaborer une méthodologie avancée pour l’évaluation quantitative et l’optimisation de la performance énergétique et des émissions de gaz à effet de serre d’une installation amont offshore en exploitation. À l’aide d’un modèle exergétique dynamique implémenté en Python, cette approche permet de simuler à la fois la dynamique du réservoir en sous-sol et le comportement des procédés en surface. Son architecture flexible prend en charge un large éventail d’interfaces et de solveurs d’optimisation. Le modèle intègre le logiciel GAP de Petex pour la modélisation des écoulements en sous-sol et la gestion du réservoir, ainsi que le logiciel BEST, propriété de TotalEnergies, adapté à la simulation des procédés en surface permettant ainsi une analyse holistique du système. Un bilan exergétique est réalisé sur l’ensemble de la chaîne de production, et les résultats du modèle sont comparés aux données historiques de production du site pour validation. Les résultats de l’étude initiale révèlent que les unités de traitement en surface, en particulier les turbines à gaz utilisées pour la réinjection de gaz lift, sont responsables de plus de 70 % de la destruction totale d’exergie. Ces zones inefficaces énergétiquement sont prioritaires par rapport aux réductions des émissions de carbone. Les variables des procédés de surface identifiées pour l’optimisation incluent la pression de séparation des hydrocarbures du premier séparateur de surface, la configuration du train de recompression du gaz et la répartition de la charge des turbines, chacune influençant de manière significative l’intensité de l’empreinte carbone du site sous contraintes opérationnelles. Les tests d’optimisation préliminaires démontrent une corrélation directe entre la minimisation des irréversibilités de procédé et les émissions de GES. Ainsi, le modèle proposé permet de prédire les interdépendances liées à l’interaction entre la surface et la subsurface afin d'optimiser l'intégration des différents éléments de l'installation industrielle tout au long de son cycle de vie, visant à une meilleure utilisation de l’énergie et à la réduction significative de son impact environnemental.

title: Exciton Diffusion in Covalent Triazine Frameworks and its Role in Photocatalytic Redox Transformations
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
summary: Abstract Covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) are promising heterogeneous photocatalysts, yet the transport of photogenerated excitons and its effect on catalytic output remains poorly understood. Here, we show that excited-state diffusivity
content: Abstract Covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) are promising heterogeneous photocatalysts, yet the transport of photogenerated excitons and its effect on catalytic output remains poorly understood. Here, we show that excited-state diffusivity is a key determinant of photocatalytic performance. We compare two quinoline-based CTFs containing adjacent phenyl or pyridine units to assess the role of backbone conjugation, supported by DFT calculations. Experimentally determined exciton diffusivities are correlated with photocatalytic Cr(VI) reduction. Enhanced conjugation improves exciton transport and catalytic efficiency, establishing excited-state mobility as a key design parameter.

title: From Farm-level Tools to State-level Assessment: A Scoping Review of Dairy Sustainability Indicators
source: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
summary: Dairy production is expected to deliver nutritious food, rural livelihoods and export earnings while reducing greenhouse gas emissions, nutrient losses and pressures on land, water, biodiversity and animal welfare. Indicators are the princi
content: Dairy production is expected to deliver nutritious food, rural livelihoods and export earnings while reducing greenhouse gas emissions, nutrient losses and pressures on land, water, biodiversity and animal welfare. Indicators are the principal means by which these expectations are translated into measurable performance, yet they are developed for different purposes and at different scales, from on-farm diagnostic tools to sector inventories and jurisdiction-wide composite indices. This critical narrative review, conducted with a scoping purpose, maps how dairy sustainability indicators are constructed, applied and aggregated across the farm, supply-chain, regional and state or national levels, and evaluates whether information generated at one level can legitimately inform decisions at another. Peer-reviewed studies, methodological reviews and authoritative institutional sources were identified through multidisciplinary, agricultural, economic and regional scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking, and were appraised qualitatively for relevance, transparency, representativeness and robustness. The synthesis shows that farm-level tools differ widely in normative framing, indicator logic, scoring and aggregation, so that tools applied to the same farms can produce divergent judgements. Environmental indicators are the most mature, but carbon footprints remain sensitive to allocation rules, emission-factor tiers and functional units, and intensity metrics often move in the opposite direction to absolute emissions that matter for state targets. Economic indicators are comparatively well supported by accountancy data, whereas social and animal-welfare indicators remain under-specified and are frequently lost or distorted during aggregation. State-level assessments follow four broad routes: weighting representative farm samples, top-down inventories, modelled regional typologies and composite indices built from administrative statistics. Each route carries characteristic risks, including unrepresentative sampling, spatial misallocation, leakage through imported feed and weighting choices that can reorder jurisdictions. Smallholder and mixed crop–livestock systems, which dominate milk supply in several countries, are poorly served by tools designed for specialised temperate farms. A nested indicator architecture, built on a verifiable core of farm data, explicit scaling rules and paired intensity and absolute metrics, is proposed as a defensible direction. Its validity remains to be demonstrated through longitudinal and cross-jurisdictional testing.

title: Evaluating the evaluators: what are the trends and patterns in studies on mangrove conservation policy effectiveness?
summary: Abstract INTRODUCTION: Mangrove forests provide critical ecosystem services but have been extensively converted or modified. With more than half of global systems at risk of collapse, global efforts are being undertaken to reforest, protect
content: Abstract INTRODUCTION: Mangrove forests provide critical ecosystem services but have been extensively converted or modified. With more than half of global systems at risk of collapse, global efforts are being undertaken to reforest, protect, and restore mangrove forests, but a comparison of the diverse interventions to conserve mangrove systems and their documented effectiveness remains lacking. Evidence regarding the effectiveness of mangrove interventions is important to support tailored programs that maximise impact, but program impact evaluations are rarely done rigorously and publicly available. METHODS: Here, we conduct a Systematic Quantitative Literature Review (SQLR) to synthesize the current state of knowledge regarding the effectiveness of mangrove program and policy interventions and address this knowledge gap. RESULTS: There were 42 papers that matched our inclusion criteria. The literature does not evenly cover global mangrove distribution; studies were disproportionately conducted across Asia (62%), with many regions containing large extents of mangroves not represented, such as Oceania. Protected areas (representing 13 / 45 studies) and community-based forest management were the most common interventions to be evaluated (representing 10 / 42 studies), though these intervention components frequently co-occurred with each other or other policy interventions. A ‘before’ and ‘after’ comparison of satellite-derived mangrove extent was the most frequently used method to measure changes in the outcome attributed to the intervention. We found four studies that used credible counterfactuals (e.g. with quasi-experimental methods). Significant geographic, methods, and outcome gaps remain in impact evaluation published literature despite significant efforts by mangrove conservation practitioners worldwide; researchers should work to strengthen meaningful collaborations with conservation groups in underrepresented areas to fill evaluation gaps. CONCLUSION: Conserving mangroves and protecting the communities that rely on them as climate change impacts intensify requires shifting focus to underrepresented but threatened systems that need protection with effective interventions.

title: Experts' and AI perspectives on the environmental sustainability of tensile membrane structures
summary: Purpose With increasing demands for sustainable construction, there is growing interest in enhancing the environmental performance of tensile membrane structures (TMS). This study aims to investigate the environmental sustainability challen
content: Purpose With increasing demands for sustainable construction, there is growing interest in enhancing the environmental performance of tensile membrane structures (TMS). This study aims to investigate the environmental sustainability challenges and opportunities of TMS across their lifecycle stages by integrating expert insights and advanced AI-generated perspectives. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative methodology was employed using semi-structured interviews with 16 experienced professionals including architects, engineers, contractors, builders, environmental sustainability experts and researchers. To enhance the reliability of findings and address potential gaps, the study also utilised artificial intelligence (AI) tools (ChatGPT and DeepSeek) to compare human expert insights with AI responses. Thematic analysis was conducted to categorise the results into core environmental sustainability themes. Findings Five interrelated themes were identified: (1) material innovation and environmental sustainability, (2) structural efficiency and lightweight design, (3) construction techniques and environmental sustainability alignment, (4) life durability management and (5) accessibility, inclusivity and waste management. These themes highlight critical performance indicators such as energy use, structural behaviour, material optimisation, user experience and maintenance strategies. The integration of AI insights helped highlight both consensus and gaps in expert knowledge. Originality/value This study provides a systematic qualitative investigation of environmental sustainability in TMS from an expert-practice perspective and is among the first to compare expert insights with AI-generated assessments of environmental sustainability within the TMS domain. The research contributes to the growing field of environmentally responsive structural design by offering actionable strategies for embedding environmental sustainability assessment practices into TMS planning and implementation. The findings provide valuable guidance for architects, engineers and policymakers seeking to enhance low-carbon design decisions in membrane architecture.

title: Drilling in ‘paradise’: environmental governance, local communities and oil exploration in the Okavango Delta, Botswana
summary: Abstract Oil exploration in ecologically sensitive landscapes presents significant environmental governance challenges, particularly where extractive development intersects with wetland conservation and community livelihoods. This study exa
content: Abstract Oil exploration in ecologically sensitive landscapes presents significant environmental governance challenges, particularly where extractive development intersects with wetland conservation and community livelihoods. This study examines how international, regional, and national policy and legislative frameworks regulate oil exploration in the Okavango Delta, Botswana, using a qualitative desk-based review of legal, policy, and documentary sources. The findings indicate that Botswana has a comprehensive but fragmented environmental governance framework in which international and regional instruments establish conservation principles and promote transboundary cooperation but depend largely on domestic implementation. National legislation focuses on licensing, environmental impact assessment, and mitigation measures rather than prohibiting exploration in ecologically sensitive areas, while ecosystem-specific policies and wildlife legislation enhance environmental protection through institutional coordination, enforcement, and community participation. The study concludes that the existing governance framework regulates, rather than prevents, petroleum exploration in environmentally sensitive landscapes and recommends strengthening legal safeguards, institutional coordination, and public participation to better balance petroleum development with environmental conservation.

title: The enemy of my enemy: A bacterial antagonist rescues Chlamydomonas by inactivating a toxin from a rival
summary: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bact
content: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bacteria that coexist in the same soil habitat. In pairwise cultures, all three interactions are amensalistic (-like): Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 antagonizes both C. reinhardtii and Pseudomonas fluorescens HKI0770 without benefit, while P. fluorescens inhibits C. reinhardtii without profiting from the alga. However, in a tripartite culture, P. fluorescens protects C. reinhardtii from P. protegens and promotes algal recovery. This protection is not stopped when the used carbon source, acetate, is supplemented. The P. fluorescens rescue effect is associated with reduced levels of the polyyne toxin protegencin produced by P. protegens . Protegencin levels, detected by Raman microspectroscopy, are decreased by application of spent medium or protein extracts from P. fluorescens , while heat- and protease-treatment abolish this activity. A heat-sensitive, proteinaceous factor, likely an enzyme(s), appears to contribute to protegencin inactivation. Our results show that P. fluorescens rescues C. reinhardtii by inactivating protegencin, despite being inhibited by P. protegens . These findings demonstrate the importance of investigating higher-order effects, since additional community members can transform pairwise antagonistic interactions into conditional protection through toxin inactivation.

title: European biogenic residues and wastes used for syngas production in a 20 kWth Chemical Looping Gasification unit
summary: Reaching the targets set by the Paris Agreement demands sustainable alternatives to fossil fuels. Biomass gasification, where syngas is generated and afterwards converted into liquid biofuels, is one of the routes to produce low-carbon fuel
content: Reaching the targets set by the Paris Agreement demands sustainable alternatives to fossil fuels. Biomass gasification, where syngas is generated and afterwards converted into liquid biofuels, is one of the routes to produce low-carbon fuels. Chemical Looping Gasification (CLG) is a promising route in this context, since the oxygen is supplied to the fuel by a solid oxygen carrier, so that a syngas free of atmospheric N 2 can be obtained without an air separation unit, which simplifies its downstream conversion into biofuels and makes CO 2 capture more feasible. In this work, syngas was generated in a 20 kW th CLG unit from a range of European biomass residues representative of agricultural, forestry, and waste streams, including olive pits, buckwheat pellets, spruce treetops and branches, and waste wood type B, using ilmenite as the oxygen carrier. The process was assessed during about 85 h of steady-state operation. The variables explored were the oxygen-to-fuel ratio, λ, (0.2-0.5), temperature (850-970 °C), and the use of steam or CO 2 as gasifying agent. The oxygen-to-fuel ratio was identified as the most influential variable, with lower values clearly favoring syngas yield, while producing minor differences among the biogenic residues, which had a similar composition. Temperatures above 900 °C enhanced the gasification process, achieving biomass conversions exceeding 90 % for all fuels tested. Carbon emissions to the atmosphere were found to depend on temperature, size and biomass reactivity. The use of CO 2 as gasifying agent enabled the production of syngas with varying H 2 /CO molar ratios, which is of interest for its subsequent use in biofuel production.

title: Energy savings versus thermal comfort in existing Mediterranean office buildings: a case study assessing the effectiveness of low-impact retrofit strategies
summary: Purpose Energy retrofit strategies based on non-invasive or minimally invasive measures are widely adopted in existing office buildings; however, their effectiveness is often assumed to be transferable across different climatic contexts. Th
content: Purpose Energy retrofit strategies based on non-invasive or minimally invasive measures are widely adopted in existing office buildings; however, their effectiveness is often assumed to be transferable across different climatic contexts. This study investigates energy savings and thermal comfort obtained by using commonly applied low-impact retrofit actions in existing Mediterranean office buildings. Design/methodology/approach A dynamic simulation model of an existing office building located in Southern Italy was developed to evaluate the impact of non-invasive retrofit measures, including indoor air temperature setpoint adjustments, daylight saving time strategies and the replacement of conventional boilers with air-to-water heat pumps. Energy performance was assessed in terms of heating, cooling and lighting demand, while thermal comfort was evaluated using Fanger theory. Findings The results show that setpoint adjustments provided the highest individual savings (up to 4.8%), followed by heat pump adoption (4.0%), while their combined application led to a maximum reduction of 7.7%. These savings seem limited since they refer to total annual primary energy consumption, but savings related to heating can reach up to 24–46%, while those related to cooling reach 18%. Moreover, a clear trade-off between energy savings and thermal comfort was identified, particularly during winter conditions. Research limitations/implications The analysis is based on a simulation model without calibration against measured data, although a good consistency with available benchmark data for office buildings has been obtained; therefore, results should be interpreted as a comparative assessment rather than absolute predictions. Practical implications The findings support decision-making in the management of existing buildings, highlighting both the potential and limitations of low-cost retrofit strategies. Originality/value The study provides an integrated evaluation of low-impact energy retrofit strategies, identifying a significant trade-off between energy savings and thermal comfort for existing Mediterranean office buildings.

title: China’s approach to tackling marine plastic pollution: an institutional analysis centered on the ecological and environmental code
summary: The governance of marine plastic pollution has long been hindered by two significant challenges: the fragmentation of international norms and the disconnect between domestic legislation. The first challenge arises from the lack of alignment
content: The governance of marine plastic pollution has long been hindered by two significant challenges: the fragmentation of international norms and the disconnect between domestic legislation. The first challenge arises from the lack of alignment among international agreements—such as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the London Convention, and the Basel Convention—regarding their scope and regulatory subjects. The second challenge is reflected in the dispersed nature of relevant regulations across various statutes and the inadequacy of the land-sea separation approach, which fails to effectively address the predominantly land-based origins of plastic pollution. The enactment of the 2026 Ecological and Environmental Code presents a new normative foundation aimed at alleviating these contradictions. This paper focuses on the Ecological and Environmental Code and employs three methodological approaches—normative analysis, comparative law, and legal hermeneutics—to explore its institutional framework. The analysis centers on two fundamental principles: integrated land-sea management and whole-life-cycle governance. It examines the Code’s provisions across three critical stages: source reduction, process control, and end-of-pipe disposal. The paper compares this Code with relevant extraterritorial legislative examples from the European Union, Japan, and South Korea. The study reveals that the Code effectively connects its General Provisions, the Pollution Prevention and Control Chapter, the Green and Low-Carbon Development Chapter, and the Legal Liability Chapter through internal coordination. This integrated land-sea management approach spans the regulatory chain from production to ocean discharge. The Code’s “multi-chapter synergy” structure offers distinct systemic advantages for comprehensive governance of marine plastic pollution across its life cycle, partially overcoming limitations in existing environmental law, which often neglects whole-life-cycle governance. Nonetheless, in comparison to standalone extraterritorial legislation, the Code shows institutional gaps in areas such as source-based total quantity control, specific operational rules for the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regime, dynamic management of new pollutant lists, and alignment with international conventions. This paper suggests recommendations for improvement in three key areas: governance philosophy, institutional specifics, and performance mechanisms. These recommendations aim to serve as a theoretical reference for future revisions of the Code and for negotiations related to the Global Plastics Treaty, while also facilitating the effective alignment of domestic regulations with upcoming international frameworks.

title: Macro- and socioeconomic indicators for technology assessment: Methods and case studies
summary: A multidimensional impact assessment makes it possible to assess the strengths and weaknesses of technology variants in relation to various indicators and to incorporate this knowledge into decisions on private or public investments. Althou
content: A multidimensional impact assessment makes it possible to assess the strengths and weaknesses of technology variants in relation to various indicators and to incorporate this knowledge into decisions on private or public investments. Although methods to quantify microeconomic and environmental impacts have been established for a long time, there are only few approaches to assess macroeconomic or socioeconomic impacts of individual technologies in a robust way. This paper therefore presents a new method on how macroeconomic indicators such as employment effects, value added, the competitiveness of national industry on the world market, and geopolitical risks can be calculated for individual technologies, based on established methods for quantifying macroeconomic indicators at the level of the economy as a whole. In addition, new methods are being developed to determine socioeconomic indicators such as transaction costs (non-monetary), opportunities for financial participation, and perceived risks and barriers. It is noticeable here that it is often not enough to rely purely on technological features to quantify the indicators; surveys, for example, must also be used. All indicators were developed in a co-design process together with stakeholders from research, industry and civil society, which, among other things, guarantees the relevance and practicality of the indicators. The newly developed indicators were tested using case studies from the areas of mobility, heating, and electricity generation. The results show that the macro- and socioeconomic indicators presented here allow integrating important new perspectives into a multidimensional impact assessment or a multi-criteria decision analysis. As these perspectives have often been neglected to date, the new indicators presented here represent new and valuable additions to multidimensional impact assessment of energy and transport technologies.

title: SOMER: an assessment tool for social acceptance in wetland conservation contexts
summary: Abstract Social acceptance plays an important role in wetland conservation, yet existing studies often rely on context-specific approaches that limit systematic assessment across wetland contexts. To fill this gap, this paper introduces the
content: Abstract Social acceptance plays an important role in wetland conservation, yet existing studies often rely on context-specific approaches that limit systematic assessment across wetland contexts. To fill this gap, this paper introduces the Social Monitor for Ecosystem Relations (SOMER), an assessment tool designed to examine social acceptance in wetland conservation contexts. In this study, social acceptance is operationalized through individuals’ perceptions of the costs and benefits of wetlands. To demonstrate the empirical applicability of SOMER, the assessment tool was applied in a survey study conducted in the Netherlands (n = 667). We included Nature Connectedness, climate-related perceptions, and contextual factors in this study to explore their associations with social acceptance. The findings indicate that social acceptance is associated with multiple factors, including Nature Connectedness, climate-related perceptions, socio-demographic characteristics, and geographic distance to wetlands. In addition, ecological and recreational dimensions of wetland perceptions were associated with different explanatory factors. By integrating ecological, social, and contextual dimensions, SOMER provides a promising standardized assessment tool for examining the social acceptance of wetland conservation initiatives and supporting more socially responsive environmental planning.

title: An edge memory-driven iterated search algorithm with bidirectional feedback for the capacitated vehicle routing problem
summary: The fixed‑fleet Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) is a canonical NP‑hard combinatorial optimization problem in logistics distribution. Conventional metaheuristic algorithms fail to fully exploit structural information embedded with
content: The fixed‑fleet Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) is a canonical NP‑hard combinatorial optimization problem in logistics distribution. Conventional metaheuristic algorithms fail to fully exploit structural information embedded within historical routes and lack effective search guidance, which readily results in premature convergence. To remedy these limitations, this paper proposes an Edge Memory‑Driven Iterative Search algorithm with Bidirectional Feedback (EMIS‑BF). A dynamic edge memory matrix embedded with decay and upper‑lower bound constraints is devised to quantify high‑quality edge patterns and alleviate search stagnation. To couple global population exploration and memory‑guided local intensification, a closed‑loop bidirectional feedback mechanism is constructed, where forward feedback disseminates elite route structures and backward feedback feeds local optimization improvements back into the memory matrix to enable cross‑stage information exchange. Furthermore, a two‑stage hybrid search framework is established that integrates 2‑opt, 3‑opt, insertion and destroy‑and‑repair neighborhood operators alongside a probabilistic inferior‑solution acceptance rule to strike a balance between global‑exploration breadth and local‑exploitation depth. Numerical experiments are carried out on 83 standard A/B/E/P benchmark instances, with more than ten representative metaheuristics employed as comparative baselines. EMIS‑BF matches published best‑known solutions (BKS) on 68 test instances. The Friedman test combined with post‑hoc Bonferroni–Dunn statistical analysis shows that EMIS‑BF achieves the second‑best average rank among the twelve algorithms ranked on Sets A, B and P. The proposed algorithm yields statistically significant performance improvements over six baseline methods, while no statistically distinguishable performance gaps are observed between EMIS‑BF and the top‑five competitive solvers. Multiple independent runs further verify its robust performance and stable convergence behavior. The edge‑memory and feedback strategies provide valuable design references for hybrid swarm‑intelligence and metaheuristic optimization algorithms.

title: Fungi-engineered metal nanoparticles for advanced therapeutics
summary: Growing concern over the environmental toxicity and biomedical risks of conventional physical and chemical nanoparticle synthesis has intensified interest in sustainable routes to metal nanoparticle production. Myconanotechnology, which use
content: Growing concern over the environmental toxicity and biomedical risks of conventional physical and chemical nanoparticle synthesis has intensified interest in sustainable routes to metal nanoparticle production. Myconanotechnology, which uses fungi as biological nanofactories, has emerged as a versatile green platform: fungi tolerate high metal concentrations and secrete abundant enzymes, proteins, and polysaccharides that act as reducing, stabilizing, and capping agents. Most existing reviews catalog producer species and nanoparticle types; here we instead integrate synthesis mechanisms, the physicochemical determinants of particle properties, and biomedical performance, and we weigh the strength of evidence behind each application. Antimicrobial and anticancer activities are currently the best supported, although the evidence is dominated by in vitro models, whereas vaccine-adjuvant and biosensing applications remain preliminary and mechanistically underdefined. Across silver, gold, copper, zinc, iron, and selenium systems, fungal biomolecules govern not only metal-ion reduction but also surface chemistry, biocompatibility, and immunological behavior, which distinguishes mycogenic NPs from plant-derived and chemically synthesized counterparts. The main barrier to translation is not a shortage of candidate materials but the absence of standardized, mechanistically informed synthesis and characterization protocols, which prevents batch-to-batch reproducibility and meaningful cross-study comparison. Closing this reproducibility gap, through defined culture conditions, quantitative surface characterization, and harmonized safety testing, is the most critical prerequisite for advancing fungi-engineered nanoparticles toward clinical and industrial use.

title: From vision to reality: How ‘sustainability’ is accomplished in projects
summary: Abstract This research investigates how the social and material features of project deliverables influence the way sustainability is carried out. It highlights how the processes through which actors implement sustainability are mediated by
content: Abstract This research investigates how the social and material features of project deliverables influence the way sustainability is carried out. It highlights how the processes through which actors implement sustainability are mediated by the specific type of project deliverable and specifically by the sociomaterial dimensions of the deliverable in question. The argument is made that sustainability is not a predefined design attribute but an emergent sociomaterial accomplishment. The empirical case leading to these results is an in‐depth ethnographic case of a construction project. Project settings are ideal places to investigate these issues as they provide a structured and systematic approach to the implementation of complex and multidimensional endeavours. The main contribution of this research lies in the exploration of how the pursuit of sustainability is strongly shaped by the evolving forms of sociomateriality throughout the project lifecycle. We make two main contributions. First, we show how the interrelation between social dynamics and material artefacts—plans, tools, technologies and the building itself—channels actors into specific forms of engagement and decision‐making. Second, by doing this, we demonstrate the dynamic nature of sustainability implementation by exploring the set of negotiations unfolding in sustainability implementation.

title: The Future of NHS Scotland’s Transportation
source: Strathprints: The University of Strathclyde institutional repository (University of Strathclyde)
summary: NHS Scotland’s transportation system underpins the delivery of health and social care across the nation, moving patients, staff, equipment, and supplies every day. Yet it faces growing pressure from ageing fleets, limited charging infrastru
content: NHS Scotland’s transportation system underpins the delivery of health and social care across the nation, moving patients, staff, equipment, and supplies every day. Yet it faces growing pressure from ageing fleets, limited charging infrastructure, rising costs, and increasing emissions. The system must adapt to meet the Scottish Government’s legally binding net-zero targets by 2045 while ensuring equitable access to healthcare in both urban and remote rural areas. Challenges include constrained budgets, fragmented transport coordination across Health Boards, workforce shortages, and persistent digital and geographic inequalities that limit alternatives such as telehealth. The need for a resilient, low-carbon, and inclusive transport system has therefore become an urgent strategic priority for NHS Scotland. This report presents scenario work exploring plausible futures for NHS Scotland’s transport system to 2040. Developed using the Intuitive Logic scenario-planning method, the study synthesised evidence from desk research, stakeholder interviews, surveys, and co-creation workshops. The analysis identifies ten high-level factors that will shape the future: funding, access to healthcare, public–private roles, digitalisation, Scottish transport and environmental policy, public attitudes to technology, demographic change, climate intensity, and availability of clean energy. Two key uncertainties — levels of funding and level of access to healthcare services — shaped four distinct future scenarios: Golden Pulse: In this optimistic 2040 future, NHS Scotland benefits from sustained economic growth and record funding (approximately £ 33 billion), enabling strong government investment in transport and environmental policy. Access is high (only ~20% unmet demand), digitalisation (telehealth, AI diagnostics, cloud administration) is widespread and well-used, public–private partnerships have shifted to fewer, mutually focused models, EV penetration and renewables are high, and new transport hubs and hospitals improve access for urban and rural populations. Triage Efficiency: In this constrained-funding but high-access future (funding c.£20bn), NHS Scotland achieves good access (c.20% unmet) through targeted, efficiency-led responses: community-focused prevention, lifestyle shifts, AI pre-screening, and robotic/specialist remote support. The economy is stagnant with pressure on public funds; CO₂ taxation is high, drone/logistics are used in joint private–public provision, and the system prioritises digital care and cost-efficient logistics while rural access depends on non-traditional models. Hypertrophic System: Here, the NHS receives high funding (c.£33bn) but access deteriorates (c.70% unmet) because investment chiefly funds hospital expansion and technologies that are poorly implemented or mistrusted. Despite large capital programmes and digital roll-outs, uptake and trust are low (several notable accidents and weak digital skills), transport remains large

title: Adoption and Impact of Climate-Smart Technologies on Agrifood Systems in Vihiga County, Kenya
source: African Journal of Climate Change and Resource Sustainability
summary: Agrifood systems in sub-Saharan Africa face significant challenges from climate change, threatening food security and rural livelihoods. Climate-smart technologies (CSTs) offer a viable way to strengthen resilience, productivity, and sustai
content: Agrifood systems in sub-Saharan Africa face significant challenges from climate change, threatening food security and rural livelihoods. Climate-smart technologies (CSTs) offer a viable way to strengthen resilience, productivity, and sustainability in smallholder farming systems. This study examines the adoption and impact of CSTs in Vihiga County, a high-potential agricultural region in western Kenya with small landholdings and high vulnerability to climate variability. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study assesses the extent of CST adoption, key drivers and barriers, and socio-economic benefits among smallholder farmers. Primary data were collected through household surveys (n=383), focus group discussions (n=5), and key informant interviews (n=15) with farmers, extension officers, and policymakers. Findings indicate that practices such as conservation agriculture (25%), agroforestry (15%), drought-resistant crop varieties (60%), and integrated soil fertility management have contributed to improved yields, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, and enhanced climate adaptation. However, adoption remains constrained by limited access to finance, inadequate extension services, and fragmented land ownership. The study highlights the role of policy support, capacity building, and public-private partnerships in scaling up CSTs for sustainable agrifood transformation. By aligning local practices with Kenya's Climate-Smart Agriculture Strategy, Vihiga County can serve as a model for climate-resilient development in similar agro-ecological zones. The research underscores the need for context-specific, farmer-centred approaches to ensure equitable and sustainable adoption of CSTs in sub-Saharan Africa's agrifood systems.

title: Emerging downhole sensing technologies for mineral exploration
summary: Abstract Recent advancements in spectroscopic, imaging, and geophysical sensors present new opportunities to gather geological information directly during drilling, potentially reducing reliance on physical core samples. These technologies
content: Abstract Recent advancements in spectroscopic, imaging, and geophysical sensors present new opportunities to gather geological information directly during drilling, potentially reducing reliance on physical core samples. These technologies have the potential to reduce drilling costs, shorten exploration timelines, and improve decision-making in early-stage mineral exploration. This review evaluates the principles, capabilities, and limitations of emerging sensing technologies applied to mineral exploration, including hyperspectral imaging, X-ray fluorescence (XRF), gamma-ray spectrometry (GRS), borehole radar (GPR), borehole transient electromagnetic method (BTEM), muon tomography, and seismic-while-drilling (SWD). Key metrics considered include detection limits, spatial resolution, and technology readiness level. Although many of these tools are well established, their integration into drilling systems is constrained by the challenging operating conditions, including narrow borehole dimensions, high vibration, high temperatures and difficulties in maintaining reliable telemetry. By comparing the technological maturity, environmental resilience, and engineering requirements of these sensors, this review identifies GRS, and SWD as having strong potential for near-term deployment during drilling, while XRF, GPR and BTEM are likely to have a transformative impact in the longer term. Realising the full potential of downhole sensing will require substantive advances and investment in sensor miniaturization, ruggedisation for high-pressure and high-temperature environments, along with the development of reliable telemetry systems for real-time data transmission. Additionally large-scale field demonstrations will also be critical for validating system performance and enabling broader industry adoption. These advancements have the potential to transform mineral exploration by improving targeting efficiency, reducing geological uncertainty, and accelerating the transition from discovery to resource development.

title: Respirable crystalline silica exposure in agate-stone workers in Khambhat, India: a human health risk assessment using a probabilistic approach
summary: Crystalline silica, a Group 1 carcinogen, is present in dust generated during cutting, polishing, chipping and drilling activities in cottage-scale agate units. This study quantified respirable crystalline silica (RCS) exposure amongst work
content: Crystalline silica, a Group 1 carcinogen, is present in dust generated during cutting, polishing, chipping and drilling activities in cottage-scale agate units. This study quantified respirable crystalline silica (RCS) exposure amongst workers in such units in Gujarat, India, and assessed associated carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic health risks. Personal respirable dust samples of workers were collected across four distinct work areas and quantified for RCS. Associated health risks were evaluated using Monte Carlo–based probabilistic inhalation risk assessment model. The activity-specific arithmetic mean RCS concentrations ranged from 0.039 to 0.359 mg/m³, surpassing occupational exposure limits in all work areas. Average carcinogenic risk estimates exceeded the US Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) screening benchmark in all work areas, with cutting exhibiting the highest observed mean modelled cancer risk ( n = 13), although differences in RCS concentrations between activities were largely not statistically significant. The non-carcinogenic hazard quotients in the cutting and polishing areas exceeded safety thresholds. Simulated implementation of engineering controls and respirator use reduced 95th percentile upper-bound health risks by 78% and 62.5%, respectively; however, mean cancer and non-cancer risks in these areas still exceeded reference values. Sensitivity analysis revealed that RCS concentration exerted significant influence and accounted for 61% of variance in carcinogenic risk and 82% in non-carcinogenic risk. Findings of this study highlight the urgent need for implementing effective exposure control measures amongst this informal workforce.

title: How Resilient Green Logistics drives Sustainable Environmental Outcomes: the multi-mediating role of governance, leadership and work ethos
source: Modern Supply Chain Research and Applications
summary: Purpose This study looks at how Resilient Green Logistics (RGL) affects Sustainable Environmental Outcomes (SEO) in the Indian dairy sector. It focuses on the roles of Sustainability-Driven Governance (SDG), Eco-Transformative Leadership (E
content: Purpose This study looks at how Resilient Green Logistics (RGL) affects Sustainable Environmental Outcomes (SEO) in the Indian dairy sector. It focuses on the roles of Sustainability-Driven Governance (SDG), Eco-Transformative Leadership (ETL) and Pro-Environmental Work Ethos (PWE) as mediators. The research also aims to show how governance, leadership and employee behavior collectively contribute to environmental sustainability in dairy supply chains. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey design was adopted, covering 189 registered dairy companies across Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab and New Delhi. Purposive sampling targeted key supply chain professionals, including senior managers, logistics/supply chain managers and sustainability/environment officers. Of 567 targeted respondents, 407 provided valid responses. The data were analyzed using SmartPLS-SEM 4.1 to examine the proposed relationships. Findings The analysis strongly indicated that RGL directly improves environmental outcomes through business and behavioral mechanisms in the dairy sector's supply chain. Furthermore, the mediating roles of SDG, PWE and ETL have been established, and these mediators strengthen the relationship between RGL and SEO. Among the above-defined mediators, SDG emerged as the strongest, followed by PWE and ETL. Practical implications Adopting and implementing sustainable logistics practices, backed by strong governance, sustainable leadership and environmentally responsible employee behavior, will help the dairy sector leverage them to gain a competitive advantage at national and international levels. These insights can support policymakers and dairy managers in developing more sustainable logistics strategies and reducing environmental harm in the dairy sector. Originality/value This study integrates the roles of SDG, ETL and PWE as mediators into an inclusive framework for the Indian dairy sector.

title: CH2Cl2 emissions from China inferred from atmospheric observations
summary: The importance of dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) on stratospheric ozone has intensified in recent years, with China suspected to be a contributor to global emissions. However, China’s post-2019 emissions remain poorly constrained. Here we show th
content: The importance of dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) on stratospheric ozone has intensified in recent years, with China suspected to be a contributor to global emissions. However, China’s post-2019 emissions remain poorly constrained. Here we show that CH2Cl2 emissions in China were 931 ± 107 gigagram per year (Gg yr−1) in 2024, an increase of 303 ± 111 Gg yr−1 relative to 2019. These values indicate a higher average growth rate of 67.0 ± 15.2 Gg yr−2 during 2019–2024, compared with the previously reported 42.0 ± 8.1 Gg yr−2 during 2011–2019, despite some measures restricting CH2Cl2 use in China since 2020. Moreover, the proportion of China’s CH2Cl2 emissions to global emissions rose from 2011 to 2024. These findings highlight the importance of continued monitoring and mitigating CH2Cl2 emissions in the context of ozone layer recovery. Measurements across China reveal that emissions of dichloromethane, a substance with a growing impact on ozone-layer recovery, rose faster during 2021–2024 than during 2011–2019, despite measures introduced since 2020 to curb its use.

title: How data asset accounting enhances inclusive finance: an evolutionary analysis using signaling game models
summary: Information asymmetry remains a major obstacle to inclusive finance for micro and small enterprises (MSEs). This study develops an evolutionary signaling game model in which boundedly rational MSEs and banks adapt their strategies through r
content: Information asymmetry remains a major obstacle to inclusive finance for micro and small enterprises (MSEs). This study develops an evolutionary signaling game model in which boundedly rational MSEs and banks adapt their strategies through repeated interactions to examine whether observable data asset disclosures can serve as a supplementary financing signal under emerging accounting systems. The results show that when banks consider observable data asset disclosures in lending decisions and set loan amounts within an appropriate range, high-potential MSEs are more likely to continue digital transformation and disclose capitalized data assets, allowing banks to improve their assessment of firm quality and achieve a separating equilibrium. However, excessively high or low loan amounts weaken the signaling mechanism. The study suggests that observable data asset disclosures may help reduce financing-related information asymmetry under appropriate institutional conditions. While the model is calibrated to China’s emerging data asset accounting framework, the proposed mechanism may also provide theoretical insights for other economies undergoing digital accounting reforms.

title: HOUSING RETROFITS IN JUST TRANSITIONS ? Emerging Contradictions in Catalonia, Spain
source: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
summary: Abstract Efforts to decarbonize residential housing are growing globally. Following ambitious targets set by the European Commission's Renovation Wave and subsidized through Covid‐19 recovery funds, Spain's housing retrofit programme deploy
content: Abstract Efforts to decarbonize residential housing are growing globally. Following ambitious targets set by the European Commission's Renovation Wave and subsidized through Covid‐19 recovery funds, Spain's housing retrofit programme deployed EUR 3.4 billion in European grants to retrofit half a million homes between 2022 and 2026. This article uncovers emerging political, economic, environmental and social contradictions around expanding housing retrofits in Spain, with a focus on Catalonia, to explore how funds were disbursed and who stands to benefit. In considering the political economy of housing in just transitions, I draw from two dozen interviews in 2023 with a range of actors, meeting observations and grey literature to highlight contradictions emerging across five domains. These include the territorial distribution of funds, the universal nature of retrofit grants, the treatment of vulnerable populations, the scale of intervention and the nature of the housing retrofit sector. Together the contradictions largely illustrate how public retrofit funding has favoured increased capital circulation alongside reinforced social relations and ideologies of private property ownership and wealth accumulation. While the overall push is towards what I term a Spanish growth economy of housing repair, some contradictions in the five domains point to possibilities for a more transformative just housing transition.

title: Sulfation Roasting for Sustainable Lithium-First Recovery from Spent NCM Batteries: Minimizing Acid Consumption, Process Time, and Energy Demand
summary: Sulfation roasting has emerged as a promising alternative for lithium-first recovery from spent lithium-ion batteries, while reducing hydrometallurgical complexity. This study investigated the sulfation roasting of nickel–cobalt–manganese o
content: Sulfation roasting has emerged as a promising alternative for lithium-first recovery from spent lithium-ion batteries, while reducing hydrometallurgical complexity. This study investigated the sulfation roasting of nickel–cobalt–manganese oxide (NCM) black mass to maximize lithium recovery while minimizing sulfuric acid consumption and thermal treatment time. The effects of preliminary calcination, sulfuric acid dosage, and roasting time were systematically investigated at 550 °C. Lithium and coextracted metals were quantified by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), while phase transformations were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Statistical evaluation identified sulfuric acid dosage as the only factor significantly affecting lithium extraction. An integrated success index was developed to assess lithium recovery, contaminant dissolution, reagent consumption, and thermal treatment time. Under the optimum conditions (nLi:nH2SO4 = 1:0.95, without preliminary calcination, 45 min), lithium recovery reached 90.8%, with a 75% reduction in thermal treatment time compared with previously reported sulfation roasting routes. A mass balance showed that sulfuric acid consumption corresponded to only 7.8% of that required for conventional hydrometallurgical leaching. These findings demonstrate that sulfation roasting substantially improves the sustainability of lithium-first recovery by reducing chemical reagent and energy while maintaining high recovery efficiency.
